t: The TLR4-2604G>A GG genotype (rs10759931) has been identified as a marker for poor cognitive outcome following COVID-19, and TLR4 signaling is proposed as the primary pathway for long-term cognitive dysfunction after COVID-19.

Injection of the S1 subunit into mouse brain via intra-cisterna magna modulated neuroimmune gene expression (Iba1, Cd11b, MhcIIα, Cd200r1, Gfap, Tlr2, Tlr4, Nlrp3, Il1b, Hmgb1) and protein levels (IFN-γ, IL-1β, TNF, CXCL1, IL-2, IL-10) for up to 7 days, producing behavioral changes resembling PASC.

Brain infusion of S protein in mice impaired cognitive function via complement-mediated synapse destruction, and genetic or pharmacological blockade of TLR4 signaling protected against this synapse elimination and memory dysfunction.
High levels of syndecan-1 (SDC-1), a glycocalyx shedding marker, were reported in convalescent COVID-19 patients, suggesting persistent endothelial damage.

Spike protein exposure induced Ca2+ influx and phenotypic changes in brain pericytes (elongated, contracted morphology, increased ACE2 and contractile/myofibrogenic protein expression), along with lipid peroxidation, oxidative/nitrosative stress, and NF-kB pathway activation, indicating pericyte-mediated microvascular injury.

Spike/RBD-triggered mast cell activation induced inflammatory factors in human brain microvascular endothelial cells and microglia, destroyed tight junction proteins, and full-length S protein (but not RBD) stimulated IL-1β, chymase, and tryptase secretion via TLR4 (IL-1β) and ACE2 (chymase/tryptase) pathways.

Spike protein can activate the NLRP3 inflammasome in LPS-stimulated microglia in an ACE2-dependent manner and prime the inflammasome via NF-κB signaling, allowing subsequent activation by ATP, nigericin, or α-synuclein, potentially increasing vulnerability to Parkinson's-like neurological symptoms.

Reductions in plasma and brain BDNF levels are common in patients with psychiatric and neurodegenerative diseases, possibly secondary to chronic brain inflammation, and decreased microglial BDNF is proposed as a mechanism in neuro-PASC.

Circulating S, S1, and N SARS-CoV-2 antigens were detectable in approximately 65% of PASC patients months after infection, with S protein detected most frequently (60%), S1 in about a fifth, and N rarely; detection was most associated with gastrointestinal and neuropsychiatric PASC symptoms.

GnRH neurons were found dying in post-mortem brains of COVID-19 patients with significantly reduced GnRH expression, and fetal olfactory/vomeronasal epithelia and GnRH neurons appeared susceptible to infection, potentially explaining post-COVID hypogonadism and cognitive symptoms.

In long COVID patients, serum cortisol and free thyroxine (FT4) levels were positively correlated with fatigue and depression scores respectively, while patients with anosmia/dysgeusia had significantly lower serum cortisol levels, and higher TSH with lower FT4/TSH ratios in initially severe cases suggested occult hypothyroidism.

In patients recovering from prior SARS-CoV infection, hypercortisolism persisted for up to 1 year in most patients, along with central hypothyroidism and low DHEAS in some, supporting chronic corticotropin deficiency attributed to reversible hypophysitis or direct hypothalamic damage.
Patients with chronic fatigue syndrome exhibited blunted HPA axis activity, including reduced 24-hour free cortisol excretion, increased sensitivity to ACTH, and an attenuated response to CRH.

Spike mRNA vaccine (BNT162b2) administered during pregnancy significantly altered WNT gene expression and BDNF levels in neonatal rat offspring, with male rats exhibiting autism-like behaviors (reduced social interaction, repetitive behavior), decreased neuronal counts, and impaired motor performance.
Following vaccination, the S1 subunit spike protein was detected in blood for up to 14 days, in CSF for up to 2.5 months, and in breast milk for up to 45 days.
Prospective studies showed that vaccination, up to two doses, before or after SARS-CoV-2 infection reduced the risk of developing PASC-prolonged symptoms and also reduced mortality risk.

High antibody titers induced by successive COVID-19 vaccinations were shown to have opposite (negative) effects on long COVID protection, contradicting the earlier protective association of vaccination.

Both expression levels and percentage of astrocytes expressing NRP1 mRNA were higher in astrocytes from COVID-19 patients compared to controls, and NRP1-mediated infection of astrocytes was confirmed using anti-NRP1 neutralizing antibody and siNRP1.

Downregulation of NRP1, potentially via ADAM9/10-mediated shedding, has been associated with iron accumulation, inhibition of cellular growth, and immunosenescence, suggesting a possible role in PASC symptoms.

Expression of DPP4 and CD147 increases in response to inflammation in reactive astrocytes, potentially contributing significantly to viral binding and entry into astrocytes, creating a positive feedback loop of viral receptor upregulation.
Elevated ADAM17 expression and activity was associated with poorer clinical outcomes and increased mortality in COVID-19, underscoring its significance in disease pathophysiology.

S1 subunit increased expression and activation of purinergic receptor P2X7 in BV-2 microglial cells and activated the TLR4 signaling pathway; Pannexin-1/ATP-dependent P2X7 activation acts as a second signal for inflammasome activation following TLR4-NF-kB pathway activation.
Single-cell phototransfection of mRNAs encoding spike and nucleocapsid in human astrocytes resulted in RNA-dependent translation interference.

The Spike protein remains in the skull-meninges-brain axis in COVID-19 patients long after virus clearance, and elevated levels of neurodegeneration biomarkers were detected in the CSF of Long COVID patients; in an animal model the Spike S1 subunit altered the proteome in this axis and induced anxiety-like behaviors, with differential expression of IL-18, MAPK, and PI3K-AKT signaling proteins, NET formation proteins, and increased caspase-3 activity.

A recent study indicates that active SARS-CoV-2 infection is not required for cognitive impairment in long COVID, supporting the role of factors other than viral proliferation as the main cause of neurological symptoms.
Patients with PASC reported greater cognitive fatigue than healthy controls throughout a 2-back working memory fMRI task.
The relationship between brain activation within the fatigue network and increased cognitive fatigue during the fatiguing task did not differ between the PASC and control groups.
As reported cognitive fatigue increased, the PASC group showed activation in more brain areas both inside and outside the fatigue network compared to controls.

The relationship between brain activation and 2-back task performance differed between groups, with the PASC group showing more frontal activation, suggesting greater mental effort during demanding cognitive tasks.
Gastrointestinal symptoms, most commonly diarrhea, occur in an estimated 20-30% of COVID-19 patients.
SARS-CoV-2 enters gastrointestinal epithelial cells via the ACE2 receptor, which is abundantly expressed in the small intestine, enabling direct viral infection of the gut.
SARS-CoV-2 RNA has been detected in stool samples of infected individuals, confirming viral presence in the gastrointestinal tract.
Acute and Long COVID are associated with decreased abundance of the beneficial commensal bacterium Faecalibacterium prausnitzii in the gut microbiome.
Acute and Long COVID are associated with an increase in pathogenic Enterococcus species in the gut microbiome.
Acute and Long COVID are associated with an increase in pathogenic Rothia species in the gut microbiome.
Gut dysbiosis in COVID-19 impairs intestinal barrier function, increasing gut permeability ("leaky gut") and allowing microbial products and inflammatory mediators into the bloodstream.
Long COVID is characterized by reduced gut-derived serotonin, which may contribute to neuropsychiatric and gastrointestinal symptoms via the gut-brain axis.
Persisting SARS-CoV-2 antigen fragments in the gut mucosa, first identified by the authors' 2022 endoscopy study, are linked to Long COVID.
A follow-up study by the authors showed that clearance of SARS-CoV-2 antigen fragments from the gut mucosa is associated with resolution of Long COVID symptoms.

A recent study found that Nirmatrelvir-Ritonavir, while generally safe, did not significantly improve specific Long COVID symptoms, despite showing post-acute benefits when given during acute infection.
A study of 60 patients suggested that fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) may be effective and safe for alleviating Long-COVID-related insomnia, though findings are preliminary.
Many Long COVID patients report symptoms consistent with dysautonomia, including features resembling POTS, such as tachycardia, dizziness, and gastrointestinal disturbances.
IBS, SIBO, and MCAS have been proposed as contributors to gastrointestinal symptoms in Long COVID, potentially via altered gut motility and immune dysregulation.
SARS-CoV-2 causes endothelial damage and microthrombi formation, leading to impaired blood flow and tissue hypoxia that may underlie fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, and muscle pain in Long COVID.

Persistence of viral antigens and gut dysbiosis in Long COVID drive chronic immune activation with elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines, contributing to systemic inflammation and symptoms such as fatigue and cognitive dysfunction.
Deficiency in gut secretory IgA, a mucosal immunity component, has been speculated to contribute to the persistence of SARS-CoV-2 antigens in the gut.

SSRIs, which increase brain serotonin levels and have anti-inflammatory properties, have been proposed as a therapeutic approach for managing post-acute COVID-19 syndrome by addressing serotonin deficiency.
Nearly all surveyed healthcare workers (93%) reported encountering patients with suspected PASC symptoms on a weekly basis.
61% of HCWs estimated that PASC patients accounted for less than 10% of their total patient load.
44% of respondents reported that PASC symptoms typically presented within six months of acute COVID-19 diagnosis, while roughly half were unsure or reported variable timing.
Persistent cough was the most frequently selected PASC symptom, chosen by 64% (n=46) of respondents as among the five most common presentations.
Shortness of breath was reported as one of the five most common PASC symptoms by 54% (n=39) of respondents.
Fatigue was selected as one of the five most common PASC symptoms by 49% of respondents.
Headache was selected as one of the five most common PASC symptoms by 44% of respondents.
Muscle or body aches were selected as one of the five most common PASC symptoms by 42% of respondents.
When ranked by frequency, headache was rated the single most commonly encountered PASC symptom by the largest share of respondents (22%, n=16).
Persistent cough was ranked as the single most frequently encountered PASC symptom by 21% (n=15) of respondents.
89% of HCWs reported routinely treating persistent shortness of breath attributed to PASC with corticosteroids, without specifying route of administration.
88% of respondents reported prescribing over-the-counter analgesics as the typical management for chronic headache attributed to PASC.
Nearly half of respondents reported prescribing antibiotics for persistent cough attributed to PASC.
29% of respondents reported uncertainty about how to manage persistent cough attributed to PASC.
36% of respondents reported uncertainty about how to manage fatigue attributed to PASC.
No survey respondent reported evaluating patients with chronic shortness of breath attributed to PASC for cardiac sequelae or pulmonary complications such as fibrosis or pulmonary embolism.
92% of respondents indicated they would attend a workplace-based training session on PASC symptom treatment.
90% of respondents stated they would refer PASC patients to multidisciplinary services such as physiotherapy, occupational therapy, and mental health services if these were available.
Persistent fatigue or tiredness after rest/sleep was reported in none of the iCPM-treated patients versus 17 of 120 placebo patients.
Headaches were significantly less common in the iCPM cohort than in the placebo group.
Difficulty concentrating or mental confusion was significantly less frequent in the iCPM cohort than in placebo.
Loss of taste or smell was significantly less common in the iCPM cohort than in placebo.
Joint or muscle pain did not differ significantly between iCPM and placebo groups.
Difficulty performing daily activities or work was significantly less common in the iCPM cohort than in placebo.
Fewer patients in the iCPM cohort sought medical attention for PACS symptoms compared to placebo.
The proportion of patients receiving any treatment for PACS symptoms did not significantly differ between iCPM and placebo groups.
The proportion of patients with at least one PASC symptom was markedly lower with iCPM (0.7%) than with placebo (72%).
The mean composite PACS symptom survey score was significantly lower in the iCPM cohort than in the placebo cohort.
No patients in either the iCPM or placebo group reported difficulty breathing, chest pain/pressure, digestive problems, skin rashes, or mood changes during follow-up.
A cited study found serum chymase, a marker of mast cell degranulation, was more elevated in hospitalized COVID-19 patients than in community cases.

Chlorpheniramine is hypothesized to act against SARS-CoV-2 via direct virucidal effects, inhibition of viral adsorption and replication, blockade of histamine release/mast cell degranulation, and bitter-taste-receptor (T2R) agonism that may stimulate sinonasal innate immunity, alongside anticholinergic, bronchodilatory, and decongestant activity.
Patients treated earlier in the disease course with iCPM appeared to have fewer long-term PASC sequelae than those treated later.

A cited veterans cohort study found that nirmatrelvir-ritonavir (Paxlovid) given during acute COVID-19 was not associated with a significant reduction in long-COVID rates compared with untreated patients.
PASC prevalence has been reported to vary widely, from about 10% among individuals infected with the Omicron variant up to 63% among those infected during initial SARS-CoV-2 variant waves.

Higher PASC rates have been reported among older individuals, females, unvaccinated individuals, smokers, obese individuals, those with recurrent infections, preexisting comorbidities, and hospitalized patients.
A systematic review (Wolff et al.) found that pre-existing asthma (in hospital-based populations) and pre-existing rhinitis were significantly associated with increased incidence of Long-COVID.
Younger and middle-age adults comprised the large majority of both post-hospitalization (71%) and non-hospitalized (90.5%) Neuro-PASC patients, while older adults were a minority of each group.
Pre-existing hypertension, dyslipidemia, cancer (in both PNP and NNP) and type 2 diabetes (in NNP) were significantly more prevalent with increasing age.
Pre-existing headaches were significantly more prevalent in younger PNP patients, decreasing with age.

Pre-existing autoimmune disease, non-diabetic endocrine disorders, cardiovascular/peripheral vascular disease, and chronic kidney disease were significantly more prevalent with increasing age in NNP patients only.
The median number of neurologic symptoms attributed to Neuro-PASC decreased with increasing age in PNP patients and showed a similar borderline trend in NNP patients.
Sensory-related neurologic symptoms including numbness/tingling, dysgeusia, and anosmia, and headache, were significantly less frequent in older NNP patients.

Non-neurologic symptoms including depression/anxiety (NNP), insomnia (PNP), chest pain, and self-reported dysautonomia (variation of heart rate, blood pressure, and/or temperature) were significantly less frequent in older PNP and NNP patients.

In contrast to the trend for symptoms, objective neurologic exam abnormalities — abnormal overall exam (PNP), sensory and motor dysfunction (NNP), and gait dysfunction (both) — were more frequent in older Neuro-PASC patients.
Younger non-hospitalized Neuro-PASC patients reported significantly worse (higher) PROMIS fatigue scores than middle-age or older NNP patients.

Younger non-hospitalized Neuro-PASC patients reported significantly worse (higher) PROMIS sleep disturbance scores, reaching mild dysfunction category, compared to older NNP patients who remained within normal limits.
Younger post-hospitalization Neuro-PASC patients showed borderline significantly worse (lower) NIH Toolbox executive function scores than older PNP patients.
Younger non-hospitalized Neuro-PASC patients had significantly worse NIH Toolbox executive function and working memory scores than older NNP patients.

Multiple correspondence analysis of 17 common Neuro-PASC symptoms showed that older patients (both PNP and NNP) had significantly larger dimension 1 values, indicating a milder, less symptomatic global symptom profile than younger or middle-age patients.
There was no significant relationship between the length of time since COVID-19 onset and subjective impression of recovery, in any age group of PNP or NNP patients.

A meta-analysis cited in the discussion (2.6 million post-COVID-19 cases, 30.4 million controls) found SARS-CoV-2 infection significantly associated with increased risk of new-onset Alzheimer's disease, dementia, and Parkinson's disease.
A Danish electronic medical record study of COVID-19 outpatients cited in the discussion found increased relative risk of Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease compared to non-COVID outpatients.

According to the CDC Household Pulse Survey cited in the discussion, PASC prevalence increases from the second to fourth decades of life and decreases steadily from the fifth to eighth decades, and 24.3% of US adults with current PASC report significant activity limitations.
Among NNP patients, the age-related distribution of female sex differed significantly, with the middle-age group having the highest proportion of females.
Individuals in the post-acute phase of COVID-19 have an increased risk and excess burden of diabetes mellitus and incident antihyperglycemic medication use compared to contemporary controls.

Individuals with persistent COVID-19 symptoms face heightened risk of multiple cardiovascular conditions including cerebrovascular disorders, dysrhythmias, ischemic and non-ischemic heart disease, pericarditis, myocarditis, heart failure, and thromboembolic disease.
Impaired vagal activity has been observed in individuals with long COVID, indicating malfunctioning signaling of the vagus nerve or brainstem.
In a study of approximately 1,000 patients with SARS-CoV-2 infection, 26% experienced mild cognitive impairment after recovering from the initial illness.
A large cohort study of over 200,000 patients found that the risk of developing dementia within 6 months after COVID-19 infection was more than twice as high as after influenza infection.
A study comparing 270 long-COVID patients to COVID patients without long COVID and uninfected controls found significant cognitive slowing in long-COVID patients that did not resolve over time.
A meta-analysis found that transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) can effectively alleviate depression symptoms.
Studies indicate taVNS has the potential to enhance attention, memory, decision-making, and cognitive control.
Human studies have demonstrated that vagal nerve stimulation can effectively decrease or halt the elevation of proinflammatory cytokines including TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, and interferon-γ.
Invasive VNS therapy showed significant improvements in depression, anxiety, and mood assessment scores, with average increases of 35%, 35%, and 25% respectively.
Over 50% of epilepsy patients treated with VNS experienced partial to complete recovery from seizures.
taVNS effectively reduced signs and symptoms in pediatric patients with mild to moderate IBD without notable side effects.
VNS has shown promising results in promoting oligodendrocyte differentiation and myelin formation in rats, a possible mechanism for treating multiple sclerosis.
VNS has an anti-inflammatory role, reducing inflammatory biomarkers and infarct size, and thereby reducing ventricular arrhythmias.
Non-invasive brain stimulation techniques including VNS and transcranial magnetic stimulation improved cognitive function, reduced fatigue, and reduced anxiety, leading to improved quality of life.
A prospective pilot study found significant improvements in cognitive function, anxiety and depression, fatigue, and sleep in female long COVID patients 10 days after starting tcVNS treatment.

A prospective randomized controlled study found that nVNS therapy lowered levels of the inflammatory biomarkers procalcitonin and C-reactive protein and was feasible to implement in a hospital setting for COVID-19 patients.

An open-label pilot study of 14 patients with chronic fatigue syndrome related to long COVID showed improved symptoms in 8 of the 14 patients treated with tcVNS, though further research was called for.

A systematic review of 51 studies and 1,322 subjects found taVNS has minimal side effects, including local skin irritation (18.2%), headache (3.6%), and nasopharyngitis (1.7%), with a low dropout rate of 2.6% due to adverse events.
A meta-analysis of 177 trials and 6,322 participants confirmed the safety of taVNS, finding no discernible difference in adverse event incidence between active taVNS and controls.
People with long COVID display an unusual, diffuse inflammatory cytokine profile lasting for months, which is not present in asymptomatic COVID-19 survivors.

SARS-CoV-2 enters via the olfactory/gustatory pathway and binds ACE2, NRP1, and TMPRSS2 receptors on cranial nerves IX and X, disrupting vagus nerve signal transmission and reducing parasympathetic activity, contributing to sympathetic-parasympathetic imbalance and systemic inflammation.
Women are more susceptible to long COVID syndrome, attributed to increased risk of autoimmune disorders and stronger immune responses.
The prevalence of long COVID as of June 2022 is estimated between 10-35% among those who had COVID-19, rising to as high as 85% in hospitalized patients.

Across 13 included studies, the reported prevalence of Long COVID-19 in pregnant women ranged widely from 9.3% to 93%, largely due to differences in study design, follow-up duration, and case definitions.
Metz et al reported a lower Long COVID-19 prevalence of 9.3% in a large multicenter cohort at a median follow-up of 10.3 months.
Malgina et al found a much higher Long COVID-19 prevalence of 93% in pregnant women with prior COVID-19 compared with 38.4% in non-COVID-19 controls.
Fatigue was the most frequently reported Long COVID-19 symptom in pregnant women, with prevalence ranging from 54.5% to 76% across studies.
Cognitive impairment and memory loss were prominent in Malgina et al, affecting nearly 50% of women with Long COVID-19.
Vetrugno et al and Muñoz-Chápuli et al reported prominent psychological symptoms, including depression and anxiety, with a significant impact on health-related quality of life.
Gu et al found a high incidence (40.6%) of liver function abnormalities in pregnant women with Long COVID-19, suggesting an organ-specific impact of COVID-19 during pregnancy.

Vásconez-González et al noted difficulty concentrating and hair loss as distinctive symptoms among pregnant women with Long COVID-19, but found no significant difference compared with non-pregnant controls.
Bruno et al found that women who contracted SARS-CoV-2 during pregnancy had a lower overall risk of developing Long COVID-19 (adjusted hazard ratio=0.85).
Among pregnant women who developed COVID-19, those with severe symptoms were more likely to develop thromboembolic events and abnormal heart rhythms, per Bruno et al.

Yao et al reported that pregnant women with long-term COVID-19 had a significantly higher risk of gestational hypertension (OR=3.344), gestational diabetes (OR=2.301), and fetal intrauterine growth restriction (OR=2.817).
Yao et al found no significant differences in rates of premature rupture of membranes, preterm delivery, or neonatal asphyxia between the long-term COVID-19 and non-COVID-19 groups.
Ghizzoni et al reported a higher rate of adverse pregnancy outcomes, including preterm birth and neonatal complications, in women with persistent Long COVID-19 symptoms.
Vetrugno et al found that 30% of pregnant women with COVID-19 tested positive for PTSD one year post-infection, using the SF-36 and IES-R scales.
Women with underlying comorbidities such as cardiac or pulmonary disease had significantly poorer health-related quality of life scores following COVID-19 in pregnancy.
Metz et al identified obesity, pre-existing mental health conditions, and severe acute infection as significantly associated with higher odds of developing Long COVID-19 in pregnant women.
Muñoz-Chápuli et al identified non-vaccination and multiparity as key risk factors for Long COVID-19 in pregnant women.
Oliveira et al found that women who experienced severe acute COVID-19 during pregnancy had a 2.43-fold increased risk of persistent fatigue compared with those with milder symptoms.
Exploratory factor analysis of the 14-item Post-COVID Cognitive Impairment Scale identified a two-factor structure (Memory and Attention, seven items each) explaining 40.38% of total variance.
The KMO measure of sampling adequacy (0.89) and Bartlett's test of sphericity (p < 0.001) confirmed that the scale item data were suitable for factor analysis.
Confirmatory factor analysis of the two-factor (Memory/Attention) model showed acceptable to good model fit across multiple indices.
The Memory subscale of the Post-COVID Cognitive Impairment Scale showed acceptable internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha = 0.81).
The Attention subscale of the Post-COVID Cognitive Impairment Scale showed acceptable internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha = 0.80).
During content validity assessment, two items were removed from the initial pool based on expert ratings falling below the content validity index threshold of 0.79, yielding a final 14-item scale.
A cited study found that 68.7% of non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients experienced post-acute sequelae within 30 days of infection, with some symptoms persisting 12 weeks or more.

A cited 7-month cohort study reported that 85.1% of 3203 long COVID participants experienced brain fog and cognitive impairment, including deficits in attention, executive function, problem-solving, and decision-making.
A cited study found that 86% of participants reported that post-COVID-19 cognitive impairment substantially impacted their everyday work capabilities.

The UK Office for National Statistics reported that fatigue (72%), difficulty concentrating (51%), muscle aches (49%), and shortness of breath (48%) were the predominant self-reported symptoms among people with long COVID.
Cited literature indicates that cognitive difficulties including memory impairment, concentration problems, and brain fog affect approximately 70% of people with long COVID.

A cited study identified specific cognitive symptom prevalences among long COVID patients: trouble concentrating (77.8%), brain fog (69%), forgetfulness (67.5%), word-finding difficulties (59.5%), and semantic disfluency (43.7%).
Fatigue is described as a prevalent and debilitating symptom of long COVID that significantly affects functioning.

Only 21 of 57 (37%) included long COVID studies provided an explicit definition of fatigue, and among these, 19 of 21 definitions involved an interplay of multiple fatigue categories rather than a single consistent construct.

Among studies using self-report fatigue measures, the Chalder Fatigue Questionnaire was the most frequently used validated tool (14/55 studies), followed by the Fatigue Severity Scale (11/55) and the Fatigue Assessment Scale (9/55).
Physical fatigue was the most assessed dimension of long COVID fatigue, evaluated in 29 of 57 studies, most commonly using the CFQ or Modified Fatigue Impact Scale subscales.
Cognitive fatigue was assessed separately from mental fatigue in long COVID studies (12/57 and 26/57 respectively) without a clear explanation of the distinction between the two constructs.
Postexertional symptom exacerbation (PESE), encompassing postexertional malaise with fatigue as a core component, was used to define fatigue in 4 studies and was directly assessed in 2 of 57 studies.

A core outcome set for long COVID recommends three unidimensional fatigue measures (FAS, FSS, FACIT-F), but appropriate adherence to the original scoring was inconsistent, particularly for the FACIT-F which was used appropriately in only 1 of 4 studies.

Of the studies using objective fatigability (non-self-report, performance-based) measures, none quantified whether their fatigability measure was associated with any self-reported fatigue measure, leaving the relationship between perceived fatigue and performance decline unestablished in long COVID.
Approximately 80% of Chinese college students reported having had COVID-19 infection in late 2022 and early 2023 after the zero-COVID policy was lifted.
47.8% of participants reported at least one long COVID somatic symptom about 2-3 months after COVID-19 onset.
35.4% of participants reported insomnia about 2-3 months after COVID-19 onset.
43.8% of participants reported fatigue about 2-3 months after COVID-19 onset.
37% of participants reported anxiety symptoms about 2-3 months after COVID-19 onset.
About 35.4% of Chinese college students reported at least one insomnia symptom roughly 2-3 months after COVID-19 onset.
About 43.8% of Chinese college students reported at least one fatigue symptom roughly 2-3 months after COVID-19 onset.
About 37% of Chinese college students reported anxiety symptoms roughly 2-3 months after COVID-19 onset.
About 54.3% of Chinese college students reported depressive symptoms roughly 2-3 months after COVID-19 onset, the highest prevalence among the measured outcomes.
The authors suggest that interventions targeting long COVID (somatic symptoms, insomnia, fatigue) may improve anxiety and depressive symptoms in Chinese college students who had COVID-19.
A regression model including cognitive failures, avoidance, rumination, and injustice experiences accounted for a significant amount of variance in psychological distress among long COVID patients.
Fatigue affects psychological distress in long COVID through a moderated mediation pathway rather than a direct effect alone.
Health resort treatment reduced self-reported fatigue by about 55% in the overall long COVID study group.
Fatigue reduction after health resort treatment was somewhat greater in men (63%) than in women (56%), though the difference in magnitude of change was not statistically significant.
Physical performance, measured by the SPPB, improved by about 10% following health resort treatment.
SPPB score increased more in women (12%) than in men (8%) after health resort treatment.
Functional status impairment (PCFS score) decreased by about 42% after health resort treatment compared with baseline.
PCFS score decreased by about 45% in women and about 37% in men after treatment.
At baseline, men scored about 8% higher on the SPPB than women, a statistically significant difference.
At baseline, women's PCFS scores (indicating greater functional impairment) were about 13% higher than men's.
At admission, fatigue level was 13% higher in women than in men, although the difference was not statistically significant.
The magnitude of SPPB improvement (delta) was numerically 29% higher in women than men, the largest sex difference among the delta variables, though not statistically significant.
Before treatment, patients aged 40-59 years had significantly better SPPB scores than those aged 70-79 years.
Health resort treatment significantly improved SPPB score in every age subgroup, with the largest improvement (14%) in the oldest group (70-79 years).
PCFS scores decreased by about 42% in each age subgroup after health resort treatment, with no significant differences between age groups.
Fatigue reduction after treatment was comparable across age groups (54% in ages 40-59, 56% in 60-69, and 57% in 70-79), suggesting the treatment mitigates fatigue regardless of age.

The magnitude of SPPB improvement (delta) was 45% higher in the youngest age group (40-59) compared with the oldest (70-79), indicating a smaller absolute delta but the authors note the oldest group had a clear relative improvement.
Hypertension was the most common comorbidity among long COVID patients undergoing health resort treatment, affecting 58.62% of patients.
Type 2 diabetes mellitus was present in 18.97% of the long COVID patients undergoing health resort treatment.
Hypothyroidism was diagnosed in 12.93% of long COVID patients undergoing health resort treatment.
Degenerative joint disease was diagnosed in 21.55% of the long COVID patients undergoing health resort treatment.
At baseline, the majority (65.52%) of long COVID patients qualifying for health resort treatment reported moderate fatigue severity.
At baseline, most long COVID patients (44.83%) reported mild functional impairment on the PCFS, contrasting with prior reports of predominantly no functional limitation.

At baseline, most long COVID patients (76.72%) showed no physical performance limitations as measured by the SPPB, consistent with prior reports of largely preserved physical performance shortly after COVID-19.
A multi-center electronic health record review of 659,286 US children and adolescents under 21 found the incidence of non-MISC pediatric PASC to be 3.7%.
Across included studies, the prevalence of pediatric PASC among infected children ranged from less than 1% to nearly 27%.
Pediatric PASC patients were predominantly adolescents, female, and Caucasian, with asthma, atopy, allergic rhinitis, and obesity as the most frequently described pre-existing conditions.
Commonly identified risk factors for developing pediatric PASC included increased age, female gender, asthma and atopy, obesity, and severe initial COVID-19 infection.
Asthma prevalence was nearly five times higher among pediatric patients with respiratory PASC than in the general population, suggesting preexisting asthma as an important risk factor.
Most (80%) pediatric patients in the included studies had mild initial COVID-19 symptoms such as fever, fatigue, cough, and shortness of breath.
Onset of PASC symptoms following acute COVID-19 illness ranged from less than 1 month to 15 months.
The most frequently reported pediatric PASC symptoms were dyspnea (26%), postexertional malaise (17%), fatigue (16%), headache (16%), and chest pain (15%).
Loss of taste or smell was significantly associated with pediatric PASC in a cohort of SARS-CoV-2 PCR-positive vs PCR-negative children (aHR 1.96).
Hair loss was significantly associated with pediatric PASC in the SARS-CoV-2 PCR-positive vs PCR-negative cohort (aHR 1.58).
Chest pain was significantly associated with pediatric PASC in the SARS-CoV-2 PCR-positive vs PCR-negative cohort (aHR 1.52).

Rare, severe neurologic and endocrine complications reported as PASC in children included Guillain-Barre syndrome, adrenal insufficiency, CNS demyelination, encephalopathy, tic disorder, stroke, seizures, and paralysis.
A 12-year-old female developed progressive limb weakness and delirium following SARS-CoV-2 infection, ultimately becoming bed-ridden.

PASC symptoms disrupted children's daily functioning, including four of nine athlete patients in a case series having to stop playing their sport, and decreased school performance reported in several studies.

Active Standing Tolerance Tests were the only diagnostic evaluation to produce abnormal findings in two cardiology-referred cohorts, leading to POTS diagnosis in 5 of 9 and 2 of 7 pediatric PASC patients.
Children evaluated for PASC had substantially lower quality of life scores on both the PedsQL Core and PedsQL Fatigue surveys compared to healthy controls.

Pediatric POTS patients treated with nonpharmacologic measures and medications (fludrocortisone, atenolol, midodrine) had nearly complete symptom resolution within one week once medication management was optimized.
About 30% of pediatric PASC patients with obstructive lung disorders were responsive to inhaled bronchodilator therapy.
Trials of nerve blocks in pediatric PASC patients with severe headaches did not appear beneficial.
Behavioral therapy, neuropsychology, and physical therapy included in a multi-disciplinary pediatric PASC clinic did not show indicated effectiveness.
Acupuncture and vitamin supplementation (vitamin D, coenzyme Q, magnesium) were trialed for pediatric PASC with little observed benefit.
At University Hospital Essex, 21 of 110 patients referred for long COVID evaluation were found to have an alternative diagnosis upon further work-up.
An Italian study reported that poor symptom recovery from PASC declined over time: 4% at 1-5 months, 1.3% at 6-9 months, and 0.7% at 12 months after symptom onset.
A prospective Canadian cohort study found that 0.67% of children who tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 remained symptomatic at 12 months compared to 0.16% of those who tested negative.
Nerve blocks were trialed for pediatric patients with severe PASC-related headaches but did not appear to be beneficial.
Acupuncture and vitamin supplementation (vitamin D, Co-enzyme Q, magnesium) were trialed in pediatric PASC patients with little observed benefit.
Across three pulmonology clinic studies, approximately 30% of pediatric PASC patients with obstructive lung disorders responded to inhaled bronchodilator therapy.
Laryngoscopy in pediatric PASC patients with respiratory symptoms identified paradoxical vocal fold motion disorder in one study and exercise-induced laryngeal obstruction in another.

The authors propose that endothelial abnormalities contribute to reduced exercise capacity in long COVID.

17.1% of patients continued to report persistent symptoms two years after mild SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Fatigue was the most frequently reported long COVID symptom, present in 26.1% of the sample.
Persistent muscle pain was reported by 8.4% of patients following mild SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Post-exercise malaise was reported by 7.5% of patients after mild SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Leg/arm weakness was reported by 3.9% of patients after mild SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Dyspnea was reported by 3.6% of patients after mild SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Persistent dry cough was reported by 3% of patients after mild SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Memory loss was reported by 6% of patients after mild SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Dizziness/lightheadedness was reported by 3.9% of patients after mild SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Concentration problems were reported by 3.6% of patients after mild SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Persistent headache was reported by 2.1% of patients after mild SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Reduced/absent/altered sense of smell and taste were reported in about 2% of patients following mild SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Among patients still symptomatic at two years, persistent fatigue remained the most frequent complaint, reported by 18% of that subgroup.
5.7% of patients reported an ongoing impact on their work or school status due to COVID-19 that persisted to the time of the interview.
17.4% of patients reported worse self-care capacity after SARS-CoV-2 infection compared to before.
16.8% of individuals reported that walking a distance of at least 1 km is harder now than before SARS-CoV-2 infection.

About 3.9% of patients reported that standing up for at least 30 minutes is harder now than before infection, and household or work/school tasks and sustained concentration were also reported as more difficult by a subset of patients.
Age distribution did not significantly differ between symptomatic (long COVID) and asymptomatic patient groups, both centered around 30-60 years with a median slightly above 40.

Men with long COVID showed a more concentrated age distribution (30-40 years), whereas women with long COVID showed greater age variability, suggesting a sex difference in the age pattern of long COVID.

The discussion cites viral persistence, immune dysregulation, and autoimmunity as proposed key mechanisms underlying long COVID pathophysiology, based on prior literature rather than this study's own data.
One-dose pre-COVID vaccination showed no significant effect on the odds of developing long COVID.
Two-dose pre-COVID vaccination was associated with a 24% reduced odds of developing long COVID.
Two-dose pre-COVID vaccination was associated with reduced odds of four specific long COVID symptoms: fatigue, headache, loss of smell, and muscle pain, out of 10 symptoms analysed.
Three-dose pre-COVID vaccination showed a statistically insignificant but potentially strong protective association against long COVID.
One-dose post-COVID vaccination (given after infection) was associated with a 15% reduced odds of long COVID.
Two-dose post-COVID vaccination showed a statistically insignificant but potentially protective association against long COVID.

FACIT-Fatigue scores (higher = less fatigue) significantly improved from baseline to 6 weeks, baseline to 12 weeks, and 6 to 12 weeks during a 12-week individualized exercise program in Long-COVID patients.
1MSTST repetitions increased significantly over the 12-week intervention, with significant improvement from baseline to 6 weeks and baseline to 12 weeks, but not from 6 to 12 weeks.
Workload (average wattage on the Total Body Trainer) improved significantly and progressively across all three time points during the intervention, with a large effect size.
No significant interaction between sex and time was found for FACIT-Fatigue, 1MSTST, or workload scores, indicating similar trainability of male and female Long-COVID patients.
Males had significantly higher mean workload scores than females averaged across all testing sessions, with a medium effect size.
Participants who completed more than 24 training sessions over 12 weeks showed a significantly greater increase in workload scores than those completing fewer than 21 sessions.

Number of completed training sessions did not significantly affect change in 1MSTST or FACIT-Fatigue scores, indicating no consistent dose-response relationship between training frequency and these outcomes.

The median PCFS score did not change significantly over the 12-week intervention, with the majority of participants remaining at a score of 3 (moderate functional limitation) both before and after training.
Moderately affected Long-COVID patients (by PCS score) showed a significantly larger increase in workload scores over 12 weeks than severely affected patients, though both groups improved.
FACIT-Fatigue and 1MSTST score changes did not significantly differ between moderately and severely affected Long-COVID patients, both groups showing comparable improvement.

At baseline, lower PCFS (functional status) scores were moderately correlated with higher FACIT-Fatigue scores (less fatigue), indicating a relationship between functional status and fatigue severity in Long-COVID patients.
Higher FACIT-Fatigue scores (less fatigue) at baseline moderately correlated with higher workload scores, suggesting less-fatigued patients tolerate more demanding exercise.
Workload scores strongly correlated with 1MSTST scores at baseline in Long-COVID patients.
PCS score did not correlate significantly with PCFS, FACIT-Fatigue, 1MSTST, or workload scores at baseline.

Almost three-quarters of participants (73.2%) reported at least one comorbidity, most commonly endocrine, nutritional, or metabolic diseases.

The red blood cell aggregation index was significantly higher in Long-COVID patients compared to non-Long-COVID controls.

Plasma fibrinogen concentration showed a moderate positive correlation with the RBC aggregation index (AI%) in Long-COVID patients.

Echinocytes/acanthocytes, the largest category of morphological abnormality, were significantly more frequent in Long-COVID patients than controls.
Dacrocytes (teardrop cells) were significantly more frequent among RBCs in Long-COVID patients compared to controls.

Standard hematological parameters (RBC count, WBC, platelets, hemoglobin, hematocrit, MCV, MCH, MCHC, and RDW) did not differ significantly between Long-COVID patients and non-Long-COVID controls.

Long-COVID patients showed a clinically relevant fatigue burden, with a mean FACIT-Fatigue score of 21.35 ± 8.4 (below the severe-fatigue cutoff of 30), and 26 of 30 participants scored below this threshold.
Serum ferritin was within the normal range in all but two Long-COVID patients, and serum fibrinogen was within normal range in all but one Long-COVID patient.

Fatigue was the second most common symptom of long COVID-19, reported in 25.9% of affected individuals.

Receiving fewer than two vaccine doses before infection was an independent risk factor for long COVID-19.
Gender was not significantly associated with long COVID-19 in univariate analysis.
Smoking history was not significantly associated with long COVID-19, differing from some earlier reports.

Reduced concentration was reported as a common functional change among persons with long-Covid.
Having had COVID-19 one year or more prior to survey was associated with a change in perceived global health, with an odds ratio of 1.5.
Being infected with COVID-19 twelve months or more prior was associated with functional decline, with an odds ratio of 1.5.
Hospitalization for COVID-19 was associated with functional decline, with odds ratios ranging from 2.2 to 2.4.
Having one or more chronic comorbid conditions was associated with functional decline, with an odds ratio of 1.6.
Obesity was associated with functional decline in persons with long-Covid, with an odds ratio of 1.6.

A Dutch matched cohort study found post-COVID symptom clusters (chest pain, dyspnea, muscle pain, ageusia/anosmia, fatigue, autonomic dysregulation) were more common in COVID survivors than in controls.
A systematic review of 120,970 people found neurological symptoms in 19.7% of long COVID patients, particularly difficulty concentrating, headache, anosmia, memory deficit, and cramps.
The same systematic review found respiratory disorders, especially dyspnea and poor exercise tolerance, present in about a quarter of long COVID participants.
Cardiac symptoms, mostly palpitations, affected 11% of long COVID participants in the same systematic review.
In a 452-patient ICU-treated COVID-19 cohort followed one year later, most patients reported persistent physical, psychological, and cognitive symptoms, with weakness the most common.
A meta-analysis of 1.2 million patients found long COVID at 3 months was roughly twice as common in women as in men over 20 years old.
A meta-analysis found older age groups had a progressively lower risk of long COVID compared to younger adults aged 18-30 years.
Daily and former cigarette smoking was associated with an increased risk of long COVID among survivors.

A Japanese multicenter study identified asthma and the need for mechanical ventilation as independent risk factors for prolonged dyspnea at 6 and 12 months post-COVID-19.
Among patients with pre-existing autoimmune disease, a study found a substantial prevalence of long COVID with high rates of neurological/psychological symptoms and quality-of-life impact.
COVID-19 was reported to increase the risk of developing new autoimmune and autoinflammatory connective tissue disorders.
A large meta-analysis found individuals with obesity (BMI>30) had a 10% higher risk of long COVID compared to those with normal BMI.

A meta-analysis of five studies including over 200,000 patients found ischemic heart disease was associated with a 1.28-fold higher risk of long COVID.
In a large sample of HIV-positive COVID-19 patients, HIV infection was associated with more than a two-fold increased risk of long COVID, and about half developed at least one long COVID symptom.

In a study of 113 long COVID patients, serum markers of endothelial activation (von Willebrand factor), red blood cell lysis, and complement activation persisted at 6-month follow-up and were associated with elevated anti-CMV and anti-EBV IgG antibody levels.
Patients treated with dexamethasone during acute COVID-19 showed a shorter duration of long COVID symptoms, hypothesized to reflect early modulation of the inflammatory state.
SARS-CoV-2 RNA was detected in the majority of examined lung samples, supporting the lung as a potential site of viral persistence in long COVID.
A systematic review of over 517 studies found that acute-phase treatment with remdesivir or nirmatrelvir/ritonavir had a protective effect against development of long COVID.

One study found long COVID fatigue and neurocognitive symptoms at 4 months post-diagnosis were independently associated with serologic evidence of recent EBV reactivation, in the absence of detectable viral DNA.
CMV seropositivity was associated with a lower risk of neurocognitive symptoms of long COVID, with no association found for other non-neurocognitive symptoms.
In HIV-positive COVID-19 patients, EBV antibody prevalence was significantly higher among those with long COVID symptoms compared to those without.
An association has been observed between long COVID and VZV reactivation, potentially explaining vesicular lesions and neuropathic manifestations seen in some long COVID patients.
Elevated cytokine levels were found in long COVID patients compared to healthy controls, suggested to be associated with symptom persistence.

A synthesis of 19 systematic reviews and 46 primary studies found strong evidence for immune system dysregulation, cerebral hypoperfusion, and altered pulmonary gas exchange as long COVID mechanisms, with moderate evidence for endothelial damage/hypercoagulation, mast cell activation, and vascular receptor autoimmunity.
Salivary creatine abundance was significantly lower in long COVID patients than in healthy controls, potentially reflecting impaired cellular energy metabolism.
The tripeptide Gly Pro Lys, an ACE-inhibitory peptide, was less abundant in saliva of long COVID patients than controls, possibly linked to cardiovascular sequelae.
Calenduloside E 6'-methyl ester (also referred to as calenduloside G methyl) was detected only in, and more abundant in, the long COVID group compared to controls.
Cyasterone, a phytoecdysteroid with antitumor and osteogenic properties, was absent/significantly reduced in the long COVID group compared to controls.
N-phenyl-1-naphthylamine was absent/significantly reduced in saliva of long COVID patients compared to controls.
Gentiobiose, a disaccharide component of gentio-oligosaccharides, was significantly less abundant in saliva of long COVID patients than controls.
D-(+)-turanose, a low-glycemic-index sucrose isomer, was significantly less abundant in saliva of long COVID patients than controls.
L-glutamic acid n-butyl ester was significantly less abundant in saliva of long COVID patients than controls.

Zygadenine, a plant alkaloid, was significantly less abundant in saliva of long COVID patients than controls.
2-dodecyl benzene sulfonic acid was significantly less abundant in saliva of long COVID patients than controls.

Of 338 salivary metabolites identified, 19 showed significantly different abundance between long COVID patients and healthy controls, and PLS-DA showed discrimination between the two groups.

Long COVID patients showed impaired quality of life 60 days post-discharge as measured by the Saint George's Respiratory Questionnaire, with reduced scores across symptom, activity, and impact domains.
No oxygen deficit was observed in arterial blood gas analysis or during the 6-minute walk test in long COVID patients.
Fatigue resistance improved significantly from baseline to day 14 across all participants, but the improvement did not differ between beetroot juice and placebo groups.
Distance walked on the 6-minute walk test increased significantly from baseline across the trial, but this change was not different between the beetroot juice and placebo groups.
Flow-mediated dilation, a marker of endothelial function, did not differ between participants receiving beetroot juice and those on placebo.
A PLS-DA model based on combined biological variables (microbiome, metabolome, inflammatory markers) correctly classified participants into beetroot juice vs placebo groups with high accuracy.
Participants who ingested beetroot juice had a greater abundance of Akkermansia compared with placebo.
Participants who ingested beetroot juice had a greater abundance of Oscillospira compared with placebo.
Participants who consumed beetroot juice had higher circulating levels of interferon gamma compared with those on placebo.

FCGR3A (V/F) genotype distribution did not differ significantly between Long COVID patients, prepandemic SFN patients, and population controls.
G1m (3/17) IgG1 allotype genotype distribution did not differ significantly between LC patients, prepandemic SFN patients, and controls.
The rs9916629 (C/T) polymorphism, which affects NK cell subpopulation composition, showed no significant difference in genotype distribution across LC, prepandemic SFN, and control groups.
HLA-E genotype distribution was similar across LC patients, prepandemic SFN patients, and controls.
Homozygous NKG2C gene deletion (del/del) was significantly more frequent in prepandemic SFN patients (24%) than in population controls (3%) or LC patients (8%).
HCMV IgG seropositivity rates did not differ significantly between LC patients (50%), prepandemic SFN patients (35%), and population controls (55%).

The higher prevalence of low NKG2C response in prepandemic SFN patients versus LC was confirmed when restricting the LC group to the subset with skin-biopsy-confirmed SFN (n=15).

Two of 46 LC patients were weakly positive for anti-GM1 IgM ganglioside antibodies, considered likely part of the natural antibody repertoire rather than pathogenic.

In the prepandemic SFN cohort, one of 24 patients had low titers of glycine receptor antibodies and another had low titers of anti-GD1a IgG ganglioside antibodies, both considered likely clinically irrelevant.
SFN was histologically confirmed by reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density on skin biopsy in 15 of 50 (30%) Long COVID patients with new neuropathic symptoms.
High certainty evidence shows that eight weeks of vortioxetine does not improve cognitive function in long covid patients.
Moderate certainty evidence suggests vortioxetine probably has little or no effect on depressive symptoms or quality of life in long covid.
No compelling evidence supported effectiveness of leronlimab, a monoclonal antibody targeting CCR5, for long covid symptoms.
Licopid (glucosaminyl muramyl dipeptide) was supported only by low or very low certainty evidence for treating long covid symptoms.
Actovegin (derived from ultrafiltered calf blood) was supported only by low or very low certainty evidence for long covid.
Intermittent aerobic exercise (3-5 times weekly for 4-6 weeks) probably improves physical function compared with continuous exercise in long covid patients.

Other physical activity/rehabilitation programmes (multicomponent exercise with physiotherapy, low vs high intensity training, in-patient rehabilitation plus acupuncture, inspiratory muscle training, physiotherapy plus breathing exercises) were supported only by low or very low certainty evidence.

The online CBT programme probably improves concentration/cognitive symptoms in long covid patients versus usual care.
A mobile app (ReCOVery) providing education on diet, sleep, and exercise, and an amygdala/insula retraining programme, were supported only by low or very low certainty evidence.
Low certainty evidence suggests the synbiotic formulation SIM01 might alleviate fatigue compared with placebo in long covid.
SIM01 might improve concentration in long covid patients compared with placebo (low certainty evidence).
SIM01 might improve dyspnoea in long covid patients compared with placebo (low certainty evidence).

Moderate certainty evidence suggests coenzyme Q10 (500 mg/day for six weeks) probably does not improve quality of life in long covid patients.
