Medical devices and technologies (hyperbaric oxygen, active high-definition transcranial direct current stimulation, photobiomodulation, active hydrogen therapy) were supported only by low or very low certainty evidence, or by trials with integrity concerns.

A combined physical and mental health rehabilitation programme probably increases the proportion of long covid patients who experience recovery or important improvement compared with a single session of advice/support.
The combined physical and mental health rehabilitation programme probably improves quality of life versus a single advice/support session.

Combined physical and mental health rehabilitation probably has little or no effect on physical and cognitive function, and may have little or no effect on anxiety, though it probably reduces depressive symptoms.
No compelling evidence of benefit was found for combined physical and mental health rehabilitation on fatigue, pain, or dyspnoea.

Investigators of the SIM01 trial previously reported that several bacterial species, including Bifidobacterium adolescentis and Bifidobacterium longum, are substantially lower in the gut of patients with covid-19 compared with healthy controls, suggesting gut dysbiosis in long covid.

Risk factors reported in the literature for developing long covid include female sex, greater comorbidity burden, and patient-reported psychological distress, whereas severity of acute covid-19 infection may not predict long covid.
In hepatitis B patients not receiving antiviral treatment, HBV DNA levels before and after COVID-19 were not significantly different.
In hepatitis B patients on antiviral therapy, HBV DNA levels significantly declined from before to after COVID-19, likely reflecting ongoing antiviral efficacy rather than a COVID-19 effect.
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) levels increased significantly after COVID-19 compared to before, in both antiviral-treated and untreated hepatitis B patients, though values remained within normal range.
Serum creatinine levels decreased significantly after COVID-19 in hepatitis B patients receiving antiviral treatment.
eGFR increased significantly after COVID-19 in hepatitis B patients receiving antiviral treatment, suggesting mild COVID-19 did not impair renal function in this group.
Long COVID symptoms were significantly more prevalent among chronic hepatitis B patients than non-hepatitis B patients after propensity score matching for age and sex.

After matching for age and sex, acute COVID-19 symptoms including sore throat, reduced sense of smell, and nasal congestion occurred less frequently in hepatitis B patients than in non-hepatitis B patients.
BMI composition differed significantly between hepatitis B and non-hepatitis B patients, with a higher proportion of overweight/obese individuals in the hepatitis B group.
COVID-19 vaccination completion rate was significantly higher in hepatitis B patients than non-hepatitis B patients.
Hepatitis B patients receiving antiviral treatment had lower incidence of sore throat and headache during the acute phase of COVID-19 compared to those not receiving antiviral treatment.
Overall incidence of long COVID symptoms was significantly lower in hepatitis B patients receiving antiviral treatment compared to those not receiving treatment.
Dry cough as a long COVID symptom was significantly less common in hepatitis B patients receiving antiviral treatment compared to those not receiving treatment.
Six hepatitis B patients showed an increase in HBV DNA after COVID-19, but none met the criteria for HBV reactivation (≥2 log increase) and none had abnormal liver function.
The most frequently reported long COVID symptoms among all patients, in descending order, were cough, fatigue, palpitations, insomnia, and reduced memory.
Among long COVID patients, there was a significant difference in gender distribution, with a higher proportion of females than males.
Across 102 long COVID clinic patients, mean ACE-III score was 91/100 (SD 6), with only 15.7% scoring at or below the threshold indicating objective cognitive impairment.

A large majority of participants achieved maximum possible scores on ACE-III attention, language and visuospatial subdomains, suggesting ceiling effects that limit sensitivity to detect impairment in these domains.
Among the subgroup completing the digital LCCAB battery, 89.47% showed significant impairment on at least one cognitive task, versus only 15.7% flagged as impaired by ACE-III.
Nearly half of the LCCAB subgroup showed significant impairment in reaction time on the simple reaction time task assessing processing speed.
Over half of the LCCAB subgroup showed significant reaction-time impairment on the go/no-go inhibitory control task.
42.1% of LCCAB subgroup participants showed significant reaction time impairment on the stimulus-oriented attention task.
42.1% of participants showed significant reaction time impairment on the SIT1 stimulus-independent attention task.
31.6% of participants showed significant reaction time impairment on the SIT2 stimulus-independent attention task.
Working memory error scores on the XNA2 task showed significant impairment in 41.1% of the LCCAB subgroup, higher than the impairment rate seen in reaction-time or baseline error measures.
A lower proportion of participants showed impairment on error-based (accuracy) scores compared to reaction-time measures for inhibitory control, attention, and working memory baseline tasks.
Sleep quality (PSQI) scores showed a strong positive correlation with performance on the SOT attention task, though this did not survive correction for multiple comparisons.
Sleep quality showed a moderate positive correlation with SIT1 attention task performance, not surviving multiple comparison correction.
Sleep quality showed a moderate positive correlation with SIT2 attention task performance, not surviving multiple comparison correction.
Overall, anxiety, depression, fatigue and sleep scores did not significantly correlate with ACE-III or LCCAB cognitive performance (aside from the specific sleep-attention correlations noted).
Fatigue scores were a marginally non-significant predictor of ACE-III Global score in a regression model.
Anxiety scores were a marginally non-significant predictor of ACE-III Fluency score in a regression model.
Sleep scores significantly predicted performance on the SOT attention task in regression modelling.
Sleep scores significantly predicted performance on the SIT2 attention task in regression modelling.
A combination of sleep, fatigue and depression scores significantly predicted performance on the SIT1 attention task.
Bioelectric Meridian Therapy (BMT) was associated with approximately 80% recovery of the patient's sense of taste and smell over six months of treatment.
BMT decreased the patient's muscle tightness and spasm, particularly in the jaw and spine muscles, reportedly improving blood and oxygen supply to affected areas.
Following initiation of BMT, the patient regained strength and energy, enabling resumption of physical activities such as swimming and cycling.
BMT was associated with subjective improvement in cognitive function, mental clarity, and reduced brain fog in the patient.
The patient exhibited positive psychological changes after BMT, including improved mood, optimism, and emotional stability, along with relief from depression.

The patient experienced persistent post-COVID symptoms including numbness, cognitive impairment/forgetfulness, fatigue, muscle weakness, and reduced pulmonary function/endurance that appeared after completing quarantine.
Standard treatments including vitamin supplementation and counseling did not improve the patient's post-COVID fatigue and mental symptoms.

Six months after COVID-19 symptom onset, and prior to substantial improvement with BMT, the patient reported a markedly reduced quality of life due to persistent sensory dysfunction and other symptoms.
Among 29 non-hospitalized PCC patients undergoing needle EMG, 18 (62%) showed myopathic findings across multiple muscles.
PCC patients with myopathic EMG findings were significantly older than those without myopathic findings.
No significant differences were found between PCC patients with and without myopathic EMG findings in sex distribution, BMI, or symptom duration.
Symptom severity for muscle pain and fatigue (VAS scores) did not differ between PCC patients with myopathic EMG findings and those without.
Quality of life (SF-36) and multidimensional fatigue (MFI) scores did not differ between PCC patients with and without myopathic EMG findings.
Nerve conduction studies showed no signs of peripheral nerve dysfunction in PCC patients with or without myopathic EMG findings.
Quantitative sensory testing (thermal thresholds) results were comparable between PCC patients with and without myopathic EMG findings.
Physical fitness, assessed by peak VO2 and 6-minute walk test distance, did not differ between PCC patients with and without myopathic EMG findings.
Upper and lower limb muscular strength was similar between PCC patients with myopathic EMG findings and those without.
In prior work by the same group, 62% of non-hospitalized PCC patients with fatigue and PEM showed myopathic EMG findings, compared to only one case among age- and sex-matched healthy controls.
Agergaard et al. reported myopathic EMG findings in 55% of PCC patients without evidence of large nerve fiber dysfunction, despite shorter symptom duration than the present cohort.
A cited study of PCC patients with symptoms lasting on average 10 months found myopathic EMG findings in 75% of patients along with muscle fiber atrophy and regeneration on biopsy.
A cited meta-analysis found that 45% of people may experience unresolved symptoms for more than 4 months following SARS-CoV-2 infection, regardless of hospitalization.
Persistent fatigue, loss of interest/pleasure, and trouble concentrating were the most common symptoms reported by children with long COVID syndrome, occurring in the majority of cases.
All five assessed cardiopulmonary/cardiovascular symptoms were significantly more frequent in children with LCS than in convalescent controls, representing 100% of that symptom category.
Children with LCS reported significantly worse total quality-of-life and functioning scores than both convalescent and uninfected control groups.
The change in quality-of-life/functioning since acute COVID-19 was significantly worse in the LCS group than in the convalescent control group, most of whom showed unaltered functioning.
Neutrophil viability, assessed by Annexin A5/Propidium Iodide staining, did not differ between LCS and convalescent control cells.

Unstimulated (basal) superoxide production by neutrophils was significantly decreased in children with LCS compared to convalescent controls, across maximal production, slope, and area-under-curve parameters.

Stimulated superoxide production (PMA or opsonized zymosan), evaluated by maximal production, slope, and area-under-curve, did not significantly differ between LCS and convalescent control neutrophils.

After normalizing stimulated superoxide production to basal (unstimulated) levels, PMA-stimulated LCS neutrophils showed significantly higher relative superoxide output than controls, roughly 1.3-1.5-fold greater.
The percentage of neutrophils actively phagocytosing GFP-expressing S. aureus was significantly decreased in children with LCS compared to controls.
The rate constants for both phagocytosing-cell and phagocytosed-bacteria saturation curves were significantly lower in LCS neutrophils than in controls, indicating slower phagocytic kinetics.
Plasma IL-6 concentration was significantly elevated in children with LCS compared to controls.
Plasma IFN-γ levels did not significantly differ between children with LCS and controls, contrasting with an adult LCS biomarker study.
Neutrophil-derived IL-8 production, at rest and after PMA or zymosan stimulation, did not significantly differ between LCS and convalescent control cells.
Neutrophil migration toward an fMLP chemoattractant gradient, unstimulated or directed, did not differ significantly between LCS and control cells.

The slope of PMA-stimulated superoxide production correlated negatively with the number of symptoms in children with LCS, indicating that greater neutrophil dysfunction paralleled greater symptom burden; unstimulated and zymosan-stimulated correlations trended similarly but did not reach significance.
PMA-induced IL-8 production negatively correlated with the number of symptoms in children with LCS, whereas zymosan-induced IL-8 showed no significant correlation.
The negative correlation between PMA-stimulated superoxide production and symptom number was significant in boys and in unvaccinated children with LCS when examined by subgroup.

In subgroup analysis, the negative correlation between PMA-stimulated IL-8 production and symptom number was significant in girls but the text's description of boys and unvaccinated children's significance was internally inconsistent with the reported statistics.

A moderate (versus mild or asymptomatic) acute SARS-CoV-2 infection course was more prevalent among children who went on to develop LCS than among convalescent controls, while asymptomatic infection was more common in convalescent controls.
Adults with ASD learned to prefer advantageous probabilistic choices at the same rate and extent as NT participants, in both choice ratio and response time.
As adults with ASD learned to favor advantageous choices, their pupillary arousal for these choices increased, in contrast to NT participants.
In NT participants, learning to favor advantageous choices caused a decrease in pupillary arousal for those choices, opposite to the pattern seen in ASD.
Greater pupil-linked arousal during decisions with higher expected value correlated with a greater self-reported degree of intolerance of uncertainty in everyday life.

Six children and one adult were found via whole genome sequencing to carry clinically significant CHD8 variants (four likely pathogenic, three variants of unknown significance) associated with autism spectrum disorder and related phenotypes.
Patients with CHD8 variants displayed the previously described phenotype spectrum including ataxia, overgrowth, ADHD, and connective tissue disorders in addition to autism spectrum disorder.
Four patients with CHD8 variants had hepatomegaly, a clinical feature not previously associated with pathogenic CHD8 variants.
Two patients with CHD8 variants had hyperbilirubinemia, a clinical feature not previously associated with pathogenic CHD8 variants.
Two patients with CHD8 variants presented with cardiovascular abnormalities, primarily arrhythmias and, in one case, cardiomyopathy, features described as uncharacteristic of CHD8-related disorder.
A novel heterozygous splice-site variant, c.436+1G>T, was identified in intron 2 of the P4HTM gene in the patient.
A previously reported missense variant, c.934G>A (p.E312K), was found in exon 6 of the P4HTM gene, forming a compound heterozygous genotype with the novel splice-site variant.
This is reported as the first case linking P4HTM gene variants to epileptic encephalopathy, expanding the known phenotypic spectrum of HIDEA syndrome beyond its classic features.
The patient presented with severe developmental delay, significant hypotonia, autistic behaviors, and abnormal eye movements since the neonatal period, alongside a happy demeanor.
Brain imaging in the patient showed cortical atrophy and a thin corpus callosum, without dystonia.
Among adolescents referred for headache to the pain clinic, significantly more girls than boys were represented, consistent with known female predominance around puberty.
Autism was diagnosed in 15% of headache patients prior to referral, and the pain team additionally attributed headaches to autism with sensory integration problems in 9% of cases.

The pain team newly diagnosed fibromyalgia/AMPS in 30% of headache patients (15% fibromyalgia, 15% AMPS), whereas only 15% had this diagnosis prior to referral and none had received condition-appropriate treatment beforehand.

71% of headache patients had a pre-existing psychiatric disorder diagnosis (depression, anxiety, PTSD, or suicide attempt/self-harm), described in the discussion as an elevated 67% prevalence relative to the general literature.
15% of headache patients had a history of hospitalization for suicidal ideation or attempted suicide.
52% of headache patients screened positive for mild to severe anxiety on the GAD7 questionnaire.
55% of headache patients had symptoms of depressive disorder based on the PHQ9 questionnaire.
The average Pain Catastrophizing Scale score was 31±14, with 57% of patients reporting a clinically relevant level of pain catastrophizing.
Patients had been experiencing headaches for an average of 52±44 months (range 1-144) before being referred to the multidisciplinary pain clinic.

Patients had tried an average of 4.5±2 (range 1-10) different medications to manage headaches and psychiatric conditions, including 3±2 headache-specific medications, before their initial pain clinic visit.
Topiramate was the most commonly prescribed medication for headache management in this cohort, followed by tricyclic antidepressants, triptans, and gabapentin.
The CHAMP trial (cited in discussion) demonstrated that topiramate provided youth with no significant reduction in headache frequency or impairment compared to placebo.
The CHAMP trial (cited in discussion) demonstrated that amitriptyline provided youth with no significant reduction in headache frequency or impairment compared to placebo.
Bilateral occipital nerve blocks were offered to three patients with occipital neuralgia (one refused); headaches improved in two of the remaining patients who underwent the procedure.
A bilateral supraorbital nerve block performed in one patient with a failed cranial vault reconstruction did not provide any pain relief.
A patient referred to a physiatrist for Botox injections experienced improved pain and better functioning.
Two patients had previously undergone unsuccessful trials of Botox for headache management before referral to the pain clinic.
Neuroimaging studies (brain MRI in 52% and CT in 8% of patients) did not demonstrate any brain pathology that could explain the headaches.
After multidisciplinary pain clinic treatment, 47% of patients reported improved headache severity/frequency, 22% felt recommendations were not effective, and 21% did not return for follow-up.
18% of headache patients had comorbid joint pain diagnosed prior to referral.

Before referral, patients saw an average of 3±1 (range 1-5) different specialists for headaches, most commonly neurologists (34%), physiatrists (15%), and neurosurgeons (5%); none had previously seen a pain specialist.
Nine of 21 patients (40.1% as stated) with psychogenic fever had a comorbid neurodevelopmental disorder.
Seven of 21 patients with psychogenic fever had comorbid autism spectrum disorder.
Four of 21 patients with psychogenic fever had comorbid intellectual disability.
Two of 21 patients with psychogenic fever had comorbid ADHD.
Four of 21 patients with psychogenic fever had comorbid orthostatic dysregulation, diagnosed by symptoms and active standing test.
Three of 21 patients with psychogenic fever had comorbid migraine.
Two of 21 patients with psychogenic fever had comorbid irritable bowel syndrome.
Among the 9 patients with comorbid neurodevelopmental disorders, 4 also had comorbid adjustment disorder related to bullying, poor friendships, or academic failure.

Only one of nine patients with comorbid neurodevelopmental disorder had been diagnosed prior to their psychogenic fever consultation; the remaining eight were diagnosed at the clinic as a result of the fever presentation.
Children and adolescents with ASD have been reported to show atypical HPA axis and autonomic nervous system function at rest and under social or nonsocial stress.
Youth with ASD have been reported to have higher rates of epilepsy and allergies, but not asthma, compared with non-ASD youth.
POTS has been reported to be prevalent among children with psychogenic fever, with enhanced sympathetic stress response potentially underlying both conditions.
The autonomic nervous system regulator tofisopam was effective (prolonged the period of normal temperature) in 5 of 8 patients treated.
The serotonin receptor antagonist tandospirone was effective in only 3 of 6 patients treated.
The antidepressant paroxetine was given to one patient and was ineffective.
Among herbal medicines tried (Hochuekkito, Shokenchuto, Ninjinyoeito), only Ninjinyoeito showed effectiveness, increasing the period of normal temperature.
The herbal medicines Hochuekkito and Shokenchuto were used but did not show effectiveness for psychogenic fever, unlike Ninjinyoeito.

Of the 21 patients treated with lifestyle counseling, environmental adjustment, and psychotherapy, 9 achieved complete remission, 4 improved, 1 discontinued treatment, and 7 were transferred to another hospital.

Psychosocial stressors identified among the 21 patients with psychogenic fever included interpersonal problems at school (n=16, e.g., bullying), learning difficulties (n=9), family problems (n=6), and sexual abuse (n=1), with 19 (90.1%) having no school attendance.

Psychogenic fever accounted for approximately 1.7% of outpatients over 22 years at this clinic, with a male-to-female ratio of 1:2, compared with a prior Japanese study reporting 1:1.19 and another reporting 1:2.2.
In a prior pediatric study, psychogenic fever accounted for 18% of all fever-of-unknown-origin cases and 2-6% of all psychosomatic disease cases.

Psychogenic fever is proposed to involve a noninflammatory cytokine-mediated pathway with sympathetic hyperactivity rather than inflammation, distinct from infection-induced fever, and is unresponsive to usual anti-inflammatory drugs.

The area covered by the center-of-pressure trajectory during quiet standing was significantly greater in children with ASD than in typically developing controls, especially under conditions of reduced or absent visual information.

Variability of COP oscillations (RMS) along both anterior-posterior and medial-lateral directions was significantly higher in ASD patients than controls, with group differences accentuated in conditions of reduced visual input.

Total sway path length did not differ significantly on average between ASD and control groups, but control subjects showed greater flexibility in modulating sway path across different postural conditions than ASD patients, suggesting reduced adaptability in ASD.

Higuchi fractal dimension of both anterior-posterior and medial-lateral COP components was significantly smaller in ASD patients than in controls, indicating reduced geometric complexity of postural sway.

Sample entropy values for both AP and ML COP components were significantly lower in ASD patients than in controls, particularly under conditions of reduced vision or unstable feet position, indicating excessive regularity/predictability of postural sway.

In children with ASD, lower sample entropy of the mediolateral COP component under the FP20 eyes-open/visual condition was strongly inversely correlated with more severe balance/vestibular dysfunction as measured by the SPM-2 Equilibrium subscale.

In the same FP20 condition, lower sample entropy of the mediolateral COP component in ASD patients was also inversely correlated with the severity of restricted and repetitive behaviors (RBS-R total score).

Under conditions of absent visual information (feet-30-degrees, eyes closed) and/or less stable feet positions, decreased sample entropy in ASD patients was significantly associated with higher (more severe) RBS-R repetitive-behavior scores.

The relationship between postural stability (area, sway path) and complexity/regularity measures (FrDim, SampEn) diverged by group: in ASD, decreased stability correlated with reduced complexity and greater regularity of COP trajectories (negative correlations), whereas in controls decreased stability correlated with increased complexity (positive correlations).

Caregiver-reported balance and motion (vestibular function) sensory profile was clinically abnormal in all ASD participants, falling within the range of definite dysfunction, and nearly all reported poor coordination and balance abilities.
Both ASD and VSD post-surgical pediatric patients had lower SDNN (a time-domain HRV measure of overall variability) compared to the non-cardiac surgical comparison group.
RMSSD, a time-domain HRV measure reflecting parasympathetic (vagal) activity, was lower in both ASD and VSD patients compared to the comparison group.
High frequency (HF) power, a frequency-domain HRV metric reflecting parasympathetic activity, was lower in both ASD and VSD patients versus the comparison group.
Low frequency (LF) power, reflecting mixed sympathetic and parasympathetic activity, was lower in both ASD and VSD patients versus the comparison group.
Very-low frequency (VLF) power was lower in both ASD and VSD patients compared to the comparison group.
SD2 (a non-linear Poincaré plot measure of long-term HRV) was lower in both ASD and VSD patients compared to the comparison group.
AVNN (average NN interval duration, inversely proportional to heart rate) was higher in both ASD and VSD patients compared to the comparison group.
ASD patients showed a lower LF/HF ratio compared to the comparison group, suggesting a shifted sympatho-vagal balance.
VSD patients showed a higher LF/HF ratio compared to the comparison group, suggesting sympathetic predominance.
ASD patients showed higher SD1 (a Poincaré plot measure of short-term HRV) compared to the comparison group.
VSD patients showed lower SD1 compared to the comparison group.
ASD patients showed higher sample entropy (SampEn), indicating greater unpredictability of the heart rate time series, compared to the comparison group.
Sample entropy (SampEn) was the only HRV parameter showing no statistically significant difference between VSD patients and the comparison group.

Overall, the pattern of HRV abnormalities in postoperative ASD and VSD patients is consistent with reduced parasympathetic (vagal) activity and sympathetic predominance, indicating autonomic imbalance.

HRV abnormalities documented in this pediatric postoperative cohort, particularly reduced SDNN and RMSSD, correlate with previously reported abnormal HRV findings in adults who underwent ASD or VSD closure in childhood.

The authors hypothesize that the observed HRV abnormalities may reflect partial vagotomy occurring during surgical dissection for clamp placement at the time of cardiac operation, an inadvertent consequence of surgical technique.
Prior literature cited by the authors describes partial normalization of HRV at 3-month follow-up after ASD/VSD surgery, potentially reflecting partial autonomic reinnervation over time.

At baseline (T1), both HCV and SARS-CoV-2 patients showed elevated IL-6 compared to healthy donors.
At baseline (T1), both HCV and SARS-CoV-2 patients showed elevated IL-22 compared to healthy donors.
Following clearance of either virus, all cohorts showed a reduction in soluble inflammatory mediator (SIM) activity relative to baseline.
At six months (T3), the SARS-CoV-2 cohort showed decreased activity of MCP1, IP-10, and ITAC compared to median SIM values.
Cirrhotic HCV patients exhibited the highest soluble inflammatory mediator activity of all cohorts at long-term follow-up after viral clearance.
IL-10, IL-22, TNFα, IFNγ, and IL-6, which were elevated during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection, normalized back to baseline levels by follow-up T2 through T5 in the longitudinal SARS-CoV-2 cohort.
Patients with acute HCV infection exhibited an overall increase in soluble inflammatory mediator levels.
Non-cirrhotic chronic HCV patients returned to soluble inflammatory mediator levels comparable to healthy donors after achieving sustained virologic response.
Chronic cirrhotic HCV patients showed persistently elevated SIM levels after SVR, with no significant change compared to baseline (T1).

IL-8 and IP-10/CXCL10 normalized to healthy levels by 3 months in SARS-CoV-2, acute HCV, and non-cirrhotic chronic HCV patients, but in cirrhotic HCV patients showed an initial decrease followed by persistent elevation without full recovery.

In cirrhotic chronic HCV patients, IP-10/CXCL10 and IL-8 concentrations decreased between T1 and T5 but remained statistically significantly elevated relative to healthy controls at the long-term follow-up.
In the longitudinal SARS-CoV-2 cohort, MIP-3β levels significantly increased at the long-term follow-up (T5) compared to T4, rebounding to nearly 80% of baseline (T1) levels.
MCP1 levels in the longitudinal SARS-CoV-2 cohort showed no long-term recovery, returning to T1 baseline levels by T5.
ITAC concentrations remained elevated at the long-term follow-up (T5) in the longitudinal SARS-CoV-2 cohort compared with baseline.
Acute HCV patients showed the most pronounced decline in MIP-3β levels, which was no longer statistically significant from healthy donors by T4.
Chronic cirrhotic HCV patients had highly significant elevation of MIP-3β compared with healthy donors, with persistence despite an apparent decrease at T5.
MCP1 levels remained elevated in both acute and chronic HCV patients, irrespective of cirrhosis status, compared to healthy donors.

Linear modeling showed that at T2 and T3, almost all SIMs in the HCV cohorts had a positive association with time relative to the SARS-CoV-2 cohort baseline, indicating persistently higher inflammatory marker levels in HCV patients at these time points.
No soluble inflammatory mediator was directly associated with fatigue scores collected during follow-up in the SARS-CoV-2 cohort.
Sex, age, and BMI did not significantly influence levels of selected SIMs (IL-6, IP-10, ITAC, MIP3β) in the SARS-CoV-2 cohort.
Steroid and/or antiviral therapy administered during the acute phase of SARS-CoV-2 infection did not significantly affect levels of selected SIMs (IL-6, IP-10, ITAC, MIP3β).

The cross-sectional cohort of patients presenting specifically for long-COVID symptoms had higher IL-6, TNFα, and IFNγ levels at month 9 compared to other cohorts, supporting a link between these mediators and long-COVID symptomatology.
Detection of EBV transcripts in nasal and PBMC compartments during the first 40 days post-admission was significantly associated with greater COVID-19 severity (trajectory group).
CMV transcript detection in nasal and PBMC samples was significantly associated with increasing COVID-19 severity.
Anelloviridae transcript detection in PBMCs was significantly associated with increasing COVID-19 severity.
Among severely ill TG4 patients, detection of CMV transcripts in any compartment (nasal, endotracheal aspirate, or PBMC) was associated with higher one-year mortality.
Detectable EBV transcripts in the upper respiratory tract of TG4 patients were associated with increased one-year mortality, as were HSV1 and HSV2 nasal transcripts.
Detection of Anelloviridae transcripts in PBMCs was positively associated with increasing age, independent of COVID-19 severity.
Hispanic/Latino ethnicity was significantly associated with detection of both CMV and EBV transcripts.
No significant associations were found between detection of chronic viral transcripts and biological sex or treatment with remdesivir or steroids.
Anelloviridae transcripts in PBMCs were significantly associated with a history of solid organ transplantation, immunosuppression, shock, and ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI).

Nasal CMV transcript detection was inversely associated with azithromycin use, while CMV in PBMCs was associated with bacteremia, pulmonary vascular disease, renal complications, shock, and stroke, and nasal CMV was linked to pneumothorax.

EBV transcript detection in the nasal compartment was associated with ICU-level care and shock, while PBMC EBV transcripts correlated with liver failure, concurrent infections, shock, and higher overall complication counts; EBV detection in either compartment was also associated with secondary infections.

Nasal HSV1 detection was significantly associated with acute venous thromboembolism and shock, and inversely associated with liver disease; nasal HSV2 was associated with shock and inversely associated with convalescent plasma treatment.
Patients with detectable EBV transcripts in PBMCs had persistently elevated serum EBV IgG and IgA antibody titers.
Circulating HSV1 proteins detected by plasma proteomics were more common in participants with nasal HSV1 transcripts and were significantly more common in patients with severe (TG4) COVID-19.
EBV transcription in PBMCs was associated with increased proportions of B-cell plasmablasts, the primary host cell of EBV.

Detection of CMV transcripts was associated with reduced frequencies of CD4 and CD8 central memory T cells, CD27low effector memory CD4 T cells, and CD56low CD16hi CD57low NK cells, while both EBV and CMV were associated with higher frequencies of activated CD4+ and CD8+ T cells.
EBV transcription in PBMCs was associated with elevated serum IL6, CCL7, CCL2, IL10, and CXCL10, cytokines previously linked to COVID-19 severity.
CXCL10, CXCL11, and IL18 were shared cytokine signatures elevated across several chronic viral reactivations (EBV, CMV, HSV1, HSV2, Anelloviridae).
CMV reactivation was associated with the greatest number of metabolomic changes, including higher levels of urea and TMAO, metabolites linked to kidney injury.
CMV and Anelloviridae reactivation were both associated with increases in long chain fatty acids (erucate, arachidate, docosadienoate) and nitric oxide synthesis regulators SDMA and ADMA.
S-methylcysteine sulfoxide and 6-bromotryptophan, metabolites involved in oxidative stress protection, were reduced with reactivation of Anelloviridae, HSV1, HSV2, CMV, and EBV.

Anelloviridae in PBMCs, CMV in PBMCs, and HSV1/2 in the nasal compartment were associated with downregulation of RNA processing and protein translation pathways and upregulation of cellular replication pathways (EBV, CMV, HSV1/2), with several viruses also linked to neutrophil degranulation signatures.

In the nasal compartment, CMV, EBV, and HSV1/2 transcripts were associated with upregulation of interleukin signaling (including IL-10 signaling), lymphocyte immunoregulatory interactions, and neutrophil degranulation, with CMV/EBV also increasing type 2 immune response and phagocytosis pathways.

During the convalescent period, Anelloviridae transcripts were significantly more prevalent in participants belonging to the Physical PASC patient-reported outcome group, characterized by physical disability and fatigue, suggesting a possible biomarker role for persistent physical PASC symptoms.

No significant relationship was found between acute-stage viral reactivation and PASC patient-reported outcome groups, though CMV reactivation trended toward lower PASC rates and EBV toward higher PASC rates.

The patient's serology showed positive EBV early antigen IgG and negative EBV nuclear antigen IgG with undetectable EBV viral load, consistent with EBV reactivation rather than active or primary infection.

The authors hypothesize that COVID-19-induced inflammation triggered EBV reactivation, which likely contributed to relapse of the patient's preexisting collagenous gastritis and slower clinical recovery.

The patient's initial HIV screening test was falsely positive, likely due to cross-reactivity of EBV and SARS-CoV-2 antibodies with HIV screening assays, and was subsequently disproven by confirmatory HIV RNA and antibody testing.
The patient was found to be iron deficient, with a low ferritin level, without accompanying microcytic anemia.
Treatment with ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily resolved the patient's leg cramps after 3 months of supplementation.
A 4-week course of oral budesonide 9 mg daily with taper, given for suspected recurrent collagenous gastritis/colitis, resulted in only minimal symptomatic improvement.
Ongoing proton pump inhibitor therapy with omeprazole 40 mg daily, combined with prior iron supplementation, was associated with the patient's steady but slow weight gain and symptom improvement.
Citing prior literature, the authors note that EBV reactivation is common among individuals with COVID-19 and may be associated with disease severity, poor clinical outcomes, and patient age.
A cited comparative meta-analysis found that EBV reactivation was associated with significantly higher mortality among hospitalized patients admitted for symptomatic COVID-19.
All 9 PASC/LC gynecologic patients evaluated had elevated baseline plasma von Willebrand factor levels above the normal reference range.
At baseline, control PASC/LC patients (non-NAC users) had significantly higher vWF levels than patients who would go on to use NAC.
At the first follow-up visit, control patients continued to show significantly higher vWF levels than NAC supplementers.
NAC supplementation was associated with normalization of elevated von Willebrand factor levels in all 3 NAC users, whereas none of the 6 control patients normalized their levels.
Patients using NAC supplementation reported subjective improvement in shortness of breath, brain fog, and fatigue compared to control patients not using NAC.
Prior studies indicate NAC has a thrombolytic effect on von Willebrand factor by reducing disulfide bonds connecting vWF monomers, decreasing multimer size and lysing vWF-rich micro-clots.

SARS-CoV-2 spike protein binding has been reported to downregulate surface expression of ACE2 and the α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, impairing the cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway and increasing platelet activation/aggregation.
A prior report by the same group found persistent elevation of von Willebrand factor and Factor VIII in PASC/LC gynecologic cancer patients.
Unlike von Willebrand factor and Factor VIII, D-dimer was not found to be persistently elevated in PASC/LC gynecologic cancer patients in the authors' prior report.

A separate case series reported that combined guanfacine and NAC treatment significantly improved memory, concentration, and executive function in 12 patients with brain fog and PASC/LC symptoms, allowing resumption of normal workload.
In a separate cited study, NAC treatment of COVID-19 pneumonia patients significantly reduced the risk of mechanical ventilation and mortality.

Post-hospitalization Neuro-PASC (PNP) patients with breakthrough infection (BTI, infection after vaccination) had a higher pre-COVID prevalence of depression/anxiety than PNP patients infected before vaccination (PVI).
Non-hospitalized Neuro-PASC (NNP) BTI patients had a higher pre-COVID prevalence of depression/anxiety than NNP PVI patients.
NNP BTI patients had a higher pre-existing prevalence of lung disease than NNP PVI patients.
NNP BTI patients had a higher pre-existing prevalence of headache disorder than NNP PVI patients.
NNP BTI patients had a higher pre-existing prevalence of gastrointestinal disease than NNP PVI patients.
NNP BTI patients had a higher pre-existing prevalence of non-diabetes endocrine disorders than NNP PVI patients.
NNP BTI patients had a higher prior history of traumatic brain injury than NNP PVI patients.
In PNP patients, anosmia was more frequently reported by BTI patients than PVI patients.
In NNP patients, anosmia was less frequently reported by BTI patients than PVI patients.
In NNP patients, dysgeusia was less frequently reported by BTI patients than PVI patients.
NNP BTI patients more frequently reported dizziness than NNP PVI patients.
NNP BTI patients more frequently reported dysautonomia symptoms than NNP PVI patients.
NNP BTI patients more frequently reported gastrointestinal symptoms than NNP PVI patients.
On neurologic examination, NNP BTI patients were more likely to show attention deficit than NNP PVI patients.
PROMIS quality-of-life scores did not differ significantly between PVI and BTI patients in either the PNP or NNP groups.
NIH Toolbox objective cognitive scores did not differ significantly between PVI and BTI patients in either the PNP or NNP groups.

Both PNP and NNP long COVID patients performed worse than a US normative population on NIH Toolbox tests of processing speed, attention, and working memory, with PNP patients additionally impaired on executive function.
PNP and NNP patients showed moderate impairment in PROMIS quality-of-life T-scores compared with a US normative population.
Time from symptom onset was not associated with subjective percent recovery compared to pre-COVID baseline in either PNP or NNP patients.

In multiple correspondence analysis of the PNP cohort, BTI patients had significantly higher values on the second dimension than PVI patients, indicating more frequent co-occurrence of anosmia and dysgeusia.

In multiple correspondence analysis of the NNP cohort, BTI patients had significantly lower values on the second dimension than PVI patients, indicating less frequent co-occurrence of anosmia and dysgeusia.

Overall, vaccination prior to SARS-CoV-2 infection made little difference to the clinical presentation, subjective quality-of-life alteration, or objective cognitive dysfunction of established Neuro-PASC, in both post-hospitalization and non-hospitalized patients.

A meta-analysis of 10,945 SARS-CoV-2 cases at 6-12 months follow-up found pooled prevalence of muscle weakness (54%), fatigue (30.94%), dyspnea (27.06%), anxiety (25.19%), sleep difficulty (24.11%), difficulty concentrating (22.47%), limited mobility (21.81%), chest tightness (21.18%), and depression (20.16%).

In a large RECOVER cohort of 9764 individuals, 37 symptoms were documented 6 months post-infection, with post-exertional malaise (87%), fatigue (85%), brain fog (64%), dizziness (62%), GI manifestations (59%), and palpitations (57%) being most common.
A systematic review found that 22% of Long COVID patients had GI-related symptoms compared to 12% during the acute phase.

In severe acute COVID-19, males showed higher pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-8, IL-18, CCL5) and lower CD8+ T cells, whereas females showed higher innate immune cytokines (IL-15, M-CSF, CXCL10) and more robust T cell activation.
In a cohort of 486,149 non-hospitalized COVID-19 cases, Black, mixed-ethnicity, and other ethnic minority groups had higher risk of developing Long COVID compared to the white population.
Among 327 acute COVID-19 patients, those admitted to ICU or requiring mechanical ventilation had a 3.6-fold higher risk of persistent symptoms and greater dyspnea during follow-up.
More than 40% of people over 65 years experienced prolonged COVID symptoms compared to 26-30% of those aged 18-64 years.
A cohort study of 418 patients found that obese women had a 57% risk of persistent Long COVID symptoms.

In 133 patients followed at 3 and 6 months post-acute COVID, Long COVID patients had less diverse gut microbiota with reduced SCFA-producing bacteria (Bifidobacterium adolescentis, Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Lachnospiraceae) and increased Candida albicans, Pseudomonas phage Pf1, and Klebsiella spp.

Higher abundance of opportunistic pathogens (Erysipelatoclostridium ramosum, Clostridium bolteae, Clostridium innocuum) persisted for up to 6 months post-COVID and correlated with higher viral load and severity markers.
Post-COVID patients showed lower levels of SCFAs and L-isoleucine, consistent with loss of beneficial bacteria involved in key biochemical pathways.

In an 84-patient cohort one year post-COVID, SCFA-producing bacteria (Eubacterium hallii group, Subdoligranulum, Ruminococcus, Dorea, Coprococcus, Eubacterium ventriosum group) declined significantly, with Ruminococcus positively correlating with lymphocytes and negatively with CRP, Dorea negatively correlating with neutrophils, and Eubacterium ventriosum group/Ruminococcus negatively correlating with NK cells.

Respiratory Long COVID symptoms were associated with increased abundance of Streptococcus anginosus, S. vestibularis, and S. gordonii, while neurological symptoms were associated with increased Clostridium innocuum and Actinomyces naeslundii.
Long COVID patients with hair loss had reduced levels of butyrate-producing bacteria Bifidobacterium pseudocatenulatum and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii.
Patients with mental stress and depression in Long COVID showed alterations in Lactobacilli and Clostridia species, with Lactobacilli significantly reduced.

Obese Long COVID patients had lower gut microbiome alpha diversity and higher pro-inflammatory markers (FGF2, IL-6, IFN-γ, MCP-1), with attenuated viral neutralization capacity linked to HMGB1 activation.

A meta-analysis of 23 studies evaluating 18 inflammatory and vascular biomarkers found CRP, LDH, D-dimer, and leucocytes remained elevated in Long COVID patients compared to recovered individuals, indicating vascular immunopathology.
In short-term PASC (2 months post-discharge), fatigue correlated with high ESR, LDH, CRP, and D-dimer, and low hemoglobin, ferritin, and albumin.

IL-6, a hallmark cytokine of acute COVID-19 and the cytokine storm, remains elevated during Long COVID sequelae in some reports, though other studies observe a progressive decline, making its role debatable.

IFN-β, Pentraxin 3, IFN-γ, and IFN-λ2/3 remained elevated in Long COVID up to 8 months post-infection, and a predictive model using inflammatory biomarkers achieved 78.5-81.6% accuracy for identifying Long COVID.
Gut-specific inflammatory biomarkers fecal calprotectin, LBP, and FABP2 are elevated in Long COVID patients, particularly those with dysbiosis.

A Spanish cohort study reported increased total CD8+ lymphocytes, driven by increased effector CD8+ T cells, in Long COVID patients, possibly reflecting EBV reactivation or chronic aberrant adaptive immune response.
CD3+ lymphocytes expressing exhaustion markers PD-1 and TIM-3 were elevated in Long COVID patients, possibly due to chronic immune activation from persistent SARS-CoV-2 antigen.
Levels of memory B cells and IgA/IgG-producing plasmablasts were increased in Long COVID patients compared to the acute phase, where IgM-producing plasmablasts predominated.

In the RECOVER cohort of 9764 individuals, the most common symptoms 6 months after infection were post-exertional malaise (87%), fatigue (85%), brain fog (64%), dizziness (62%), GI manifestations (59%), and palpitations (57%).

A meta-analysis of 10,945 SARS-CoV-2 cases at 6-12 months follow-up found pooled prevalences of muscle weakness (54%), fatigue (30.94%), dyspnea (27.06%), anxiety (25.19%), sleep difficulty (24.11%), difficulty concentrating (22.47%), limited mobility (21.81%), chest tightness (21.18%) and depression (20.16%), with additional myalgia/joint pain (34.52%), rhinorrhea (30.93%) and neurological symptoms (23.85%) persisting beyond 12 months.
Frequently reported neuropsychiatric manifestations of Long COVID include fatigue (37%), brain fog (32%), memory impairment (28%), sleep disturbances (31%), anxiety (23%), and depression (17%).

In a systematic review, 22% of participants had GI symptoms during Long COVID compared to 12% in the acute phase, including loss of taste (10%), loss of appetite (9%), abdominal pain (7%), nausea/vomiting (6%), and diarrhea (5%).
Males with more severe acute SARS-CoV-2 infection had higher levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines including IL-8, IL-18, and CCL5, along with lower CD8+ T cell levels.

Females with more severe acute disease had higher levels of innate immune cytokines including IL-15, M-CSF, and CXCL10, along with a more robust T cell activation response and higher IFNγ from CD8+ T cells compared to age-matched males.

A cohort study of 486,149 non-hospitalized, confirmed COVID-19 cases found that Black, mixed-ethnicity, and other ethnic minority patients were more susceptible to developing Long COVID symptoms than white patients.
A US study found Black participants experienced higher rates of dyspnea, myalgia, and arthralgia compared to other ethnicities.

Among 327 acute COVID-19 patients of differing severity, those admitted to the ICU or receiving mechanical ventilation had a 3.6-times higher risk of persistent symptoms and higher dyspnea during follow-up.

A cohort study of Long COVID patients found that obese individuals had lower gut microbial alpha diversity and higher pro-inflammatory markers (FGF2, IL-6, IFNγ, MCP-1) with attenuated viral neutralization capacity via activation of HMGB1, suggesting a disturbed microbiome-immune axis contributing to Long COVID.

In a study of 133 patients at 3 and 6 months post-acute COVID infection, those with Long COVID had a less diverse gut microbiome with lower abundance of SCFA-producing bacteria (Bifidobacterium adolescentis, Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Lachnospiraceae) and higher abundance of Candida albicans, Pseudomonas phages Pf1, and Klebsiella spp.

Persistent SARS-CoV-2 gut microbiome effects up to 6 months included higher abundance of opportunistic pathogens Erysipelatoclostridium ramosum, Clostridium bolteae, and Clostridium innocuum, which were associated with higher viral load and increased severity markers, with these changes relatively stable over time.

Low gut microbial diversity, measured by the Chao1 index, in the post-acute convalescence phase correlated with high inflammation scores, and full microbial diversity was not restored until six months or longer post-illness.

In a cohort of 84 recovered COVID-19 patients one year post-illness, SCFA-producing taxa (Eubacterium hallii group, Subdoligranulum, Ruminococcus, Dorea, Coprococcus, Eubacterium ventriosum group) were significantly decreased and positively correlated with lymphocytes but negatively correlated with CRP (Ruminococcus), neutrophil count (Dorea), and NK cells (Eubacterium ventriosum group, Ruminococcus).
Respiratory symptoms in Long COVID were associated with increased abundance of Streptococcus anginosus, Streptococcus vestibularis, and Streptococcus gordonii.
Individuals with neurological symptoms in Long COVID showed increased levels of Clostridium innocuum and Actinomyces naeslundii.
Patients with mental stress and depression in Long COVID showed alterations in Lactobacilli and Clostridia species, with Lactobacilli being significantly reduced.
Long COVID patients experiencing hair loss had reduced levels of butyrate-producing bacteria such as Bifidobacterium pseudocatenulatum and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii.

A meta-analysis of 23 studies evaluating 18 inflammatory and vascular biomarkers found that CRP, LDH, D-dimer, and leucocytes remained elevated in Long COVID patients compared with those who recovered, pointing to ongoing vascular immunopathology.
In short-term PASC (2 months post-discharge), fatigue was correlated with high levels of ESR, LDH, CRP, and D-dimer, along with low hemoglobin, ferritin, and albumin.

Cytokines of the acute inflammatory response including IFN-β, Pentraxin 3, IFN-γ, and IFN-λ2/3 remained elevated during Long COVID up to 8 months post-infection, and a predictive model based on these biomarkers achieved 78.5-81.6% accuracy for Long COVID.

Contrary to the reduced/impaired type I interferon seen in severe acute COVID-19, levels of type I IFN (IFN-β) and type III IFN (IFN-λ1) remained elevated in Long COVID, indicating high activity of plasmacytoid dendritic cells.

Gut-specific inflammatory biomarkers including fecal calprotectin, lipopolysaccharide-binding protein, and fatty acid-binding protein 2 are elevated in Long COVID patients, particularly those with dysbiosis.
In a study of 612 individuals, adherence to the Mediterranean diet was associated with a marked decrease in pro-inflammatory markers CRP and IL-17.

Consumption of the Mediterranean diet shifted gut microbiota composition toward higher abundance of SCFA-producing bacteria such as Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Eubacterium, taxa otherwise depleted in Long COVID.
A large smartphone-based study found that a plant-based diet was associated with decreased risk of severe COVID-19 infection and joint-related complications.
A randomized clinical trial of hospitalized acute COVID-19 patients found that administering calcifediol (vitamin D) at admission markedly reduced ICU admission compared with untreated patients.

A cross-sectional retrospective cohort study found vitamin D levels were lower in Long COVID patients than non-Long COVID patients 6 months after discharge, and vitamin D was the only independent factor associated with Long COVID development.
Consumption of cranberry oligosaccharides as a prebiotic induced production of short-chain fatty acids (acetate, propionic acid, butyrate) from Lactobacillus strains.
Prebiotic inulin administration was associated with higher serum glucagon-like peptide 2 (GLP-2) and lower serum zonulin concentration, indicating improved intestinal barrier function.
In severe acute COVID-19 patients, gut dysbiosis was characterized by reduction of Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron, which persisted throughout hospitalization.

A meta-analysis reported a 51% reduction in symptom severity in COVID-19 patients receiving probiotic strains (Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium, Bacillus coagulans, Bacillus subtilis, Bacillus clausii), with significant improvement in headache, cough, diarrhea, fatigue, and cognitive symptoms.

A probiotic/prebiotic preparation containing Bifidobacteria strains, given 5 weeks after COVID-19 infection, decreased viral load and reduced levels of IL-6, MCP-1, M-CSF, IL-1RA, and TNF-α while increasing beneficial Bifidobacteria.
A clinical trial of Limosilactobacillus reuteri DSM 17,938 given for 6 months to mRNA-vaccinated individuals found higher serum anti-RBD IgA levels in the probiotic arm compared with placebo.

Fecal metagenomic profiling showed higher levels of antibiotic resistance genes (tetracycline, vancomycin) in bacteria from patients who received antibiotics, alongside elevated pathogenic Klebsiella associated with Long COVID.
Certain strains of Klebsiella, such as Klebsiella quasipneumoniae, were found to be elevated in patients with severe COVID-19 infection.
Treatment with the psychobiotic Lactobacillus plantarum strain PS128 reduced previously elevated serum corticosterone levels and stabilized neurotransmitters dopamine and serotonin.
Computational modeling showed that Lactobacillus plantarum probiotics and its metabolites blocked the receptor binding site for the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein RBD.
Animal studies using Lactobacillus plantarum showed enhanced vaccine-induced antibody production through T and B cell activation, along with reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6 and TNF-α.
Long COVID patients show dysregulation of the HPA axis with decreased cortisol levels that are not accompanied by a compensatory increase in adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH).
Hypercortisolemia during the early phase of acute COVID-19 disease is suggested as a possible risk factor for the later development of Long COVID.

Studies in germ-free mice showed that perturbation of normal gut microbiota composition reduced expression of Occludin and Claudin-5 proteins, increasing blood-brain barrier permeability, and that administering the SCFA-producing bacterium B. thetaiotaomicron restored blood-brain barrier integrity.

Mice deficient in the α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor showed significantly impaired regulation of TNFα in non-bone-marrow derived cells, indicating a role for this receptor in the vagal anti-inflammatory reflex independent of T cells.

Vitamin D is proposed to support gut microbiota and gut homeostasis by enhancing the ACE2/Ang1-7/MAS system, promoting the growth of beneficial Bifida and Firmicutes species, and reducing hyperinflammation.
Pre-COVID use of respiratory system medications was associated with significantly higher odds of persistent fatigue at 3-6 months post-infection.
Pre-COVID cardiovascular system medication use showed a non-significant trend toward lower odds of long COVID fatigue.
Pre-COVID systemic antiinfective use showed a non-significant trend toward reduced odds of long COVID fatigue.
Pre-COVID respiratory medication users had higher but non-significant odds of persisting respiratory symptoms in long COVID.
Pre-COVID cardiovascular system medication use showed a non-significant trend toward fewer neurological symptoms in long COVID.
Pre-COVID use of systemic antiinfectives was significantly associated with lower odds of persistent neurological symptoms in long COVID.
Pre-COVID cardiovascular system medication use was significantly associated with fewer persistent LC symptom categories.
Pre-COVID systemic antiinfective use was significantly associated with fewer persistent LC symptom categories.
Pre-COVID respiratory medication users had higher but non-significant odds of pulmonary radiological abnormalities.
Pre-COVID nervous system medication use was significantly associated with fewer pulmonary radiological abnormalities.
At 3-6 months post-infection, the most commonly reported persistent long COVID symptoms in this cohort were respiratory, neurological, and fatigue complaints.
Systemic corticosteroid use rose sharply during acute COVID-19 and then dropped markedly post-COVID, indicating predominantly short-term use for acute inflammatory control.
Anticoagulant (antithrombotic) use markedly increased during acute COVID-19 and then decreased post-COVID, consistent with management of COVID-19-associated coagulopathy.
Use of agents acting on the renin-angiotensin system (RAS inhibitors, C09) declined from pre-COVID to acute COVID-19, then increased back to baseline post-infection.

Overall use of alimentary tract and metabolism medications remained relatively stable and comparatively high across pre-COVID, acute, and post-COVID phases, despite large shifts within specific subgroups.
GP registrars considered long COVID as a differential diagnosis in 80% of consultations where fatigue was a presenting symptom.
Registrars judged long COVID to be the likely cause of fatigue in 18% of encounters where it was considered as a differential.
Consultations conducted via telehealth were associated with greater odds of registrars both considering long COVID as a differential and considering it the likely cause of fatigue.
Registrars who trained in Australia had lower odds of considering long COVID as the likely cause of fatigue compared with overseas-trained registrars.
No patient-level variables were significantly associated with either registrars considering long COVID as a differential or as the likely cause of fatigue.
Across 11 studies (14,979 workers), the pooled prevalence of Long Covid-19 among workers was 38% (95% CI 22.5–56.2), ranging from 10% to 54% across individual studies.
Dyspnoea at moderate activity was the most commonly reported symptom among workers with Long Covid-19, with a pooled prevalence of 51%.
Mental symptoms (e.g. anxiety, depression, PTSD-related symptoms) were reported by a pooled 38% of workers with Long Covid-19 across two studies.
Dyspnoea at mild activity had a pooled prevalence of 35% among workers with Long Covid-19.
Fatigue had a pooled prevalence of 26% among workers with Long Covid-19 across ten studies.
Effort intolerance had a pooled prevalence of 24% among workers with Long Covid-19.
A total of 43 distinct symptoms associated with Long Covid-19 were identified among workers across the 11 included studies.

The pooled prevalence of Long Covid-19 among workers (38%) was lower than that reported in general-population meta-analyses (42-57%), possibly reflecting a healthy worker effect and younger worker age.
Presence of Long Covid-19 symptoms was associated with a lower likelihood of working full-time (adjusted OR 0.84).
Long Covid-19 symptoms were associated with a higher likelihood of unemployment (adjusted OR 1.23).

Subgroup analyses found no significant difference in the prevalence of Long Covid-19 by industrial sector, follow-up duration, worker age, gender, diagnostic method, symptom assessment method, presence of a control group, Long Covid-19 definition, or study design.
Funnel plot asymmetry and a significant Egger's test (P<0.05) indicated possible publication bias in the prevalence estimates.

A prospective cohort of SARS-CoV-1 survivors showed notable declines in diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide, exercise capacity, and overall health status at 24 months post-infection, more pronounced among healthcare workers.
Workers who contracted SARS-CoV-1 reported significantly elevated burnout, psychological distress and PTSD between 13 and 26 months after infection.
Even 18 years after SARS-CoV-1 infection, fatigue remained the predominant symptom among affected workers.
Despite persistent fatigue and reduced respiratory function, emotional and mental health fully recovered at the 18-year follow-up of SARS-CoV-1 survivors.
Among MERS-CoV survivors, 48% continued to experience fatigue at 1 year, decreasing to 33% at 18 months of follow-up.
88% of MERS-CoV survivors returned to work, though the study did not specify part-time versus full-time employment status.
At 12 months post-infection, 27% of MERS-CoV survivors reported depression and 42% had PTSD.
A South Korean study found that 57% of nurses who treated MERS-CoV patients suffered from PTSD.
Persistent Long Covid-19 symptoms make it difficult for returning workers to focus on job tasks, leading to decreased work productivity.
Workers with Long Covid-19 have increased rates of sickness absenteeism, further impeding return to work.
Cognitive impairment, present in 49% of the long-COVID sample, was not associated with quality of life.
Fatigue was a significant contributor to quality of life variance in long-COVID patients, accounting for 7% of the explained variance.
Psychological distress (depression-anxiety-stress) was a significant contributor to quality of life variance, accounting for 11% of the explained variance in long-COVID patients.
Gender, along with fatigue and psychological distress, was part of a model accounting for 42% of the variance in quality of life among long-COVID patients.
Troponin T levels were significantly higher in patients with the PEM-fatigue symptom cluster compared to asymptomatic controls.
Relative telomere length (T/S ratio) in PBMCs was significantly shorter in patients with PEM-fatigue symptoms compared to asymptomatic controls.

Mitochondrial DNA copy number (mtDNAcn) in PBMCs was significantly lower in patients with PEM-fatigue symptoms compared to asymptomatic controls, though it did not significantly predict symptoms in regression models.

Global DNA methylation, assessed via LINE-1 methylation in PBMCs, did not significantly differ between Long-COVID patients (including PEM-fatigue cluster) and asymptomatic controls, nor did it predict symptoms.

None of the 14 plasma cytokines measured (including IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-2, IL-4, IL-10, IL-13, GM-CSF, IL-9, IL-17A, IL-17E, IL-17F, IL-21, MIP-3α, IL-22) differed significantly between Long-COVID patients and asymptomatic controls, nor predicted PEM-fatigue symptoms.
C-reactive protein levels did not significantly differ between Long-COVID patients and asymptomatic controls.
Troponin T was significantly higher in women than men, and higher with older age.
Older age predicted shorter telomere length in the cohort.
Linear regression showed shorter telomere length, together with troponin T and age, significantly predicted PEM-fatigue symptom severity.
Troponin T significantly predicted PEM-fatigue symptom severity in linear regression models.

Principal component analysis of 26 symptoms identified six independent symptom clusters: PEM-fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, autonomic symptoms, visceral problems, neurological symptoms, and immune disturbances.
Approximately 35.5% of SARS-CoV-2-infected participants developed persistent Long-COVID symptoms 4 to 24 months after infection, with PEM-fatigue being the most prevalent cluster (15.9%).
Acute infection severity, measured as need for ICU admission, was not associated with the prevalence of persistent Long-COVID symptoms or with physical function (6-minute walk test distance).
Significantly more women were represented in the Long-COVID group compared with the asymptomatic control group.
Across the 13 included studies, fatigue was the most frequently reported Long COVID symptom, appearing in 61.5% of studies.
Dyspnoea was reported in 46.1% of the included studies as a prevalent Long COVID symptom.
Changes in smell and/or taste (anosmia/dysgeusia) were reported in 38.6% of included studies.
Cognitive impairment/dysfunction was reported in 30.7% of the included studies.
Anxiety was reported as a Long COVID symptom in 15.3% of the included studies.
Diabetes mellitus and hypertension were the most predominantly reported comorbidities among people with Long COVID symptoms in the studies that described comorbidities.

Anosmia-dysgeusia was associated with younger age (under 65 years) rather than older age in a post-acute COVID-19 cohort.
Total blood triglycerides and the metabolites lactate and pyruvate were higher, while lipoproteins were lower, in Long COVID patients compared to healthy controls.
Lipoproteins were lower in Long COVID patients compared to healthy controls.

Long COVID patients show decreased serotonin caused by reduced tryptophan absorption, thrombocytopenia and increased expression of monoamine oxidase, leading to reduced vagal and hippocampal activation and cognitive impairment.
Reduced serotonin and vagus nerve dysfunction have been suggested as a pathway subsequent to viral infection contributing to Long COVID.
Cardiopulmonary symptoms including postural orthostatic tachycardia are described as common features of Long COVID, associated with significant disability and increased anxiety.

Menopause is associated with increased risk of Long COVID, with postmenopausal women showing higher COVID-19 incidence than premenopausal women, suggesting estrogen, a negative regulator of ACE2 expression, is linked to disease severity.

TLR7, an X-chromosome immune gene regulating interferon production, causes greater IFN signalling and better viral clearance in women, but continuous signalling is thought to predispose women to greater risk of developing Long COVID.
A reduced number of CD4+ and CD8+ effector memory T cells persisted for at least 13 months in individuals with Long COVID who had mild COVID-19, in both sexes.
PD1 protein expression was elevated in central memory cells and persisted for at least 13 months in individuals with mild COVID-19 who developed Long COVID.
A decrease in immunoglobulin M (IgM) was detected from primary infection to 6-month follow-up in individuals who developed Long COVID.

Immunoglobulin G3 (IgG3) was lower in Long COVID patients while IgG1 remained unchanged, an inverse pattern to that seen in mild and severe acute COVID-19, and an immunoglobulin signature combined with age, asthma history and five acute symptoms could predict Long COVID risk.
Early vaccination (before infection) using SARS-CoV-2-specific IgG titres was found to be more effective than late vaccination in reducing persistent symptoms.
Double vaccination was associated with a temporary beneficial effect on long-lasting COVID symptoms lasting between 21 and 67 days.

Vaccination against COVID-19 administered before infection was associated with a significant reduction in the incidence of Long COVID, though vaccination after infection was associated with lower chances of recovery from Long COVID.

Long COVID prevalence estimates diverge widely across populations, from around 1 in 8 people in the general population of the northern Netherlands to 9 out of 10 patients with at least one symptom 60 days after recovery in an Italian cohort.

In a rehabilitation cohort, 75 of 147 Long COVID patients had symptoms associated with overactive bladder 4-7 weeks after COVID-19, with 44 newly diagnosed and 22 worsening cases, and all reporting nocturia.

In a cohort of hospitalised COVID-19 patients, individuals with dyspnoea 4 months post-diagnosis were younger, had more severe initial COVID-19 episodes, longer hospital stays, and more frequent ICU admissions than those without dyspnoea.

In a study of intestinal microbiota, no significant differences in age, gender, comorbidities, medication use, or COVID-19 severity were found between patients with and without post-acute COVID-19 syndrome.

After multivariate adjustment, no baseline clinical characteristics, ICU admission, length of hospital stay, or treatment behaved as independent predictors of post-COVID-19 syndrome in one cohort, although anosmia-dysgeusia was associated with younger age and neurological symptoms occurred in 11.9% of patients.

After multivariate adjustment, female gender, pre-existing hypertension, and length of hospital stay were associated with increased risk of new or persistent symptoms after COVID-19 hospital discharge.

In a Korean cohort, difficulty concentrating, cognitive dysfunction, amnesia, depression, fatigue, and anxiety were the most frequent symptoms persisting up to 12 months post-COVID-19, with older age, female gender, and disease severity as risk factors for persistent neuropsychiatric symptoms, which had a greater impact on quality of life than other symptoms.
Diastolic blood pressure and rate-pressure product were significantly higher in post-acute COVID-19 participants compared to controls.
Fatigue is one of the most prevalent and debilitating symptoms of Long COVID, affecting up to 63% of patients.
18F-FDG PET imaging demonstrated hypometabolism patterns in multiple brain regions of Long COVID patients, with marked variability over time.
Temporal tensor decomposition captured progression of brain network reorganization in chronic fatigue syndrome with 82% accuracy versus 64% for traditional static analytical approaches.
Diffusion MRI (DTI) identified widespread microstructural white matter changes in COVID-19 patients.
Long COVID has been associated with over 200 distinct symptoms, with fatigue presenting in notably different patterns across patient subgroups.
Combining MRI with FDG-PET increased detection sensitivity for neurological manifestations of Long COVID to 94%, compared with 68% for MRI alone.
Early metabolic changes detected by PET often preceded and predicted subsequent structural alterations on MRI in Long COVID, with a median lag time of 3.2 months.
A deep learning framework for Long COVID multimodal neuroimaging achieved 87% accuracy identifying disease-specific patterns compared to 63% for conventional methods.
An attention-based neural network integrating PET and MRI features distinguished different phenotypes of Long COVID fatigue with 91% classification accuracy.
A graph neural network combining PET-MRI data identified distinct patterns of brain network disruption that strongly correlated with fatigue severity in Long COVID.
An AI model incorporating PET and MRI features predicted recovery trajectories in Long COVID patients at 6 months with 89% accuracy.

AI-driven multimodal analysis identified distinct Long COVID imaging subtypes with different therapeutic responses: patients with predominant metabolic disruption responded better to certain interventions than those with primarily structural changes.

A recurrent neural network analyzing sequential PET-MRI scans predicted symptom progression in Long COVID with 85% accuracy at 3 months, particularly identifying patients at risk of developing chronic fatigue.

In a cohort of 86 post-COVID patients versus 36 healthy controls assessed ~11 months after infection, attention and working memory were the most affected cognitive domains (up to 44.2% of patients), followed by memory (up to 40.7%) and executive functions (up to 39.5%).

Hospitalized Long COVID patients (33.72% of the cohort) exhibited more pronounced cognitive deficits than non-hospitalized patients, with neurological changes persisting regardless of vaccination status.
Functional connectivity was reduced between bilateral orbitofrontal-cerebellar areas and between parahippocampal regions in post-COVID patients.
Post-COVID patients showed decreased gray matter volume in cortical, limbic, and cerebellar areas, along with white matter alterations in axial and mean diffusivity.

Gray matter volume reductions correlated strongly with attention and processing speed deficits, while functional connectivity changes were specifically associated with memory performance in post-COVID patients.
A systematic review found that 51% of Long COVID patients fulfill ME/CFS diagnostic criteria, supporting COVID-19 as a major trigger for ME/CFS.
Prevalence estimates of long COVID in adults range widely from 2.3% to 53%.
According to systematic reviews, fatigue, post-exertional malaise and dyspnoea are the symptoms most commonly reported in long COVID.
In predominantly mild-to-moderate, non-hospitalised COVID-19 cases, roughly 12%-23% of affected persons remained absent from work or had prolonged absences 3-7 months after acute illness.
A meta-analysis of RCTs through December 2023 found moderate certainty evidence that an online cognitive-behavioural therapy programme probably improves fatigue and concentration in long COVID.

The same meta-analysis found moderate certainty evidence that a combined programme of physical and mental health rehabilitation probably increases the proportion of long COVID patients experiencing recovery or important improvement.
The meta-analysis found moderate certainty evidence that intermittent aerobic exercise, compared with continuous exercise, probably improves physical function in long COVID.

A prior 2022 feasibility study found that, following Energy Management Education, the mean difference in self-efficacy for performing energy conservation strategies at post-intervention (T2) was 1.9 points.
In May 2021, nine occupational therapists reported that the EME protocol was feasible and appropriate for persons with long COVID-related fatigue, though some optimisations were necessary.
