The lived experience of long-COVID neuropsychological sequelae shares similarities with chronic fatigue syndrome and fibromyalgia, though long COVID is narrated more as an abrupt rupture than a gradual transformation.
Participants highly valued being involved in scientific studies about their condition, describing that it helped them recover a sense of self and agency.
Patients who received at least one dose of COVID-19 vaccine showed statistically significant improvement in all ten of the most common Long COVID symptoms compared to never-vaccinated patients.
No statistically significant difference in Long COVID symptom recovery rates was found between patients who received CoronaVac, BNT162b2, or a heterologous CoronaVac+BNT162b2 regimen.
In univariate logistic regression, vaccination status was the only significant factor associated with recovery from the three most common Long COVID symptoms: dyspnea, fatigue, and forgetfulness.
Dyspnea, fatigue, and forgetfulness were identified as the three most common Long COVID symptoms among the ten symptoms tracked in the cohort.

Although not statistically significant, patients who received the mRNA vaccine BNT162b2 showed a trend toward higher recovery rates from Long COVID symptoms compared to the inactivated CoronaVac vaccine.
72.1% of patients hospitalized for acute COVID-19 had at least one persisting symptom (Long COVID) at a median follow-up of 35 days after symptom onset.
Fatigue was the most frequently reported persistent symptom, occurring in 41.7% of patients at follow-up.
Shortness of breath was reported in 31.2% of patients as a persistent symptom of Long COVID.
Cough persisted in 27.1% of patients following acute COVID-19 hospitalization.
Sleep disturbances were reported in 15% of patients as part of Long COVID symptomatology.
Patients with symptom duration greater than 7 days before hospital admission had significantly higher odds of developing Long COVID on multivariate analysis.
Patients hospitalized for more than 10 days had significantly increased odds of developing Long COVID on multivariate analysis.
Age 70 or older was associated with 2.2 times increased odds of Long COVID on bivariate analysis, but this association was not significant after adjusting for confounders in multivariate analysis.
Sex was not significantly associated with development of Long COVID in this cohort.
Above-normal BMI (overweight/obesity) was not found to be significantly associated with Long COVID in this study.
ICU admission during acute illness was not significantly associated with Long COVID in this cohort.
Having one or more comorbidities such as diabetes mellitus or chronic lung conditions was not significantly associated with Long COVID.
Lymphopenia persisted in 17.8% of patients during follow-up after acute COVID-19.
Leukocytosis was observed in 14.6% of patients at follow-up.
Raised CRP was present in 8.5% of patients during follow-up, comparable to a prior meta-analysis finding of 8%.
Among patients who had follow-up chest X-rays, fibrosis was the most common abnormality, detected in 42.6% of those imaged.
Ground-glass opacities were seen in 39.7% of patients who had a follow-up chest X-ray.
Low oxygen saturation (SpO2 <90% on room air) was present in 3.6% of patients at follow-up.
Cluster analysis of long COVID symptoms in 746 hospitalized COVID-19 patients identified five distinct symptom-based phenotype clusters one year after diagnosis.

Patients in the severe multi-organ dysfunction symptom cluster, which included many patients with malaise, were more likely to have poor psychosocial status (anxiety, depression, PTSD, QOL) one year after onset compared to other clusters.
The olfactory and gustatory disturbance symptom cluster had the second highest depression and anxiety scores among the five clusters, after the multi-organ dysfunction cluster.

The authors conclude that the multi-organ dysfunction phenotype with malaise and the olfactory/gustatory disturbance phenotype have distinct psychosocial consequences and require more extensive follow-up and intervention.
Among 370 adults with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection, 66.2% reported at least one persistent symptom (long COVID) at 18-month follow-up.
Female sex was statistically associated with a higher proportion of long COVID (73.91%).
Lower family income (below two minimum wages) was strongly associated with long COVID (94.74%).
Lack of physical activity was associated with a higher proportion of long COVID (83.33%).
Poor self-reported sleep quality was strongly associated with long COVID (93.33%).
Long-term medication use was associated with a higher proportion of long COVID (85.90%).
Needing health care in the last six months was associated with a higher proportion of long COVID (87.32%).
Needing professional and/or family support during recovery was associated with a higher proportion of long COVID (79.31%).
ICU treatment during acute COVID-19 was associated with a higher proportion of long COVID (78.99%).
Use of ventilatory support in the acute phase was associated with a higher proportion of long COVID (77.50%).
Presence of comorbidity was not statistically significantly associated with long COVID in this sample.
During the acute phase of COVID-19 infection, neurological symptoms were the most common symptom cluster, followed by respiratory, musculoskeletal, digestive, psychological, and endocrine symptoms.
Unlike most other symptom clusters, which decreased over time, skin and circulatory symptoms increased in frequency by the 18-month follow-up compared to the acute phase.
Memory loss was the single most prevalent persistent symptom at 18-month follow-up, affecting 42.70% of participants.
Fatigue was the second most prevalent persistent symptom at 18 months, affecting 32.16% of participants.
Anxiety was reported by 23.51% of participants at 18-month follow-up, part of the psychological symptom cluster present in 28.38%.
Dyspnoea was reported by 19% of participants at 18 months as part of the respiratory symptom cluster (29.46% overall).
Hair loss was reported by 19.73% of participants as part of the endocrine symptom cluster (12.43% overall) at 18 months.
Digestive symptoms were reported by 30.54% of participants at 18 months, including change in appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and altered stool.
Patients with headache after COVID-19 did not have a significantly different number of brain T2-hyperintense lesions than those without headache.
The proportion of patients with an age-adjusted pathological number of T2-lesions did not significantly differ between headache and no-headache groups.
Patients with chronic fatigue did not have a significantly different number of brain T2-hyperintense lesions than those without fatigue.
The proportion of patients with an age-adjusted pathological number of T2-lesions did not significantly differ between fatigue and no-fatigue groups.
Post-COVID-19 syndrome in this cohort showed a strong female predominance, consistent with prior long-COVID literature.
Despite a clear female predominance in post-COVID-19 syndrome, no sex-specific differences were found in brain MRI findings.
Chronic fatigue remained highly prevalent at the first post-COVID-19 follow-up, affecting the large majority of patients who had also reported it acutely.
Recurrent headaches, sleep disorders and depression were commonly reported post-COVID-19 symptoms at first consultation.
Mean fatigue severity scores in the post-COVID-19 cohort exceeded the clinical cutoff for significant fatigue.
Mean FSMC scores indicated a substantial fatigue-related impact on motor and cognitive function, exceeding the clinical cutoff.
Mean BDI-II scores exceeded the clinical cutoff for depressive symptoms in the post-COVID-19 cohort.
Mean daytime sleepiness scores in the cohort were below the clinical cutoff for pathological sleepiness, despite over a third of patients reporting daytime sleepiness.
T2-hyperintense lesions, mostly located in subcortical and periventricular white matter, were common brain MRI findings in this post-COVID-19 cohort, consistent with prior literature.

Central vein sign, a marker more specific to multiple sclerosis, was absent in the majority of post-COVID-19 patients with white matter lesions, and no paramagnetic rim or enhancing lesions were identified by either rater.
Post-infectious myelitis on spine MRI was a rare finding, occurring in only a small number of patients, consistent with transverse myelitis being an uncommon post-COVID-19 complication.
Pooled prevalence of persistent COVID-19 symptoms across 16 sub-Saharan African studies was 42.1%.
Hospitalized COVID-19 patients had a higher pooled prevalence of long COVID sequelae than the general population.
Studies with sample size greater than 400 reported higher pooled prevalence of long COVID sequelae than smaller studies.
South Africa exhibited the highest pooled prevalence of long COVID sequelae among sub-Saharan African countries, followed by Nigeria.
Fatigue was the most prevalent constitutional symptom of long COVID in sub-Saharan Africa.
Myalgia was the second most common constitutional symptom identified in the meta-analysis.
Brain fog was the most prevalent neurological sequela of long COVID in the pooled analysis.
Persistent loss of taste was identified as a common neurological sequela of long COVID.
Persistent loss of smell was identified as a common neurological sequela of long COVID.
Lack of concentration was the least prevalent neurological symptom of long COVID identified in the review.
Blurring of vision was reported as a neurological sequela of long COVID.
Headache was reported as a neurological sequela of long COVID.
Sleep disturbance was the most common psychiatric consequence of long COVID identified in ten studies.
Anxiety was the second most prevalent psychiatric issue among long COVID patients.
General pulmonary complications were the most common respiratory sequela of long COVID.
Shortness of breath was a common respiratory sequela of long COVID.
Cough was identified as a respiratory sequela associated with long COVID.
Chest pain was a common cardiovascular sequela of long COVID assessed across ten studies.
Palpitations were a common cardiovascular sequela of long COVID.
Joint pain was identified as a musculoskeletal sequela of long COVID pooled from eight studies across four countries.
Fever was reported as a persistent constitutional symptom of long COVID.
Loss of appetite was among the constitutional symptoms of long COVID reported in the pooled analysis.
Sore throat was identified as an ENT-related sequela of long COVID from four primary studies.
Presence of comorbidities (diabetes and hypertension) was significantly associated with increased risk of developing long COVID-19 sequelae.
Older age was not significantly associated with long COVID-19 sequelae in this pooled analysis, in contrast to some prior studies.
Long hospitalization was not significantly associated with long COVID-19 sequelae, contrasting with prior literature.

A higher proportion of participants from the earlier (2020-2021) COVID cohort reported at least one lingering symptom than those from the later (2021-2022) cohort, despite a longer average time since diagnosis in the earlier cohort.
In multivariate regression, female participants reported a significantly greater number of symptoms than males.
Female participants reported significantly higher symptom severity than males in multivariate analysis.
Female participants reported significantly greater symptom interference with daily activities than males in multivariate analysis.
Participants diagnosed with COVID-19 in outpatient settings reported significantly lower symptom severity and interference than those diagnosed in emergency departments.

After adjusting for demographic and clinical characteristics in multivariate regression, patient cohort (2020-2021 vs 2021-2022, corresponding to earlier vs later SARS-CoV-2 variants) had no independent effect on number, severity, or interference of symptoms.
Fatigue was the most commonly reported lingering symptom among symptomatic participants.
Difficulty remembering things was among the most commonly reported lingering symptoms.
Shortness of breath was among the most commonly reported lingering symptoms.
Joint/muscle pain was among the most commonly reported lingering symptoms and was also the most severe of the top symptoms.
A moderate proportion (43%) of participants remained symptomatic nearly a year after their COVID-19 diagnosis.
A cited study from Northern Spain found mild elevations of C-reactive protein and other biomarkers in patients with long COVID syndrome, suggesting underlying low-grade inflammation.
Omega-3 supplementation did not significantly improve shortness of breath at week 12 compared to placebo.
Omega-3 supplementation did not significantly improve cough at week 12 compared to placebo.
Omega-3 supplementation did not significantly improve fatigue at week 12 compared to placebo.
Omega-3 supplementation did not significantly improve lack of taste at week 12 compared to placebo, though the odds ratio approached significance.
Omega-3 supplementation did not significantly improve lack of smell at week 12 compared to placebo, though the odds ratio approached significance.
The blood omega-3 index rose more from baseline to week 12 in the omega-3 supplement group than in the placebo group.

The AA:EPA ratio, a marker of chronic inflammation, declined more markedly in the omega-3 supplement group than in the placebo group over 12 weeks, though this did not correlate with symptom improvement.
Adverse events were less frequent in the omega-3 supplement group (1/16) than in the placebo/soybean-oil group (5/16), with no serious adverse events in either arm.
The pilot trial demonstrated that omega-3 supplementation is feasible, safe, and well tolerated as a proof-of-concept intervention for long COVID symptoms in healthcare workers.
Recent research cited in this review found that circulating serotonin levels are inversely associated with the severity of post-COVID-19 syndrome.

The authors propose that serotonergic psychedelics, acting mainly via the 5-HT2A serotonin receptor, may alleviate PCS symptoms through effects on inflammation, neuroplasticity, gastrointestinal function, and endothelial dysfunction.

Post-COVID-19 syndrome (Long COVID) presents with debilitating symptoms including fatigue, disordered sleep, olfactory dysfunction, and cognitive issues ("brain fog"), and currently has no approved treatments.
Adolescents infected during the pre-Omicron phase reported a significantly higher mean number of persistent symptoms than those infected during the Omicron phase.
Adolescents with moderate or severe acute COVID-19 reported a significantly higher mean number of persistent symptoms than those with mild acute disease.
Fatigue was the most commonly reported persistent symptom among adolescents with long-COVID.
Dyspnea was the second most commonly reported persistent symptom among adolescents with long-COVID.
Fatigue was significantly more common among adolescents infected during the Omicron phase than those infected pre-Omicron.
Dyspnea showed a non-significant trend towards being more common in adolescents infected during the pre-Omicron phase compared to the Omicron phase.
Thoracic pain showed a non-significant trend towards being more common in adolescents infected during the pre-Omicron phase compared to the Omicron phase.
Fatigue was significantly more common among adolescents without comorbidities than those with comorbidities.
Thoracic pain was significantly more common among adolescents with previous comorbidities than those without.
Palpitations/tachycardia were significantly more common among adolescents with moderate or severe acute COVID-19 than those with mild disease.
Muscular pain showed a non-significant trend towards being more common among adolescents with more severe acute disease.
Fever showed a non-significant trend towards being more common among adolescents with more severe acute disease.

The overall persistent-symptom profile differed markedly between adolescents and 1297 contemporaneously enrolled adults, with headache, thoracic pain, diarrhea, and fever significantly more frequent in adolescents.

Memory loss, sleep disturbances, depressed mood, cough, anxiety, weight loss, paresthesias, and gait/equilibrium disturbances were significantly more common in adults than adolescents with long-COVID.

Two-step cluster analysis identified two adolescent long-COVID phenotype clusters: cluster 1 had a lower prevalence of Omicron-phase infection and a higher overall number of symptoms, with all dyspnea cases occurring only in this cluster.
At follow-up (mean 340 days from acute infection), 45.3% of adolescents still had persistent symptoms.
Among adolescents who remained symptomatic, the mean number of persistent symptoms significantly decreased between first evaluation and follow-up.
The proportion of adolescents becoming symptom-free at follow-up was inversely correlated with the number of symptoms reported at first evaluation.

In multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, phase and severity of acute disease, and comorbidities, only the number of symptoms at first evaluation was independently associated with symptom persistence at follow-up.

Nine adolescents (9.3%) were diagnosed with new conditions considered related to COVID-19, including pericarditis, low blood pressure, pancreatitis, sleep disturbances, a psychiatric cluster (anxiety, depression, psychosis, PTSD), polyneuropathy, fasciculations, and asthma, most of which resolved by follow-up.
One adolescent was newly diagnosed with low blood pressure (hypotension) considered related to COVID-19, which resolved by follow-up.
No cases of the most severe form of fatigue, chronic fatigue syndrome/myalgic encephalomyelitis, were diagnosed in this adolescent long-COVID cohort.

Fatigue prevalence decreased roughly three-fold over follow-up but remained the most common persistent symptom, at a final prevalence of about 20%, and was significantly more common among more recently (Omicron) infected adolescents.
At 6 months, the remotely delivered weight management intervention produced a significant improvement in the patient-selected dominant long COVID symptom score compared with wait-list control.
The treatment effect on the primary outcome was larger and highly significant at 3 months compared with 6 months.
Fatigue (Chalder Fatigue Scale) improved significantly more in the intervention group than in the control group at 6 months.
Breathlessness (MRC Dyspnoea Scale) improved significantly more in the intervention group than control at 6 months.
Pain (P4 Pain Rating Scale) did not significantly differ between intervention and control groups at 6 months, unlike other secondary symptoms.
Combined anxiety and depression scores (HADS) improved significantly more in the intervention group than control at 6 months.
The improvement in combined anxiety/depression scores was mostly driven by the depression subscale.
The HADS anxiety subscale showed no clear treatment effect at 6 months.
The physical fatigue subscale improved significantly with the intervention at 6 months.
The mental fatigue subscale improved significantly with the intervention at 6 months.
Self-nominated 'other' long COVID symptoms (rated on a 10-point VAS) improved significantly more with the intervention than control.
Health-related quality of life (EQ-5D VAS) improved significantly more in the intervention group at 6 months.
The EQ-5D health utility score did not differ significantly between groups at 6 months, although QALY gain calculated from it was significant.
QALY gain over the 6-month study period was significantly greater in the intervention group.
Hours of work missed per week due to health problems were not significantly different between groups at 6 months, though numerically favored the intervention.
The weight management intervention produced substantial mean weight loss (~10 kg / 10.3%) compared with minimal change in controls at 6 months.
Systolic blood pressure decreased significantly more in the intervention group than control at 6 months, coinciding with weight loss.
Diastolic blood pressure decreased significantly more in the intervention group than control at 6 months.
Serious adverse events were similarly distributed between groups with no deaths, indicating the intervention was safe.
Two serious adverse events (gallstone events) were judged related to the rapid weight loss intervention but were an expected, known risk.
There was no evidence that the treatment effect on the primary outcome differed by age, socioeconomic deprivation, baseline BMI, sex or the main symptom selected.
A post-hoc analysis found no evidence that the magnitude of weight loss mediated/interacted with the intervention's effect on the primary long COVID symptom outcome.
A large proportion of trial participants reported weight gain following their COVID-19 infection, with roughly a third changing NICE weight class category.

A sensitivity analysis restricted to participants with a confirmed positive COVID-19 test showed a similar but slightly attenuated and non-significant treatment effect on the primary outcome, reflecting reduced power.
Compared to healthy controls, PACS patients showed reduced gut microbial diversity and richness across multiple observational studies.
Bacteroides is consistently positively associated with PACS across multiple studies.
Flavonifractor is consistently positively associated with PACS across multiple studies.
Bifidobacterium is consistently negatively associated with PACS across multiple studies.
Dorea is consistently negatively associated with PACS across multiple studies.
Ruminococcus gnavus has consistently shown a positive association with PACS at the species level across studies.
Faecalibacterium prausnitzii has consistently shown a negative association with PACS at the species level across studies.
Opportunistic fungal pathogens including Candida were increased in patients with severe COVID-19, with emerging evidence of a link between gut candidiasis and PACS.

A meta-analysis of 41 studies including 860,783 subjects found that female sex, older age, higher BMI, smoking, comorbidities, and prior hospital or ICU stay were associated with increased risk of PACS.
Receiving two doses of COVID-19 vaccination was associated with a lowered risk of developing PACS compared to being unvaccinated.

FMT from PACS patients into germ-free mice caused lung inflammation without SARS-CoV-2 infection, worsened lung pathology following Klebsiella pneumoniae infection, and induced cognitive impairment, supporting a causal role of PACS-associated dysbiosis.
Probiotic supplementation of Bifidobacterium longum partially reversed coronavirus infection-induced memory impairment in a murine model.

In a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial of 463 PACS patients, 6 months of the synbiotic SIM01 significantly alleviated fatigue, memory loss, difficulty concentrating, gastrointestinal upset, and general unwellness compared to placebo.

SIM01 treatment increased bacterial diversity and richness, elevating Bifidobacterium species, Roseburia intestinalis, Roseburia hominis, Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, and Akkermansia muciniphila while reducing Ruminococcus gnavus and Klebsiella species, alongside enrichment of short-chain fatty acid production pathways.

Following SIM01 treatment, Bifidobacterium adolescentis abundance correlated with improvement in fatigue, GI upset, and memory loss; Bifidobacterium bifidum correlated with fatigue and general unwellness improvement; and Bifidobacterium longum correlated with concentration improvement.

A 14-day RCT of 200 post-COVID fatigue patients found that a Bacillus-based probiotic combined with systemic enzymes significantly improved fatigue resolution and Chalder Fatigue Scale scores versus placebo.

A pilot study of 6 PACS patients given 4 weeks of non-viable 'paraprobiotics' (30 species of Bifidobacterium, Lactobacillus, Streptococcus, and Saccharomyces) showed improvement in dysautonomia, fatigue, and depression scores, plus increased daily steps and better sleep quality.
Paraprobiotic treatment reduced expression of activation markers on several immune cells and reduced toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2) expression on T cells.

A case report of a PACS patient with GI symptoms found that high-fiber nutritional intervention NBT-NM108 was associated with alleviation of loss of appetite, nausea, and anxiety, along with increased short-chain fatty acid-producing bacteria.

A randomized placebo-controlled trial of 52 patients found no significant difference in post-COVID symptoms at 6 months between synbiotic and placebo groups, though the synbiotic prevented the acute-phase decline in microbial diversity seen in the placebo group.

A 28-day randomized placebo-controlled probiotic trial of 73 patients found no significant improvement in post-COVID symptoms at 3 months, though the intervention reduced duration and severity of acute COVID-19 symptoms.
A retrospective cohort study of 211 patients found that early antibiotic treatment during acute COVID-19 was associated with shorter time to symptom resolution.

In a murine coronavirus infection model, probiotic supplementation with Bifidobacterium longum partially reversed virus-induced memory impairment, suggesting neuroprotective potential of microbiome-based therapeutics.

A large randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (n=463) found that the synbiotic SIM01 (three Bifidobacterium species plus prebiotics) significantly alleviated fatigue, memory loss, difficulty concentrating, gastrointestinal upset, and general unwellness compared to placebo over 6 months.

SIM01 treatment increased relative abundance of Bifidobacterium species, Roseburia intestinalis, Roseburia hominis, Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, and Akkermansia muciniphila, while reducing Ruminococcus gnavus and Klebsiella species.
After SIM01 treatment, microbial pathways involved in short-chain fatty acid production, such as pyruvate fermentation to acetate and lactate (PWY-5100), were enriched.
Bifidobacterium adolescentis abundance was positively correlated with improvement in fatigue, gastrointestinal upset, and memory loss following SIM01 treatment.
Bifidobacterium bifidum abundance was positively correlated with improvement in fatigue and general unwellness following SIM01 treatment.
Bifidobacterium longum abundance was positively correlated with improvement in concentration following SIM01 treatment.
SIM01 was well tolerated in the phase 2 trial with no statistically significant difference in adverse event rates compared to placebo, and no adverse event was deemed related to treatment.

A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (n=200) of a probiotic (three Bacillus species) combined with systemic enzymes for 14 days significantly improved resolution of fatigue and total, physical, and mental Chalder Fatigue Scale scores in post-COVID fatigue patients, without adverse events.

A small pilot study (n=6) of a 4-week paraprobiotic mixture improved dysautonomia, fatigue, and depression scores, daily steps, and sleep quality, and reduced expression of activation markers on immune cells and TLR2 expression on T cells.

A case report of a PACS patient with gastrointestinal symptoms showed that a high-fiber nutritional intervention (NBT-NM108) was associated with alleviation of loss of appetite, nausea, and anxiety, alongside an increase in potential short-chain fatty acid producers in the gut.

A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (n=52) of a synbiotic formula (Bifidobacterium, Lactobacillus, prebiotics, quercetin, calcium butyrate) for 35 days found no significant difference in post-COVID symptoms at 6 months versus placebo, though it prevented the acute-phase decrease in microbial diversity seen in the placebo group.

A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (n=73) of a 28-day probiotic (Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus species) intervention showed no significant improvement in post-COVID symptoms at 3 months compared to placebo, although it was linked to reduced duration and severity of acute COVID-19 symptoms.
A retrospective cohort study (n=211) found that early antibiotic treatment during acute COVID-19 was associated with shorter duration to symptom resolution.
Another study (n=311) identified antibiotic treatment during acute COVID-19 as a risk factor for developing PACS.
Longitudinal gut microbiome analysis of COVID-19 patients (n=142) showed that antibiotic treatment was linked to an increased abundance of antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs).
Antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) were found to be significantly higher in PACS patients compared to healthy controls.

A non-randomized, open-label prospective interventional study (n=60) found that fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) was effective and safe in alleviating post-COVID insomnia and anxiety, improving sleep quality, and reducing daytime sleepiness, with significant improvements in ISI, PSQI, GAD-7, and ESS scores at 12 weeks versus untreated controls.

After FMT, metagenomic analyses showed increased Gemmiger formicilis, Coprococcus comes, and bacterial richness, alongside decreased microbial pathways producing menaquinol derivatives such as menaquinol-7 (vitamin K2).

A case report (n=11) of oral capsule FMT administration (4 days, 10 capsules daily) relieved post-COVID gastrointestinal symptoms, fatigue, mood disturbance, and sleep disturbance, with significantly enhanced Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance following FMT.

COVID-19 vaccination was shown to have protective effects against PACS across multiple studies, though these effects varied depending on vaccine type, and only prophylactic (not therapeutic) benefits have been demonstrated.
The patient developed isolated ACTH deficiency with very low baseline ACTH concentration after COVID-19 infection.
Baseline and ACTH-stimulated peak serum cortisol concentrations were decreased, consistent with adrenal insufficiency secondary to ACTH deficiency.
Intravenous and oral hydrocortisone treatment resolved the patient's symptoms and corrected hyponatremia, with no recurrence of adrenal insufficiency.
Pituitary MRI showed no structural abnormalities despite the presence of isolated ACTH deficiency.
Receptive vocabulary scores (PPVT-4) significantly increased from pre- to post-treatment with the SEQEX ELF-EMF device.
Expressive vocabulary scores (EOWPVT-4) significantly increased from pre- to post-treatment.
Parent-rated externalizing problem scores significantly decreased after ELF-EMF treatment in the 1.5–5 year age group.
Parent-rated overall Total Problems score significantly decreased after treatment in the 1.5–5 year age group.
Parent-rated internalizing problems did not significantly change after treatment in the younger age group.
Parent-rated attention problems significantly decreased after treatment in the younger age group.
Parent-rated aggressive behavior significantly decreased after treatment in the younger age group.

Parent-rated externalizing problems significantly decreased after treatment in the older age group.
Parent-rated anxious/depressed scores significantly decreased after treatment in the older age group.
Parent-rated social problems significantly decreased after treatment in the older age group.
Parent-rated attention problems significantly decreased after treatment in the older age group.
Parent-rated anxiety problem scores significantly decreased after treatment in the older age group.
Parent-rated ADHD-oriented problem scores significantly decreased after treatment in the older age group.
Teacher-rated ASD symptom scale scores significantly decreased after treatment in the younger age group, corroborating parent reports.
Teacher-rated thought problems scores significantly decreased after treatment in the older age group.
None of the teacher-rated DSM-5 oriented scales (depressive, anxiety, somatic, ADHD, oppositional defiant, conduct problems) showed statistically significant change in the older age group.
No participant experienced any adverse effects from the 15-week ELF-EMF total-body treatment protocol.
The authors cite prior literature indicating that 2 Hz ELF-EMF exposure reduces IL-1β and TNF-α, proposed as a mechanism by which the treatment could reduce CNS inflammation in ASD.

The authors cite an older animal study showing low-frequency magnetic field exposure increased dopamine and serotonin turnover in rat frontal cortex, proposed as a mechanism underlying observed behavioral effects.
Flat feet were significantly more common in children with ASD compared to healthy controls.
Flat feet were significantly more common in children with ADHD compared to healthy controls.
Flat feet were significantly more common in children with Tourette syndrome compared to healthy controls.
Tactile, visual, auditory, olfactory, or gustatory hypersensitivity was significantly more prevalent in children with ASD than controls.
Sensory hypersensitivity was significantly more prevalent in children with ADHD than controls.
Sensory hypersensitivity was significantly more prevalent in children with Tourette syndrome than controls.
Myopia or drooping eyelids (ptosis) were significantly more prevalent in children with ADHD than in the other groups and controls.
Use of orthodontic appliances showed a borderline non-significant trend toward being more frequent in children with Tourette syndrome.

In the familial analysis, myopia and ptosis were present in patients and were more frequently found in fathers than mothers, though no formal statistic was reported for this comparison.

Autistic adults without a diagnosed central sensitivity syndrome scored significantly higher on the CSI than the non-autistic, non-CSS comparison group, with the mean score well above the clinical cutoff.
CSI scores did not differ significantly between autistic and non-autistic adults who both had a diagnosed central sensitivity syndrome.
Non-autistic participants with a diagnosed central sensitivity syndrome scored significantly higher on autistic traits than the comparison group, though below the autism cutoff.
There was no significant difference in autistic trait scores between autistic people with and without a diagnosed CSS.

Autistic people with a diagnosed CSS reported greater sensory sensitivity than people with a CSS diagnosis alone.
Sensory sensitivity levels were comparable between autism-only and CSS-only groups.
Participants with a CSS-only diagnosis reported significantly higher depression scores than autism-only participants.
Depression scores were comparable between the dual autism-and-CSS group and the CSS-only group.
All three diagnostic groups (autism only, CSS only, autism+CSS) reported significantly more anxiety than the comparison group, with no significant differences between the clinical groups themselves.

Women scored significantly higher than men on the CSI across the whole sample.
Women scored significantly higher than men on depression across the whole sample.
Autistic traits (AQ score) significantly predicted CSS symptom severity, explaining an additional 19.4% of variance in CSI scores beyond age and gender.

Path analysis showed that gender predicted sensory sensitivity, anxiety, and CSS symptoms, and autistic traits predicted sensory sensitivity and anxiety, with all three (autistic traits, sensory sensitivity, anxiety) directly predicting CSI scores rather than being mediated as in the prior autism-only model.

On the AQ Imagination subdomain, the CSS-only group did not differ significantly from the comparison group, unlike the other AQ subdomains where CSS-only participants scored higher than the comparison group.
Among participants with a formally diagnosed central sensitivity syndrome, 93% scored at or above the CSI clinical cutoff of 40.
Among participants with a formal autism diagnosis, 86% scored at or above the AQ cutoff of 145 suggested to be specific for autism.
Two-thirds (67%) of the overall sample reported at least one formally diagnosed central sensitivity syndrome, with many participants having more than one CSS diagnosis.
Early studies in small cohorts of SARS-CoV-2-infected individuals reported ANA seroprevalence ranging from 34.5% to 54.5%.
Larger cohort studies estimated ANA prevalence at approximately 35.6%, 25%, and 57.5% in SARS-CoV-2-infected individuals.
Taeschler et al. observed a higher trend of ANA antibodies in individuals with severe COVID-19 compared to those with milder infections.
A longitudinal cohort study of 106 convalescent individuals identified ANA antibodies as a predictor of long-COVID.
A large study found an increased risk of receiving an autoimmune pathology diagnosis after COVID-19 among individuals with detectable ANA antibodies.
ANA antibodies are also found in 14-27% of healthy individuals without symptomatic presentations, limiting their specificity as a COVID-19 marker.

In a cohort of 987 individuals with severe COVID-19, 10.2% had detectable autoantibodies against type I interferon, which were absent in mild/asymptomatic cases and present in only 0.33% of healthy individuals.
Chang et al. used a multiplex protein array to identify autoantibodies targeting IL-1, IL-6, IL-10, IL-15, IL-17A, IL-22, IL-21, MIP-α, and VEGF-B in severe COVID-19.
Among several detected anti-cytokine antibodies, only anti-IL-12p70, anti-IL-22, and anti-IL-6 were found to be neutralizing.
Arthur et al. found anti-ACE2 antibodies in 93% of inpatients and 81% of convalescent controls, but in none of the healthy controls.
IgM antibodies to ACE2 were detected in 27.2% of individuals with severe COVID-19 versus 3.8% with mild disease, similar to the 4% control rate.
Anti-ACE2 antibodies detected in COVID-19 patients have not shown significant capacity to inhibit ACE2 enzymatic activity.
Immunization of mice with recombinant SARS-CoV-2 RBD induced anti-ACE2 autoantibodies, suggesting molecular mimicry between spike RBD and ACE2.
Chang et al. did not find elevated anti-ACE2 autoantibodies in hospitalized SARS-CoV-2 patients compared to other autoantibodies.
In a cohort of 464 individuals, anti-ACE2 IgG, IgA, and IgM autoantibodies were detected at 10.3%, 6.3%, and 18.8% respectively, with no association found with SARS-CoV-2 vaccination or infection.
Critically ill COVID-19 patients exhibited elevated levels of anti-phospholipid antibodies, including IgA against cardiolipin and IgG/IgA against β2-glycoprotein-1.
Trahtemberg et al. found that anti-phospholipid antibodies were associated with increased disease severity in patients with respiratory failure regardless of SARS-CoV-2 infection status.
Helms et al. identified anti-phospholipid antibodies in 87.7% of 57 SARS-CoV-2 patients with coagulation abnormalities.
IgG fractions containing anti-phospholipid antibodies from COVID-19 patients induced neutrophil extracellular trap release in healthy neutrophils and promoted venous thrombosis in mice.
Serrano et al. observed elevated anti-β2GP1 antibody levels in COVID-19 patients but found no association with thrombosis.
Xu et al. detected rheumatoid factors in 20% of a cohort of 129 individuals infected with COVID-19.
Multiple studies reported a variable rheumatoid factor seroprevalence among COVID-19 patients, ranging from 20% to 50%.
RF-positive COVID-19 patients had higher rates of death, ICU admission, and mechanical ventilation, suggesting a link between RF positivity and disease severity.
A study identified novel polyreactive rheumatoid factors in COVID-19, including one able to bind epitopes on both IgG and the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein.
Using human exoproteome display against thousands of putative self-antigens, Klein et al. found no significant differences in autoantibody levels or enrichment in individuals with long COVID.
High-throughput profiling in severe COVID-19 revealed a broad range of autoantibodies targeting lymphocyte function proteins, cytokines, complement factors, growth factors, and cell surface proteins.

Woodruff et al. showed severe COVID-19 is associated with expansion of antibody-secreting B cell populations with low somatic hypermutation, which contract upon recovery, indicating a transient reduction in selection pressure.

Seroconversion to Epstein-Barr virus was associated with a 32-fold increased risk of subsequently being diagnosed with multiple sclerosis, illustrating a virus-autoimmunity link cited as precedent for SARS-CoV-2.
Molecular mimicry between EBV nuclear antigen 1 (EBNA1) and the neural protein GlialCAM generates cross-reactive antibodies detectable in about 25% of multiple sclerosis patients.

Computational analyses identified linear hexapeptide epitopes shared between SARS-CoV-2 proteins and 460 human proteins, suggesting molecular mimicry hot-spots that could drive cross-reactive autoantibodies.
Immunization of mice with the SARS-CoV-2 receptor-binding domain generated antibodies capable of binding ACE2, suggesting cross-reactive epitopes consistent with molecular mimicry.

Severe COVID-19 is associated with expansion of antibody-secreting B cell populations bearing low somatic hypermutation, which contract upon recovery, indicating a transient loss of selection pressure that may permit autoreactive clone escape.

A similar expansion of low-somatic-hypermutation antibody-secreting B cells was seen in acute respiratory distress syndrome caused by bacterial pneumonia, suggesting this is a general physiological response to severe pulmonary infection rather than SARS-CoV-2-specific.

Data from Jaycox et al. suggest that increased autoantibody production seen in SARS-CoV-2 infection is not a feature of mRNA vaccination, implying severe infection itself, not the vaccine antigen, drives autoantibody induction.

A study stratifying participants by disease severity, including healthy controls, found increased prevalence of autoantibodies against cardiolipin, claudin, and platelet glycoproteins with escalating COVID-19 severity and advancing age.

Anti-cytokine autoantibodies were more prevalent in critically ill patients with non-SARS-CoV-2 respiratory infections compared to non-infected critically ill individuals, indicating autoantibody generation is a broader feature of critical illness, not COVID-specific.
Retrospective analysis of unvaccinated individuals reported a 42.6% higher likelihood of being diagnosed with an autoimmune disease following SARS-CoV-2 infection.

Autoantibodies targeting type I interferons associated with severe COVID-19 were shown by Bastard et al. to be present in individuals prior to infection rather than induced by it, indicating a pre-existing predisposition rather than de novo generation.
Using human exoproteome display autoantigen profiling, Klein et al. found no significant differences in autoantibody levels or specific enrichment in individuals with long COVID compared to controls.

Lebedin et al. demonstrated that some autoantibodies associated with COVID-19 are non-specific, polyreactive IgG that can interfere with accurate quantification of target-specific, functionally relevant autoantibodies.
In systemic lupus erythematosus patients, a reduction of anti-TNFα autoantibodies was linked with disease exacerbation, suggesting these autoantibodies can have a regulatory, disease-limiting role.

In lupus patients, autoantibodies against type I IFN correlated with lower IFN bioactivity and reduced downstream IFN pathway signaling, which in turn correlated with a lower disease activity score, again suggesting a regulatory autoantibody role.

Autoimmune-associated conditions such as myocarditis, arthritis, vasculitis, and encephalitis have been reported following SARS-CoV-2 infection, though no definitive mechanistic studies have linked these conditions to specific autoantibodies.
Despite anecdotal reports and small cohort studies identifying autoantibodies after SARS-CoV-2 vaccination, vaccination overall remains protective against the development of autoimmune diseases.

Although hypothesized that anti-spike antibodies could act as Ab1 generating anti-idiotype Ab2 antibodies capable of binding ACE2, no experimental evidence currently supports this mechanism in the context of SARS-CoV-2.
Overall cumulative symptom severity score significantly decreased at week 16 compared with week 6 and week 14 over the 16-week observation period.
Fatigue was the most frequently reported symptom throughout the 16-week study, followed by difficulty concentrating.
Cognitive function assessment scores significantly improved from baseline through week 16, with further improvement between week 4 and later time points.
Dyspnoea severity, measured via the MRC Dyspnoea Scale, remained unchanged across the 16-week study period.
FAS scores indicated severe fatigue at baseline that improved to a mild-to-moderate level over the study period, though scores fluctuated between time points.
Total MFIS fatigue impact scores significantly decreased from baseline through week 10, fluctuating thereafter across the 16 weeks.
The MFIS physical fatigue subscale significantly improved from baseline through week 16.
The MFIS cognitive fatigue subscale significantly improved from baseline to week 8, 10, 14 and 16.
The MFIS psychosocial fatigue subscale significantly improved from baseline to weeks 4, 8, 12 and 16.
The EQ-5D-5L utility index score did not significantly change across the 16-week study period despite a wide range of scores.
EQ-5D-5L visual analogue scale self-rated health scores significantly improved at week 16 compared with weeks 6, 10, and 14.
Post-COVID-19 Functional Status Scale scores significantly improved (lower limitation) from baseline to week 14 and week 16.
6-Minute Walk Test distance significantly improved from baseline to week 16, with further improvements between week 4/8 and week 16.
Timed Up and Go completion time significantly decreased (improved) from baseline through week 16.
Maximum inspiratory pressure (MIP) significantly improved from baseline to week 16, with no significant change at other time points.
Lung function measures FEV1, FEV1/FVC ratio, and FVC showed statistically significant overall change across the 16 weeks, but no individual pairwise time-point comparisons were significant.
Peak expiratory flow showed no significant change across the 16-week study period.

In a subset of 44 long COVID patients, individual minimum/maximum blood values (though group means were within normal range) showed some markers exceeding expected ranges, suggesting biochemical disturbance.
Long COVID symptoms and functional status followed an episodic, relapsing-remitting pattern with frequent fluctuations rather than a steady linear improvement over the 16-week study.
The majority (89%) of long COVID study participants had one or more comorbidities.
Individuals with post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC) had significantly lower flow-mediated dilation (a measure of endothelial function) than healthy individuals.

An 8-week combined exercise training program (aerobic, resistance, and inspiratory muscle training) significantly improved endothelial function in individuals with PASC compared to a non-exercising control group, reaching levels similar to healthy individuals.
Combined exercise training significantly increased peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak) in individuals with PASC.
Combined exercise training reduced dyspnea and fatigue in individuals with PASC compared to the control group.

An ACE2 polymorphism (p.Arg514Gly), identified in a genomic analysis of ~81,000 genomes, was more frequent in African/African-American populations and was linked to cardiovascular and pulmonary conditions.
A prevalent TMPRSS2 polymorphism (p.Val160Met) was associated with an increased risk of severe COVID-19, particularly in male patients and those with cancer.
In a Pakistani cohort of 300 patients, the ACE2 rs2285666 SNP was associated with increased susceptibility to SARS-CoV-2 infection, particularly in older males.
No significant association was found between TMPRSS2 SNPs and COVID-19 susceptibility in the same 300-patient Pakistani cohort.
In an Egyptian cohort of 317 patients, no significant link was found between the ACE2 rs2285666 polymorphism and COVID-19 severity.
In the Egyptian cohort, the TMPRSS2 rs12329760 T allele and CT/TT genotypes were associated with a lower risk of severe COVID-19, suggesting a protective role.
A review analyzing 33 studies found 10 SNPs and 21 mutations in ACE2, plus 13 SNPs and 12 variants in TMPRSS2, potentially linked to COVID-19 susceptibility and progression.

The CARGENCORS study identified 14 new SNVs linked to coronary artery disease, thrombosis, and inflammation that were significantly associated with severe COVID-19, with a meta-analysis using SCOURGE and UK Biobank cohorts confirming five key SNVs.
Pulmonary embolism was estimated to affect about 15% of COVID-19 patients.
A case study reported a link between death from pulmonary embolism and heterozygous mutations in the MTHFR and SERPINE1 genes in a COVID-19 patient.

In 25 Italian patients, the ACE D/D genotype was significantly more prevalent among those with pulmonary embolism (72%) than those without thromboembolic complications (46.5%), suggesting genetic susceptibility to thromboembolism potentially linked to higher ACE/angiotensin II levels.

In a cross-sectional study of 140 patients, severe COVID-19 cases had significantly higher frequencies of heterozygous mutations in F2, F5, and MTHFR, with FV R506Q carrying the highest risk for severe disease progression, and elevated D-dimer levels were more common in patients with FV R506Q, FV R2H1299R, or F2 G20210A mutations.
Pulmonary hypertension is estimated to occur in about 22% of COVID-19 patients.

Integration of protein-protein interaction and transcriptomic data identified RUNX1, HIF1A, JUN, STAT1, STAT3, and NFKB1 as shared molecular mechanisms/transcriptional regulators common to both COVID-19 and pulmonary arterial hypertension.

Bioinformatics and machine learning analyses identified SELE and CCL20 as key factors in immune/inflammatory responses shared between COVID-19 and pulmonary hypertension, linked to activation of dendritic cells and T cells.
Bioinformatics and machine learning analyses identified SELE as a key gene involved in immune and inflammatory responses shared between COVID-19 and pulmonary hypertension.
CCL20 was identified as a key gene involved in immune and inflammatory responses shared between COVID-19 and pulmonary hypertension, linked to dendritic cell and T cell activation.

A bioinformatics analysis of a GWAS dataset for COVID-19 respiratory failure identified eight genes (GATA4, ID2, MAFA, NOX4, PTBP1, SMAD3, TUBB1, WWOX) forming the largest connected network, associated with pulmonary and cardiac diseases including pulmonary hypertension.
Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) was estimated to occur in about 1.2% of COVID-19 patients according to a UK national surveillance study.

Factor V Leiden and prothrombin G20210A appear to contribute differently to CTEPH development compared to pulmonary embolism alone, with younger PE patients carrying Factor V Leiden potentially at reduced risk of developing CTEPH; this finding was not linked to SARS-CoV-2 infection.

A GWAS on CTEPH found a significant association with a SNP within the ABO blood group gene, confirming non-O blood types as a known risk factor for CTEPH development, though not linked to SARS-CoV-2 infection.

The same GWAS found significant genetic variants in fibrinogen and coagulation factor XI genes, crucial to the coagulation cascade, and genetic overlap between CTEPH and patients with pulmonary embolism or deep vein thrombosis, along with a novel SNP near HLA-DRA implicated in immune response.

A study identified ten key genes (IL-1B, CXCL8, CCL22, CCL5, CCL20, TNF, IL-12B, JUN, EP300, and CCL4) as highly relevant to CTEPH progression, linked to inflammatory responses, thrombus formation, and endothelial cell dysfunction, with NF-κB, AP-1, and TNF signaling pathways implicated.

The 4G4G genotype of the PAI-1 promoter 4G/5G polymorphism was associated with higher PAI-1 levels, suppressed fibrinolysis, and increased NFκB activation, contributing to endothelial dysfunction in COVID-19 patients.
The 5G5G genotype of the PAI-1 promoter polymorphism posed risk due to inflammation-induced overactivation of the fibrinolytic system, contributing to endothelial dysfunction in COVID-19 patients.

The ACE2 rs2285666 variant can increase ACE2 expression, enhancing viral entry, inflammation, and imbalance in the renin-angiotensin system favoring elevated angiotensin II, contributing to endothelial dysfunction, vascular remodeling, and pulmonary hypertension.

The TMPRSS2 rs12329760 polymorphism can alter protease activity, either facilitating viral activation or modifying immune responses, potentially intensifying endothelial damage and thrombotic risk driving pulmonary vascular complications.

Inflammatory gene polymorphisms such as IL6 -174G>C and TNF -308G>A can lead to excessive or prolonged cytokine production during COVID-19 infection, driving a cytokine storm that increases vascular permeability and endothelial injury, contributing to pulmonary endothelialitis and chronic vascular inflammation.

Polymorphisms in coagulation-related genes F5 (R506Q) and F2 (G20210A) can increase susceptibility to thromboembolic events, synergizing with the hyperinflammatory state of COVID-19 to drive excessive clot formation in pulmonary vessels, leading to pulmonary thromboembolism.

The IL6 -174G>C polymorphism is associated with elevated pro-inflammatory cytokine levels, contributing to asthma severity and prolonged inflammation in long COVID, illustrating a shared genetic link between asthma and long COVID.
Variants in ADRB2, such as Gln27Glu and Arg16Gly, are linked to airway hyperresponsiveness in asthma and may exacerbate respiratory symptoms in long COVID due to altered smooth muscle function.
HLA-DRB1*04 alleles, which play a role in immune regulation, have been implicated in both asthma and severe COVID-19 through dysregulated immune responses.

One study reported a protective effect of genetic predisposition to asthma on COVID-19, finding individuals genetically predisposed to asthma may have a lower risk of contracting SARS-CoV-2 and experiencing severe outcomes, potentially due to a compensatory immune mechanism, contradicting other findings of asthma worsening COVID-19 severity.

A bioinformatics study investigating shared pathways in COPD and COVID-19 comorbidity identified critical genes CCL2, MMP9, IL1A, and HIF1A playing pivotal roles in immune responses, angiogenesis, and inflammation, with cytokine-cytokine receptor interactions, chemokine activity, and IL-17 signaling central to progression of both diseases.

Dexamethasone, estradiol, progesterone, and nitric oxide were highlighted as potential therapeutic agents for COVID-19/COPD comorbidity, supported by their ability to modulate key inflammatory and angiogenic processes.
Individuals with obesity may experience heightened ACE2 expression in adipose tissue, further facilitating SARS-CoV-2 viral entry and potentially promoting severe pulmonary vascular symptoms.
PASC subjects showed a larger difference in wave V latency between slow and fast ABR click rates than controls, suggesting diminished nerve conduction efficiency.
PASC subjects had smaller wave I amplitude than controls in the grand mean waveform and at the fast click rate, potentially reflecting age differences between groups.
Across the entire cohort, the V/I amplitude ratio, a measure of central auditory gain, did not differ significantly between PASC and control subjects.
When stratified by age, younger PASC subjects (18-45 years) showed heightened V/I amplitude ratios (central auditory gain) compared to younger controls, a pattern not seen in the older subgroup.
Younger PASC subjects had significantly smaller wave I amplitude than younger controls, suggesting possible subclinical cochlear or auditory nerve dysfunction.
In the younger subgroup, wave III latency and the I-V interpeak interval were significantly shorter (earlier) in PASC subjects than in age-matched controls.
Older PASC subjects and older controls did not differ on any ABR peak or interpeak measure.

In mixed-effects models, the wave V slow-fast latency difference significantly predicted PASC group membership and subjective cognitive fatigue on both the Chalder Fatigue Scale and Neurobehavioral Symptom Inventory.
Frequent tinnitus perception significantly predicted higher cognitive fatigue scores on both the CFQ and NSI, but did not significantly predict PASC group membership itself.

In the younger subgroup, higher ABR V/I amplitude ratio significantly predicted PASC group membership and Chalder Fatigue Scale scores, but not NSI cognitive scores; no such association was found in the older subgroup.

PASC subjects were significantly more likely than controls to report frequent (more than once a week) tinnitus, with this effect especially pronounced in the younger subgroup; no controls reported constant tinnitus versus 30% of PASC subjects.
PASC subjects reported greater subjective hearing handicap (AIAH) than controls overall and in the older subgroup, but not in the younger subgroup, despite matched peripheral hearing thresholds.
PASC subjects had significantly higher levels of depression, anxiety, and negative affect than controls, both overall and within each age subgroup.
Among younger PASC subjects, those with higher perceived tinnitus had smaller wave V amplitude.
Age was a significant predictor of reduced wave I amplitude across the entire cohort and within the older subgroup, consistent with age-related presbycusis independent of PASC status.
Subjective cognitive fatigue (Chalder Fatigue Scale) and subjective cognitive functioning (NSI-cog) were significantly higher in the PASC group compared to controls.
Somatosensory complaints (NSI-ss subscale) were significantly higher in the PASC group compared to controls.

The authors propose, based on prior literature, that decreased GABA (the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter in the central auditory system) reported in PASC could be a mechanistic driver of the heightened central auditory gain observed, though GABA was not directly measured in this study.
Corneal nerve branch density (CNBD), measured by in vivo corneal confocal microscopy, was lower in PASC-SFN patients than in healthy controls across all three studies that assessed it.
Corneal dendritic cell density (DCD) was higher in PASC-SFN patients with neurological symptoms compared to controls in two of the studies using corneal confocal microscopy.
Bandinelli et al. found a reduction in the peripapillary retinal nerve fiber layer on optical coherence tomography in half of PASC-SFN patients.
Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) was reported as a comorbid dysautonomia manifestation in nearly 30% of PASC-SFN patients across studies.
In tilt testing, PASC-SFN patients showed a higher heart rate response with lower end-tidal CO2, and cerebral Doppler testing showed lower cerebral blood flow compared to healthy controls.
Cognitive and memory impairment ('brain fog') was reported in 3 of 14 studies, with prevalence ranging from 32.5% to 100% of PASC-SFN patients.
CRP was more elevated in PASC-SFN patients than in post-COVID painful patients without SFN, and a separate study confirmed increased CRP in patients with moderate-to-severe SFN.
In McAlpine et al.'s cohort of ten PASC-SFN patients, three were positive for TS-HDS IgM antibodies and three were positive for FGFR3 IgG antibodies.
Bandinelli et al. found a mildly higher prevalence of antinuclear antibodies (ANA) in PASC-SFN patients compared to PASC patients without SFN (87.5% vs. 50%).
Anti-spike protein and anti-SARS-CoV-2 antibody levels did not differ between PASC-SFN patients and PASC patients without SFN.
Using quantitative sensory testing (TSA-2 QST), Azcue et al. found that the ability to detect heat was lower in PASC patients than in healthy controls.

EMG in PASC-SFN patients showed motor unit action potential abnormalities characterized by short duration, small amplitude, and polyphasic morphology, without spontaneous fibrillation or positive sharp waves.
Falco et al. reported that the severity and duration of acute COVID-19 disease were independent of subsequent PASC-SFN manifestations.
In 8 of 14 studies examining evolution, PASC-SFN symptoms were persistent over time and did not appear to be self-limiting.

On histological follow-up at about six months, IENF/mm remained stable in PASC-SFN patients regardless of symptom change, whereas patients initially negative on skin biopsy but with persistent symptoms showed a progressive decrease in IENF/mm on repeat biopsy.
IVIG treatment led to a higher percentage of improvement or resolution of symptoms after six months in PASC-SFN patients, but with possible relapse after treatment was weaned.
Duloxetine, pregabalin, and gabapentin showed controversial results in PASC-SFN patients and seemed more effective in PASC patients with normal skin biopsies (Abrams et al.).

Bandinelli et al. demonstrated efficacy of a long-term combination therapy of vitamin B6, B12, D3, folate, homotaurine, phosphatidylserine, and alpha lipoic acid for PASC-SFN, particularly for brain fog symptoms.
Steroid therapy, commonly used in acute SFN, carries a high risk of symptom recurrence after withdrawal, as shown in the Panagiotides case report.
Immunomodulators and immunosuppressive drugs, including hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine, methotrexate, and mycophenolate, have been used in PASC-SFN with controversial results.
Arthritis and arthralgia were reported as accompanying manifestations in 4 of 14 studies, with evolution into established arthritis described in one study.
'Visual fog' and ocular discomfort were frequent accompanying symptoms in PASC-SFN patients, reported in 4 of 14 studies, including visual impairment, dry eye, and eye pain/redness/burning.
Patients with PASC-related cognitive impairment had significantly lower DTI-ALPS index in the left hemisphere compared with healthy controls, indicating glymphatic dysfunction.
In contrast to the left hemisphere, the right hemisphere DTI-ALPS index in PASC patients remained within normal limits and did not differ significantly from controls.
Within PASC patients, there was a significant asymmetry in DTI-ALPS index between the left and right hemispheres.
There was no statistically significant change in the left hemisphere DTI-ALPS index between the 3-month and 12-month timepoints within PASC patients.
Central white matter K trans (a marker of blood-brain barrier permeability) was positively correlated with DTI-ALPS on the side of abnormal ALPS.
Whole-brain mean K trans scores did not correlate with DTI-ALPS scores.
Dx diffusivity values in projection fibers were mildly decreased in PASC patients compared with controls, contributing to the reduced DTI-ALPS index, with a trend toward significance.
Prior research by the authors indicated that BBB disruption and white matter integrity changes in PASC/long COVID patients are likely triggered by glutamatergic excitotoxicity.

Glutamatergic excitotoxicity is known to impair aquaporin-4 water channels, resulting in impaired CSF influx and disrupted CSF-interstitial fluid turnover, mechanistically linking BBB and glymphatic dysfunction in PASC.
Participants' subjective feasibility/acceptance ratings of the VNS device improved (numerically decreased, indicating improvement) from a score of 3 at 4 weeks to 2 at 12 weeks on a 1–5 scale.

The 10 Hz stimulation group showed the greatest improvement in subjective treatment ratings, decreasing by 0.5 points, compared to smaller change in the 25 Hz group and a worsening in the 2 Hz control group.
72% of participants found VNS to be subjectively effective, 14% considered it ineffective, and 14% were unsure.
Heart rate variability (SDNN) remained stable across the 12-week VNS intervention, with baseline and 12-week values both at 59 ms.
Median RMSSD decreased only slightly from 38 ms at baseline to 37 ms at 12 weeks, suggesting minimal change in parasympathetic modulation.
Mean heart rate pressure product increased slightly from baseline to 12 weeks but remained within normal reference limits throughout.
Resting pulse rate remained within normal limits, averaging 75 bpm at baseline and 77 bpm at 12 weeks.
Morning salivary cortisol remained within the normal reference range throughout the study, with a slight increase from baseline to 12 weeks.
Post-COVID-19 functional status improved during the 12-week VNS intervention, with median scores decreasing from 3 to 2.
Dyspnea severity decreased from a median score of 3 at baseline to 2 after 12 weeks of VNS.
Fatigue levels measured by the Brief Fatigue Inventory decreased from a mean of 5.5 at baseline to 4.5 after 12 weeks of VNS.
Sleep quality improved during VNS treatment, with ISI scores decreasing from a mean of 13.7 at baseline to 11.1 at 12 weeks.
Physical health-related quality of life (SF-36 physical component summary) improved from 32 to 36 points over the 12-week VNS treatment period.
Mental health-related quality of life (SF-36 mental component summary) improved from 40 to 45 points over the 12-week VNS treatment period.

No serious adverse events or suspected unexpected serious adverse reactions occurred; mild adverse events (tinnitus, insomnia, ear pain, itching, headache, restless legs, tingling) were reported in 27-42% of participants across groups.
Among 609 male Japanese patients hospitalized with COVID-19, 116 (19.0%) reported erectile dysfunction symptoms at the one-year, two-year, or both post-infection surveys.
Most patients who developed ED did so early after infection: 79 (68.1%) within 28 days of COVID-19 infection and 6 (4.3%) at 2-5 months post-infection.
Of the 116 patients with ED, 29 (25.0%) showed improvement of symptoms by the two-year survey, while 57 (49.1%) showed no apparent improvement.

No significant associations were found between ED and traditional organic risk factors (age, smoking, diabetes, hypertension, BMI, ICU admission, oxygen administration) in cross-sectional comparisons between ED+ and ED- patients.
At the two-year survey, patients with ED were significantly older than those without ED (median 61 vs 55 years), whereas no significant age difference was seen at the one-year survey.
Patients with ED reported significantly lower self-rated awareness of recovery than those without ED at both the one-year and two-year surveys.
Patients with ED had significantly higher (worse) self-rated breathlessness scores than those without ED at both surveys.
Patients with ED had significantly higher (worse) fatigue scores than those without ED at both one-year and two-year surveys.
Patients with ED reported significantly lower overall wellness (0-100 scale) than those without ED at both one-year and two-year surveys.
At the one-year survey, patients with ED had significantly higher HADS-Anxiety scores than those without ED.
At the two-year survey, there was no significant difference in HADS-Anxiety scores between patients with and without ED.
Patients with ED had significantly higher HADS-Depression scores than those without ED at both one-year and two-year surveys.

The EQ-5D-5L usual-activities domain score was significantly worse (higher) in patients with ED than without ED at the one-year survey; a significant difference was also reported at the two-year survey.
At the two-year survey, patients with ED reported significantly higher pain/discomfort scores than those without ED.
EQ-5D-5L anxiety/depression scores were significantly worse in patients with ED than without ED at both the one-year and two-year surveys.
In hierarchical cluster analysis of the one-year survey, erectile dysfunction clustered together with sleep disorder, hair loss, skin rash, and eye symptoms among the post-acute symptoms.
In hierarchical cluster analysis of the two-year survey, erectile dysfunction clustered with sore throat, rhinorrhea, cough, arthralgia, myalgia, hair loss, and skin rash.
Patients with ED reported a high overall burden of concurrent post-acute symptoms: a median of 9 other symptoms at the one-year survey and 4 other symptoms at the two-year survey.
Vaccination prior to infection and early antiviral treatment for COVID-19 showed no significant association with, and no apparent protective effect against, developing erectile dysfunction.

None of the patients who developed ED as a post-acute COVID-19 symptom reported seeking medical evaluation or receiving any treatment (rehabilitation, psychological counseling, or pharmaceutical treatment) for it.
In patients with long COVID/PCC treated with hochuekkito, mean fatigue assessment scale (FAS) scores decreased from baseline to 8 weeks, indicating improvement in general fatigue.
Secondary endpoint FAS scores at 1, 2, and 4 weeks did not show a consistent monotonic improvement trend relative to baseline, unlike the significant decrease seen at 8 weeks.
In cited animal studies, hochuekkito enhanced locomotor activity in normal mice and in a mouse model of chronic-fatigue-syndrome-like behavior induced by Brucella abortus antigen injection.
Ginsenoside, a main constituent of Ginseng contained in hochuekkito, has been reported to have anti-fatigue, anti-stress, and tonic effects and is used to improve qi deficiency.
Astragalus Root, an ingredient of hochuekkito, has been reported to improve fatigue and malaise.
General fatigue was reported as the most common symptom of long COVID/PCC, with incidence estimates ranging from 58% to 64%.
Several study patients had experienced long COVID/PCC symptoms for more than one year, suggesting a chronic course resembling myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome.
Expectation of the amount of energy needed for the next 3 hours predicted subsequent physical activity, fatigue, and recalled demandingness of that period.
Currently feeling positive predicted slightly more subsequent physical activity and less fatigue 3 hours later.
Feeling negative was not predictive of subsequent physical activity or fatigue.
Feeling negative predicted subsequent recall of the period as emotionally demanding.
Feeling more anxious predicted greater fatigue 3 hours later.
Feeling more anxious was not predictive of reduced subsequent physical activity.
A one-point increase in anticipated energy demand for the next 3 hours (on a 1-7 scale) was associated with an additional 2.2 minutes of moderate or vigorous physical activity in that period.
A one standard deviation increase in momentary anxiety was associated with a one-point increase in fatigue (on a 0-100 scale) three hours later.
Overall, expectation and affect had little detectable effect on subsequent physical activity or fatigue in the day-to-day experience of people with Long Covid.
People with inflammatory arthritis and long COVID reported significantly worse (higher) modified Health Assessment Questionnaire disability scores than those without long COVID.
RAPID-3 self-reported disease activity scores were significantly higher (worse) in inflammatory arthritis patients with long COVID than in those without.
SF-12 physical health scores were significantly lower (worse) in those with long COVID compared to those without.
SF-12 mental health scores were significantly lower (worse) in those with long COVID compared to those without.
Fatigue, measured by the Fatigue Symptom Inventory, was significantly worse in individuals with long COVID compared to those without.
Pain, measured by the short form McGill Pain Questionnaire, was significantly worse in individuals with long COVID compared to those without.
Among those with long COVID, the most commonly reported persistent symptoms were fatigue, altered smell/taste, difficulty breathing, and headache.
This randomized controlled trial is designed to evaluate whether repetitive anodal transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) improves cognitive fatigue in patients with long COVID.
Among healthcare workers with a history of SARS-CoV-2 infection, 64.1% reported having experienced long COVID.
Extreme fatigue was the most commonly reported long COVID symptom after persistent cough, affecting 57.0% of participants.
Cognitive dysfunction (brain fog, memory/concentration problems) was reported by 42.6% of participants with long COVID.
Shortness of breath was reported by 27.4% of participants with long COVID.
Persistent cough was the most commonly reported symptom, affecting 60.6% of participants with long COVID.
In univariate analysis, long COVID showed a marginal association with lower life satisfaction (SWLS) scores.
In the multivariate model, long COVID was significantly associated with lower life satisfaction (SWLS) scores, indicating a negative impact on quality of life.
Having a Master's or PhD degree was significantly associated with higher SWLS (life satisfaction) scores in univariate analysis, but this did not remain significant after multivariate adjustment.
Clinical secretaries had significantly lower SWLS (life satisfaction) scores than medical doctors, and this association remained significant after multivariate adjustment.
Nurses showed a non-significant trend towards lower SWLS scores than medical doctors in univariate analysis.
Having two or more chronic diseases was associated with lower SWLS (life satisfaction) scores in univariate analysis, but this did not remain significant in the multivariate model.
Non-hospital healthcare facility workers did not differ significantly from hospital-based workers in life satisfaction (SWLS) scores.
In univariate analysis, long COVID was significantly associated with decreased workplace performance among healthcare workers.
Older age was associated with lower workplace performance in univariate analysis, but this association did not persist after multivariate adjustment.
Female sex showed a borderline univariate association with lower workplace performance, which was not significant after multivariate adjustment.
Having a Master's or PhD degree was positively associated with workplace performance in univariate analysis, but not significant after multivariate adjustment.
Nurses showed significantly lower workplace performance than medical doctors in univariate analysis, but the association did not persist after multivariate adjustment.
Clinical secretaries showed significantly lower workplace performance than medical doctors in univariate analysis, but the association did not persist after multivariate adjustment.
Having two or more chronic diseases was significantly associated with lower workplace performance in univariate analysis, with a trend persisting after multivariate adjustment.
Extreme fatigue was strongly and significantly associated with decreased workplace performance in both univariate and multivariate analyses.
Cognitive dysfunction was strongly and significantly associated with decreased workplace performance in both univariate and multivariate analyses.
Shortness of breath was significantly associated with decreased workplace performance in univariate analysis, but this association was not significant after multivariate adjustment.
There was no significant difference in the frequency of external incentives between the Pass, Intermediate, and Fail performance validity test groups.
Patients in the performance validity test Fail group reported slightly greater somatization symptoms on the PAI SOM-S subscale than those in the Pass group.
Modified Fatigue Impact Scale scores did not significantly differ between the Pass, Intermediate, and Fail performance validity test groups in Long COVID patients.
Among 175 Long COVID patients undergoing neuropsychological evaluation, 84.57% passed all performance validity tests, 9.14% failed one, and 6.29% failed two or more.
Pulmonary rehabilitation significantly improved 6-minute walking test distance compared to controls in long COVID-19 patients across 14 RCTs.
Pulmonary rehabilitation significantly improved 30-second sit-to-stand test performance compared to controls.
Pulmonary rehabilitation significantly improved handgrip strength compared to controls.
Pulmonary rehabilitation improved FEV1 (both absolute and % predicted) compared to controls, and this finding reached sufficient statistical strength on trial sequential analysis.
Pulmonary rehabilitation improved FVC compared to controls, but the trial sequential analysis did not confirm sufficiency of evidence for this outcome.
Pulmonary rehabilitation improved maximal inspiratory pressure compared to controls, with trial sequential analysis confirming sufficient evidence.
Pulmonary rehabilitation improved maximal expiratory pressure compared to controls, but trial sequential analysis did not confirm sufficiency of evidence.
Pulmonary rehabilitation reduced dyspnea scores compared to controls in long COVID-19 patients.
Pulmonary rehabilitation improved health-related quality of life in both physical and mental health dimensions compared to controls.
Pulmonary rehabilitation reduced fatigue scores compared to controls in long COVID-19 patients.
Pulmonary rehabilitation reduced anxiety scores compared to controls in long COVID-19 patients.
Pulmonary rehabilitation showed no significant effect on depression scores compared to controls.
Pulmonary rehabilitation decreased perceived exertion as measured by the modified Borg Scale compared to controls.
PR programs lasting ≤4 weeks improved 6MWT distance (larger magnitude than longer programs) but did not significantly improve FEV1, FVC (%pred), HRQoL, or fatigue.
PR programs lasting 4-8 weeks significantly improved 6MWT, FEV1, FVC, HRQoL, and fatigue.
PR programs lasting more than 8 weeks led to further improvements in HRQoL and fatigue but not additional gains in 6MWT, FEV1, or FVC.
Breathing exercises improved 6MWT, lung function (FEV1, FVC), and HRQoL but had no effect on fatigue.
Multicomponent exercises enhanced 6MWT performance and reduced fatigue but did not impact lung function or HRQoL.
The combination of breathing and multicomponent exercises improved 6MWT, FEV1, FVC (%pred), HRQoL, and reduced fatigue, showing the broadest benefit of any exercise type.

Pulmonary rehabilitation was generally safe, with most RCTs reporting no adverse events, while a minority reported minor issues such as oxygen desaturation, and adverse events including disability, hospitalization, or reinfection occurred more often in control groups.
Fatigue was the most commonly reported neuropsychiatric long COVID symptom among included Reddit posts, present in 47.3% of posts.
Cognitive impairment was reported in 46.4% of included Reddit posts describing long COVID symptoms.
Depression was reported in 30.0% of included Reddit posts describing long COVID symptoms.
The majority of posters (78.2%) reported some improvement in long COVID neuropsychiatric symptoms after psilocybin use.
A minority of posters (11.8%) reported worsening of long COVID symptoms after psilocybin use.
Among those reporting improvement, 77.9% described symptom improvement persisting beyond the acute psilocybin experience.
A small subset (5.8%) of posters with improvement reported the effect only during the acute psilocybin experience, without lasting benefit.
32.4% of the 173 primary-care patients (n=56) reported at least one persistent COVID symptom lasting ≥8 weeks at some point during the two-year follow-up.
