At the 2-year data collection point, 23.1% of patients still had at least one long COVID symptom, with arthralgia, anosmia and asthenia each present in ≥15%.
Among symptomatic patients, asthenia (fatigue) was the most common persistent symptom (about half), followed by anosmia in more than a third, then dysgeusia, dyspnea and arthralgia.
Women reported persistent COVID symptoms more often than men (36.7% vs 26.3%), but this difference did not reach statistical significance.
Anosmia and dysgeusia were the longest-lasting persistent symptoms (4-5 months), followed by dyspnea, arthralgia and concentration problems (about 3 months).
Multivariate logistic regression found that symptomatic (vs asymptomatic) primary infection significantly increased the likelihood of developing persistent COVID symptoms.
Younger age was significantly associated with a higher probability of persistent COVID symptoms in multivariate logistic regression.
Reinfection with SARS-CoV-2 was significantly associated with a higher probability of persistent COVID symptoms.
Among the 56 symptomatic patients, 78.3% had two or more persistent symptoms, with a mean of 3.37 symptoms per patient.
The mean number of persistent symptoms was higher in women than men, but the difference was not statistically significant.
Multivariate linear regression showed that patients with depression had significantly more persistent COVID symptoms.
Overall self-perceived health-related quality of life measured with EuroQol-5D was high, with mean score 83.25 and median 90 out of 100.
Patients without long COVID reported no pain/discomfort more often than those with long COVID (85.5% vs 71.4%), and had an EQ-VAS score nearly 9 points higher (86.15 vs 77.72).
Patients with long COVID reported significantly higher rates of severe anxiety/depression than those without (12.5% vs 4.2%).
There was no significant sex difference in overall EQ-VAS quality-of-life score (83.35 in men vs 83.18 in women).

In multivariate linear regression for EQ-VAS score, being female was associated with at least 5.75 points higher score, older age and more vaccine doses were associated with higher scores, while more comorbidities were associated with a lower score.
A greater number of comorbidities was associated with a lower EQ-VAS quality-of-life score in multivariate regression.
Odds of exhibiting long-COVID symptoms increased with the severity/number of previous COVID-19 infections.
Hypertension as a co-morbidity was associated with increased odds of exhibiting long-COVID symptoms.
Vaccination against COVID-19 decreased the likelihood of developing long-COVID.
Long-COVID sufferers exhibited higher IL-6 signalling activity than healthy control individuals.
The rs2228145 genotype of the IL-6R gene was not associated with long-COVID odds-ratios across the entire study cohort.
In the summer sub-cohort, the rs2228145 AA genotype was significantly over-represented among individuals reporting long-COVID symptoms.
In the summer sub-cohort, individuals carrying the CC or AC genotypes of rs2228145 had significantly reduced odds of long-COVID compared to other genotypes.
In the winter sub-cohort, no significant association was found between rs2228145 genotype and long-COVID symptoms, in contrast to the summer sub-cohort.
The authors propose that circulating IL-6 levels and/or rs2228145 genotype could serve as future biomarkers predictive of long-COVID risk.
Across a 6-country collaborative study (4 in Europe, 2 in North America), the incidence of Long COVID ranged from 46% in Mexico to 17% in Ukraine, with an average incidence of 25%.
Fatigue was the most frequently reported Long COVID symptom overall across the 6-country cohort, occurring in 47% of cases.
Hair loss was the second most frequent Long COVID symptom overall, reported in 39.2% of cases across the 6 countries.
Myalgia was the third most frequent Long COVID symptom overall, reported in 35% of cases across the 6 countries.
Despite common symptoms overall, no two of the six countries shared the same top-3 clinical signs/symptoms, indicating substantial international variability in Long COVID presentation.
The authors propose that Long COVID is a multi-organ inflammatory chronic condition partly attributable to retention of the virus or viral particles in several organs.
SLE patients had a significantly higher incidence of long COVID than matched healthy controls after SARS-CoV2 infection.
Worsening of memory as a long COVID symptom was significantly more common in SLE patients than in controls.
Chest pain as a long COVID symptom was significantly more common in SLE patients than in controls.
Palpitation as a long COVID symptom was significantly more common in SLE patients than in controls.
Arthralgia as a long COVID symptom was significantly more common in SLE patients than in controls.
Among SLE patients, ever use of hydroxychloroquine was the only factor significantly associated with occurrence of long COVID.
The most frequently reported long COVID symptoms across all participants were fatigue, worsening of memory, difficulty concentrating, cough and insomnia.
Less than 2% of participants with a history of Long COVID reported resolution, with a mean duration of illness exceeding 2 years before resolution.
Participants with current Long COVID had significantly worse PROMIS-29 physical health scores than those who never had Long COVID.
Participants with current Long COVID had significantly worse PROMIS-29 mental health scores than those who never had Long COVID.
Current Long COVID was associated with higher odds of moderate-to-high perceived stress compared with never having Long COVID.
Current Long COVID was associated with higher odds of moderate-to-high loneliness compared with never having Long COVID.
Current Long COVID was associated with substantially higher odds of moderate-to-severe fatigue compared with never having Long COVID.
Current Long COVID was associated with worse nutrition and physical activity scores compared with never having Long COVID.
Current Long COVID was associated with modestly worse exercise vital sign scores compared with never having Long COVID.
Current Long COVID was strongly associated with worse dyspnea scores compared with never having Long COVID.
Participants with resolved Long COVID had significantly worse physical health scores than those who never had Long COVID, despite resolution of symptoms.
Participants with resolved Long COVID had significantly worse mental health scores than those who never had Long COVID, despite resolution of symptoms.
Resolved Long COVID was associated with slightly better nutrition and physical activity scores compared to never having Long COVID, unlike other outcomes which showed no significant difference.

Prolonged Long COVID (>12 months) versus short Long COVID (≤12 months) showed no significant difference across most outcomes, except a slightly better PROMIS physical health score in the prolonged group.
Vaccination prior to Long COVID onset was associated with better PROMIS physical and mental health scores among participants with current Long COVID.
Across all participants, receiving more total COVID-19 vaccine doses was associated with progressively better scores on multiple physical and mental health PROMs.
Among participants with current Long COVID, symptom trajectories varied, with nearly half reporting waxing-and-waning symptoms and only about a quarter reporting improvement.

Alterations in gut bacteria including Ruminococcus gnavus, Bacteroides vulgatus, Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, and Veillonella have been associated with long COVID symptoms such as respiratory dysfunction, fatigue, and chest tightness.
Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Intestinimonas butyriciproducens were identified as protective gut microbiota against long COVID symptoms.
Long COVID patients show reduced bacterial diversity and lower levels of SCFA-producing bacteria even one year after infection.
Ethnic minorities in Denmark, particularly individuals of Iraqi, Turkish, and Somali origin, had significantly higher risk of COVID-19 infection compared to the native Danish population.
US Household Pulse Survey data showed long COVID was more prevalent among females, Black individuals, and Hispanics compared to males, non-Hispanic individuals, and Whites.

A 12-state US study found Black individuals had the highest levels of virus-associated hospitalizations, while Hispanic, Alaska Native, and Native American populations also showed high hospitalization prevalence.
The anti-inflammatory Christensenellaceae bacterial family has shown a protective role in long COVID, with Dutch populations exhibiting the highest levels.
A US student study found Black students had higher rates of toxin-producing, pro-inflammatory Bacteroides, while White students had higher levels of anti-inflammatory Faecalibacterium and Roseburia.
In mice, ACE2 knockout increases certain gut microbiota levels, while ACE2 overexpression increases anti-inflammatory probiotics and SCFA-producing microbiota.

SARS-CoV-2 binding downregulates ACE2 expression, disrupting the renin-angiotensin system and gut microbiota homeostasis, contributing to chronic cough, shortness of breath, and chest pain in long COVID.
Patients with cardiovascular disease and hypertension demonstrate increased ACE2 expression, heightening susceptibility to COVID-19 infection and worsening cardiovascular complications.
Individuals with HIV show decreased CD8+ T cells and increased PD-1+ expression (a marker of immune exhaustion), leading to compromised immune responses and heightened inflammation.
TLR5-deficient mice show increased periosteal bone formation, suggesting a link between TLR5 signaling, the microbiome, and bone remodeling relevant to musculoskeletal pain in long COVID.
IL-6, IL-10, TNF-α, and IFN-γ were identified as predictive cytokines for musculoskeletal pain in the knees, shoulders, and cervical spine among long COVID patients.
Higher levels of Adlercreutzia bacteria were associated with increased inflammation and greater likelihood of developing lower back pain, particularly in individuals with higher BMI.
Pathogenic microbiota including Pseudomonas veronii, Pseudomonas stutzeri, and Streptococcus anginosus have been linked to intervertebral disk degeneration.
Patients with acute kidney disease associated with long COVID face a threefold increase in mortality risk.
Patients with pre-existing chronic kidney disease and long COVID experienced a median reduction in glomerular filtration rate of 2.96 mL/min/1.73 m2.
A GFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 correlates with higher hospital mortality rates in long COVID patients.
COVID-induced kidney injury impairs tryptophan reabsorption, and resulting tryptophan deficiency via the kynurenine pathway is linked to brain fog, fatigue, and muscle weakness in long COVID.
Elevated lipopolysaccharide-binding protein, a marker of gut microbiota dysfunction, is closely associated with respiratory failure in COVID-19 patients.

TLR5 signaling activated by gut microbiota modulates the osteoclast-osteoblast balance, and TLR5-deficient mice show increased periosteal bone formation, suggesting a mechanistic link between dysbiosis and musculoskeletal pain in long COVID.
Higher levels of Adlercreutzia bacteria were associated with increased inflammation and a greater likelihood of developing lower back pain, particularly in individuals with higher BMI.

Pathogenic microbiota including Pseudomonas veronii, Pseudomonas stutzeri, and Streptococcus anginosus have been linked to intervertebral disk degeneration, potentially contributing to chronic musculoskeletal pain in long COVID.
IL-6, IL-10, TNF-alpha, and IFN-gamma were identified as predictive cytokines for musculoskeletal pain in the knees, shoulders, and cervical spine in long COVID patients.

COVID-19-associated downregulation of ACE2 increases vulnerability to viral entry in brain regions lacking the blood-brain barrier and compromises blood-brain barrier integrity in protected regions, contributing to neurological effects.

In long COVID, gut dysbiosis may reduce butyrate production, weakening gut barrier integrity and contributing to systemic inflammation that impacts brain function and neurocognitive symptoms such as brain fog.
Human and mouse model studies show a high prevalence of acute kidney disease associated with long COVID, and patients with AKD face a threefold increase in mortality risk.
Patients with pre-existing chronic kidney disease and long COVID experienced reductions in glomerular filtration rate, with a median decrease of 2.96 mL/min/1.73 m2 in virus-infected patients.

Dysregulation of gut microbiota in long COVID patients is linked to accumulation of uremic toxins such as indoxyl sulfate, p-cresyl sulfate, and trimethylamine N-oxide, contributing to chronic inflammation and endothelial dysfunction.

COVID-induced kidney injury impairs proximal tubular cell reabsorption of tryptophan, which is crucial for the tryptophan-kynurenine pathway and melatonin/serotonin production, potentially contributing to brain fog, fatigue, and muscle weakness.
Lipopolysaccharide-binding protein, a marker of gut microbiota dysfunction, has been closely associated with respiratory failure in COVID-19 patients.
80% of patients with severe COVID-19 experienced some level of cardiac symptoms, and 25% reported persistent symptoms three months post-diagnosis.

A systematic review found that COVID-19-infected patients with pre-existing cardiovascular disease had significantly higher risks of long COVID, with hypertension and heart failure serving as the strongest predictors.

SCFAs act on endothelial cells to prevent VCAM-1 and IL-6/IL-8 pro-inflammatory expression, reducing inflammation and cell adhesion to prevent atherosclerosis, and also decrease triglyceride, cholesterol, and LDL while increasing HDL.

The gut microbial metabolite TMAO, derived from microbial metabolism of dietary choline, L-carnitine, and betaine, is implicated in cardiovascular disease through inhibition of cholesterol metabolism, arterial plaque formation, platelet aggregation, and thrombosis, with Clostridiales bacteria instrumental in its production.

COVID-19 infections can exacerbate gut dysbiosis by decreasing anti-inflammatory Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and increasing pathogenic Clostridium ramosum and Clostridium hathewayi; higher F. prausnitzii levels are associated with reduced coronary heart disease and ischemic stroke and decreased plasma LPS levels.

A 12-country study found that patients more likely to be hospitalized with COVID-19 exhibited lower levels of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and higher levels of pro-inflammatory bacteria, exacerbating cardiovascular issues.
A study of 2,871 adult subjects from 16 countries identified a significant association between low levels of butyrate-producing bacteria and COVID-19 mortality.
Chinese herbal medicine showed a small, non-significant reduction in dyspnea severity on the Borg Dyspnea Scale compared to control, with the confidence interval crossing the null.
Chinese herbal medicine significantly reduced fatigue on the Borg Scale compared to control, though certainty of evidence was low.
Chinese herbal medicine produced a clinically meaningful reduction in depression scores on the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale compared to control, with moderate certainty.
Chinese herbal medicine produced a clinically meaningful reduction in anxiety scores on the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale compared to control, with moderate certainty.
Chinese herbal medicine showed a numerical reduction in insomnia severity compared to control, but the confidence interval crossed zero indicating no significant treatment effect.
Meta-analysis of two RCTs suggested CHM may improve exercise intolerance as measured by 6-minute walking distance, but with substantial heterogeneity and low certainty of evidence.
The overall safety of Chinese herbal medicine for treating long COVID symptoms remains uncertain based on the included trials.
In the primary intention-to-treat analysis, the Listen intervention showed a borderline, non-significant improvement in routine daily activities compared with usual care at three months.
In a per-protocol analysis restricted to participants attending at least three sessions, the improvement in routine activities reached nominal statistical significance.
Participants receiving the Listen intervention showed a statistically significant improvement in emotional wellbeing compared with usual care at three months.
The Listen intervention was associated with significant improvement in the mental health component of the SF-12 compared with usual care.
The Listen intervention significantly reduced fatigue impact compared with usual care at three months.
Self-efficacy to manage daily struggles was significantly increased in participants receiving the Listen intervention compared with usual care.
There was no significant between-group difference in social engagement or physical health component of the SF-12 following the Listen intervention.
After adjusting for baseline score, age, gender, ethnic group, employment status, and number of long covid symptoms, the improvement in routine activities became statistically significant.
Adjusted secondary analyses (model B) confirmed significant improvements with the Listen intervention across emotional wellbeing, fatigue, self-efficacy, and mental health domains.
After full covariate adjustment, no significant between-group differences remained for social engagement or physical health.
In a responder analysis, a higher but non-significant proportion of intervention participants achieved a clinically important improvement in routine activities compared with usual care.
Adherence to the Listen intervention was high, with most participants attending the minimum required sessions.
Adverse events, including serious adverse events, were rare and none were judged related to the Listen intervention.
Participants rated the Listen intervention as acceptable, feasible, and appropriate.
Trial participants reported a substantial symptom burden, with most having tested positive for covid-19 and experiencing a median of 12 long covid symptoms across 10 organ systems.
Sensitivity analysis using multiple imputation for missing data produced effect estimates similar to the main analysis, suggesting missing data did not bias the results.

The Listen intervention's theoretical model proposes self-efficacy, symptom control and stability, and knowledge as key mechanisms mediating improved everyday functioning and emotional wellbeing in long covid.

Exercise (strength and aerobic training) produced significantly larger improvements in the physical domain of health-related quality of life than a WHO self-management leaflet control, but not the mental health domain.
A second Jimeno-Almazán trial replicated the significant improvement in the physical domain of HRQoL with exercise relative to control.
Li et al reported significant improvement in HRQoL treatment effect after pulmonary telerehabilitation, sustained at 28-week follow-up.
Okan et al reported a non-significant improvement in HRQoL (St George's Respiratory Questionnaire) in the exercise group relative to control.
Exercise produced significantly larger improvements in fatigue (multiple fatigue scales) relative to control.
A greater proportion of exercise participants than controls no longer met fatigue caseness criteria after intervention.
Rodriguez-Blanco et al reported significantly greater fatigue improvement in the exercise group compared with control.
Two Jimeno-Almazán trials found no between-group differences in change in dyspnoea with exercise versus control.
Li et al found significantly greater improvements in dyspnoea with pulmonary rehabilitation versus no-treatment control at baseline-to-postintervention but not at interim weeks or 28-week follow-up.
Okan et al reported significantly larger pretest-to-post-test improvement in dyspnoea in the walking/breathing exercise group than control.
Rodriguez-Blanco et al reported significantly larger pretest-to-post-test improvement in dyspnoea with telerehabilitation exercise than control.
Exercise significantly improved functional limitations (Post-COVID-19 Functional Status) relative to control in two related trials.
6-minute walk-test distance improved with exercise relative to control groups in both studies that assessed it.
Pulmonary function (spirometry) and VO2 max did not consistently improve following exercise relative to control across studies.
Measures of muscular strength and endurance generally improved with exercise across included studies.
No significant between-group differences in anxiety and depressive symptom change (HADS) with exercise versus control.
A significantly greater proportion of exercise participants no longer met depressive symptom threshold (PHQ-9) versus control, but no difference in anxiety.
No significant between-group differences were found in change of ME/CFS-type symptoms following exercise versus control.
Concurrent (strength+aerobic) training significantly reduced total long COVID symptom count compared with respiratory muscle training only and control.
Strength and aerobic training produced significant improvements in all dyspnoea measures (Multidimensional Dyspnoea Profile) relative to standard physiotherapy.
Strength and aerobic training improved the SF-12 physical dimension of HRQoL relative to standard physiotherapy, but not the total score or mental dimension.

No significant differences were found between in-person and virtual-reality-delivered pulmonary rehabilitation in pulmonary function, walk distance, breathlessness, fatigue after walk-test, or stress.
Inpatient pulmonary rehabilitation produced greater improvement than home-based rehabilitation in some fatigue outcomes, but not in dyspnoea, exercise capacity, or other fatigue subscales.

Exercise interventions were generally well tolerated, with no serious adverse events reported in four of five studies reporting adverse events, and mostly mild adverse events (chest tightness, weakness, cough) in the fifth.
Discontinuation of exercise intervention due to tolerance-related issues was rare, occurring in 1 of 252 participants across seven studies with adequate reporting.

A total of 40 PCPs submitted 47 eConsults through Champlain eConsult BASE and 197 PCPs submitted 228 cases through Ontario eConsult to the long COVID specialist group, representing a small proportion of each service's overall case volume.
Specialists responded to long COVID eConsults with a median turnaround of 0.6 days, demonstrating rapid access to specialist advice.
Specialists spent an average of 27.5 minutes of billed time responding to each long COVID eConsult.
Among 47 Champlain eConsult BASE cases, fatigue was the most frequently reported presenting symptom, followed by dyspnea, cough, altered sense of smell (anosmia/parosmia), and cognitive changes.
The most common clinical question categories posed by PCPs to the long COVID eConsult group concerned management of chronic COVID-19 symptoms and the need for additional work-up or follow-up testing.
eConsult confirmed the PCP's initially contemplated course of action in about a third of cases and provided new or additional management advice in nearly two-thirds of cases.

Use of the long COVID eConsult service was associated with avoidance of a previously contemplated face-to-face specialist referral in over a third of cases, while an actual referral remained necessary in fewer cases.
A GWAS of 6,450 long COVID cases and over a million controls identified the FOXP4 SNP rs9367106 as associated with increased risk of long COVID and increased FOXP4 expression in lung tissue.
SNPs in NR1H2 (liver X receptor beta) and SLC6A20 (amino acid transporter facilitating viral entry) were associated with neurological complications in acute and long COVID.
COVID-19 patients had a 92% increased risk of experiencing first-time insomnia compared to influenza patients.
The risk of any nerve, nerve root, or plexus disorder is increased by 64% in COVID-19 patients compared to influenza patients.
The risk for any mood, anxiety, or psychotic disorder is 46% higher in COVID-19 patients versus influenza, and 73% higher in patients with encephalopathy.
A 12-month longitudinal study of 171 COVID-19 survivors without prior mental health history found a 24.6% prevalence of PTSD with 24% co-occurring self-reported impaired cognition.

In a retrospective study of 236,379 COVID-19 survivors, 13.66% were diagnosed with a mood disorder (4.22% first-time), with hospitalized patients showing 21%/53% increased risk (any/first-time) and ICU patients showing 15%/106% increased risk.
Patients with encephalopathy had a 73% increased risk of any mood, anxiety, or psychotic disorder and a 228% increased risk of a first-time diagnosis of these disorders.
In a cohort of 134 patients examined at a median of 113 days post-infection, 47.8% experienced anxiety and 39.6% reported low mood, both significantly elevated.
An observational study of 1,142 COVID-19 patients at approximately seven months post-infection reported 16.2% self-rated anxiety symptoms and 19.7% depressive symptoms.
FDG-PET imaging shows hypometabolic patterns in nearly half of long COVID patients, localized to olfactory gyrus, right amygdala, hippocampus, right thalamus, brainstem, and cerebellum.
PET scans reveal increased microglial activity in the brainstem with increased uptake of radioligands targeting microglial activation in long COVID patients.

MRI abnormalities including white matter hyperintensities, frontal/parietal lesions, and microhemorrhages persisting up to one year were found in up to 71% of long COVID patients symptomatic at four months.
A three-month follow-up MRI study found increased gray matter volumes in olfactory cortices, hippocampi, and cingulate gyri in COVID patients, potentially related to loss of smell.

COVID-19 patients had lower individual alpha frequency and greater cortical current source density in bilateral frontal and central-temporal regions than uninfected individuals, plus higher linear lagged connectivity across regions.

Transcranial Doppler with breath-holding test in a cross-sectional study of 49 COVID-19 patients with mild neurological symptoms 300 days post-acute phase showed statistically significantly reduced cerebrovascular reactivity compared to controls.
Transcranial sonography found 28.6% of a 70-patient long COVID cohort had hypoechogenic brainstem raphe, which was associated with higher depression and anxiety scores.
Autoimmune markers including anti-SSA/Ro antibodies and antinuclear antibodies are heightened in severe COVID-19 cases, supporting an autoimmune hypothesis for LC neurological sequelae.
Comprehensive immune profiling revealed elevated antibody responses against herpesvirus antigens, notably EBV, in long COVID patients, suggesting a role for latent viral reactivation.

A systematic review pooled cumulative incidence estimates of herpesvirus reactivation among long COVID patients: 38% herpes simplex virus, 19% cytomegalovirus, 45% Epstein-Barr virus, and 44% human herpesvirus 7.

Mast cells colocalize with IL-1 and TNF-alpha and may degranulate during COVID-19 cytokine storm, suggesting a link between mast cell activation and the multisystem inflammatory response in long COVID.
High levels of VEGFA have been reported in long COVID, potentially linked to a positive feedback loop between neuroinflammation, vascular permeability, and chronic inflammation.
LC brain fog correlates with increased expression of GFAP, TGF-beta, and IL-8, markers of inflammation and BBB dysfunction, alongside disruption of the BBB in temporal lobes.
Serum S100beta, an astrocytic protein, is elevated in infected individuals with acute cognitive impairment, indicating a disrupted BBB.
A brain autopsy study of COVID-19 fatalities found significant findings regarding MMP-9, which degrades collagen IV, an essential basement membrane component, implicating BBB breakdown.

A two-hospital cohort study in China found significantly altered gut microbiome composition in COVID patients versus non-COVID patients, with depletion of Bacteroidaceae, Lachnospiraceae, and Ruminococcaceae and enrichment of opportunistic pathogens like Enterococcus, Staphylococcus, Serratia, and Collinsella, correlating with inflammatory marker levels.

Fecal transplant from long COVID patients into germ-free mice caused compromised lung immune responses, increased susceptibility to K. pneumoniae infection, and dysbiosis-induced memory impairment resembling long COVID, providing causal evidence linking gut dysbiosis to LC symptoms.

A GWAS of 6,450 long COVID cases and 1,093,995 controls across 24 studies in 16 countries found the FOXP4 SNP rs9367106 associated with higher risk of developing long COVID, increasing FOXP4 expression in lung tissue independent of acute severity.
GWAS SNP analysis found NR1H2 (liver X receptor beta) and SLC6A20 gene variants associated with neurological complications in acute and long COVID cases.
Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (Paxlovid), effective for acute COVID-19, did not decrease the incidence of long COVID when given to vaccinated adults.
The antihistamine famotidine has shown efficacy in reducing a wide range of long COVID symptoms, supporting the role of histamine in symptom severity.

Modafinil has shown promise for improving fatigue and cognitive function in conditions like multiple sclerosis and narcolepsy, with reviews suggesting potential benefit for long COVID brain fog and central hypersomnia.

Early anticoagulation with aspirin has been shown to protect vascular endothelium, reduce thrombotic sequelae, and significantly reduce 28-day in-hospital mortality in COVID-19, though evidence for long COVID prophylaxis specifically is mixed.

Long COVID is characterized by fibrinolysis-resistant microclots up to 200 um in diameter formed via interaction of spike protein, fibrinogen, serum amyloid A, and envelope protein, sufficient to contribute to neuronal injury.

NINDS RECOVER study data show only four symptoms previously considered unique to ME/CFS (motor disturbances, tinnitus/double vision, lymph node pain, sensitivity to chemicals/foods/medications/odors) are now also reported in long COVID patients, suggesting a shared post-viral pathophysiology.
The risk for any nerve, nerve root, or plexus disorder is increased by 64% in COVID-19 patients compared to those with influenza.

Hospitalized long COVID patients have a 128% increased risk of developing dementia, rising to 66% additional increased risk within 6 months for ICU patients, and 325% increased risk for patients with encephalopathy.
Hospitalized long COVID patients had a 65% increased risk of ischemic stroke and 263% increased risk of Parkinsonism; ICU patients had 193% and 390% increased risk, respectively.
Long COVID, defined per WHO criteria using ISARIC symptoms, was present in 77.7% of ICU survivors of severe COVID-19 one year after discharge.
One year after ICU discharge, 20.5% of survivors had physical impairments (modified MRC score ≥ Grade 2) and 42.7% overall had some functional impairment.
Mental disorders (anxiety, depression, or PTSD) were present in 35.0% of ICU survivors one year after infection.
Loneliness, as measured by the Three-item Loneliness Scale, affected 21.8% of survivors at one year.
Quality of life at the time of survey, measured by EQ-5D-5L, averaged 0.831, indicating reduced quality of life relative to full health.
Patients who required ventilatory management during ICU admission had a significantly higher prevalence of long COVID than those who did not.

There was no difference in the prevalence of physical impairments or mental disorders between the ventilatory and non-ventilatory management groups, though loneliness was higher and QOL lower in the ventilated group.
Persistent fatigue/malaise was an independent risk factor for physical impairment at one year, more than quadrupling the odds after adjustment.
Persistent cough was an independent risk factor for physical impairment at one year.
Persistent dyspnea was an independent risk factor for physical impairment at one year.
Persistent chest pain showed the strongest association with physical impairment at one year among long COVID symptoms, though with a wide confidence interval.
Persistent palpitations were an independent risk factor for physical impairment at one year.
Persistent myalgia was an independent risk factor for physical impairment at one year.
Persistent muscle weakness was an independent risk factor for physical impairment at one year.
Persistent sleep disorder was an independent risk factor for physical impairment at one year.
Persistent decreased concentration was an independent risk factor for physical impairment at one year.
Persistent dizziness was strongly associated with physical impairment at one year.
Persistent fatigue/malaise was an independent risk factor for mental disorders at one year.
Persistent sore throat was an independent risk factor for mental disorders at one year.
Persistent cough was an independent risk factor for mental disorders at one year.
Persistent palpitations were an independent risk factor for mental disorders at one year.
Persistent myalgia was an independent risk factor for mental disorders at one year.
Persistent muscle weakness was an independent risk factor for mental disorders at one year.
Persistent sleep disorder was an independent risk factor for mental disorders at one year.
Persistent decreased concentration was strongly associated with mental disorders at one year.
Persistent brain fog was an independent risk factor for mental disorders at one year.
Persistent dizziness was an independent risk factor for mental disorders at one year.

Physical impairments were more prevalent among patients with obesity, higher SOFA scores, prolonged mechanical ventilation, continuous neuromuscular blockade, ECMO use, tracheostomy, and lower educational attainment.
A history of smoking was associated with a higher prevalence of mental disorders among ICU survivors.
Just over half of children referred to a long COVID clinic for long-term post-infectious symptoms were seropositive for SARS-CoV-2 receptor-binding domain antibodies.
Pre-existing somatic disease (present in 42.5% of the whole cohort) was significantly more common among seronegative than seropositive children with suspected long COVID.
Asthma was the most common pre-existing somatic disease, present in 19.5% of the cohort.
Neuropsychiatric or psychiatric disorder prevalence (23.9% overall) did not differ significantly between seronegative (18.5%) and seropositive (28.8%) children.
Among children with a neuropsychiatric/psychiatric diagnosis, ADHD was most common (10 patients), followed by anxiety disorder (7) and autism spectrum disorder (5).
The proportion of children with ADHD or autism spectrum disorder in this long COVID cohort (13.3%) was higher than that reported for the general child population in Stockholm 2015-2020 (6.3%).
Self-reported health-related quality of life (EQ-5D-Y VAS) was low overall (mean 51.1) but did not differ significantly by SARS-CoV-2 antibody status in linear regression.
Children with SARS-CoV-2 antibodies had significantly lower odds of school absence compared with seronegative children with suspected long COVID.
Children with SARS-CoV-2 antibodies had significantly lower odds of complete interruption of leisure activities compared with seronegative children.
Children with SARS-CoV-2 antibodies reported significantly fewer long-term symptoms than seronegative children, confirmed by multivariable regression.
Almost all children referred to the clinic (94.7%) reported more than one long-term symptom, with a median of 10 symptoms per child.
Fatigue was the most common reported symptom and its prevalence did not differ by antibody status.
Boys were more likely than girls to report diarrhoea as a long-term symptom, the only gender difference found in symptom presentation.
Heart palpitations were common (47%) but did not differ between antibody-positive and antibody-negative children.
Seronegative children more frequently reported sore throat, chest pain, intermittent fever and rash than seropositive children.
More than half of the children, regardless of antibody status, reported post-exertional malaise, a hallmark symptom also seen in ME/CFS.
Standard inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR, albumin, ferritin) were consistently normal across the cohort.
IDO2 was upregulated in PBMCs of long COVID patients and associated with mitochondrial dysfunction, reduced oxygen consumption rates, and reduced Krebs cycle metabolites and amino acids.
Taenzer et al. reported a lower kynurenine/tryptophan ratio, with decreased kynurenine, tryptophan, phenylalanine, and tyrosine, in LC patients with fatigue.

López-Hernández's study found 53 and 27 metabolites dysregulated in LC compared to acute COVID-19 and healthy controls respectively, with lactic acid, lactate/pyruvate, ornithine/citrulline, and arginine distinguishing LC, indicating mitochondrial dysfunction and redox imbalance 2 years post-infection.
Elevated plasma IL-17 levels were observed in long COVID patients 2 years post-infection, indicating ongoing immune activation, and correlated with pre-existing hypertension.

CXCL10 was significantly upregulated in LC patients relative to COVID-19 convalescents and healthy controls, corroborated by an independent study also reporting elevated blood CXCL10 reflecting sustained interferon-induced inflammation.

Gene expression changes in muscle biopsies of LC patients indicated matrix remodeling, angiogenesis, and immune dysregulation linked to type I/III interferons and the complement system, alongside decreased mitochondrial activity and energy production capacity, with no sex-related influence found on principal component analysis; serum complement protein levels were also increased in LC.

Clustering of 162 differentially regulated proteins in LC revealed clusters related to viral infections (SARS-CoV-2, Epstein-Barr) and immune responses (NK cell cytotoxicity, Fc epsilon R1 signaling), plus affected mitochondrial dysfunction pathways; LC and ME/CFS showed similar protein profiles including B2M, BCL2, CD4, and HLA-DRB1.

Genomic analysis linked LC fatigue risk to SNPs in ATP9A, CLOCK, SLC15A14, INSR, and GPC5, more abundant in LC than in ME/CFS, involving metabolic/JNK signaling, insulin, and circadian rhythm regulation.

Longitudinal blood transcriptomics in COVID-19 convalescents by Ryan et al. found downregulation of genes related to platelet factor 4, platelet glycoprotein IX, thrombopoietin receptor, and coagulation in platelet-related pathways at 6 months post-COVID in those who developed long COVID.
Clostridium innocuum and Actinomyces naeslundii in fecal samples collected 6 months post-COVID were significantly associated with fatigue and neuropsychiatric symptoms in long COVID.

Plasma miR-9-5p and miR-486-5p were linked to impaired lung diffusion capacity (<80%) in LC and involved in inflammation, angiogenesis, tissue repair, and cell senescence pathways, with associated target genes upregulated (PXDN, ITGA2, MXRA7, TMEM200A, RNF187, FAT1) and downregulated (NELL2, RAI14, SLC24A2, PPP1R9A, CHRM3).

Airway proteomics in LC patients with persistent radiological abnormalities 3-6 months post-discharge showed abnormal presence of CASP3, EPCAM, KRT19, and TGFA, indicative of epithelial injury and apoptosis, which were absent in healthy controls; increased cytotoxic lymphocytes were associated with epithelial damage and impaired lung function.
Genetic association analysis identified SNPs in FURIN and SLC6A20 linked to neurological symptoms in long COVID.

Taylor et al. identified 73 genes related to severe long COVID and fatigue-dominant cohorts (5 shared: D2HGDH, GUCY1A2, PCSK2, CCDC146, PGPEP1); combinatorial analytics highlighted 42 genes as potential therapeutic targets (13 already drug-linked), and TLR4 was proposed for drug repurposing.
Greene et al. found significantly increased concentrations of S100β, a marker of blood-brain barrier dysfunction, in acute COVID-19 patients, positively associated with age.

Transcriptomics of LC patients with brain fog showed upregulated genes related to T-cell activation, angiogenesis (HIF1A, HES1, DLL1) and TGF-signaling (SMAD3, SNAI1, SMURF1), and downregulated genes involved in platelet activation and hemostasis, compared to recovered individuals.

Saito et al. reported an inverse correlation between reduced plasma sarcosine and LC symptoms including cognitive dysfunction and depression scores, while lower serine levels were inversely associated with anxiety and depression in LC patients with ME/CFS.

Gut microbiome analysis of LC patients with persistent GI symptoms at 3 months post-COVID showed decreased alpha and beta diversity, with reduced Proteobacteria, Fusobacteria, Spirochaetes, Actinobacteria, and Uroviricota, plus ectopic colonization of the oral cavity by gut microbes (27 differentially abundant Proteobacteria genera) linked to potentially harmful serum metabolites.

At 3 months post-infection, recovered (non-LC) individuals showed increased Prevotella abundance compared to LC patients, potentially revealing a protective effect, while butyrate-producing bacteria (Roseburia, Faecalibacterium prausnitzii) increased and lower alpha diversity during acute infection was related to subsequent LC.

At 3 months post-COVID, gene expression analysis revealed upregulation of proteoglycan synthesis, extracellular matrix alteration, and viral mRNA replication pathways related to vascular smooth muscle cell dysfunction and vascular fibrosis in LC, with Rho-kinase inhibitors proposed as a potential therapeutic option.

Cervia-Hasler et al. found increased complement activation during acute infection persisting into LC, with elevated von Willebrand factor at 6 months indicating endothelial activation and red blood cell lysis, and increased monocyte-platelet aggregates and platelet activation markers at 6 months in patients whose LC symptoms persisted at 12 months, indicating a pro-thrombotic environment.

Proteomic analysis of fibrin amyloid microclots in LC patients found elevated von Willebrand factor and increased platelet factor 4 activation, while plasma kallikrein levels were reduced compared to healthy controls, with antibodies detected within the microclots suggesting a possible autoimmune response.

In LC patients with or without POTS, proteomic analysis showed similar dysregulation affecting coagulation/hemostasis, immune response, angiogenesis, and metabolism, with SERPINE linked to increased clotting susceptibility and CCL5 associated with hyper-inflammation and T-cell involvement, suggesting a shared pathophysiological profile.

Microbiome analyses revealed significant gut flora differences between POTS and LC patients compared to controls, including variations in microbial diversity and specific taxa, with LC associated with altered abundance of the phyla Ascomycota and Firmicutes compared with controls.

Multi-omics analysis found increased soluble C5bC6 complement complexes and decreased C7-containing terminal complement complexes in LC serum, alongside thrombo-inflammation; single-cell transcriptomics of monocytes showed decreased NR4A1 and increased interferon-induced transcripts including IFITM3.

Wang et al. identified increased plasma levels of microbiota-derived metabolites trimethylamine and phenylacetylglutamine associated with cardiovascular disease in LC, alongside altered acute phase proteins, platelet degranulation, and TCA cycle/glucose metabolism dysregulation across proteomic and metabolomic layers.

Unsupervised clustering of omics profiles identified three distinct LC disease phenotypes, with cluster B characterized by a triglyceride/organic acid signature, and cluster C (with a higher proportion of women) associated with molecules enriched in the HIF-1α pathway, indicating gender-specific differences.

Elevated plasma IL-17 levels in long COVID patients two years post-infection were correlated with pre-existing hypertension, suggesting interaction between chronic post-COVID manifestations and pre-existing health conditions.

CXCL10 was significantly upregulated in long COVID patients relative to COVID-19 convalescents and healthy controls, a finding corroborated by an independent study showing elevated CXCL10 in blood indicating a sustained interferon-induced inflammatory response.

A proteomic study identified Sirtuin 1, Natriuretic Peptide B, Hemopexin, and Arachidonate 5-Lipoxygenase as inflammation-related proteins showing significant multivariate changes from healthy controls, proposed as potential biomarkers for long COVID, while heterogeneity was also observed among patients.

Serum proteomics in a multi-omics study showed increased soluble C5bC6 complexes and decreased C7-containing terminal complement complexes in long COVID patients, indicating complement activation alongside thrombo-inflammation.
Single-cell transcriptomic analysis of monocytes in long COVID showed decreased NR4A1 and increased interferon-induced transcripts including IFITM3, suggesting an ongoing inflammatory response.

A combined proteomics and metabolomics study found significant alteration in acute phase proteins and platelet degranulation reflecting inflammatory and immune responses, alongside persistent dysregulation of TCA cycle and glucose metabolism metabolites reflecting adjustments to inflammation.

Unsupervised clustering identified three distinct long COVID disease phenotypes based on multi-omics profiles: cluster B characterized by triglycerides and organic acids, and cluster C, which included a higher proportion of women, associated with molecules enriched in the HIF-1alpha pathway, indicating gender-specific differences.

In patients with persistent pulmonary abnormalities, pathways of tissue repair including focal adhesion, MET signaling, and L1CAM interaction were identified, with increased proteins involved in tissue repair at the proteomic level.

Among the 73 genes Taylor et al. identified related to neurological and cardiometabolic disease pathways in long COVID, 14 were also differentially expressed in an independent transcriptomic study of whole blood from long COVID patients.
Ectopic bacterial colonization of the oral cavity was correlated with serum metabolite levels, illustrating a link between microbiome disturbances and systemic metabolic changes in long COVID.
Mast cell activation has been associated with immune dysfunction post-COVID, cited as a possible additional mechanism contributing to long COVID pulmonary/inflammatory phenotypes.
Neutrophil extracellular traps were identified in patients with respiratory long COVID sequelae at 6 months post-COVID, suggesting a role in pulmonary inflammatory phenotypes.
Severe COVID-19 and long COVID have been associated with elevated type I IFN-alpha responses through cGAS-STING pathway activation, contributing to sustained inflammation.

The burden of long COVID at 3 years post-infection is highest among previously hospitalized patients, demonstrating the impact of acute COVID-19 severity heterogeneity on long-term long COVID outcomes.
An integrated multi-omics approach identified long COVID biomarkers emphasizing latent virus reactivation and autoantibodies as key factors, and classified patients into distinct immune endotypes.
Severe COVID-19 was related to an increased risk of developing neuropsychiatric disorders, specifically Alzheimer's disease.

SARS-CoV-2-positive adolescents/young adults had more severe fatigue at baseline than SARS-CoV-2-negative individuals, though median fatigue severity converged by six months while a greater proportion of positives remained in the upper severity quartile.
In bivariate (univariate) analyses, SARS-CoV-2 infection status alone was not significantly associated with six-month fatigue severity.
Higher baseline fatigue was the strongest bivariate risk factor for fatigue severity at six months, explaining the largest proportion of variance among all predictors tested.
Higher neuroticism scores at baseline were a moderate risk factor for greater fatigue severity at six months.
Higher trait worry at baseline was a moderate risk factor for greater fatigue severity at six months.
Greater loneliness at baseline was a strong social/behavioural risk factor for fatigue severity at six months.
Female sex was independently associated with greater fatigue severity at six months among constitutional factors.
Older age was independently associated with greater fatigue severity at six months among constitutional factors.

Baseline interleukin-4 was retained as an independent predictor of fatigue severity at six months in the final multivariable model, though post-hoc analysis suggested this may reflect residual confounding by baseline symptom severity rather than a true independent effect.

Baseline interleukin-7 was retained as an independent predictor of fatigue severity at six months in the final multivariable model, though post-hoc analysis suggested this may reflect residual confounding by baseline symptom severity.

Baseline C3bc (complement C3 activation product) was retained as an independent predictor of fatigue severity at six months in the final multivariable model, though post-hoc analysis suggested this may reflect residual confounding by baseline symptom severity.

In post-hoc analysis controlling only for higher-order confounders, SARS-CoV-2 infection status remained a small but statistically significant independent risk factor for fatigue severity at six months.
The final multivariable regression model (including baseline symptom severity, SARS-CoV-2 status, IL-4, IL-7, and C3bc) explained 34.1% of variance in fatigue severity at six months.

PCA-derived 'symptom severity' and 'emotional maladjustment' composite scores were both strong risk factors for six-month fatigue severity and were highly correlated with one another, suggesting shared psychosocial underpinnings rather than infection-specific ones.

Baseline symptom severity, the study's major risk factor, correlated only weakly with SARS-CoV-2 status but more strongly with psychosocial factors not specific to infection, such as personality traits, loneliness, and recent negative life events.
As cited from an external randomised controlled trial (Kuut et al.), cognitive behavioural therapy had a sustained positive effect on post-COVID-19 fatigue at 12 months.

As cited from an external cohort study (Schneider et al.), adolescents with 'high loneliness' had markedly increased odds of persistent post-COVID symptoms compared to those with 'no loneliness', independent of baseline loneliness and health.
Fatigue was the most frequently reported symptom among Long-COVID patients at the outpatient neurology clinic, affecting 94.3% of patients.
Anxiety was reported by 79.2% of Long-COVID patients.
Myalgias were reported by 75.5% of Long-COVID patients.
Concentration difficulties were reported by 71.7% of Long-COVID patients.

Long-COVID patients clustered into a high symptom-number group and a low symptom-number group, with the high-number cluster reporting significantly worse depression, anxiety, stress, and sleep quality than the low-number cluster.
Overall, 60.4% (32 of 53) of Long-COVID patients were found to have poor well-being.
Reporting more than 17 symptoms (58.6% of patients) predicted poor well-being with 37.5% sensitivity and 95.2% specificity.
Mean single-fiber EMG jitter did not differ significantly among controls, LC-no, and LC-yes groups.
The percentage of abnormal individual jitter values (>10%) did not differ significantly between controls, LC-no, and LC-yes groups.
In situ muscle fiber conduction velocity in the tibialis anterior muscle was within reference limits and did not differ significantly between controls, LC-no, and LC-yes groups.
The fastest-to-slowest muscle fiber conduction velocity ratio (F/S ratio) did not differ significantly between the three groups.
Fatigue/postexertional malaise (F-PEM) frequency was 100% in the LC-yes group compared with 25% in LC-no and 29.7% in controls, a highly significant difference.
The mean F-PEM severity score (sum of 5 questions, 0-4 scale) was markedly higher in the LC-yes group than in LC-no and control groups.
A higher proportion of acute-phase SARS-CoV-2 symptoms (≥6 symptoms) during the initial infection was significantly associated with subsequent development of long COVID.
Acute-phase tiredness or fatigue was more frequently reported by patients who went on to develop long COVID than by those who did not.
All subjects with abnormal jitter parameters, across controls and both long COVID groups, tested negative for acetylcholine receptor antibodies, arguing against myasthenic NMJ pathology.
Among 102 long COVID survivors, 13%-30% reported clinically significant impairments in cognitive, emotional and physical functioning.
Over 10% of participants experienced persistent symptoms including diarrhoea, sleep problems, dyspnoea, nausea, fatigue and pain 6-9 months after COVID-19 diagnosis.

Functional impairments and long COVID symptoms were associated with greater acute COVID-19 symptom severity, presence of chronic disease, overweight status, regular exercise and living without a partner.
Donepezil did not significantly reduce fatigue severity compared with placebo at 3 weeks as measured by change in Chalder Fatigue Scale score, the trial's primary outcome.

Donepezil showed no significant effect on secondary outcomes including CFS at 8 weeks, anxiety/depression (HADS), PTSD-like symptoms (IES-R), quality of life (EQ-5D-5L), depression severity (PHQ-9), or daily health status (DHS) at 3 and 8 weeks compared with placebo.
The rate and nature of adverse events did not differ significantly between donepezil and placebo groups, with no serious adverse events occurring in either group.

In a prior mouse model of COVID-19 (intranasal S1 protein administration), reduced numbers of acetylcholine-producing cells and lower brain acetylcholine concentrations were associated with brain inflammation and fatigue/depression-like symptoms.

SITH-1, a protein encoded by an intermediate-stage transcript of human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6), has been proposed to exacerbate psychiatric symptoms by reducing acetylcholine-producing cells and brain acetylcholine concentration, and HHV-6 reactivation is more frequent after COVID-19 infection.
Fatigue is the most commonly reported symptom in post-COVID-19 condition, affecting 40% to 60% of patients, and impairs functional reintegration into society.
Subgroup analyses based on age, sex, medical history, and disease severity showed no significant difference in donepezil's effect on outcomes compared with placebo.
Individuals with long COVID after severe acute COVID-19 walked significantly less distance during the 6-minute walk test than matched controls without symptomatic COVID-19.
Total mechanical work performed during the 6-minute walk test was significantly lower in the severe long COVID group than controls.
Peak oxygen uptake during the 6-minute walk test was significantly lower in the severe long COVID group than in controls.
Minute ventilation during the 6-minute walk test was significantly lower in the severe long COVID group compared to controls, with group differences emerging after 80% of the test.
Heart rate response during the 6-minute walk test was blunted (attenuated) in the severe long COVID group compared to controls, with significant differences appearing after 60% of the test.
At rest prior to exercise, the severe long COVID group reported greater lower limb fatigue and dyspnea than controls.
At the end of the 6-minute walk test, perceived exertion was significantly higher in the severe long COVID group than controls.
All SF-36 quality-of-life domains were significantly reduced in the severe long COVID group compared to controls, with functional capacity and physical limitation showing the largest differences.
The FEV1/FVC ratio significantly differed between the severe long COVID group and controls, while other spirometry values did not show notable pulmonary dysfunction.
Respiratory muscle strength and resistance (maximum inspiratory and expiratory pressures) did not differ significantly between the severe long COVID group and controls.
No cardiac function abnormalities were detected on echocardiogram in the severe long COVID group.
The severe long COVID group predominantly reported grade 2 dyspnea on the mMRC scale, while controls reported grade 0.
Hypertension was the most common comorbidity (41%) in the severe long COVID group, followed by anxiety and diabetes (18% each).
Resting Borg fatigue score was significantly associated with walked distance in the 6-minute walk test, explaining 43% of the variance.
Resting Borg dyspnea score was significantly associated with walked distance in the 6-minute walk test, explaining 30% of the variance.
VO2 and heart rate were significantly associated with 6-minute walk distance, explaining 16% and 25% of its variance respectively.
Functional capacity, physical limitation, pain, vitality, and mental health SF-36 domains were significantly associated with walked distance, explaining between 25% and 38% of its variance.
A multiple linear regression model including VO2, resting Borg fatigue, functional capacity, physical limitation, vitality, and mental health explained 91% of the variance in 6-minute walk distance.
Fatigue was the most commonly reported long COVID symptom, occurring in 18.2% of women with long COVID.
Malaise was reported by 12.2% of women with long COVID.
Memory problems were reported by 12.1% of women with long COVID.
Brain fog was reported by 11.2% of women with long COVID.
Women who tested positive for COVID-19 had lower unadjusted physical function scores than those who never tested positive.
Women who tested positive for COVID-19 were less likely to be able to perform all ADLs without help compared to those who never tested positive.

Women who tested positive for COVID-19 were less likely to report being able to perform all Activities of Daily Living without help compared to those who never tested positive, in unadjusted analysis.
After adjusting for covariates including pre-COVID functioning, post-COVID physical function scores did not differ significantly by COVID-19 status.
Pre-COVID physical function scores were significantly associated with post-COVID physical function scores, independent of COVID-19 status.
After adjustment for covariates, the odds of being able to perform all Activities of Daily Living without help did not differ significantly by COVID-19 status.
Pre-COVID ADL status was significantly associated with post-COVID ADL status, independent of COVID-19 status.
Participants with severe fatigue (top quartile FAS scores) had 3.2 times higher odds of meeting clinical thresholds for anxiety compared with those with milder fatigue.
Participants with severe fatigue had 2.8 times higher odds of meeting clinical thresholds for depression compared with those with milder fatigue.
Cluster analysis using GAD-7, PHQ-4 and somatoform (SSEQ) scores identified four distinct Long COVID psychological phenotypes differing in anxiety/depression severity and somatoform symptom burden.
Cluster 3 (high anxiety/depression, high somatoform symptoms) reported more neurological symptoms and vascular/lymph node symptoms than other clusters.
Clusters 2 and 3 showed the highest rates of headache/migraine symptoms among the four Long COVID psychological clusters.
No significant gender differences were found between the four psychological symptom clusters.
Epilepsy prevalence significantly differed between clusters, being highest in Cluster 3 (2.4%) and absent in Cluster 2.
History of depression was reported more frequently in the high-symptom-severity Clusters 3 and 4 compared with Clusters 1 and 2.
Previous PTSD was more prevalent in Cluster 3 than in the other psychological symptom clusters.
Cluster 4 had the highest prevalence of ADHD history among the four clusters.
Cluster 3 had a significantly higher prevalence of past burnout than Clusters 1 and 4.
Cluster 3 showed a markedly higher prevalence of prior anxiety disorder diagnosis than Cluster 1.
Cluster 3 exhibited a higher prevalence of prior adjustment disorder than Clusters 1 and 4.
Cluster 3 had a significantly higher prevalence of prior phobia than Cluster 1.
Cluster 3 had a higher prevalence of prior OCD than Cluster 2.
Cluster 3 had the lowest proportion of individuals who felt they could live with their current health state long-term, compared with Clusters 1 and 4.
Clusters 2 and 3 had higher proportions of individuals unable to return to professional activity without complications compared with Clusters 1 and 4.
Deterioration in personal relationships was most pronounced in Clusters 3 and 4 compared with Clusters 1 and 2.
Medication use was higher in Clusters 2 and 3 compared with Clusters 1 and 4.
Vaccination status did not significantly differ between the four psychological symptom clusters, although unvaccinated rates were nominally highest in Cluster 3.
Family living situation differed significantly between clusters, though with a low effect size and no clear pattern.
Individuals with a prior COVID-19 infection had significantly higher Brain Fog Scale (BFS) scores than those never infected.
Brain Fog Severity Score (BFSS) did not differ significantly between individuals with and without prior COVID-19 infection.
MIND diet adherence score did not differ significantly between individuals with and without prior COVID-19 infection.
Participants reinfected with COVID-19 more than once had significantly higher BFS scores than those infected only once.
BFSS was only marginally, non-significantly higher in participants with COVID-19 reinfection compared with single infection.

BFSS scores trended higher, but not significantly, with greater COVID-19 disease severity (severe home symptoms/hospitalization) at p=0.055, while BFSS differed significantly across severity groups when tested separately, with severe-home-symptom participants scoring higher than mild cases.
MIND diet score did not differ significantly by COVID-19 disease severity.
Women showed significantly higher brain fog (BFS, BFSS), MIND diet score, GSRS, and BMIS Pleasant-Unpleasant scores than men, indicating greater brain fog severity in women.
Sleep quality (SQS) was negatively correlated with brain fog (BFS) scores, indicating poorer sleep quality with higher brain fog severity.
Gastrointestinal symptom severity (GSRS and its Abdominal Pain, Reflux, Diarrhea, Indigestion, and Constipation dimensions) was positively correlated with brain fog (BFS) scores.
Age was negatively correlated with brain fog (BFS), Abdominal Pain Dimension, Diarrhea Dimension, and BMIS Pleasant-Unpleasant Dimension scores.
BMI was negatively correlated with MIND diet score and several mood (BMIS) sub-dimensions (Pleasant-Unpleasant, Arousal-Calm, Negative-Relaxed).
Regression analysis identified GSRS, BMIS Pleasant-Unpleasant, and BMIS Arousal-Calm as significant predictors of brain fog symptoms, explaining 35.8% of variance.

The negative correlation between sleep quality and brain fog became non-significant in regression when controlling for mood, diet, and gastrointestinal symptoms, suggesting the sleep-brain fog relationship may be mediated by these other factors rather than direct.
Autistic children showed a shorter RR interval (faster heart rate) than neurotypical children, a difference that was only a statistical tendency after FDR correction.
Autistic children showed significantly lower LF peak frequency in heart rate variability than neurotypical children, a result that survived FDR correction.
No significant group differences were found between autistic and neurotypical children for HF peak frequency, HF absolute power, LF absolute power, or RMSSD.

There was a non-significant tendency toward higher tonic EDA in autistic children compared to neurotypical children, which did not survive FDR correction; other EDA parameters (peak number, AUC, peak amplitude) showed no group differences.

In a small subgroup of 8 autistic children with usable pupil data, none of the three pupillary parameters (median pupil diameter, hippus frequency, hippus amplitude) differed significantly from age-matched neurotypical children.
Autistic adults showed a larger median resting pupil diameter than neurotypical adults, though this only remained a tendency after FDR correction.
Autistic adults showed significantly greater pupil hippus amplitude than neurotypical adults, a result that survived FDR correction.
Autistic adults had a significantly shorter RR interval (faster heart rate) than neurotypical adults, though this became only a tendency after FDR correction.

Autistic adults showed non-significant tendencies toward lower RMSSD and lower HF absolute power (both indices of parasympathetic activity) compared to neurotypical adults; neither survived FDR correction.
Autistic adults exhibited significantly higher tonic electrodermal activity (sympathetic tone) than neurotypical adults, a finding that survived FDR correction.
Autistic adults showed fewer spontaneous phasic EDA peaks than neurotypical adults, a result that was only marginally significant after FDR correction.

A group-by-sex interaction on RR interval in adults showed that neurotypical females had a higher RR interval than autistic females, with a tendency for autistic males to have higher RR interval than autistic females; no difference was found between neurotypical males and females.

BMI interacted with autism group status to affect electrodermal parameters in adults, with BMI positively correlated with EDA measures in autistic adults but negatively correlated in neurotypical adults.
In autistic adults, AQ scores showed only non-significant tendencies toward positive correlation with median pupil diameter and LF peak frequency, and no correlation with other autonomic parameters.

In autistic adults, pupil hippus amplitude was positively correlated with verbal IQ, but this correlation did not survive FDR correction; no other autonomic-verbal IQ correlations were found, and none were found in autistic children.
In autistic children, no autonomic parameters (pupil, cardiac, or electrodermal) correlated significantly with CARS-rated autism severity.

The authors propose that autistic children show a sympathetic/parasympathetic co-inhibition pattern at rest, while autistic adults show a sympathetic/parasympathetic co-activation pattern, suggesting an atypical maturational trajectory of autonomic regulation in autism, potentially linked to locus coeruleus functioning.
Disrupted oxytocinergic signaling has been implicated as a potential contributing factor in autism spectrum disorder.
Approximately 30% of individuals with autism have co-occurring intellectual disability, yet nearly all prior oxytocin trials have excluded this subgroup, limiting generalizability.

Prior single- and multiple-dose oxytocin trials in autism show inconsistent efficacy, with some reporting improved social and repetitive behaviors and others finding no significant difference versus placebo.
Across prior trials, moderate-duration (4-6 week) intermittent dosing regimens of 24-32 IU intranasal oxytocin every other day have shown the most promise in autism.
Oxytocin's therapeutic outcomes in autism appear context-dependent, with better efficacy reported when administration occurs in socially supportive settings.
Sex-related differences in response to oxytocin treatment in autism remain an understudied area of research.
Emerging evidence suggests younger children with autism may derive greater benefit from oxytocin administration than older individuals.
DNA methylation at three specific CpG sites (-934, -924, -914) of the oxytocin receptor gene OXTR has previously been reported to be altered in autism.
In a prior trial, oxytocin's beneficial effect on social functioning (SRS-2) in autistic children was detected only after adjusting for baseline plasma oxytocin levels as a covariate.

A pooled meta-analytic effect size of Cohen's d = 0.84 for chronic intranasal oxytocin's effect on SRS-2 outcomes was calculated from four prior trials in young autistic children without intellectual disability.
hcASD gene expression was significantly enriched in enteric neurons and their progenitors (ENCCs) compared to all other cell types in single-cell RNA-seq data from developing human prenatal gut.
Across sixteen hcASD gene patient cohorts in Simons Searchlight, caregivers reported GI symptoms in an average of 51.7% of affected individuals compared to only 0.4% of unaffected family members.

In Citizen Health medical records, over 80% of individuals carrying variants in SYNGAP1, SCN2A, CHD2, SLC6A1, or STXBP1 had GI-related diagnoses, and over 60% had dysmotility symptoms, particularly constipation.
CRISPR/Cas9 mutagenesis of syngap1 in Xenopus tropicalis significantly reduced ENCC migration area compared to the uninjected control side.
CRISPR/Cas9 mutagenesis of chd8 in Xenopus tropicalis significantly reduced ENCC migration area.
CRISPR/Cas9 mutagenesis of scn2a in Xenopus tropicalis significantly reduced ENCC migration area.
CRISPR/Cas9 mutagenesis of chd2 in Xenopus tropicalis significantly reduced ENCC migration area.
CRISPR/Cas9 mutagenesis of dyrk1a in Xenopus tropicalis significantly reduced ENCC migration area.
Both CRISPR and an independent validated translation-blocking morpholino against dyrk1a produced the same ENCC migration-reduction phenotype, confirming gene specificity.
Dyrk1a is expressed in ENCCs during their migration and persists in mature enteric neurons, localizing particularly to the primary cilium, an organelle required for ENCC migration.
Dyrk1a knockdown by CRISPR or morpholino caused defects in the early neural crest marker sox10 at NF stage 15, indicating a requirement for Dyrk1a earlier in neural crest development.
Morpholino knockdown of chd8 caused significant defects in sox10 expression, indicating a role in earlier neural crest development beyond ENCC migration.
Morpholino knockdown of chd2 caused significant defects in sox10 expression, indicating a role in earlier neural crest development.
Morpholino knockdown of syngap1 caused a moderate defect in sox10 expression, a weaker effect than chd8/chd2.
Morpholino knockdown of scn2a showed no significant effect on sox10 expression, unlike chd8, chd2, and syngap1.

Pharmacological inhibition of Dyrk1a (TG003 or harmine) after neural crest specification, at the onset of vagal neural crest migration, still disrupted ENCC migration to a similar extent as CRISPR perturbation or a Ret inhibitor (Hirschsprung's disease model), indicating an independent later requirement for Dyrk1a in migration.
Developmental inhibition of Dyrk1a with TG003 caused decreased fluorescent bead excretion (a measure of gut motility) in Xenopus tadpoles compared to DMSO vehicle control.

In a targeted screen of 8 FDA-approved serotonergic drugs, only the SSRI escitalopram oxalate (10 µM) increased gut motility (bead excretion) by more than 1 standard deviation compared to DMSO in wildtype tadpoles.
Acute exposure to escitalopram oxalate fully rescued the decreased gut motility caused by developmental Dyrk1a inhibition, restoring excretion to levels comparable to DMSO controls.

Acute exposure to the serotonin receptor 6 (5-HTR6) agonist WAY-181187 partially rescued decreased gut motility from developmental Dyrk1a inhibition, though excretion remained modestly lower than DMSO controls.

Both Dyrk1a and serotonin receptor 6 (5-HTR6) localize to the primary cilium in enteric neurons, suggesting a shared subcellular site linking Dyrk1a function to serotonergic modulation of ENCC migration and gut motility.
Knockdown of the hcASD genes chd8 and chd2 caused significant defects in the early neural crest marker sox10, with a moderate effect from syngap1 knockdown.
SCN2A knockdown had no significant effect on expression of the early neural crest marker sox10, unlike chd8, chd2, and syngap1.
Prior work in zebrafish showed that disruption of chd8 caused reduced colonization of enteric neurons into the gut and gut dysmotility.
A prior zebrafish study of SHANK3 found no significant change in gut neuron number but identified disrupted serotonergic signaling in the gut.

From 1 month to 3 months post infection, MFI-20 total score and general fatigue significantly decreased, suggesting partial recovery, though other subscales decreased non-significantly.

At 3 months post infection, MFI-20 total score, physical fatigue, mental fatigue, and reduced activity remained significantly higher than healthy controls, though reduced motivation and general fatigue no longer differed significantly, indicating a long-lasting fatigue effect.
At 1 month post infection, patients with long COVID showed significantly increased whole-brain network integration compared to healthy controls, measured using the nested-spectral partition method.

At 1 month post infection, patients with long COVID showed significantly decreased whole-brain network segregation compared to healthy controls, with consistent decreases across nearly all networks (FPN, VAN, DMN, DAN, SMN, limbic, VN, SCN).

No significant differences in segregation or integration were found between the 1-month and 3-month post-infection groups at whole-brain, network, or regional scales, despite improvement in fatigue scores.
At 3 months post infection, whole-brain network integration was no longer significantly different from healthy controls, suggesting partial normalization.

At 3 months post infection, whole-brain network segregation remained significantly decreased compared to healthy controls, with this decrease significant in seven of eight networks except the subcortical network.

At 3 months post infection, 14 regions of interest including right precentral gyrus, superior temporal gyrus, left parahippocampal gyrus, insular gyrus, left superior frontal gyrus, lateral occipital cortex, left hippocampus, left basal ganglia, right inferior frontal gyrus, and left thalamus showed significant differences in both integration and segregation versus healthy controls.

In the 1-month post-infection group, physical fatigue was significantly negatively correlated with whole-brain network segregation, while the correlation with total MFI-20 score and integration were not significant.
At 1 month post infection, physical fatigue was significantly negatively correlated with segregation of the visual network.
At the regional scale, left medioventral occipital cortex and lateral occipital cortex showed significant negative correlations with physical fatigue at 1 month post infection.

At 3 months post infection, the correlation pattern reversed: MFI-20 total score and nearly all subdimensions were significantly negatively correlated with network integration and positively correlated with segregation, opposite to the 1-month pattern.
At 3 months post infection, MFI-20 total score was positively correlated with segregation and negatively correlated with integration in DAN, DMN, FPN, and VN networks.
Reduced motivation showed significant positive correlation with segregation and negative correlation with integration in DAN and VN networks at 3 months post infection.

At the regional level, integration of left posterior superior temporal sulcus and left lateral occipital cortex was negatively correlated with reduced motivation, while segregation of these regions was positively correlated with reduced motivation, at 3 months post infection.

Whole-brain gene expression profiles from the Allen Human Brain Atlas were correlated with fatigue-related network integration/segregation effects; 4,604 significant genes were identified at 1 month (1,561 integration-related, 3,043 segregation-related) and 4,133 at 3 months (4,111 integration-related, 22 segregation-related).

Gene Ontology enrichment analysis of fatigue-associated genes revealed human disease phenotypes of abnormal social behavior and abnormal communication at both 1-month and 3-month post-infection timepoints.

No significant pre- to post-infection differences were found for depression (PHQ-9), anxiety (GAD-7), perceived stress (PSS), or cognitive complaints (FLei) in the total cohort.

In the Long-COVID subgroup, quality of life, sleep, fatigue, depression, anxiety, stress, and cognitive complaint scores were all significantly worse after SARS-CoV-2 infection compared to before, with mild to strong effect sizes.

Among Long-COVID patients, the most common symptoms were concentration disorders (60%), fatigue (55%), reduced exercise capacity (50%), shortness of breath (40%), chest pain (20%), and brain fog (15%).
Fatigue, reduced exercise capacity, shortness of breath, and concentration disorders were significantly more common in Long-COVID patients than in recovered patients.

Among patients homozygous for the ATP7B p.H1069Q mutation, 47.1% had a neurological or mixed phenotype.

Participants with Long Covid in Kenya reported disabling fatigue, memory inconsistencies, and acute pain in muscle, gut, or tissues.
