Participants felt dismissed or disbelieved by family, friends, and clinicians, and turned to online social support groups such as Facebook for validation and support.
Some participants appreciated clinicians who offered experimental treatments for Long Covid, while others expressed trepidation when treatments made them feel sicker.

The most common pediatric Long COVID subphenotype, 'Respiratory/cardiac symptoms', comprised 53.8% of patients and was distinguished by a significantly higher proportion (56.7%) of respiratory diagnoses than any other subphenotype.
A 'Musculoskeletal pain' subphenotype comprising 13.9% of the cohort was distinguished by pain-related diagnoses, with 'other chronic pain' the most common specific code.
A 'Neuropsychiatric conditions' subphenotype (10.9% of patients) showed significantly higher neuropsychiatric diagnosis rates, with anxiety disorder the most common specific diagnosis.
A 'Gastrointestinal symptoms' subphenotype (9.3% of patients) showed significantly higher rates of gastrointestinal diagnoses than other subphenotypes.

A 'Headache' subphenotype (7.1% of patients) had significantly more headache diagnoses and elevated neuropsychiatric comorbidity, with the highest post-acute healthcare utilization aside from the severe lower-respiratory cluster.

A 'Fatigue' subphenotype (5.0% of patients) was defined by significantly elevated fatigue/malaise diagnoses (41.7%) and Long COVID diagnoses (63.5%), with common comorbid chest pain, arrhythmias, and respiratory symptoms.

The fatigue subphenotype's co-occurring constellation of fatigue, cardiac symptoms, headache, musculoskeletal pain, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and POTS-like symptoms (dizziness, giddiness) is suggested to reflect underlying ME/CFS, though a strict ME/CFS diagnosis could not be established within the 28-179 day observation window.
Children younger than 4 years were almost exclusively classified into the respiratory/cardiac subphenotype, particularly the more severe lower-respiratory and upper-respiratory clusters.

Female patients were underrepresented in the respiratory/cardiac and musculoskeletal pain subphenotypes but overrepresented in the fatigue, headache, gastrointestinal, and neuropsychiatric subphenotypes.

Race/ethnicity was associated with subphenotype membership: Hispanic patients were overrepresented in respiratory/cardiac and neuropsychiatric subphenotypes; non-Hispanic Black patients were overrepresented in neuropsychiatric, musculoskeletal pain, and respiratory/cardiac subphenotypes; and non-Hispanic White patients were overrepresented in fatigue, headache, and musculoskeletal pain subphenotypes.
Patients with more severe acute SARS-CoV-2 infection were classified almost entirely into the respiratory/cardiac subphenotype, specifically the severe lower-respiratory cluster.

Patients with a pre-existing non-complex chronic condition were overrepresented in the gastrointestinal and neuropsychiatric conditions subphenotypes, suggesting possible risk factors or exacerbation of existing chronic conditions.

The six identified subphenotypes were reproduced in similar proportions across the independently trained development (Cohort A) and validation (Cohort B) cohorts, supporting the robustness of the clustering approach.

Compared with clusters from a matched SARS-CoV-2-negative control cohort, the neuropsychiatric and gastrointestinal long COVID subphenotypes were relatively similar to control clusters, while headache, fatigue, and respiratory/cardiac subphenotypes were more distinct, suggesting the latter three may be more specifically attributable to COVID-19.

The severe cardiorespiratory cluster identified in this pediatric cohort overlapped with the multisystem+lab cluster and cardiac/renal subtype reported in prior adult EHR-based Long COVID subtyping studies, while musculoskeletal, gastrointestinal, and neuropsychiatric symptoms tended to form composite subphenotypes in adults rather than the distinct subphenotypes seen here.

Unlike a prior prospective survey-based pediatric clustering study, this EHR-based analysis identified a predominant respiratory/cardiac subphenotype and a distinct neuropsychiatric subphenotype, but did not identify clusters characterized by loss of taste/smell or sleep impacts that were found in the prior study.

Cronbach's alpha for the total ABNAS score and its subsets was 0.814 in this long COVID cohort, indicating good internal reliability of the tool.

A more severe acute COVID-19 course was independently associated with a higher risk of developing long COVID in kidney transplant recipients.
Male sex was independently associated with a lower risk of developing long COVID.
Higher body mass index was independently associated with increased risk of developing long COVID.

Maintenance corticosteroid use in kidney transplant recipients was independently associated with a nearly three-fold increased risk of developing long COVID, though 93% of the cohort was on corticosteroids limiting interpretation.
Targeted antiviral or monoclonal antibody treatment during acute COVID-19 was not associated with lower odds of developing long COVID.
No association was found between SARS-CoV-2 vaccination status and risk of developing long COVID or change in its symptom pattern in kidney transplant recipients.
The integumental and psychiatric long COVID phenotypes were significantly more common among female kidney transplant recipients.
Higher BMI was found in patients who developed the cognitive, fatigue, fibromyalgia-like, and psychiatric long COVID phenotypes compared to those without long COVID.
Worse pre-infection kidney allograft function (lower eGFR) was found in kidney transplant recipients who developed the fatigue long COVID phenotype.
A longer time from kidney transplantation to COVID-19 infection was associated with development of the cognitive long COVID phenotype.
Long COVID phenotype proportions did not differ across COVID-19 pandemic periods (wild-type/alpha/delta/omicron), reinfection status, or vaccination status.
Symptom frequency did not change with time since symptom onset except for joint/muscle pain and decreased appetite, which showed a significant change over time.

A logistic regression model using symptom-cluster factor scores accurately predicted patient-reported significant health deterioration, with strong discriminative performance in training and an independent validation cohort.

Compared to kidney transplant recipients without long COVID, those with long COVID were older, had more severe acute COVID-19, lower pre-infection eGFR, higher BMI, and higher Charlson Comorbidity Index.

The ten most commonly reported persistent symptoms after COVID-19 in kidney transplant recipients spanned fatigue, exertional intolerance, respiratory, musculoskeletal, sleep, visual, cognitive, dermatologic, and reproductive/sexual domains.
Nearly a quarter of kidney transplant recipients reported significant worsening of health and decreased quality of life more than 3 months after COVID-19.
SARS-CoV-2 infection triggers an exaggerated immune response marked by release of proinflammatory cytokines including IL-6, IL-1, and TNF-α along with reactive oxygen species in PCC patients.
Cited studies report alterations in CD4+ and CD8+ T cell populations along with NK lymphocytes in PCC patients.

Fatigue severity has been significantly correlated with increased monocyte counts, upregulation of CCL2, CCL7 and SERPINB2 in monocytes, elevated serum galectin-9, and increased CD8+ T-lymphocyte counts.

Kynurenine, a metabolite increased in COVID-19 patients, is associated with depression and contributes to neuroinflammation, whereas kynurenic acid cannot cross the blood-brain barrier and may protect against depression.
Omega-3 fatty acids act as precursors of specialized pro-resolving mediators (SPMs) that resolve inflammation and restore immune homeostasis by counteracting pro-inflammatory signaling.
In vitro studies show that Resolvin D1 and Resolvin D2 potently reduce production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, suggesting a potential therapeutic role for lipid mediators in PCC.
A cohort study found that personalized rehabilitation programs improved the overall condition of PCC patients, drawing parallels with treatment approaches used in ME/CFS.
A systematic review reported that telerehabilitation is effective in improving quality of life in a manner similar to face-to-face treatment.
A meta-analysis found that omega-3 supplementation benefits muscle mass and physical performance (walking speed) in older adults, though this was not studied specifically in PCC.

In a small uncontrolled pre-post study, COVID-19 survivors given a dietary supplement containing 19 nutrients (including arginine, carnitine, minerals, B vitamins, and plant extracts) showed improved muscle strength and physical performance, though without a control group or exercise program.
Nutritional supplements such as L-arginine plus vitamin C, or anhydrous enol-oxaloacetate, have been reported effective in controlling PCC symptoms and reducing fatigue.

A review concluded that omega-3 fatty acid deficiency is associated with an increased risk of mental disorders, though evidence on omega-3 effects on depressive symptoms remains contradictory across studies.
Among 1,129 children with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection, 68.6% reported at least one post-COVID-19 symptom, and 16.2% met criteria for long COVID.
Respiratory symptoms were the most commonly reported post-COVID category, affecting 43.4% of children, with 7.4% persisting beyond three months.
Neurological and cognitive dysfunction was the second most common post-COVID issue, reported by 27.7% of children, with 4.5% lasting over three months.
Gastrointestinal symptoms were reported in 22.1% of children, with 3.2% persisting beyond three months.
Fatigue was reported by 21.6% of children, with 3.5% experiencing it beyond three months.
Sleep disturbances were reported by 18.8% of children, with 2.7% persisting beyond three months.
Poor appetite was reported by 15.4% of children, with 2.0% persisting beyond three months.
Cardiovascular long COVID symptoms were significantly more prevalent in females than males.
Neurological and cognitive dysfunction symptoms were significantly more prevalent in females than males.
Cardiovascular long COVID symptoms increased significantly with age.
Neurological and cognitive dysfunction increased significantly with age.
Fatigue symptoms increased significantly with age.
Respiratory long COVID symptoms decreased significantly with increasing age.
Time-to-event analysis found no significant overall difference in long COVID symptom-free survival between males and females or across age groups.
Time-to-event analysis showed neurological and cognitive dysfunction symptoms occurred significantly more frequently in females.
Time-to-event analysis showed cardiovascular symptoms occurred significantly more frequently by sex among less-frequent symptom categories.
Neurological/cognitive dysfunction and fatigue showed an overall increased risk with age in time-to-event analysis.
Older children (6-17 years) showed a significantly higher risk of musculoskeletal pain than younger children.
Cardiovascular symptoms were significantly higher in the 12-17 years age group compared to younger children.
Sleep disorders and sensory symptoms showed borderline significant age-related differences.
Comorbidities, most commonly atopic dermatitis, rhinitis, asthma, gastrointestinal manifestations, and food allergies, were present in 36.9% of the pediatric cohort prior to SARS-CoV-2 infection.

The observed pediatric long COVID occurrence of 16.2% was lower than rates reported in prior meta-analyses of pediatric long COVID (25.24% and 23.36%), potentially reflecting the milder Omicron-era disease course in this cohort.
In female patients, BFHX treatment significantly increased 6-minute walk distance compared to placebo at 2 and 3 months of follow-up.
In male patients, there was no significant difference in 6-minute walk distance between BFHX and placebo groups after 3 months of treatment.

In patients younger than 60 years, BFHX showed no significant difference in 6-minute walk distance compared to placebo.

In patients with severe COVID-19, BFHX significantly improved 6-minute walk distance versus placebo after 3 months.

In patients younger than 60 years, BFHX treatment was associated with a significant decrease in mean CT value versus placebo at 3 months.
In subgroups defined by illness severity and neutralizing antibody status, BFHX treatment did not significantly improve mean CT value compared to placebo.
The population prevalence of chemical intolerance meeting QEESI criteria significantly increased between the 2020 and 2022 surveys.
Respondents with high chemical intolerance reported substantially higher COVID-19 prevalence than those with low or medium chemical intolerance.
Respondents over age 60 reported lower COVID-19 prevalence than younger respondents, contrary to typical age-risk literature.
Hispanic/Latino respondents reported significantly higher odds of COVID-19 than non-Hispanic respondents.

Overall Black/African American respondents had lower COVID-19 prevalence than non-Black respondents, but those with high chemical intolerance showed a significant interaction with markedly increased odds of reporting COVID-19.
Across multiple severity cutoff models, respondents with high chemical intolerance had at least four-fold higher odds of severe COVID-19 symptoms compared with those with low chemical intolerance.
Respondents with high chemical intolerance had markedly increased odds of reporting long COVID-19 relative to those with low chemical intolerance.
Hispanic/Latino and Black/African American respondents reported higher odds of long COVID-19 than non-Hispanic white respondents.

Respondents with mid or high chemical intolerance reported significantly greater rates of moderate and/or severe COVID-19 vaccine reactions than those with low chemical intolerance, who were also more likely to be vaccinated in the first place.

Women reported worse COVID-19 symptom severity than men, contrary to some prior reports of male-predominant severity, which the authors suggest may reflect chemical intolerance as an unmeasured confounder in earlier studies.
Asian respondents were least likely to report severe COVID-19 symptoms compared with white respondents in the 8+ severity cutoff model.

The authors cite prior work showing approximately half of mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS) patients also have chemical intolerance, with overlapping symptoms, proposing that heightened/sustained mast cell immune responses provide a biological mechanism linking chemical intolerance to COVID-19 and vaccine reaction severity.

In prior work cited by the authors, an 'Environmental House Calls' intervention that assessed indoor air quality and reduced household VOC/fragrance sources in the homes of 37 people with chemical intolerance led to reported symptom improvement at post-intervention follow-up.

A 12-week open-label trial of propranolol, a beta-adrenergic antagonist that inhibits the stress response, was associated with reduced gastrointestinal symptoms in some but not all individuals with ASD.
Participants with higher heart rate variability showed a wider cone of direct gaze during cardiac systole, when cardiac afferent signals are maximally represented in the brain.

The HRV-related widening of the cone of direct gaze during systole was independent of individual differences in autistic traits.

Somatic (autonomic) arousal was directly and positively related to depression symptoms in the path model.
Insomnia symptoms were positively and directly related to anxiety symptoms in the path model.
Insomnia symptoms were positively and directly related to depression symptoms in the path model.
Anxiety symptoms were directly and positively related to depression symptoms in the path model.
Autism traits had a significant indirect effect on depression mediated through anxiety, with anxiety fully mediating this relationship.
Intolerance of uncertainty had a significant indirect effect on depression mediated through anxiety.
Insomnia had a significant indirect effect on depression mediated through anxiety, in addition to its direct effect.
Sensory sensitivity had significant indirect effects on depression through insomnia alone and through insomnia then anxiety.
Somatic (autonomic) arousal had significant indirect effects on depression through insomnia alone and through insomnia then anxiety.

The best-fitting transdiagnostic path model (model 1) explained 29% of variance in insomnia, 37% of variance in anxiety, and 48% of variance in depression symptoms among autistic adolescents and adults.

Female autistic participants scored significantly higher than male participants on autism traits, intolerance of uncertainty, autonomic arousal, sensory sensitivity, insomnia, anxiety, and depression measures, leading sex to be included as a covariate in the models.
Over half of the sample reported a current anxiety diagnosis, about 40% reported a current depression diagnosis, and about a third of the sample was currently taking antidepressant medication.

Contrary to hypothesis, intolerance of uncertainty did not have a significant direct or indirect path to insomnia in the best-fitting model, despite a significant correlation between the two variables.
Endorsement of the EMA item 'I have an emotion I cannot name,' indexing alexithymic emotion-identification difficulty, was roughly three times lower after DBT than before.
The EMA item 'I have no emotion' did not significantly change between pre- and post-DBT assessments.
Rates of negative emotions such as anxiety and sadness did not significantly differ before versus after DBT.
Autistic adults reported significantly higher rates of joy after DBT than before.
Autistic adults reported significantly higher rates of feeling calm after DBT than before.
Autistic adults reported significantly higher rates of feeling interest after DBT than before.
Post-DBT, autistic adults reported selecting more than one emotion at a time significantly more often than pre-DBT.
Contrary to expectations, the proportion of conflicting (mixed-valence) emotions reported was significantly higher after DBT than before.
Self-reported need to decrease, maintain, or increase current emotional state did not significantly differ before versus after DBT.
Multilevel modelling showed that time (post-DBT) was a significant positive predictor of momentary self-reported emotion control.
Higher subjective emotional arousal was associated with lower momentary emotion control, independent of DBT timepoint.
Intense physical activity, compared to no activity, was associated with increased momentary emotion control.
Baseline heart rate did not significantly differ between pre- and post-DBT assessments.
Baseline heart rate variability did not significantly differ between pre- and post-DBT assessments.
Baseline skin conductance level did not significantly differ between pre- and post-DBT assessments.
Higher momentary subjective emotional arousal was positively associated with higher heart rate variability.
The presence of social interaction in the preceding 15 minutes was positively associated with heart rate.
The presence of social interaction in the preceding 15 minutes was positively associated with heart rate variability.
Older age was associated with lower heart rate.
Psychotropic medication intake was associated with increased heart rate levels, controlling for anticholinergic burden.
Intense physical activity was the only variable that positively predicted all three physiological measures (HR, HRV, and SCL) in the models.
Retrospective total and all six subscale scores of the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale significantly decreased from pre- to post-DBT.
Retrospective alexithymia scores (GAFS-8) significantly decreased from pre- to post-DBT.

The authors propose that reduced connectivity within the insular cortex in autism leads to vagal withdrawal and sympathetic hyperarousal, driving chronic hypervigilance and lowering the threshold for meltdowns.
Vagal withdrawal and sympathetic hyperarousal are proposed as autonomic correlates of chronic hypervigilance in autism, contributing to meltdown susceptibility.
The paper argues that meltdowns reflect an altered neuroceptive process in autism, in which contextual evidence such as social cues is integrated differently when assessing ambiguous signs of danger.
The authors hypothesize that differences in sensory attenuation and interoceptive inference underlying meltdowns may be linked to oxytocin deficiency during infancy.
Neuroligin transcripts were found to be expressed and extensively alternatively spliced in mouse, rat, and human gut during both fetal and adult life.
Neurexin transcripts were found to be expressed and extensively alternatively spliced in mouse, rat, and human gut during both fetal and adult life.
When transfected into non-neuronal cells, neuroligins were sufficient to recruit presynaptic elements, supporting a role in enteric synaptogenesis.
When transfected into non-neuronal cells, neurexins were sufficient to recruit postsynaptic elements, supporting a role in enteric synaptogenesis.

An engineered soluble neurexin that competitively interferes with endogenous neurexin-neuroligin binding inhibited formation/stabilization of enteric synapses and recruitment of neurotransmitter receptors.
Alternative splicing of neuroligin and neurexin was shown to contribute to establishment of ENS synaptic specificity, with some isoforms preferentially inducing cholinergic synapses.
Alternative splicing of neuroligin and neurexin transcripts contributes to establishing synaptic specificity in the enteric nervous system.
Certain neuroligin and neurexin splice isoforms preferentially induced formation of cholinergic synapses in the enteric nervous system.
Other neuroligin and neurexin splice isoforms preferentially promoted formation of serotonergic synapses in the enteric nervous system.
Nasal cytology showed significantly higher lymphocyte grading in the olfactory dysfunction group compared to both control groups.
Neutrophil grading on nasal cytology was significantly higher in the olfactory dysfunction group than in either control group.
Eosinophils and mast cells were rare in all groups and showed no significant difference between the olfactory dysfunction group and controls.
Ciliocytophthoria, a marker of epithelial degeneration, was much more prevalent in the olfactory dysfunction group than in either control group and absent in the never-infected control group.
No significant correlation was found between cytological grading of lymphocytes or neutrophils and TDI (smell test) scores in any study group.

A mild but statistically significant increase in lymphocyte grading was also observed between the two control groups, suggesting subclinical inflammation persists in some COVID-recovered individuals even without olfactory dysfunction.

The predominant lymphocytes observed in the OD group had morphology (increased euchromatin, prominent nucleoli, vacuolated cytoplasm) characteristic of type II lymphocytes actively producing immunoglobulin.

The authors note that prior research found anti-endothelial cell antibodies in patients with persistent post-viral olfactory impairment, supporting a localized autoimmune/vascular inflammatory mechanism consistent with their own findings.
The authors cite prior work showing elevated nasal circulating calprotectin levels in post-viral olfactory dysfunction patients, supporting sustained inflammation in the olfactory cleft.

The authors hypothesize, without directly testing, that long-term local (topical) corticosteroids might modulate the localized lymphocytic and neutrophilic inflammation identified in the olfactory cleft, potentially aiding neuroepithelial regeneration.
Among 319 non-depressed patients who had cognitive symptoms during acute COVID-19, 27.9% continued to experience these symptoms beyond 24 weeks, while 72.1% had remission by 24 weeks.
Female sex was independently associated with higher odds of persistent cognitive symptoms and longer symptom duration after COVID-19 in multivariate models.

Infection during the second COVID-19 wave (Delta/Gamma-predominant) was independently associated with higher odds of persistent cognitive symptoms compared with infection during the third (Omicron-predominant) wave.
Patients with persistent cognitive symptoms beyond 24 weeks were more likely to report loss of ability to carry out daily tasks compared to those whose symptoms remitted.
Patients with persistent cognitive symptoms had a substantially greater proportion of post-COVID functional limitation compared to those who remitted.

The predominant type of cognitive symptom shifted over time: concentration problems were most common in the acute and remission phases, whereas memory problems and word-finding difficulty were more prevalent among patients with symptoms persisting beyond 24 weeks.
Difficulty thinking clearly and concentration problems had the highest remission rates, whereas memory problems and difficulty finding words had the highest persistence rates.
The proportion of patients with cognitive symptoms did not significantly differ according to the presence of PTSD, depressive, or anxiety symptoms.
Unlike other psychiatric symptoms assessed, insomnia symptoms showed a statistically significant association with the pattern of cognitive symptom persistence.

There was no statistically significant association between SARS-CoV-2 vaccination status and persistence of post-COVID-19 cognitive symptoms, contrasting with prior evidence of a protective effect of vaccination on long COVID.
Pre-existing comorbidities, assessed via a modified Charlson comorbidity index, were not significantly associated with development of persistent cognitive symptoms after COVID-19.

A substantial proportion (13.0%–58.7%) of patients with post-acute COVID-19 syndrome meet diagnostic criteria for myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), reflecting overlapping pathophysiology between the two conditions.

Longitudinal UK Biobank brain imaging data showed that individuals who had COVID-19 exhibited reduced gray matter thickness in the orbitofrontal cortex and parahippocampal gyrus, decreased overall brain volume, and accelerated cognitive decline compared to controls, even among non-hospitalized cases.
A trend toward a higher proportion of sedentary patients was observed in the persistent cognitive symptom group compared to the remission group, though this did not reach statistical significance.
A trend toward a lower proportion of smokers was observed among patients with persistent cognitive symptoms compared to those with remission, though this did not reach statistical significance.
Approximately 10% of all SARS-CoV-2 infections, an estimated 65 million people globally, go on to develop post-acute SARS-CoV-2 (PASC) neuropathic sequelae.
PASC neuropathic symptoms are reported to be associated with greater disease severity, elevated body mass index, preexisting psychological conditions, and a history of addiction.
Sex differences appear to influence the prevalence of PASC-related neuropathic pain.
Mood disorders, fatigue, and cognitive dysfunction are described as contributing to altered pain perception in the multisystem presentation of PASC.
Proposed mechanisms underlying PASC-related neuropathic pain include immune dysregulation, persistent effects of viral proteins, and neuroanatomical changes.
Management of PASC-related neuropathic pain typically involves a multimodal treatment approach.

Mice inoculated with IAV alone (MC group) had a survival rate of 75% by dpi14, with deaths at dpi8, dpi12 and dpi13, whereas all Model group mice (which received oseltamivir plus fatigue induction) and all NC mice survived.

Both MC and Model group mice lost body weight rapidly during the first 7 days post-infection then slowly recovered, with significantly lower average body weight than NC mice, but no significant difference between MC and Model groups overall.
The MC group (infected, untreated) had a significantly higher pulmonary index than both the NC group and the Model group (infected, treated and fatigue-induced).
IAV NP mRNA expression was low and did not differ significantly between the NC, MC, and Model groups, indicating negative/resolved viral expression consistent with the convalescent phase.
Lung IL-10 expression was considerably higher in the Model group (fatigue-induced convalescent mice) than in both the NC and MC groups.
TNF-α and IL-6 lung expression were highest in the MC group (untreated infection) compared with NC and Model groups, and were reduced in the Model group relative to MC.

Histology showed the MC group had fused alveolar septa, thickened alveolar walls, and heavy macrophage infiltration, while the Model group had partially destroyed but largely intact alveolar structure with only limited neutrophil/macrophage infiltration and no substantial exudate, consistent with a recovering rather than acutely inflamed lung.
NC group mice swam significantly longer before exhaustion than both the MC and Model groups, while no significant difference was found between MC and Model, confirming a shared fatigue phenotype.
Serum LDH and MDA levels were highest in the MC group, followed by the Model group, both higher than NC, indicating oxidative stress and tissue damage persisting into convalescence.
Serum SOD activity was lowest in the MC group and highest in the NC group, inversely tracking LDH and MDA levels across groups.

Electron microscopy showed normal mitochondrial morphology in NC mice, whereas both MC and Model groups exhibited mitochondrial swelling, autophagosomes and autolysosomes, indicating mitochondrial damage and increased autophagy in both infected/fatigued groups.
The Model group (post-infection fatigue model) had the lowest spleen and thymus indices of the three groups, with significant differences compared to NC and MC, indicating immune organ atrophy.

Histology showed the Model group had markedly reduced thymocyte density in the medulla, significant thymic atrophy, and fuzzy cortex-medulla boundaries, more severe than the unclear thymic corpuscles and mild atrophy seen in the MC group.

Administering oseltamivir (0.2275 mg per 10 g body weight per day, oral gavage for 5 days) within 24 h of viral inoculation in the Model group avoided the severe lung damage and high mortality seen when IAV infection was combined with the subsequent fatigue-induction regimen, improving model reproducibility and stability.

The authors propose that this influenza-convalescence fatigue mouse model, while not fully equivalent to post-viral fatigue syndrome, shares symptom similarities (fatigue, mitochondrial dysfunction, chronic inflammation) with post-viral fatigue syndrome and post-COVID-19 condition, and may have reference value for future Long COVID or other post-viral pneumonia animal models.
A genome-wide significant locus upstream of FOXP4 was identified for long COVID, with the C allele of rs9367106 increasing risk.
The FOXP4 association replicated in an independent set of eight cohorts.
The FOXP4 lead variants replicated in the VA Million Veteran Program using the broad control definition.
The FOXP4 lead variants also replicated in VA MVP using the strict (recovered SARS-CoV-2) control definition.

Consistent, though sub-genome-wide-significant, associations of rs9367106-C with long COVID were seen across the other three GWAS meta-analysis case/control definitions (broad/broad, strict/strict, broad/strict).
The long COVID risk allele (proxy rs12660421-A) was associated with increased FOXP4 expression in lung tissue.
The long COVID risk allele was also associated with increased FOXP4 expression in the hypothalamus.
Colocalization analysis showed that the long COVID association signal at the FOXP4 locus is the same signal driving differential FOXP4 expression in lung.
The FOXP4 locus association with long COVID was shown by colocalization to represent the same genetic signal as the association with COVID-19 hospitalization severity.

In blood samples collected without active SARS-CoV-2 infection, higher FOXP4 expression was associated with increased risk of long COVID, providing orthogonal (protein/transcript) evidence supporting the genetic finding.
FOXP4 expression levels measured during acute COVID-19 infection were not associated with subsequent long COVID risk.
Single-cell atlas data showed FOXP4 expression was highest in type 2 alveolar cells (and nearly as high in granulocytes), independent of SARS-CoV-2 infection status.

Statistical fine mapping identified rs9381074 as the variant with the highest posterior probability of being causal at the FOXP4 locus, supported by regulatory/methylation and transcription factor binding evidence.
The long COVID risk allele at FOXP4 was also associated with lung cancer in a PheWAS of Biobank Japan.
Colocalization analysis supported that long COVID and lung cancer associations at the FOXP4 locus share the same underlying genetic signal.
Long COVID showed nominally significant positive genetic correlations with insomnia symptoms, depression, risk tolerance, asthma, diabetes and SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Long COVID showed negative genetic correlations with red and white blood cell counts.
SNP-based heritability estimates for long COVID were low overall, varying by case/control definition.

Mendelian randomization suggested earlier smoking initiation, more cigarettes consumed per day, higher HDL cholesterol and higher BMI as nominally significant causal risk factors for long COVID, though none survived multiple-testing correction.
Mendelian randomization showed a causal relationship between genetically predicted SARS-CoV-2 infection susceptibility and long COVID risk, with no evidence of pleiotropy.

Mendelian randomization showed a causal relationship between genetically predicted COVID-19 hospitalization and long COVID risk; the FOXP4 variant's effect on long COVID was larger than expected from this relationship alone.
Bayesian mixture modeling showed the ABO and 3p21.31 loci had shared genetic effects on both SARS-CoV-2 susceptibility and long COVID.
Bayesian mixture modeling showed the FOXP4 variant has a joint effect on COVID-19 severity and long COVID, but with a disproportionately larger effect on long COVID than other severity variants.

Long COVID showed nominally significant positive genetic correlations with insomnia symptoms, depression, risk tolerance, asthma, diabetes and SARS-CoV-2 infection, and negative genetic correlations with red and white blood cell counts.

SNP-based heritability of long COVID on the observed scale ranged from 0.97% to 12.36% depending on case/control definition, with the highest heritability seen using the strict case and strict control definitions.

Mendelian randomization suggested genetically predicted earlier smoking initiation, more cigarettes consumed per day, higher HDL cholesterol and higher BMI as nominally significant causal risk factors for long COVID, though none survived correction for multiple comparisons.
Two-sample Mendelian randomization showed that genetic susceptibility to SARS-CoV-2 infection causally increases risk of long COVID, with no evidence of horizontal pleiotropy.
Mendelian randomization showed that COVID-19 hospitalization (a proxy for disease severity) causally increases risk of long COVID, robust to sensitivity analyses.

The effect of the FOXP4 variant on long COVID was significantly larger than expected based on its association with COVID-19 hospitalization alone, indicating an independent contribution of FOXP4 to long COVID risk beyond acute disease severity.
Bayesian mixture modeling indicated that the ABO locus contributes to both SARS-CoV-2 infection susceptibility and long COVID with high posterior probability of a shared genetic signal.
The 3p21.31 locus (rs73062389), a known SARS-CoV-2 susceptibility locus, also showed a high posterior probability of a shared genetic effect on long COVID.

Bayesian mixture modeling of COVID-19 severity variants and long COVID showed that the FOXP4 variant has a joint effect on both traits but with a disproportionately larger effect on long COVID compared to other severity-associated variants.

The FOXP4 risk allele showed a stronger association with long COVID before COVID-19 vaccination and with wild-type/Alpha SARS-CoV-2 strains, though the signal remained even after adjusting for vaccination status or severity.
In the Estonian Biobank, higher long COVID risk associated with the FOXP4 locus was replicated for earlier SARS-CoV-2 strains, particularly the Alpha variant.
A time-to-event Cox proportional hazards analysis in FinnGen from 2020 to spring 2023 showed a significant temporal association between the FOXP4 risk variant and long COVID diagnosis.

Homozygosity for the FOXP4 risk allele conferred a substantially increased risk of long COVID under a recessive model, with consistent patterns observed in the Estonian Biobank and MexGene-COVID cohorts.

In symptom-stratified analyses of FinnGen and MVP, the FOXP4 risk variant was consistently associated with long COVID cases having fatigue, asthma diagnoses, and use of beta-adrenergic inhalants and proton pump inhibitor medications, replicating across both cohorts.
Participants with long COVID had significantly lower EQ-5D-5L utility scores at the 4-month visit compared to recovered participants, with no improvement over time relative to recovered participants.
Long COVID status was associated with a lower perceived global health score (EQ-VAS) at the 4-month follow-up compared to recovered participants, without significant change over time.
Long COVID status was associated with significantly lower Personal Wellbeing Index scores at the 8-month visit, with no significant change in this difference over time.
Participants with long COVID had markedly lower odds of agreeing they had fully recovered from COVID-19 at 8 months compared to recovered participants.

Participants with long COVID had lower odds of agreeing they had returned to pre-COVID-19 work at 8 months compared to recovered participants, although a greater proportion agreed with return to work at later visits.
Participants with long COVID had lower odds of agreeing they had returned to usual daily activities at 8 months compared to recovered participants, with sustained impairment through 24 months.
Participants with long COVID had lower odds of agreeing they had returned to normal exercise levels at 8 months compared to recovered participants, with sustained impairment through 24 months.
Long COVID status was associated with higher anxiety/depression symptom scores at 4 months postinfection, with no significant change in this difference over time.
Long COVID status was associated with higher chronic fatigue symptom scores at 4 months postinfection compared to recovered participants.
Among participants with long COVID, chronic fatigue symptoms showed a significant reduction over time through 24 months postinfection, unlike most other measured domains.
Participants with long COVID had substantially higher odds of reporting more severe breathlessness compared to recovered participants, with no change in this difference over time.

Non-COVID-19 control participants (those with other respiratory infections or epidemiological SARS-CoV-2 exposure) had similar SPHERE anxiety/depression and chronic fatigue scores compared to recovered COVID-19 participants.

Among 172 participants with mild/moderate index SARS-CoV-2 infection, 37% (64/172) met the study's long COVID definition (persistent chest pain, shortness of breath, or fatigue/malaise) at a median of 132 days postinfection.
A greater proportion of participants with long COVID had EQ-5D-5L utility scores below the lower 95% CI of Australian population norms at all visits compared to recovered participants.
A greater proportion of participants with long COVID had global health scores below the lower 95% CI of population norms at all visits compared to recovered participants.
In situ hybridization of epipharyngeal mucosa showed IL-6 mRNA expression was significantly lower in patients treated with EAT compared with untreated patients with chronic epipharyngitis.
TNF-alpha mRNA expression in epipharyngeal mucosa was significantly lower in EAT-treated patients than untreated patients with chronic epipharyngitis.
Sialylated Cav1.2 mRNA expression, a receptor targeted by influenza A virus, was significantly decreased in epipharyngeal mucosa of EAT-treated patients.
ACE2 mRNA expression, the SARS-CoV-2 cell-entry receptor, was significantly decreased in epipharyngeal mucosa after EAT treatment.
TMPRSS2 mRNA expression, required for SARS-CoV-2 cell entry, was significantly decreased in epipharyngeal mucosa after EAT treatment.
Residual SARS-CoV-2 spike mRNA detected in epipharyngeal mucosa of a long COVID patient disappeared after EAT, concurrent with decreased IL-6 and TNF-alpha mRNA.
Exhaled nitric oxide concentration positively correlated with the severity of endoscopic epipharyngeal inflammation, and continued EAT reduced exhaled NO alongside symptom and endoscopic recovery.

CD4 cell numbers in epipharyngeal leak fluid were significantly higher in chronic epipharyngitis patients than in healthy subjects, and repeated EAT significantly decreased CD4 cell numbers in parallel with symptom recovery.
