Among 604 hospitalized COVID-19 patients during the Delta wave, 66 (10.9%) died during hospitalization while 538 (89.1%) were discharged.
Male patients had a higher in-hospital mortality rate (27.1%) than female patients (19.9%).
Patients over 60 years had the highest mortality both during admission (34.9%) and post-discharge (22.8%), while no post-discharge deaths occurred among patients under 18.
Unvaccinated patients had the highest mortality rates during admission (38.1%) and post-discharge (13.4%), whereas vaccinated patients, even with a single dose, had no reported deaths.
Patients with severe disease and those requiring invasive ventilation both had a 44.8% in-hospital mortality rate.

Antiviral treatment was associated with a higher unadjusted in-hospital mortality rate (25.2%), likely reflecting confounding by indication since antivirals were preferentially given to sicker patients.
Patients with hospital stays longer than two weeks had the highest post-discharge mortality rate (66.7%).
Male sex was associated with higher odds of severe illness in the unadjusted model, but this association lost significance after adjustment for other factors.
Patients over 60 had significantly higher adjusted odds of severe illness compared to younger patients.
Patients who did not receive antiviral treatment had significantly higher adjusted odds of severe illness.
Unvaccinated patients had significantly higher adjusted odds of severe illness than vaccinated patients.
Male patients had significantly lower adjusted odds of survival compared to females.
Patients over 60 had much lower adjusted odds of survival than younger patients.
Lack of antiviral treatment was strongly associated with lower adjusted odds of survival.
At one-year post-discharge follow-up, shortness of breath was the most commonly reported long COVID symptom, affecting 14 of 331 patients (4.2%), most frequently in the >60 age group.
Chronic cough was reported by 5 of 331 patients (1.5%) at one-year follow-up, distributed across age groups.
At the one-year mark, the large majority of patients (79.15%) reported no long COVID symptoms, while only a small minority reported multiple persisting symptoms.
Age significantly affected quality-of-life scores at one year: patients under 18 had the highest PCS and MCS, while patients over 60 had lower PCS but similar MCS.
Gender showed no significant differences in either PCS or MCS scores at one-year follow-up.
Contrary to expectation, patients with severe initial illness and those with comorbidities scored higher on PCS than others at one-year follow-up.
Occupational group significantly differed in PCS scores, with government/healthcare workers reporting higher physical quality-of-life scores.
Longer hospital stays (>2 weeks) were associated with drastically reduced physical quality-of-life scores at one year, while shorter stays were associated with better PCS and MCS.
In multivariate analysis, being aged under 60 (versus over 60) was significantly associated with higher odds of better physical component summary scores.
Normal BMI was significantly linked to better physical component summary scores compared to being overweight.
Absence of comorbidities significantly improved physical component summary scores at one year.
Employed individuals had significantly lower physical component summary scores than unemployed individuals.
No significant associations were found between mental component summary scores and gender, age, BMI, comorbidity, or employment status.
Minor long COVID symptoms including palpitations, vertigo, loss of taste and smell, and hair loss were each reported by only one patient (0.3%), all within the 18-60 age group, at one-year follow-up.
Poor sleep, brain fog, and constipation were each reported by 2 patients (0.6%) in the 18-60 age group at one-year follow-up.
The majority of patients (79.15%) had no long COVID symptoms at one-year follow-up, with only a small minority reporting two or more symptoms.
Gender showed no significant difference in Physical or Mental Component Summary quality-of-life scores among discharged patients.
Age significantly affected quality-of-life scores, with patients under 18 having the highest physical and mental scores and patients over 60 having lower physical scores but comparable mental scores.
Severity of illness and presence of comorbidity were associated with higher Physical Component Summary scores, contrary to expectation.
Occupational group significantly affected physical quality-of-life scores, with government/healthcare workers reporting higher PCS scores.

Longer hospital stay (>2 weeks) was associated with drastically reduced physical quality-of-life scores at one-year follow-up, while shorter stays were associated with better physical and mental scores.
Being aged under 60 was significantly associated with higher Physical Component Summary scores compared to patients over 60 in multivariate analysis.
Normal BMI was associated with better Physical Component Summary scores compared to being overweight.
Absence of comorbidities significantly improved Physical Component Summary scores in multivariate analysis.
Employed individuals had lower Physical Component Summary scores compared to unemployed individuals.
Gender and disease severity level were not significantly associated with Physical Component Summary scores in multivariate analysis.
No significant associations were found between Mental Component Summary scores and gender, age, BMI, comorbidity, or employment status.
Moderate severity cases showed a non-significant trend toward higher Mental Component Summary scores.
Skin biopsy showed abnormal small nerve fiber findings in 14 of 17 (82%) long COVID patients with post-infectious neuropathic pain, supporting a diagnosis of small fiber neuropathy.
Among patients with post-infectious neuropathic pain, 12/17 (70%) reported autonomic complaints, and all of these had abnormal skin biopsy findings consistent with small fiber neuropathy.
Quantitative sensory testing (QST) had the highest diagnostic performance among noninvasive tests for detecting small fiber neuropathy, with 79% sensitivity and 67% specificity.
Laser evoked potential (LEP) recording showed moderate diagnostic performance for small fiber neuropathy, with 71% sensitivity and 67% specificity.
Electrochemical skin conductance (Sudoscan) performed poorly as a screening tool for small fiber neuropathy, with only 7% sensitivity and 50% specificity.
At 6-month follow-up, 10 of 17 patients reported subjective improvement in pain and/or dysautonomia, with or without pharmacological or non-pharmacological treatment.
In a case-control comparison of 100 COVID-19 survivors, those with long COVID had significantly lower serum vitamin D levels than those without long COVID six months after hospitalization.
Vitamin D deficiency in NHS healthcare workers was associated with a greater number and longer duration of COVID-19 symptoms, particularly fatigue and body aches.
In long COVID outpatients, zinc deficiency and vitamin D deficiency co-occurred, with a significant positive correlation between zinc and vitamin D levels.

An 8-week double-blind RCT of weekly high-dose vitamin D supplementation (60,000 IU) in post-COVID-19 syndrome significantly improved fatigue, anxiety, and cognitive function, but showed no effect on depression, sleep quality, or inflammatory markers.

A 24-week RCT of combined vitamin K2/D3 supplementation in long COVID significantly reduced symptoms, improved inflammatory and oxidative stress markers, decreased fungal translocation, and enhanced gut barrier integrity.
Combined magnesium and vitamin D supplementation in long COVID patients significantly improved depression, with a much higher remission rate than vitamin D alone.

Multiple observational studies (Townsend, Kaddah, Hikmet, Wu, CovILD cohort) found no significant association between vitamin D levels and long COVID symptom burden, fatigue, exercise tolerance, or inflammatory markers, despite high rates of deficiency.
A multicenter RCT of a single high dose of vitamin D3 in hospitalized COVID-19 patients found no benefit on persistent symptoms or quality of life at 6- and 12-months post-discharge.
A pilot study combining oral vitamin A supplementation with olfactory training improved smell function and neural activity in the olfactory network in long COVID.
An open-label RCT of high-dose vitamin B1 (600 mg/day) significantly improved fatigue, myalgia, anosmia, and sleep issues in long COVID.
A 19-nutrient multinutrient formula reduced fatigue and improved quality of life, strength, and endurance in long COVID patients over 28 days.
An 8-week multicomponent amino acid and Krebs cycle intermediate supplement significantly improved muscle mass, physical performance, and quality of life in COVID-19 survivors compared to controls.
A supplement combining acetyl-L-carnitine, hydroxytyrosol, and vitamins B, C, and D significantly improved self-perceived energy and reduced tiredness and tension after 15 days compared to non-users.

A supplement with vitamins, trace elements, probiotics, lactoferrin, lysozyme and resveratrol improved six-minute walking distance more than controls after six weeks in long COVID patients with reduced exercise capacity, but showed no difference in strength or symptoms.
A randomized placebo-controlled trial found that fermented papaya and Noni supplementation significantly reduced fatigue, cognitive symptoms, and joint pain in post-COVID-19 patients over 20 days.
Fermented papaya and Noni supplementation decreased IL-6, TNF-alpha, and oxidative stress markers in post-COVID-19 patients.
A 14-day micronutrient formula given at illness onset corrected deficiencies but did not reduce long COVID prevalence at 180 days compared to placebo.
A 2-month placebo-controlled trial of a botanical/micronutrient oral food supplement reduced inflammatory markers, improved vitamin D status, and improved fatigue and quality of life.

A 28-day RCT of L-arginine plus liposomal vitamin C significantly improved serum L-arginine concentrations and L-arginine/ADMA ratios in long COVID patients, suggesting enhanced nitric oxide bioavailability and vascular function.

In the LINCOLN nationwide survey of 1390 long COVID patients, those given L-arginine with vitamin C reported significantly lower symptom scores after 30 days compared to those given a multivitamin formulation.
In routine care, arginine-based formulations (Astenor Energy and Astenor Forte) taken for three months led to significant reductions in fatigue among long COVID patients.
An 8-week double-blind trial of creatine supplementation increased brain creatine levels and significantly improved long COVID symptoms including fatigue, headaches, and cognitive issues.

A separate 6-month RCT of daily creatine supplementation increased creatine levels in muscle and brain tissue and reduced fatigue and other long COVID symptoms including ageusia and breathing difficulties.

A 28-day RCT of L-arginine plus liposomal vitamin C significantly increased serum L-arginine concentrations and L-arginine/ADMA ratios in long COVID patients, suggesting improved nitric oxide bioavailability.
In the nationwide LINCOLN survey of 1390 long COVID patients, those receiving L-arginine with vitamin C reported significantly lower symptom scores after 30 days than those receiving a multivitamin.

In routine care, 505 patients treated with arginine-based formulations (Astenor Energy or Astenor Forte) showed significant reductions in fatigue after three months, with 68.7% reporting no fatigue compared to 27.7% at baseline.

An 8-week double-blind trial found that creatine supplementation (with or without glucose) increased brain creatine levels and significantly improved fatigue, headaches, and cognitive issues in long COVID patients compared to placebo.

A separate 6-month RCT of 4 g daily creatine in 12 patients significantly increased creatine levels in muscle and brain tissue and reduced fatigue and other long COVID symptoms including ageusia and breathing difficulties.

A six-week open-label trial of anhydrous enol-oxaloacetate (500-1000 mg up to three times daily) significantly improved Chalder Fatigue Questionnaire scores in both ME/CFS and long COVID patients, with dose-dependent reductions and up to 46.8% fatigue improvement in the long COVID group.

The Phyto-V RCT found that a phytochemical-rich nutritional capsule plus probiotic significantly reduced fatigue and cough and improved well-being in symptomatic COVID-19 patients, especially those with prolonged symptoms, older age, sedentary lifestyle, prior hospitalization, and GI issues.
A four-week pilot paraprobiotic intervention in six long COVID patients showed improvements in fatigue, dysautonomia, and depression along with reduced immune activation markers.

In a large RCT of 463 individuals with long COVID, the synbiotic SIM01 significantly alleviated fatigue, memory loss, brain fog, gastrointestinal disturbances, and general unwellness after six months, alongside increased gut microbial diversity, enrichment of Bifidobacterium adolescentis and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, and suppression of urea cycle and antimicrobial resistance gene pathways.

A 14-day RCT of nitrate-rich beetroot juice in 31 patients found no significant between-group differences, though the beetroot group showed improved fatigue resistance, walking distance, and increases in beneficial gut bacteria (Akkermansia, Roseburia) and shifts in cytokines including interferon-gamma and MIP-1beta.

High adherence to the Mediterranean diet was correlated with lower LDL cholesterol, glucose, and LDH levels and beneficial gut microbiota shifts, with extra virgin olive oil intake associated with anti-inflammatory microbiome-mediated effects.

A three-month RCT in 26 patients with post-COVID ME/CFS found that a synbiotic containing probiotics, prebiotics, and zinc led to greater reductions in post-exertional malaise and increased brain choline and creatine levels compared to controls, with both groups improving in fatigue.

In a large UK Biobank cohort, adherence to 6-10 healthy behaviors—including a diet high in fruits and vegetables, adequate oily fish intake, and low processed meat consumption—was associated with a 36% lower risk of developing multisystem post-COVID-19 sequelae, with protective effects across fatigue, cardiometabolic, neurological, and respiratory symptom domains.

In the NUTRICOVID study, 76% of 199 ICU survivors were at nutritional risk at hospital discharge by MUST criteria, with 35% still at risk one year later and approximately 25% showing sarcopenia despite nutritional support.

In a French cohort of 288 post-hospitalized COVID-19 patients, 36% remained malnourished six months after discharge, with 15% reporting persistent muscle weakness and reduced physical performance; obesity and ICU admission predicted worse outcomes.

Among 48 ICU survivors followed for one year in the Netherlands, most regained baseline weight and physical performance, but body composition remained altered, with elevated fat mass index in half and low fat-free mass index in 19%, alongside nutritional intake below resting energy expenditure and protein needs.

Among 66 Mexican COVID-19 pneumonia survivors referred for rehabilitation, protein deficiency, muscle thickness, handgrip strength, respiratory function, and quality of life improved over time, though delayed referral and excess weight were associated with poorer six-minute walk performance.

In a Malaysian cohort, young adults recovered from COVID-19 exhibited significantly lower dietary diversity than healthy controls, while sleep quality and weight change did not differ significantly, and neither factor correlated with weight outcomes.

In a Serbian cross-sectional study of 76 working-age adults within six months of PCR-confirmed COVID-19, physical activity (especially aerobic/high-intensity exercise) was reduced and fatigue was reported by 23.7%, while dietary patterns remained largely stable except for a significant increase in water intake.

In Portugal, a 30-day multidisciplinary program combining physiotherapy, speech therapy, and individualized ESPEN-guided nutritional support improved BMI, handgrip strength, and MNA® scores among 118 older adults, particularly ICU survivors.

An 8-week lifestyle program in Brazil for 55 overweight/obese COVID-19 survivors, combining psychoeducation, physical activity, and group-based nutritional education, produced significant improvements in psychological well-being, anxiety, depression, and quality of life.

A companion study of the same Brazilian lifestyle program reported physical benefits including reduced fat mass, increased lean mass, enhanced handgrip strength, and smaller waist circumference, relevant to post-COVID-19 fatigue and functional recovery.

In a secondary analysis of a 12-week RCT in Germany involving 46 individuals with post-COVID-19 fatigue, participants showed healthier eating habits (greater Mediterranean diet adherence, higher omega-3 and vitamin C intake) than controls, but no clear association emerged between nutrient intake and fatigue severity.

The ReDIRECT RCT in the UK evaluated a remotely delivered weight-loss program (12 weeks of 850 kcal/day total diet replacement) in 234 adults with long COVID-19 and found significantly greater improvement in participants' dominant long COVID-19 symptom compared to controls.

In the BioICOPER study, higher adherence to the Mediterranean diet among 305 adults with long COVID-19 in Spain was significantly associated with lower BMI, waist circumference, uric acid levels, and fewer metabolic syndrome components, as well as higher HDL cholesterol.

Global background epidemiology indicates roughly 400 million cumulative long covid cases with prevalence estimates spanning ~5% in selected volunteer samples to 87% in hospitalised patients assessed two months post-infection.
Over 90% of individuals with long covid had mild acute COVID-19 and did not require hospitalisation, highlighting a gap in understanding of long covid in the general (non-hospitalised) population.

Long covid (ongoing symptomatic COVID-19/post-COVID-19 syndrome) was defined per NICE guidelines as one or more symptoms consistent with COVID-19 persisting 4-12 weeks or beyond 12 weeks with no alternative diagnosis, and cases did not need to be symptomatic at clinic attendance to be classified as having had long covid.

The CONVALESCENCE deep phenotyping study recruited 349 participants from ALSPAC and TwinsUK: 141 long covid cases and three control groups (89, 75 and 44 participants) defined by combinations of long covid symptom status and SARS-CoV-2 serostatus.
Mean BMI was numerically higher in long covid cases (27.1±6.3 kg/m²) than in the three control groups (25.8-26.4 kg/m²), though no inferential statistical test was reported.
Hypertension prevalence was similar between long covid cases (20%) and the three control groups (16%-21%), with no formal statistical comparison presented.
Asthma prevalence was broadly similar between long covid cases (18%) and control groups (13%-23%), with no formal statistical comparison presented.
Mean resting systolic blood pressure was similar across groups, ranging 117-122 mmHg, with long covid cases at 118±16 mmHg.

The study's primary hypothesis-testing outcome is a composite multiorgan abnormality score (summed severity 0-3 across lung, vascular, heart, kidney, brain, autonomic function, muscle strength, exercise capacity and physical performance domains), designed to test whether long covid is associated with multiorgan abnormalities; results are not yet reported in this cohort profile.

The study's key hypotheses are that long covid may be associated with multiorgan abnormalities, that multiorgan abnormalities may relate to symptom patterns, and that prepandemic characteristics (eg, subclinical disease) may predict susceptibility to long covid and its sequelae.
In people with Long COVID, time spent in light physical activity significantly increased between fifteen and eighteen months post-discharge.
Moderate-to-vigorous physical activity significantly decreased at fifteen months in people with Long COVID and this reduction was maintained at eighteen months.
Daily step count declined between twelve and eighteen months in people with Long COVID, though the change did not reach statistical significance.
Sedentary time decreased at fifteen months and this reduction was sustained at eighteen months in people with Long COVID.
The proportion of people with Long COVID walking fewer than 5000 steps per day increased significantly from 36% at twelve months to 61% at eighteen months.
In the control group (COVID survivors without Long COVID), no significant changes in physical activity or sedentary time were observed across the follow-up period.
Greater dyspnoea severity at twelve months was associated with lower light physical activity at eighteen months.
Greater dyspnoea severity was associated with fewer daily steps at eighteen months.
Impaired quadriceps muscle strength (QMVC ≤70% predicted) at twelve months was associated with fewer daily steps at eighteen months.
People with Long COVID consistently showed lower 6-minute walk distance than controls throughout the follow-up period.
Both people with Long COVID and controls showed significant improvement in 6-minute walk distance between twelve and eighteen months.
The proportion of people with Long COVID with impaired 6-minute walk distance significantly decreased from 27% to 17% over follow-up.
No significant changes in quadriceps muscle strength (QMVC) were observed in either the Long COVID or control group throughout the follow-up period.

A significantly higher proportion of participants with Long COVID experienced clinically relevant dyspnoea, fatigue, anxiety, depression, and impaired health-related quality of life compared to controls throughout the follow-up period.
The proportion of people with Long COVID reporting fatigue significantly decreased from 83% at twelve months to 67% at eighteen months, though remaining substantial.
At eighteen months, a substantial proportion of people with Long COVID remained symptomatic with dyspnoea, fatigue, anxiety, and depression, and half reported impaired health-related quality of life.
Only hospitalised participants (ICU and hospital ward) significantly reduced their time spent in moderate-to-vigorous physical activity between twelve and eighteen months.
The proportion of participants walking fewer than 5000 steps per day increased across all COVID-19 severity subgroups, reaching significance only in the non-hospitalised group.
People with and without Long COVID remained physically inactive throughout the 12-18 month follow-up period, not meeting WHO physical activity recommendations.
Roughly half of participants still reported at least one COVID-19-related symptom at 6 months, declining to about a third by 12 months and remaining detectable at 18 and 24 months.
Fatigue, pain, sore throat, headache, and loss of strength were the most frequently reported COVID-19-related symptoms at enrollment.

Fatigue, stiff joints, wheeziness, headaches, sleep difficulties, dizziness, and loss of strength were reported more often in participants who had severe/critical acute COVID-19 than those with mild/moderate infection.

Time to complete recovery from COVID-19-related symptoms was significantly longer for participants who had severe/critical acute infection than those with mild/moderate infection, with median recovery of 234 versus 206 days.
Participants aged 40-64 years had significantly slower recovery from COVID-19-related symptoms than those under 40 years.
Participants with tertiary education recovered from COVID-19-related symptoms almost twice as fast as those with only primary education.
There was no statistically significant difference between males and females in time to recovery from COVID-19-related symptoms.
Female participants were more likely than males to report a greater number of long COVID symptoms over time.
Individuals with tertiary education were less likely to report a higher number of long COVID symptoms compared to those with only primary education.
Having one or more comorbidities was associated with a higher risk of reporting a greater number of long COVID symptoms over time compared with having no comorbidity.
Individuals with mild/moderate initial COVID-19 severity were less likely to report a higher number of long COVID symptoms compared to those with severe/critical infection.
Each additional day since a positive PCR test was associated with a small but statistically significant reduction in the risk of reporting a greater number of long COVID symptoms.
Fatigue was significantly more likely to be reported by female participants than males over the follow-up period.
Employed participants had approximately half the adjusted odds of reporting fatigue compared to unemployed individuals.
Individuals with high socioeconomic status were 50% less likely to have fatigue compared with those with low socioeconomic status.
Individuals with mild/moderate acute SARS-CoV-2 infection were 61% less likely to have fatigue compared to those with severe/critical infection.
Each additional day since a positive PCR test was associated with a small but statistically significant decrease in risk of fatigue.
Quality of life at 12 months was significantly lower among participants who experienced COVID-19-related symptoms compared with those without symptoms.
Time since infection was not significantly associated with quality of life at 12 months after adjusting for other factors.
Participants with diagnosed or self-reported long covid had significantly higher fatigue than those without long covid, with a medium-to-large effect size.
Both the diagnosed and self-reported long covid groups reported significantly greater limitations in social roles and activities than those without long covid.
Both the diagnosed and self-reported long covid groups reported significantly greater pain interference than those without long covid.
The diagnosed long covid group had significantly greater physical function problems than the no long covid group, but the self-reported group did not differ from the other groups.
Participants with self-reported (but not diagnosed) long covid had significantly greater anxiety than the no long covid group.
Participants with self-reported (but not diagnosed) long covid had significantly greater depression than the no long covid group.
There were no significant differences between long covid groups (diagnosed, self-reported, no long covid) in sleep disturbance.
There were no significant differences between long covid groups (diagnosed, self-reported, no long covid) in eating disorder symptoms.

Both diagnosed and self-reported long covid groups reported significantly greater COVID-19 pandemic-related distress than the no long covid group, with no difference between the two long covid groups.
Hispanic adults had significantly higher odds of self-reported long covid than non-Hispanic adults, with no ethnic differences observed for diagnosed long covid.
Women reported significantly greater fatigue and pain interference than men.
Higher BMI was positively associated with greater pain interference and greater eating disorder symptoms.

Greater COVID-19 pandemic-related distress was independently associated with worse mental and physical health, including anxiety, depression, fatigue, social role limitations, pain interference, poor sleep, and eating disorder symptoms.
Children with post-COVID-19 condition (PASC) had significantly lower peak oxygen uptake than controls at initial assessment, consistent with the authors' prior cross-sectional study.
At 6-month follow-up the previously observed VO2peak deficit in PASC children compared to controls was no longer detectable, and VO2peak had significantly increased in the combined cohort over time.

Peak O2 pulse, a surrogate for cardiac stroke volume/output, improved significantly over 6 months in the combined cohort, though the improvement did not reach significance within either subgroup alone.

The VE/VCO2-slope, an index of ventilatory efficiency, decreased significantly (improved) over 6 months in the combined cohort, though this change was not significant within either subgroup individually.

The time needed for VO2peak to decrease by half (T1/2VO2), reflecting muscle/mitochondrial oxidative recovery, increased significantly over 6 months in the combined cohort, though comparable between groups at both time points.
The VO2/P-slope, reflecting oxygen delivery/utilization during exercise, improved significantly over 6 months in the control group but not in the PASC group.

No pulmonary CPET parameter (peak minute ventilation, minute ventilation at first ventilatory threshold, or breathing reserve) differed significantly between PASC and control groups at baseline or at 6-month follow-up.

Cardiac parameters including peak O2 pulse, peak heart rate, heart rate recovery, VE/VCO2-slope, and chronotropic index were comparable between PASC and control groups both at baseline and at 6-month follow-up.
Children with PASC rested from physical activity for significantly longer after SARS-CoV-2 infection than the control group.
A significantly higher proportion of children with PASC reported worse subjective exercise tolerance after SARS-CoV-2 infection compared to controls.
At the 6-month follow-up, 3 of 13 (23%) children with PASC still reported symptoms, most commonly dyspnea and cough.

Baseline cardiopulmonary exercise test parameters did not differ significantly between PASC participants who were lost to follow-up and those who completed the study, suggesting minimal attrition bias.

The combined VE/VCO2 and petCO2 parameter at the ventilatory threshold, proposed as an indicator of pulmonary hypertension, did not differ between PASC and control groups at either time point, but improved significantly within the whole cohort after 6 months.

The authors note, citing external literature, that certain genetic variants linked to endothelial dysfunction, coagulation pathways, and inflammatory responses have been associated with pulmonary hypertension in adults with long COVID, though no such genetic association was tested in this pediatric cohort.
Exercise time during CPET was significantly shorter in the PASC group than in controls at baseline, but this difference resolved by the 6-month follow-up.
The pooled prevalence of COVID-19 survivors experiencing at least one unresolved symptom 3 years after SARS-CoV-2 infection was 20%.
At least one unresolved respiratory symptom was present in 35% of survivors 3 years after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
42% of survivors had DLCO below 80% of predicted value at 3 years post-infection, the most frequent significant pulmonary function finding.
10% of survivors had FEV1 below 80% of predicted value at 3 years post-infection.
Dyspnea was present in 12% of survivors 3 years after SARS-CoV-2 infection, the most frequent significant symptom.
Fatigue was present in 11% of survivors 3 years after SARS-CoV-2 infection, a substantial reduction from 27%-28% reported at 2-year follow-up.
Smell disorder was present in 7% of survivors at 3 years, showing a worsening trend compared to 3.5% at 2 years.
Cough was present in 6% of survivors 3 years after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Expectoration was present in 4% of survivors 3 years after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Sleep difficulty prevalence of 11% at 3 years was not statistically significant, though showing decline from 25% at 2 years.
Taste disorder prevalence of 7% at 3 years was not statistically significant.
Anxiety prevalence of 6% at 3 years was not statistically significant.
Myalgia prevalence of 4% at 3 years was not statistically significant.
Hospitalized COVID-19 patients had an increased risk of death 3 years after infection compared with population controls, while nonhospitalized patients showed no significant increase.
Long COVID contributed substantially more disability-adjusted life years per 1000 persons in hospitalized than nonhospitalized survivors at year 3.
Mortality was higher among COVID-19 patients with neurological signs than those without, at 3 years post-hospitalization.

Key risk factors identified for long COVID persistence included older age, higher COVID-19 severity score at hospitalization, female sex, smoking, substance use, allergy, and having comorbidities (congestive heart failure, chronic kidney disease, hypertension, diabetes).
Use of renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system blockers before and during the pandemic had no discernible effect on reported long COVID symptoms postinfection.

Patients with substantial neurological findings after COVID-19 (e.g., stroke, new seizures) were at greater risk of worse long-term outcomes including higher mortality, neurodegenerative disease, higher readmission risk, and higher age-adjusted brain volume loss compared to those without neurological findings.

Generation of autoantibodies is proposed as a mechanism contributing to long COVID, triggering inflammation and tissue damage that could explain persistent fatigue, neurological dysfunction, and cardiovascular issues.
Persistence of SARS-CoV-2 RNA in tissues is proposed to drive ongoing immune activation and inflammation contributing to chronic long COVID symptoms.
A US CDC national survey found that 26% of long COVID patients experienced significant limitation to daily activity relative to pre-COVID period.
Across seven studies, olfactory dysfunction at 12 months post-COVID-19 ranged from 0.9% to 51% of individuals, varying by assessment method.
Four studies reported gustatory dysfunction prevalence at 12 months ranging from 1.1% to 11.76%.
Anxiety was more prevalent than depression at 12 months post-COVID-19, ranging from 3.5% to 29% across studies compared to 3.5%-26% for depression.
Fatigue was the most dominant neurocognitive complaint at 12 months, ranging from 8.2% to 56.3% across included studies.
Headache and dizziness were relatively less prevalent at 12 months, ranging 2%-16% and 3.2%-13.95% respectively across studies.
Sleep disturbances were relatively common at 12 months, ranging from 3.8% to 50% across studies, while impaired memory ranged from 3.5% to 25%.
Caspersen et al. reported that 16.9% of individuals had altered smell and taste sensations at 12 months, with a risk ratio of 49.4 versus baseline/reference.
Fortunato et al. observed loss of smell in 25.8% and loss of taste in 21.3% of individuals, with sensory symptoms persisting in 3 out of 10 patients after 12 months.

Huang et al. found significant improvement in olfactory dysfunction over time (from six to 12 months, p<0.0001), though symptoms persisted in 4% of individuals, and taste impairment improved from 6% at six months to 3% at 12 months (p<0.0001).
Strahm et al. found a higher incidence of impaired taste and smell among infected healthcare workers compared to controls (16% versus 6%).

Strahm et al. reported a statistically significant incidence of anxiety and depression in infected healthcare workers compared to non-infected controls at 12 months (p<0.001), using the GAD scale and Patient Health Questionnaire.
Zhao et al. reported a significantly higher incidence of fatigue in patients with severe acute COVID-19 (51.16%) compared to mild disease (29.41%) at 12 months (p=0.032).

Rass et al. objectively assessed olfactory function using the Sniffin' Sticks identification test and found hyposmia in 51% of patients after one year, with anxiety in 29%, depression in 6%, headache in 16%, dizziness in 12%, sleep difficulty in 22%, fatigue in 38%, and forgetfulness in 25% of patients.
The discussion cites proposed mechanisms for persistence of olfactory/neurological symptoms, including ACE2 receptor expression levels and chronic inflammation.
The severity of depressive symptoms was reported to correlate with systemic inflammation during acute COVID-19 infection, per a cited study by Mazza et al.

Zhang et al. found higher rates of severe anxiety (12.1%) compared to non-severe anxiety (10.3%), and higher fatigue prevalence in the severe acute disease group (35.9%) versus non-severe group (25.8%).

Zhao et al. and Zhou et al. found statistically non-significant differences in the persistence of headache, dizziness, sleep disturbance, and fatigue between mild and severe acute-disease groups (p-values ranging 0.067-0.563), except for fatigue in Zhao et al. which was significant.
Under the WHO long COVID definition, naïve prevalence (67.4%) and confounder-adjusted prevalence (66.1%) were similar among ARCOVID participants.
At 3 months post-infection, naïve LC prevalence (80.2%) was similar to the bivariate-probit-adjusted prevalence (81.1%).
At 6 months post-infection, naïve LC prevalence (79.6%) closely matched adjusted prevalence (79.7%).
The bivariate probit selection-outcome correlation (Rho) was positive and statistically significant for LC at 3 months and 6 months, indicating meaningful residual sample selection bias.
Under the WHO definition, the selection-outcome correlation (Rho) was not statistically significant, indicating an absence of detectable sample selection bias for that definition.
Female sex significantly more than doubled the odds of developing long COVID across all three LC definitions modeled.
Individuals aged 40-50 had substantially greater odds of long COVID at 3 and 6 months compared with those aged 18-30, though age was not a significant predictor under the WHO definition.
Pre-existing cardiovascular disease significantly increased the odds of long COVID under the WHO definition, but not under the 3- or 6-month symptom definitions.
Pre-existing metabolic disease significantly increased odds of long COVID at 3 and 6 months post-infection, but was not significant under the WHO definition.
Pre-COVID use of antiplatelet (antiaggregant) medication was associated with markedly reduced odds of long COVID under the WHO and 3-month definitions.
Pre-COVID statin use was associated with a protective effect against long COVID at 6 months.
Pre-COVID use of hypoglycemic agents, particularly metformin, was consistently protective against long COVID across all definitions.
Use of antiretroviral therapy during the acute phase of COVID-19 was protective against long COVID across all definitions.

Hydroxychloroquine, antibiotics, and COVID-19 vaccination during/around the acute phase were each identified as risk factors increasing the odds of long COVID, with similar effect magnitudes across all definitions.
Fatigue was the most prevalent long COVID symptom overall, followed by dyspnea and joint/muscle pain.

Dyspnea showed a significant residual sample-selection effect even after adjustment, suggesting unmeasured (possibly neurological or brain-related) factors contribute to its persistence as a long COVID symptom.

After accounting for confounders and selection bias, there was no significant effect of pandemic wave (first vs second) on the likelihood of developing long COVID, although crude prevalence was lower in the second wave.

In mice, FOXP2 acts as a negative regulator of MEF2C during the early postnatal period, likely promoting synaptogenesis in the cortical striatum.

Polymorphisms in the FARS2-LYRM4 bidirectional promoter region have been shown to be associated with cognitive deficit and schizophrenia.

A Kenyan Long Covid patient (Kawera) reported hallucinations, deteriorating eyesight, hair loss, cognitive changes, and profound fatigue following overexertion after apparent recovery from acute COVID-19, describing a post-exertional 'crash'.

A second Kenyan Long Covid patient (Awiti) developed new-onset diabetes, pneumonia with pulmonary fluid accumulation, chronic cough, fatigue, memory loss, hallucinations, and progressive loss of mobility in the months following her acute COVID-19 illness.

Long Covid patients in Kenya, exemplified by Awiti, experienced social stigma and disbelief, being labeled 'lazy' or disorganized rather than recognized as having a genuine post-viral illness, which contributed to isolation.

Clinicians dismissed Kawera's persistent post-COVID symptoms as psychological, telling her that COVID-19 only causes symptoms for a few days and suggesting she seek therapy for personal issues instead, reflecting a broader pattern of medical gaslighting reported among Long Covid patients.

Joining a peer-led Long Covid Facebook support group and hearing another patient (Kawera) publicly describe matching symptoms helped Awiti recognize her symptoms as real rather than laziness or depression, which she associated with improved mental and subsequent physical wellbeing.

Kawera reported that a combination of medications, mental health treatment, and life changes recommended by a functional medicine doctor was associated with improvement in her physical Long Covid symptoms.

Awiti reported that local herbal remedies (ginger, garlic, aloe vera) combined with a dietary shift toward fruits and protein were associated with resolution of most of her Long Covid symptoms by mid-2023, including hair regrowth and improved cold/heat tolerance.
Despite reporting near-complete healing, Awiti later experienced a return of some Long Covid symptoms months after the initial interview, illustrating a relapsing course of the condition.

Digital and socioeconomic access differentiated Kenyan Long Covid patients' ability to obtain diagnosis, functional medicine testing, and treatment: 'elite' patients with international network access and financial resources (e.g., Kawera) had greater ability to investigate and treat their illness than less digitally-connected 'non-elite' patients.
Long Covid is rarely formally diagnosed in Kenya, so few people identify with the condition even though many are likely managing persistent post-viral symptoms.

Some projections cited by the authors estimate that up to two in three people on the African continent had been infected with COVID-19 by 2021, despite official reports suggesting lower prevalence and milder disease attributed to younger populations.
Nasal epithelial transcriptomes from long COVID patients at both 3-6 months and 12-18 months post-COVID were associated with inflammatory pathways.
Transcriptomic and cellular clusters identified in the nasal epithelium of long COVID patients were related to inflammation and ciliogenesis.
Comparison of nasal epithelial transcriptomes from long COVID patients with versus without pulmonary radiological abnormalities revealed 613 significantly differentially expressed genes.
Patients with pulmonary radiological abnormalities showed upregulation of inflammatory genes in the nasal epithelium compared with those without abnormalities.

SMURF1 expression was significantly increased in the nasal epithelium of long COVID patients with pulmonary radiological abnormalities compared with those without abnormalities and compared with healthy controls.
CRISPR/Cas9-generated SMURF1 mutant primary nasal epithelial cells produced significantly lower levels of proinflammatory cytokines upon virus exposure compared with control cells.
Long COVID is presented as an infection-associated chronic condition that is heterogeneous and best conceptualized as a group of related conditions rather than a single entity.
Greater fatigue severity was significantly correlated with worse self-reported (subjective) cognitive abilities in PASC patients.
Fatigue severity was not significantly correlated with objectively measured cognitive performance despite correlating with subjective cognitive complaints.
Greater fatigue severity was significantly correlated with greater depression symptoms in PASC patients.
Fatigue severity was significantly correlated with several measures of rest-activity rhythm disruption measured by wrist actigraphy.
Fatigue severity was significantly correlated with measures of light exposure disruption measured by wrist actigraphy.
Fatigue severity was significantly correlated with greater actigraphy-measured total sleep time and time in bed.
In a multivariable model, fatigue severity was independently and significantly associated with subjective cognitive abilities, depression symptoms, and rest-activity rhythm disruption.

Plasma IL-10 levels were consistently higher in PASC patients reporting gastrointestinal symptoms, chest pain, change in sense of smell/taste, brain fog, fatigue, or palpitation compared with patients without these symptoms.
VEGF levels were commonly elevated in participants experiencing gastrointestinal symptoms, chest pain, post-exertional malaise, fatigue, or brain fog compared with those without these symptoms.

Participants with gastrointestinal symptoms showed the widest cytokine variation of any symptom examined, with significantly higher IL-10, VEGF, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, MIP-1α, MCP-1, granzyme A, and IL-9 compared with those without gastrointestinal symptoms.
FasL levels were significantly higher in participants with post-exertional malaise or fatigue than in those without these symptoms.
I-TAC (CXCL11) levels were significantly higher in participants with post-exertional malaise or fatigue than in those without these symptoms.
IFN-α levels were significantly higher in participants with post-exertional malaise or fatigue than in those without these symptoms.
sCD40L levels, alongside VEGF, were increased in participants with PASC symptoms, consistent with prior reports linking platelet activation to vascular damage in PASC.
Elevated levels of CX3CL1 and RANTES, ligands of CX3CR1 and CCR5 respectively, were observed, suggesting a role for monocyte-mediated vessel damage in PASC pathophysiology.
Symptom cluster 3, comprising chronic cough, dizziness, dyspnea, and hair loss, showed no significant differences in cytokine levels compared to participants without these symptoms.
Plasma SARS-CoV-2 spike S1 IgG antibody titer was not associated with the presence of any PASC symptom, in contrast to cytokines which showed symptom-specific profiles.
Individuals meeting PASC criteria had a higher proportion of prior tocilizumab use during acute infection than those without PASC.
The PASC group showed a trend toward a higher proportion of individuals with multiple (reinfection) SARS-CoV-2 infections compared with the non-PASC group, though not statistically significant.
Cardiopulmonary symptoms (PEM, chronic cough, chest pain) tended to decrease in prevalence with increasing time since COVID-19 diagnosis.
Unlike cardiopulmonary symptoms, fatigue prevalence did not show a statistically significant change over the 6-month follow-up period.
Fatigue was the most frequently reported PASC symptom overall, followed by post-exertional malaise, chronic cough, thirst, brain fog, and chest pain.

Symptom cluster 2 (thirst, cognitive dysfunction, and changes in sexual desire/capacity) was associated with a distinct cytokine expression pattern that did not involve the IL-10/VEGF/inflammatory cytokine elevations seen in cluster 1 symptoms.
Worse pre-COVID global mental health score was associated with increased odds of PASC-related diarrhea/nausea.
Worse pre-COVID global mental health score was associated with increased odds of PASC-related lack of concentration/brain fog.
Worse pre-COVID global physical health score was strongly associated with increased odds of PASC-related diarrhea/nausea.
Worse pre-COVID global physical health score was associated with increased odds of PASC-related fatigue.
Worse pre-COVID global physical health score was associated with increased odds of PASC-related exertional intolerance.
Worse pre-COVID global physical health score was associated with increased odds of PASC-related joint pain/body aches.
Patients with PASC had significantly worse pre-COVID global mental health scores than propensity-score-matched controls.
Patients with PASC had significantly worse pre-COVID global physical health scores than propensity-score-matched controls.
At 1-year follow-up, the disparity in both mental and physical global health between PASC patients and controls was even greater than at pre-COVID baseline.
From pre-COVID to 1-year post-diagnosis, PASC patients worsened significantly in both mental and physical health, whereas matched controls worsened only in mental health, not physical health.
The most common PASC symptoms reported at the reCOVer Clinic visit were fatigue, exertional intolerance, lack of concentration/brain fog, and memory deficits, experienced by the majority of patients.
The most prevalent symptoms at initial COVID-19 infection among patients who later developed PASC were fatigue, cough, flu-like symptoms, and shortness of breath.
Pre-COVID HRQL of the study sample was worse than general population norms, indicating patients who later developed PASC already had below-average mental and physical health before infection.
Elevated IL-6 levels in long COVID patients correlate with cognitive dysfunction, fatigue, and mood disorders, suggesting persistent low-grade inflammation drives post-viral neurocognitive syndromes.
TNF-α contributes to synaptic disruption and excitotoxic neuronal damage and is linked to cognitive dysfunction and fatigue in long COVID.
Serum and CSF neurofilament light chain (NFL) is elevated in long COVID patients with cognitive symptoms, memory loss, and peripheral neuropathy, reflecting axonal degeneration.
Serum levels of NfL and GFAP (markers of axonal and astrocytic injury) were significantly elevated in individuals with PASC and positively correlated with IL-6 and TNF-α, per Peluso et al.
CCL2/MCP-1 recruits monocytes across the blood-brain barrier, sustaining chronic CNS inflammation in long COVID.
Tight junction proteins claudin-5 and occludin are weakened during COVID-19 by inflammatory cytokines, oxidative stress, and endothelial injury, increasing blood-brain barrier permeability.
Elevated S100B and matrix metalloproteinases (MMP-9 and MMP-2) in serum and CSF serve as biomarkers of blood-brain barrier disruption in COVID-19 patients.
Elevated autoantibody titers targeting adrenergic (β1/β2) and muscarinic (M2/M4) receptors have been reported in post-COVID POTS patients, suggesting functional disruption of autonomic signaling.
Increased levels of IL-6, CCL2/MCP-1, and soluble CD30 support a chronic inflammatory microenvironment that impairs autonomic function in post-COVID POTS.
Ganglioside-targeting autoantibodies (e.g., anti-GM1) have been detected in Guillain-Barré syndrome cases following SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Anti-NMDA receptor autoantibodies were detected in CSF of some post-COVID autoimmune encephalitis patients, even without prior autoimmune predisposition.

Skin biopsy studies in long COVID patients demonstrated reduced intra-epidermal nerve fiber density, a hallmark of small fiber neuropathy, correlating with increased circulating complement components and anti-neuronal autoantibodies.

Elevated levels of α-synuclein, total tau, phosphorylated tau, and amyloid beta 42 have been detected in CSF and serum of long COVID patients with progressive cognitive or motor symptoms, suggesting possible acceleration of neurodegeneration.
CXCL13, a B-cell-attracting chemokine, is emerging as a potential marker of chronic intrathecal inflammation in long COVID, especially in patients with encephalopathy and cognitive slowing.

Depletion of short-chain fatty acid-producing gut microbiota taxa has been linked to worsened neurocognitive outcomes in long COVID, potentially via systemic inflammation and impaired microglial regulation.
Immunophenotyping studies revealed T-cell exhaustion in long COVID, characterized by persistent expression of inhibitory receptors PD-1 and TIM-3, alongside dysregulated B-cell maturation.
Certain HLA alleles, including HLA-B*15:01 and DRB1*04:01, have been associated with heightened CD8+ T-cell responses, potentially skewing toward autoimmunity following SARS-CoV-2 infection.

Females with long COVID demonstrate higher levels of autoantibodies (e.g., anti-IFN-α and anti-phospholipid), especially those with persistent fatigue and cognitive dysfunction, suggesting estrogen-enhanced immunity may become maladaptive post-virally.
D614G-infected brain models showed induction of interferon-stimulated genes and upregulation of CXCL10, IL-6, and TNF-α, indicating robust innate immune activation with this early SARS-CoV-2 variant.

Exposure of microglia-like cells to SARS-CoV-2 spike protein, including the Omicron variant, activates the NLRP3 inflammasome and secretion of IL-1β without need for additional priming, even absent viral replication.
POTS is diagnostically defined by a sustained heart rate increase of ≥30 bpm upon standing (≥40 bpm in adolescents), frequently accompanied by fatigue, palpitations, light-headedness, and brain fog.

Targeted immune therapies such as intravenous immunoglobulin, steroids, or β-blockers have been used in select post-COVID POTS cases, drawing parallels with autoimmune autonomic ganglionopathy treatment.
Small observational studies suggest benefits of immunomodulatory agents such as corticosteroids, IVIG, and low-dose naltrexone for long COVID, but randomized controlled trials remain scarce.
Broad-spectrum anti-inflammatory treatments such as corticosteroids and tocilizumab have shown some benefit for neuro-COVID, but may not be effective or safe across all patient populations.
X-linked genes including TLR7, a key viral RNA sensor, may confer females an immunological advantage in pathogen detection at the cost of increased autoimmune susceptibility post-infection.

SARS-CoV-2 infection can trigger production of autoantibodies against cytokines, membrane receptors, and components of the autonomic nervous system in susceptible individuals, disrupting neuroimmune homeostasis.

The authors propose that immune imbalance in Long COVID may impair anti-inflammatory regulatory pathways such as the cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway, contributing to chronic inflammation and autoimmunity.

Inflammaging, a chronic low-grade inflammation associated with aging, is proposed as a contributor that may predispose individuals to Long COVID and be amplified by persistent immune activation in the condition.
Heart rate variability is discussed as an emerging biomarker relevant to the autonomic dysfunction axis in Long COVID.
Inflammatory cytokines are proposed as emerging biomarkers reflecting sustained immune dysregulation in Long COVID.
Among 295 long COVID patients assessed, 100 (33.9%) exhibited positive signs of functional limb weakness, comprising 38 men and 62 women.
Paradoxical wrist flexion was the most frequently observed positive sign among long COVID patients with positive signs, followed by give-way weakness.
More women than men had positive signs of functional limb weakness among long COVID patients.
Patients infected after 2022 (Omicron-dominant era) were more likely to have positive signs of functional limb weakness.
Comorbidity of psychiatric diseases was significantly more common in long COVID patients with positive signs than in those without.
The number of months from infection to first clinic visit was significantly higher in patients with positive signs than in those without.
Fatigue was significantly more common in long COVID patients with positive signs than in those without.
Headache was significantly more common in long COVID patients with positive signs than in those without.
Among 24 patients who reported subjective muscle weakness, 16 had positive signs and 8 did not, a significant association.
In multivariate logistic regression, time from infection to first visit remained independently associated with positive signs.
In multivariate logistic regression, comorbid psychiatric diagnosis remained independently associated with the presence of positive signs.
In multivariate analysis, female sex showed a trend toward association with positive signs but did not reach statistical significance.
Patients with positive signs on supportive care alone were followed up for significantly longer (median 13.0 months) than those without positive signs (median 6.5 months).
There was no significant difference in the rate of perceived symptomatic improvement between long COVID patients followed with (n=28) versus without (n=33) positive signs.

Among 39 patients with positive signs followed for clinical course, diminishment of positive signs was strongly associated with perceived symptomatic improvement; signs did not diminish in any patient who did not perceive improvement.
Using the Fatigue Severity Scale, more than half of long-COVID patients showed a high level of fatigue.
The mean total score on the DUKE-UNC-11 perceived social support questionnaire was above the low-support threshold, indicating overall moderate-to-normal perceived support in this long-COVID sample.
Over a quarter of participants scored below the cut-off, indicating low perceived social support.
Total perceived social support score was significantly associated with neurological, psychological, locomotor symptoms, and pain in long-COVID patients.
The confidential support subscale of perceived social support was significantly associated with neurological, psychological, locomotor symptoms, and pain.
The affective support subscale of perceived social support was significantly associated with neurological, psychological, cardiovascular symptoms, and pain.
Stepwise linear regression identified fatigue severity (FSS score) as a predictor variable in the model for total perceived social support score.
Patient age was retained as a predictor in the stepwise regression model for the confidential support subscale.
Fatigue severity (FSS score) remained a component of the regression model for the affective support subscale.
A binary logistic regression model correctly classified approximately 74.7% of individuals as having low versus normal perceived social support, with greater specificity than sensitivity.
The majority of long-COVID patients had persistent symptoms lasting more than a year, with nearly all reporting ongoing symptoms at the time of the survey.
A substantial proportion of long-COVID patients were experiencing temporary work disability at the time of the survey.
Neurological symptoms and pain were the most frequently reported symptom categories among long-COVID patients.
Self-assessed overall health status was low among long-COVID patients on a 0-10 scale.
Among the 80 long-COVID patients who were hospitalized during acute infection, 17.4% required ICU admission.
In PASC patients undergoing 2-day submaximal CPET, oxygen consumption (VO2) at the first ventilatory threshold declined by 6.8% from Day 1 to Day 2.
O2 pulse, a surrogate for stroke volume and peripheral oxygen extraction, declined by 8.5% from Day 1 to Day 2 of submaximal CPET in PASC patients.
PETCO2, reflecting combined pulmonary perfusion, alveolar ventilation, and cardiac output, decreased by 2.6% between Day 1 and Day 2 of submaximal CPET in PASC patients.
Along with the declines in VO2, O2 pulse, and PETCO2, PASC patients showed a lower workload and modest reductions in minute ventilation and CO2 production at VT1 on Day 2 of submaximal CPET.
No notable differences between Day 1 and Day 2 were observed at peak-level exercise in the submaximal CPET protocol, with significant changes confined to the first ventilatory threshold.

Invasive CPET studies in long COVID identified a preload failure endotype characterized by low biventricular filling pressures and reduced cardiac output in the upright position at peak and submaximal exercise, with normal left ventricular function.
Invasive CPET evaluation of long COVID subjects identified impaired systemic oxygen extraction as a distinct physiological endotype, alongside preload failure.

In a separate 2-day peak-exercise CPET study of 15 PEM-enriched participants, VE/VCO2 was reduced at the gas exchange threshold between test days, but no other significant physiological changes were found at GET or peak exercise.
Approximately 6.9% of US adults reported long COVID symptoms in 2022, with higher prevalence among women and individuals of Hispanic descent.
The review describes long COVID pathogenesis as multifactorial, involving endothelial dysfunction, chronic inflammation, immune dysregulation, and potential viral persistence.
The authors note that early antiviral interventions and vaccination are emphasized in current research as strategies to mitigate the risk of developing long COVID.
The review states that anti-inflammatory agents and metabolic enhancers are promising therapies for long COVID, though lack of established biomarkers complicates diagnosis and treatment.
Patients with persistent long COVID symptoms scored lower on all eight SF-36 health domains compared to asymptomatic post-COVID controls, indicating worse quality of life.
Habitual physical activity level, assessed by the IPAQ-SF, did not differ between Long COVID and Control patients, arguing against deconditioning as the cause of persistent symptoms.
Thigh volume, quadriceps femoris muscle mass and whole-body composition were not different between Long COVID and Control patients.
The ultrasound-derived sarcopenia index of the vastus lateralis muscle did not differ between Long COVID and Control patients.
Isometric maximal voluntary contraction torque of the knee extensors was similar between Long COVID and Control patients.
Resting common femoral artery diameter did not differ between Long COVID and Control patients.
Microvascular/endothelial function, assessed as the hyperaemic blood flow response to passive leg movement in the common femoral artery, was not different between Long COVID and Control patients.

Both post-COVID groups (Long COVID and Control) showed lower AUC and Δpeak blood flow responses to passive leg movement than a reference group of healthy elderly sedentary individuals, suggesting persistent microvascular/endothelial dysfunction more than 2 years after infection, though not linked to symptom status.
During constant work rate moderate-intensity exercise, breathing frequency and rating of perceived exertion were significantly higher in Long COVID patients than Controls.
The time constant of pulmonary VO2 on-kinetics and the associated O2 deficit during moderate-intensity exercise were not different between Long COVID and Control patients.
In vivo skeletal muscle oxidative metabolism, assessed by NIRS-derived VO2m recovery kinetics (τ and k), was not different between Long COVID and Control patients.

Maximal cardiorespiratory function variables, including peak work rate, VO2peak, HRpeak, cardiac output peak, SpO2peak and maximal peripheral O2 extraction, showed no significant differences between Long COVID and Control patients.
Ventilatory threshold variables (gas exchange threshold and respiratory compensation point) did not differ between Long COVID and Control patients.
The mechanical efficiency of cycling, calculated as the VO2 versus work rate slope, was not different between Long COVID and Control patients.

Ventilatory inefficiency indices (VE/VCO2 slope, VE/VCO2 at GET, and ventilatory equivalent for CO2 at peak exercise) were significantly higher in Long COVID than Control patients, an effect attributable to a subgroup of four Long COVID patients with markedly abnormal values.

Long COVID patients showed a steeper ventilation/tidal volume relationship than Control patients during incremental exercise, reflecting a greater reliance on breathing frequency rather than tidal volume increases to achieve the same ventilation.

The four Long COVID patients identified with ventilatory inefficiency did not differ from other Long COVID patients in symptoms, physical activity, muscle mass/force, exercise tolerance, or microvascular/endothelial function variables.

More than two years after mild-to-moderate SARS-CoV-2 infection, persistent fatigue and exercise-intolerance symptoms in some patients could not be explained by any of the physical activity, muscle, cardiorespiratory, microvascular, or skeletal muscle oxidative metabolism mechanisms investigated, suggesting these symptoms may instead involve neurological/psychological factors not assessed in this study.

A related study of a larger overlapping cohort (230 patients, including those in the present study) found approximately 40% prevalence of persistent fatigue symptoms at 2-year follow-up after acute COVID-19, along with several neuropsychiatric symptoms.
Pathological levels of fatigue, as measured by the MFIS-21, were observed in 95% of Long COVID patients.
Poor sleep quality, indicated by scores above the clinical PSQI threshold, was reported by 81% of patients.
Over 70% of Long COVID patients exceeded the clinical significance threshold for psychological distress on the OQ-45.
81% of patients had problematic (75th percentile or above) quality-of-life scores compared to normative healthy data.
Long COVID patients reported an approximately 60% impact on daily activities and 54% impact on work/study on the WPAI instrument.
Forty percent of participants reported severe subjective problems with attentional and executive functioning on the BRIEF-A.
Thirty-five percent of participants reported severe subjective memory problems on the MMQ.
The mean MoCA score was 27.3 (range 20-30), and only 15.4% of patients scored below the standard cutoff of 26, far fewer than the 72% who showed impairment on the full neuropsychological battery.
Seventy-two percent of patients scored below a conservative pathological threshold on at least one cognitive task, substantially exceeding the ~48% expected by chance from multiple testing.
61% of patients had at least one sub-threshold attentional score, with divided attention most frequently impaired (45%).
41% of patients had at least one sub-threshold executive function score, most often on the Brown-Peterson interference task (26%).
15% of patients had at least one sub-threshold memory task score, most frequently on the BVMT-R visuospatial memory test (13%).
Subjective executive complaints (BRIEF-A Metacognition Index) correlated moderately with objective executive performance and weakly with attentional performance.
Subjective memory complaints (MMQ Ability subscale) correlated moderately with objective executive performance and weakly with attentional performance.

Psychological distress (OQ-45) showed a large correlation with subjective behavioral-regulation complaints (BRIEF-A BRI), indicating higher cognitive complaints are linked with higher psychological distress.

Latent profile analysis identified three distinct cognitive performance profiles differing with large effect sizes on processing speed, executive-attentional function, delayed verbal long-term memory, updating, and interference in working memory.
Profile 1 patients (28% of sample) had the lowest performance across nearly all cognitive factors and the highest level of cognitive and fatigue complaints.
Profile 2 patients (52% of sample) also showed a widespread pattern of cognitive difficulties, but less pronounced than Profile 1.

Profile 3 patients (20% of sample) showed a specific impairment in verbal long-term memory without deficits in other domains and with fewer complaints, suggesting reduced awareness of their memory difficulties.
Profile 3 had significantly more men (52%) than Profiles 1 (20.6%) and 2 (28.1%), a small but significant sex effect on cognitive profile membership.
Fewer Profile 2 patients had been hospitalized in the acute phase compared with Profiles 1 and 3.

The three cognitive profiles did not differ significantly in sleep quality, psychological distress, quality of life, or activity impairment, suggesting these psychosomatic difficulties are common across all Long COVID cognitive phenotypes.
MoCA global scores differed significantly across profiles, with Profile 1 lower than Profile 2 and Profile 3 lower than Profile 2.
Profile 1 patients reported the highest level of executive function complaints on the BRIEF-A global score and Metacognition Index compared to the other profiles.
Profile 3 patients reported the fewest fatigue complaints on the MFIS compared with the other profiles, consistent with their reduced awareness of overall difficulties.
The three cognitive profiles differed significantly by sex, with a greater proportion of men in Profile 3 (specific verbal long-term memory impairment) than in Profiles 1 or 2.
