IDH3A, an enzyme in the citrate (TCA) cycle, was up-regulated in the Long-COVID group.
PCK2, a mitochondrial enzyme in the citrate cycle pathway, was up-regulated in the Long-COVID group.
Ribosomal protein RPL35 was among the up-regulated proteins enriched in both the ribosome and coronavirus disease-COVID-19 KEGG pathways.
Ribosomal protein RPL31 was among the up-regulated proteins enriched in both the ribosome and coronavirus disease-COVID-19 KEGG pathways.
Ribosomal protein RPL7A was among the up-regulated proteins enriched in both the ribosome and coronavirus disease-COVID-19 KEGG pathways.
FCGBP was also identified among the dysregulated inflammation-related proteins in COPD patients with long COVID.

Reactome pathway analysis of the differentially expressed proteins identified enrichment in pathways including disease of glycosylation, viral infection, nervous system development, platelet activation, interferon signalling, and interleukin signalling, pathways previously linked to long COVID in other studies.
FCGBP was noted as one of several dysregulated inflammation-related proteins distinguishing elderly COPD patients with long COVID from controls.

A support vector machine model built on five combined clinical and proteomic features (wheezing severity, duration of SARS-CoV-2 infection, EIF2S3 expression, current FEV1/FVC%, and course of COPD) achieved the best discriminative performance for identifying long COVID in elderly COPD patients.
A greater proportion of patients in the Long-COVID group had a COPD disease course longer than 5 years compared with the Control group.
Patients who developed long COVID had a longer duration of acute SARS-CoV-2 infection than those who did not, despite similar infection severity between groups.
Inhaled corticosteroid use was numerically higher in the Long-COVID group than the Control group, but this difference did not reach statistical significance.
Anxiety symptom scores measured by the GAD-7 did not differ significantly between elderly COPD patients with and without long COVID.
A prior systematic review and meta-analysis reported that pre-existing COPD was associated with a 32% increased odds of developing long COVID.
The proportion of participants reporting at least one persistent physical symptom was similar at 12 months (87%) compared to 3 months (90%) post-hospitalization.
Fatigue was reported as the most common symptom at all four time points from 3 to 12 months following COVID-19 hospitalization.
Group mean scores on all PROMIS measures and the Impact of Events Scale-Revised did not indicate clinical dysfunction across the follow-up period.
About 37% of participants reported that their symptoms had somewhat or a lot of impact on their normal daily routines.
At least half of participants reported currently experiencing quality of life worse than prior to COVID-19 at each of the four time points up to 12 months.
Among long COVID patients with a mild acute phase, complete pulmonary function testing showed 32% normal results, 16% mild restriction, and 47% mild obstruction.
Mild diffusion (gas exchange) defects were identified in 26% of patients tested, sometimes combined with mild obstruction or restriction.
The majority of patients (68%) achieved a 6-minute walk test distance below their predicted lower limit of normal, indicating reduced functional exercise capacity.
Approximately 80% of patients reported some sensation of dyspnea (moderate to severe), while 21% reported no dyspnea.
Following the 6-minute walk test, 63% of patients reported slight to severe fatigue, while 26% reported no fatigue and 11% reported very slight fatigue.
A weak, non-significant negative correlation was found between the severity of airway impairment on pulmonary function testing and the severity of reported dyspnea.
A weak, non-significant correlation was found between the severity of gas exchange (DLCO) impairment and the reported severity of dyspnea.
No significant relationship was found between experiencing dyspnea and achieving a lower-than-normal 6-minute walk test distance.
A significantly strong positive correlation was found between reported dyspnea and reported fatigue following the 6-minute walk test.
Most patients seeking pulmonary evaluation for long COVID after a mild acute phase had preexisting comorbidities, including asthma, hypothyroidism, fibromyalgia, diabetes, and cardiac conditions.

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for fatigue in patients with multiple sclerosis or inflammatory rheumatic conditions was either dominated by usual care (i.e., more costly and less effective) or had an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio exceeding £30,000 per QALY.

A personalized exercise program (PEP) for fatigue dominated CBT in cost-effectiveness terms (i.e., was both less costly and more effective) in patients with multiple sclerosis or inflammatory rheumatic conditions.
The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio for the personalized exercise program compared with usual care ranged from £13,159 to £35,424 per unit of effectiveness across the included studies.
In female participants, G1899 produced a significantly greater reduction in anxiety (GAD-7) scores than placebo.
In men, GAD-7 anxiety scores decreased more with G1899 than placebo, but the difference did not reach statistical significance.
Women receiving G1899 showed significantly greater improvement in chronic fatigue symptoms than women on placebo.
In men, chronic fatigue symptom reduction with G1899 versus placebo did not reach statistical significance.
Anti-spike antibody levels rose substantially in both G1899 and placebo groups over 12 weeks, with no significant between-group difference, indicating G1899 did not enhance humoral antibody response.
In men, the increase in anti-spike antibody levels was greater with G1899 than placebo, but the difference did not reach significance.
In women, anti-spike antibody levels increased similarly in both groups with no significant between-group difference at Visit 4.
No significant differences were observed in CD8+ T cell population changes between G1899 and placebo groups across visits.
The CD4+ T cell percentage increased significantly in the G1899 group from Visit 1 to Visit 4.
In the placebo group, CD4+ T cell percentage increased only slightly and non-significantly from Visit 1 to Visit 4.
The CD4/CD8 ratio increased significantly in the G1899 group from Visit 1 to Visit 4, suggesting attenuation of chronic inflammation.
In the placebo group, the CD4/CD8 ratio changed only slightly and non-significantly from Visit 1 to Visit 4.
In the G1899 group, the Treg population showed no statistically significant change from Visit 1 to Visit 4, suggesting stability.
In the placebo group, the Treg population significantly declined from Visit 1 to Visit 4.
ALT levels decreased more in the placebo group than in the G1899 group over the 12-week period.
Blood cortisol levels increased more in the placebo group than in the G1899 group over 12 weeks, a statistically significant difference.
No adverse events were reported in association with G1899 intake during the trial.

The newly developed long COVID questionnaire showed excellent internal consistency across its two main sections (development/course of infection and post-COVID-19 psychophysical condition), with a Cronbach's alpha of 0.97.

Self-rated severity of the acute COVID-19 illness was predominantly mild-to-moderate, with 40% of participants each rating it as level 2 or level 3 on a 1-5 scale, and only 1.6% rating it as critical (level 5).

Persistent fatigue/asthenia severity decreased from the acute phase (mean 2.60) to the post-viral long COVID phase (mean 2.20), though it remained one of the most commonly reported symptoms in both phases.
Excessive tiredness severity decreased from the acute phase (mean 2.76) to the post-viral phase (mean 2.36), remaining among the most commonly reported symptoms.
Muscle weakness severity decreased from the acute phase (mean 2.77) to the post-viral phase (mean 2.25), remaining one of the most frequently reported symptoms.
Muscle and joint pain severity decreased from the acute phase (mean 2.79, the highest acute-phase value) to the post-viral phase (mean 2.25).
Headache severity decreased from the acute phase (mean 2.35) to the post-viral phase (mean 1.94).
Nasal congestion or runny nose during the acute phase had a mean severity of 2.52.
Mood disorders during the acute phase had a mean severity of 2.17, and were also highlighted among organ-specific manifestations in the post-viral phase.
Intermittent fever during the acute phase had a mean severity of 2.19.
Smell disturbances during the acute phase had a mean severity of 2.27.
Tachycardia during the acute phase had the lowest mean severity (1.74) among reported acute symptoms, but was also highlighted as one of the notable organ-specific manifestations of long COVID.
Difficulty concentrating during the acute phase had a mean severity of 2.09, and was also noted among organ-specific long COVID manifestations.
Swallowing and taste dysfunction during the acute phase had a mean severity of 2.18.

"Long cold", defined by the authors as prolonged mild respiratory symptoms (cough, nasal congestion, runny nose) persisting after the acute phase, had a mean severity of 2.15, though the term is not a standardized clinical entity.
A persistent dry cough during the acute phase had a mean severity of 2.28.

Among organ-specific manifestations, the most commonly reported post-COVID symptoms were dyspnea at rest and after light exertion, headache, tachycardia, mood disorders, sleep disorders, difficulty concentrating, and chest tightness.
The majority of the sample reported that persistent symptoms significantly influenced their daily lives, particularly affecting work, study, recreational activities, and health management.
The vast majority of participants (95.6%) reported no pre-existing health conditions prior to their COVID-19 infection.
Only one participant out of 250 had been hospitalized during the acute phase of COVID-19, limiting the study's ability to characterize long COVID symptoms in previously hospitalized patients.
EBV reactivation, detected via EBV genetic material (BamHI/LMP2 primers), was significantly more common in patients with persistent post-COVID fatigue than in recovered controls.
EBNA-1 IgG antibody titers were significantly elevated in patients with persistent post-COVID fatigue compared to recovered controls.
EA-D IgG antibody titers were significantly elevated in patients with persistent post-COVID fatigue compared to recovered controls, consistent with EBV reactivation rather than primary infection.
Initial hospitalization during acute COVID-19 infection was significantly associated with the development of post-COVID fatigue.
Diabetes and hypertension as pre-existing risk factors showed no significant association with post-COVID fatigue.
Peak work rate improved by 20% following completion of the hybrid pulmonary rehabilitation programme.
VO2peak improved by 15% (approximately 2.4 mL/min/kg) following the hybrid PR programme.
In the usual care group, there was no significant change in peak work rate between baseline and 12-week reassessment.
At iso-work rate during incremental cycling after PR, patients showed lower minute ventilation compared to baseline, indicating improved ventilatory efficiency.
Breathing frequency at iso-work was reduced after the PR programme compared to baseline.
Inspiratory time, expiratory time and duty cycle time at iso-work were all increased following PR compared to baseline.
Dyspnoea and leg fatigue at iso-work were reduced after PR compared to baseline peak work.
6-minute walk distance increased substantially in the PR group, exceeding the minimum clinically important difference reported for chronic respiratory disease.
In the usual care group there was no significant change in 6-minute walk distance at 12-week follow-up.
Quadriceps force increased in the PR group following completion of the programme.
Handgrip strength increased in the PR group following completion of the programme.
No significant change in quadriceps force or handgrip strength was observed in the usual care group.
Respiratory muscle strength (PImax and PEmax) was not significantly affected by the hybrid PR programme and was similar between groups before and after.
A trend of improvement in SPPB total score was observed in the PR group but individual SPPB components were not significantly affected.
The number of repetitions during the 60-second sit-to-stand test significantly increased in the PR group after the programme.
General fatigue score assessed via FACIT improved significantly in the PR group after the programme.
COPD Assessment Test (CAT) symptom intensity score improved significantly in the PR group after the programme.
Chronic dyspnoea assessed via the modified Medical Research Council (mMRC) scale improved in the PR group after the programme, with a smaller improvement also seen in the usual care group.
Both the PR and usual care groups reported similar reductions in depression and anxiety at 12-week follow-up, but these did not reach statistical significance.
Adherence to the remote home-based exercise sessions was very high, with patients completing 23 of 24 sessions.
At baseline, long COVID survivors in this cohort had an impaired VO2peak corresponding to approximately 65% of predicted normal levels.
Patients with post-COVID condition showed increased intra-network functional connectivity in the default mode network compared with healthy controls.
Patients with post-COVID condition showed increased intra-network functional connectivity in the executive control network compared with healthy controls.
Patients with post-COVID condition showed increased intra-network functional connectivity in the salience network compared with healthy controls.
Patients with post-COVID condition showed increased intra-network functional connectivity in the auditory network compared with healthy controls.
Patients with post-COVID condition showed increased intra-network functional connectivity in the superior parietal lobule network compared with healthy controls.

Patients with post-COVID condition showed increased intra-network functional connectivity in the anterior cingulate cortex compared with healthy controls, contrasting with prior reports of decreased frontal FC in PCC.
Patients with post-COVID condition showed increased intra-network functional connectivity in the basal ganglia network compared with healthy controls.
PCC patients showed increased inter-network connectivity between the sensorimotor network and default mode network, with loss of the normal anticorrelation seen in controls.

Within the PCC group, higher connectivity strength in seven cognitively relevant resting-state networks (anterior ECN, superior parietal, auditory network, salience network, anterior cingulate) correlated positively with MoCA scores after FDR correction.
In the PCC group, connectivity strength across all significant networks correlated positively with the time interval between infection and MRI acquisition, most strongly in the basal ganglia network.
Within the PCC group, subjective memory failure scores correlated positively with connectivity strength in the anterior cingulate, DMN, anterior ECN, basal ganglia network, and salience network.

Within the PCC group, fatigue severity correlated positively with connectivity strength in the anterior ECN, anterior cingulate, salience network, DMN, auditory network, superior parietal, and basal ganglia network.
Inter-network connectivity between the sensorimotor and default mode networks did not correlate with any clinical or neuropsychological variable examined in the PCC group.
Depression (PHQ-9) and anxiety (GAD-7) scores were not significantly correlated with resting-state network connectivity strength in the PCC group.

The PCC group performed significantly worse than healthy controls across multiple cognitive domains including global cognition, verbal learning/memory, attention, processing speed, executive function, and smell identification.
Using a threshold of impairment on two or more cognitive tests, 67 of 121 (55.4%) PCC patients were classified as cognitively impaired.

No significant intra- or inter-network functional connectivity differences were found between cognitively impaired and non-impaired PCC patients, despite objective classification by neuropsychological testing.
Intra-network functional connectivity did not differ between PCC patients hospitalized during acute infection and those who were not, after accounting for demographic and motion covariates.
The PCC group reported significantly higher levels of depression, anxiety, subjective memory failure, and fatigue than healthy controls.
In this sample, 36.36% of PCC participants (44 of 121) remained symptomatic beyond 2 years post-infection, a higher proportion than the 4% reported in prior longitudinal literature.
Among non-hospitalised long COVID patients, 69.5% reported new-onset pain compared with recovered COVID-19 survivors and healthy controls.
Widespread Pain Index scores were markedly higher in the long COVID group compared to recovered COVID survivors and healthy controls.
Pain intensity scores were significantly higher in the long COVID group than in recovered COVID-19 survivors and healthy controls.
The long COVID group showed higher pain and anxiety/depression scores and lower mobility, self-care, usual activities, and VAS scores compared to recovered and healthy groups.
Women with new-onset long COVID pain reported around 20% higher medication use than men, particularly NSAIDs and metamizole, while men more often used NSAIDs and paracetamol.

Myalgia experienced during acute COVID-19 hospital admission was associated with a higher likelihood of developing persistent musculoskeletal pain as a post-COVID sequela, with 73.2% of post-COVID MSK pain cases classified as new-onset.
In hospitalised COVID-19 survivors, new-onset musculoskeletal pain was not significantly associated with anxiety, depressive level, or sleep quality.
Among COVID-19 ICU survivors, chronic pain manifested predominantly as musculoskeletal, post-traumatic, neuropathic, visceral, and orofacial pain.
COVID-19 ICU survivors with new-onset chronic pain had significantly lower physical and mental quality-of-life scores than those without new-onset pain.
Intubation during acute COVID-19 illness was identified as a factor linked to new-onset chronic pain among ICU survivors.
Two years after infection, post-COVID patients had higher pain intensity than recovered COVID-19 survivors and healthy controls.
Post-COVID patients at 2 years had markedly worse depression scores than recovered survivors and healthy controls.
Post-COVID patients showed markedly worse fear-avoidance beliefs about physical activity and work compared with healthy controls and recovered survivors.
All participants with long COVID and new-onset chronic musculoskeletal pain reported continuous, high-interference pain most impacting enjoyment of life, work and mood.
Following long COVID with chronic musculoskeletal pain, the prevalence of anxiety, depression and PTSD increased substantially from pre-COVID to post-COVID.
Functional disability scores rose sharply from before COVID-19 infection to after, in patients with new-onset chronic musculoskeletal pain.
Most patients with new-onset chronic musculoskeletal pain in long COVID were physically inactive.
In a large household survey in Bangladesh, chest, joint, muscle, headache and abdominal pain occurred at varying but generally low prevalence among long COVID symptomatic individuals.
Higher pain scores were strongly and negatively correlated with quality of life across physical, psychological, social and environmental domains in long COVID patients in Bangladesh.
Fatigue was identified as a risk factor associated with the later development of new-onset/late-onset pain one year after COVID-19 hospitalisation.

Across all seven included studies, new-onset pain following COVID-19 was consistently associated with lower health-related quality of life, including worse physical, psychological and social well-being.
K-means clustering of PLQS symptom factor scores identified a severe-symptom cluster (Cluster 5) and a mild-symptom cluster (Cluster 6) with markedly different overall symptom burden.
The mild-symptom PTLD subgroup was significantly more male than the severe-symptom subgroup.
The mild-symptom, male-enriched PTLD subgroup had a higher rate of initial Lyme arthritis than two female-enriched subgroups, which had none.
The 'Fatigue/Cognitive' PTLD subgroup had a higher incidence of flu-like illness during acute Lyme infection than several other subgroups.
Multivariate clustering of 34 serum cytokines/chemokines showed heterogeneity across participants but this did not correspond to PTLD status or symptom subgroup.
No individual serum cytokine or chemokine differed between the PTLD cohort as a whole and healthy controls, and none correlated with PLQS symptom factor scores.
CXCR5-expressing naive CD4 T cells were significantly reduced in the peripheral blood of PTLD patients compared to healthy controls.
CD4+ EMRA T cells (also CD57+HLA-DR+) were increased in PTLD patients relative to healthy controls.
CD8+ Th1-like cells defined by CXCR3+CCR6-CCR4- expression were markedly increased in PTLD patients compared to healthy controls.
CD8+ Th1/17-like cells defined by CXCR3-CCR6+CCR4+ were significantly decreased in PTLD patients relative to healthy controls.

CXCR5+ naive CD4 T cell frequency was positively correlated with musculoskeletal pain symptom scores in PTLD patients but negatively correlated with the same factor in healthy controls, indicating an opposite relationship between groups.
NK cell frequencies were significantly correlated with multiple PLQS symptom factor scores in PTLD patients.

In female PTLD patients only, central memory CD8 T cells were elevated in a specific fatigue/cognitive-dominant symptom subgroup compared to other subgroups, an effect not seen in males or in the combined-sex analysis.

An elastic net classifier combining flow cytometry and cytokine data moderately distinguished PTLD from healthy controls, but performance was driven entirely by flow cytometry data with no contribution from cytokines.

In the multimodal PTLD classifier, CXCR5+ naive CD4 T cells were the most heavily weighted feature, followed by CD8 Th1-like and Th1/17-like cells, with no cytokine features contributing predictive weight.
Elastic net regression models using flow cytometry and cytokine data were unable to meaningfully predict any of the six PLQS symptom factor scores.
Multivariate clustering of flow cytometry immune features did not separate PTLD participants from healthy controls or by symptom subgroup.
In a randomized controlled trial of 78 hospitalized COVID-19 patients, two weeks of synbiotic supplementation significantly reduced serum IL-6 compared with placebo.
The same RCT reported improvements in white blood cell counts in the synbiotic-treated group of hospitalized COVID-19 patients.

A cohort study of prophylactic probiotics, prebiotics, and synbiotics in high-risk individuals found no significant difference in COVID-19 incidence or antibody levels between supplemented and placebo groups.

In an open-label study, a greater proportion of hospitalized COVID-19 patients receiving the synbiotic SIM01 for 28 days developed SARS-CoV-2 IgG antibodies by Day 16 compared with untreated controls.

The SIM01 group of hospitalized COVID-19 patients showed significantly reduced levels of pro-inflammatory markers including IL-6 and TNF-α compared to controls, alongside metagenomic evidence of increased beneficial bacteria and suppressed pathogens.
A Hong Kong clinical trial of the synbiotic SIM01 for post-acute COVID-19 syndrome (PACS/Long COVID) reported significant reductions in several long COVID symptoms.

Research on long COVID shows a significant increase in mast cell activation, which contributes to persistent inflammation and recurring symptoms, with gut dysbiosis implicated as a key trigger via the gut-immune axis.

Sex-based differences in COVID-19 severity are attributed to testosterone's immune-suppressive effects weakening T-cell activity and antibody production in men, while estrogen's immune-enhancing properties and X-chromosome gene redundancy may protect women.

Aging-related immunosenescence, reduced naïve T- and B-cell production, and chronic low-grade inflammation ('inflammaging'), combined with comorbidities like diabetes and heart disease, delay viral clearance and heighten immune activation, increasing severe COVID-19 outcome risk in older individuals.

COVID-19 infection is associated with notable changes in the gut microbiome, typically a decrease in microbial diversity and an increase in harmful bacteria, which is linked to systemic inflammation, cytokine storms, and immune exhaustion that can worsen infection severity.

In Long COVID, ongoing gut dysbiosis is proposed to contribute to persistent inflammation and immune dysfunction, keeping the immune system in a state of continuous activation that worsens long-term symptoms.
In healthy individuals, an 8-week synbiotic regimen altered immune markers including IL-10 and secretory IgA (sIgA), indicating a gut microbiota shift associated with reduced inflammation.

Butyrate, a short-chain fatty acid produced by gut bacteria, reduces pro-inflammatory cytokines TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6 by inhibiting NF-κB signaling, while also activating regulatory T cells and strengthening the gut barrier.
Synbiotic supplementation may increase glutathione availability by boosting cysteine bioavailability via probiotic strains, supporting antioxidant defenses relevant to COVID-19 recovery.

Prolonged reactive oxygen species (ROS) production during acute and post-acute SARS-CoV-2 infection, including Long COVID, can overwhelm endogenous antioxidant systems, contributing to immune exhaustion, persistent inflammation, and fatigue.
Only 24% of patients hospitalized for COVID-19 reported complete recovery at 3 years.
At 3 years, patients rated their average recovery level at 80% compared to their pre-COVID-19 health status.
The prevalence of impaired fitness, fatigue, and muscle weakness decreased significantly over the total 3-year follow-up period.
The prevalence of memory problems significantly increased between the 2- and 3-year visits.
Self-reported fatigue score significantly worsened between the 2- and 3-year visits.
Cognitive failures score significantly worsened between the 2- and 3-year visits and overall over follow-up.
SF-36 mental component summary (MCS) score significantly worsened between the 2- and 3-year visits.
Outcomes for fatigue, participation, return to work, and health-related quality of life improved significantly over the total follow-up period.
Post-exertional malaise (PEM) was reported by 36% of patients at 3 years after hospitalization for COVID-19.
Almost all patients with PEM (98%) also experienced co-occurring health problems, with 42% reporting concurrent fatigue, cognitive failures, and dyspnea.
Patients with PEM reported a much lower average recovery level (55%) at 3 years than those without PEM (88%).
Female sex was a significant risk factor for post-exertional malaise at 3 years.
Pre-existing pulmonary disease was a significant risk factor for post-exertional malaise at 3 years.
Pre-COVID-19 physical inactivity was a significant risk factor for post-exertional malaise at 3 years.
ICU admission during hospitalization for COVID-19 was a significant risk factor for post-exertional malaise at 3 years.
Younger age showed only a non-significant trend toward association with post-exertional malaise.
Patients with PEM showed significantly worse fatigue, physical HRQoL, and mental HRQoL trajectories over the 3-year follow-up compared to patients without PEM.
In patients without PEM, cognitive failures and SF-36 mental component summary scores still worsened significantly in the third year.
44% of patients with a paid job before infection had not fully returned to work at 3 years.
At 3 years, poor sleep quality, fatigue, cognitive failures, depression, and anxiety remained prevalent among patients.
More than half of patients experienced fatigue, impaired fitness, memory problems, or concentration problems at 3 years, and severity was substantial in a substantial minority.
Patients with PEM at 3 years were characterized by a higher proportion of females, more comorbidities, and more frequent pre-COVID-19 physical inactivity compared to those without PEM.
The authors note that long COVID is linked to new-onset conditions such as dysautonomia, particularly POTS, and ME/CFS.
TL infants looked more to the left side of the face than EL infants, both across the full trial and specifically in the 500-1000 ms window, indicating a reduced left-side gaze bias in EL infants.
In the 500-1000 ms window, a significant left-versus-right side looking difference was observed only in the TL group, indicating that EL infants lacked this typical side asymmetry.
A group-by-age interaction in pupil responses was found, with EL infants showing a larger increase in pupil size over time compared to TL infants.
People with fibromyalgia reported higher levels of sensory processing sensitivity, central sensitisation symptoms, and autistic traits than a general population sample.
Sensory processing sensitivity, central sensitisation symptoms and autistic traits were all significantly positively correlated with one another.
Central sensitisation symptoms fully mediated the relationship between sensory processing sensitivity and autistic traits in the fibromyalgia sample, as predicted.
Contrary to expectation, central sensitisation symptoms also fully mediated the relationship between sensory processing sensitivity and autistic traits in the general population control sample.

The strength of the relationship between central sensitisation symptoms and autistic traits was moderated by sample group, with autistic traits increasing more rapidly with central sensitisation symptoms in people with fibromyalgia than in the general population sample.

The authors suggest autism may be prevalent among people with fibromyalgia with very high central sensitisation symptoms, but caution that elevated CS symptoms could cause self-reported autistic traits to be misdiagnosed as autism in this population.
All 51 patients with heterozygous CNOT3 variants exhibited developmental delay, particularly affecting language development.
Intellectual disability, typically mild to moderate, was found in 87% of patients with CNOT3 variants.
Behavioral issues including autism spectrum disorders and attention deficits were common in patients with CNOT3 variants, affecting over half of the cohort.
Dysmorphic facial features were noted in patients with CNOT3 variants and may aid diagnosis.
Epilepsy was an uncommon feature, occurring in 10% of patients with CNOT3 variants.
Twenty-eight novel CNOT3 variants were identified across the cohort, including missense, nonsense, frameshift, intronic variants, and a 12-exon deletion.
Missense variants clustered at the N- and C-terminal regions of the CNOT3 protein, indicating these regions have critical functional roles.
No clear genotype-phenotype correlation was observed among CNOT3 variant carriers, suggesting that all identified variants likely result in a loss-of-function effect.
Among the 28 novel variants identified, one was a large deletion spanning 12 exons of CNOT3.
CNOT3 is a subunit of the CCR4-NOT complex, which plays a crucial role in the regulation of gene expression.
RMSSD at rest increased significantly from pre- to post-intervention across both sequences after the 10-day VR intervention.
SD1 (Poincaré plot short-term variability, a parasympathetic marker) increased significantly from pre- to post-intervention at rest.
Mean RR interval showed only a marginally significant increase from pre to post intervention at rest.
During the abstract (webcam) VR task, SDNN decreased significantly compared to resting baseline, whereas this decrease was not seen in the concrete task group.
HF power (a marker of vagal/parasympathetic modulation) decreased significantly during the abstract VR task compared to rest, indicating vagal withdrawal.
SD2 (long-term Poincaré variability) decreased significantly during the abstract VR task compared to rest.
The LF/HF ratio (sympathovagal balance index) increased significantly during the abstract VR task compared to rest, indicating greater sympathetic dominance.
Comparing interface types irrespective of sequence, the LF/HF ratio was marginally higher during abstract (webcam) tasks than during concrete (touchscreen) tasks.
In the group practicing the concrete (touchscreen) task first, SDNN showed a non-significant trend of increase from day 1 to day 5 of practice.
In participants who practiced the concrete task first, switching to the abstract task in the second sequence block produced a significant increase in SDNN.
In the concrete-first sequence, LF n.u. increased significantly when participants switched to the abstract task.
In the concrete-first sequence, HF n.u. decreased significantly when participants switched to the abstract task, indicating reduced parasympathetic modulation.
Participants who practiced the abstract (webcam) task first showed no significant HRV changes when subsequently switching to the concrete (touchscreen) task.
Regression analysis found that age, BMI, IQ, autism severity (CARS), and functional ability (PEDI) had no significant influence on changes in HRV indices (SDNN, RMSSD, LF/HF).

Adolescents with ASD are reported in prior literature to exhibit lower parasympathetic activity and higher sympathetic activity than typically developing peers, consistent with autonomic nervous system dysregulation (dysautonomia).
Thapa et al. reported reduced HRV, including lower RMSSD and other time- and frequency-domain indices, in adults with ASD compared to reference populations.
Kalfiort et al. found higher SDNN (global HRV variability) in typically developing children compared to children with ASD.
PTSD symptom severity (PCL-5 total score) was not significantly correlated with circulating PACAP levels.
PTSD symptom severity was not significantly correlated with late acquisition fear-potentiated startle to the conditioned danger cue (CS+).
PTSD symptom severity was not significantly correlated with late acquisition fear-potentiated startle to the conditioned safety cue (CS-).
PTSD symptom severity was not significantly correlated with heart rate during fear extinction.
PTSD symptom severity was not significantly correlated with heart rate variability during fear extinction.
Circulating PACAP levels did not differ significantly between participants meeting full (threshold) versus subthreshold PTSD criteria.
Late acquisition fear-potentiated startle to the CS+ did not differ significantly between threshold and subthreshold PTSD groups.
Extinction heart rate variability did not differ significantly between threshold and subthreshold PTSD groups.
Heart rate during fear extinction was higher in participants meeting full PTSD criteria compared with those with subthreshold PTSD, though this was significant only at an uncorrected threshold.
Higher circulating PACAP levels were associated with higher fear-potentiated startle to the conditioned danger cue (CS+) during late fear acquisition, controlling for age.
The interaction between PACAP level and sex was not significant in the model predicting fear-potentiated startle to the CS+.
Higher circulating PACAP levels were associated with higher fear-potentiated startle to the conditioned safety cue (CS-) during late fear acquisition, indicating diminished fear inhibition.
The interaction between PACAP level and sex was not significant in the model predicting fear-potentiated startle to the CS-.
Higher circulating PACAP levels were associated with higher heart rate during fear extinction, controlling for age.
The interaction between PACAP level and sex was not significant in the model predicting heart rate during extinction.
Higher circulating PACAP levels were associated with lower heart rate variability during fear extinction, controlling for age.
The interaction between PACAP level and sex was not significant in the model predicting heart rate variability during extinction.

Overall, PACAP was associated with heightened fear responding and autonomic dysregulation similarly in men and women, failing to replicate a prior study's sex-specific PACAP-fear associations found only in females.
Autistic individuals have been reported to show reduced heart rate variability, suggesting sympathetic dominance or impaired parasympathetic regulation relative to neurotypical individuals.

Longitudinal wearable ECG monitoring found elevated sympathetic tone and reduced parasympathetic activity in autistic individuals during social and sensory stressors, linking these autonomic patterns to core ASD traits such as anxiety and emotional reactivity.
Real-time HRV was examined and validated as a clinically relevant, non-invasive biomarker for sensory processing difficulty and social withdrawal in autism.
Wearable multisensor tracking of HRV, skin conductance, and breathing patterns in autistic children during behavioral therapy revealed phase-locked physiological responses to intervention intensity.

A simulated ASD-like cardiovascular subcohort, defined using low HRV and sympathetic dominance as documented autonomic markers of autism, was extracted from the MIT-BIH and PPG-DaLiA datasets to test model generalization; the proposed CGSE+DCTA model achieved an F1 score of 85.53% and RMSE of 0.103, outperforming LSTM and GRU baselines.

On an Autism Cardiovascular Dataset, the proposed CardioGraph Synaptic Encoder (CGSE) outperformed LSTM, GRU, Transformer, and Informer baselines in predicting cardiovascular health metrics such as HRV, ECG signals, and blood pressure in autistic patients.

In a small clinician evaluation study (n=8 licensed cardiology practitioners), the CGSE+DCTA model's outputs were rated highest for interpretability (4.3/5), trust (4.5/5), explanation accuracy (>83%), and had the fastest average interpretation time (21.3 seconds) compared to LSTM, GRU, Informer, and Autoformer baselines.
Higher baseline heart-rate variability (STD HR) was positively correlated with greater clinician-rated improvement in anxiety after 12 weeks of propranolol.
Lower baseline pNN50, reflecting reduced parasympathetic/vagal tone, predicted greater clinician-rated anxiety improvement after propranolol.

Among high responders to propranolol, higher baseline SDNN was associated with greater improvement in peer interaction.

Meta-analytic evidence cited by the authors indicates that autistic individuals generally show blunted vagally-mediated HRV at rest, consistent with chronic sympathetic predominance.
Individuals with a genetic risk profile in the IL1RN, IL1A, and IL1B genes show more frequent recent EBV reactivation among those with long COVID symptoms.
Genetic risk carriers for EBV reactivation show an elevated ratio of IL-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1Ra) to IL-1β.

High levels of anti-viral capsid antigen (VCA) IgA serve as a strong marker of recent EBV reactivation in the long COVID cohort.

Serum neurofilament light chain (NfL) levels were moderately elevated in post-COVID-19 patients with persistent olfactory dysfunction compared to post-COVID-19 patients without residual olfactory deficits.

No significant Spearman correlations were found between serum NfL levels and individual olfactory test scores (odor identification, discrimination, threshold) or the composite TDI score in Od-post-COVID-19 patients.
Two-way ANOVA showed no significant effect of sex on serum NfL levels among the study participants.
Based on TDI score classification, nearly all Od-post-COVID-19 patients were categorized as hyposmic, with one patient meeting criteria for functional anosmia.
Pooled analysis of three RCTs found a mean reduction in VAS symptom scores with Chinese herbal medicine versus control that did not reach statistical significance.
Pooling three RCTs, CHM showed a non-significant trend toward higher rates of cough relief compared to control.
In two RCTs, CHM showed a non-significant trend toward higher fatigue remission rates versus control.
Pooling two RCTs, CHM significantly increased insomnia remission rates compared to control.
Across three RCTs, CHM showed a non-significant trend toward greater dyspnea relief versus control.
In two RCTs, CHM significantly increased chest tightness relief rates compared to control.

Subgroup analysis found short-term CHM treatment (≤7 days) significantly reduced VAS symptom scores compared to control.
Subgroup analysis reported long-term CHM treatment (≥14 days) associated with a larger, though CI-crossing-zero, reduction in VAS scores compared to control.
Pooled analysis across ten RCTs found no significant difference in adverse event risk between CHM and control groups, indicating good tolerability.

Ephedra, especially combined with Gypsum, has been reported to inhibit pro-inflammatory cytokines and improve hypothalamic homeostasis, contributing to the anti-inflammatory effect of Lianhua Qingwen formula on cough.
Platycodon is described as promoting salivary and bronchial secretions and suppressing airway hyperreactivity, supporting its role in cough-relief herbal formulas.
Forsythia, honeysuckle, and Scutellaria are described as having antiviral and anti-inflammatory activity relevant to airway remodeling and post-infectious inflammation.

Ginseng, Codonopsis, and Astragalus are described as enhancing mitochondrial function, promoting ATP production, and boosting immune resilience, proposed mechanisms for fatigue and exercise intolerance improvement.
Ginseng is proposed to alleviate central fatigue by modulating hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis hyperactivity, improving physical endurance.
Suanzaoren is proposed to enhance sleep quality through modulation of GABAergic and serotonergic pathways, while Acanthopanax exerts sedative and anti-fatigue effects.

A six-week virtual mindfulness-based group therapy program (Post-COVID Resilience Program) did not produce a statistically significant improvement in depressive or anxiety symptoms among long-COVID patients when comparing pre- and post-intervention questionnaire scores.

Fatigue was the most common symptom reported in this Long COVID cohort, present in 93% of participants.
Subjective cognitive impairment ("brain fog") was reported by 79% of the cohort.
New onset muscle and/or joint pain was reported by 78% of participants.
Headache was reported by 74% of participants as part of the neuropsychiatric symptom cluster.
Insomnia or sleep disturbance was reported by 58% of participants and was strongly linked to PTSD-related symptoms.
Coughing or shortness of breath persisted in 81% of participants as part of the acute COVID-19 symptom cluster.
Loss of smell (58%) and loss of taste (54%) persisted as long COVID symptoms in this cohort.
Gastrointestinal symptoms including diarrhea (43%), nausea/vomiting (38%), and weight loss (58%) were reported and contributed to the Long COVID fatigue-related cluster.
Rash, considered an autoimmune-cluster symptom, was reported by 21% of participants.
Only 25% of participants were currently exercising at the time of evaluation, reflecting functional limitation in the cohort.
The cohort was stratified into high (mean=11) and low (mean=8) Symptom Score subgroups by median split, which were significantly different from each other.
Despite a higher proportion of females with above-median Symptom Score, biological sex did not significantly predict Symptom Score.
Patient age did not predict Long COVID Symptom Score.
BMI did not predict Long COVID Symptom Score.
No race or ethnicity category was associated with Symptom Score, despite over half the cohort identifying as Hispanic.
PCL-5 screening revealed that 44% of the cohort experienced stress-related symptoms rising to the level of PTSD.
GAD-7 screening showed 69% of participants had at least mild anxiety and 18% had severe anxiety.
PHQ-9 screening showed 74% of participants had at least mild depression, and 28% had moderately severe to severe symptoms.
Approximately 41% of the cohort reported slight to extreme dissatisfaction with life.
Symptom Score was positively correlated with PCL-5 (PTSD/stress) scores.
Symptom Score was positively correlated with GAD-7 anxiety scores, the strongest of the three psychiatric correlations.
Symptom Score was positively correlated with PHQ-9 depression scores.
Duration of Long COVID symptoms since infection was not correlated with PCL-5, PHQ-9, or GAD-7 scores.

Headache (11/20 PCL-5 items) and subjective cognitive impairment (9/20 items) were significantly correlated with individual PTSD symptom items, with item 8 (trouble remembering the stressful experience) most broadly correlated across symptoms.
Currently exercising was negatively correlated with 5 PCL-5 items, suggesting a protective association between exercise and stress-related symptoms.

Higher PHQ-9, PCL-5, and GAD-7 scores were positively correlated with current prescriptions for mood stabilizer (valproate, carbamazepine, lamotrigine) and stimulant (methylphenidate, amphetamine/dextroamphetamine, modafinil, lisdexamfetamine) medication classes.
There was a negative but non-significant correlation between PHQ-9 score and blood pressure medication use.
Patients prescribed mood stabilizers had significantly higher GAD-7 and PHQ-9 scores than those not taking them, but no significant difference in PCL-5.
Patients prescribed stimulants had significantly higher GAD-7 and PHQ-9 scores than those not taking them, but no significant difference in PCL-5.
41% of participants endorsed taking respiratory care medications (e.g., albuterol, salmeterol/fluticasone, fluticasone, tiotropium) well after initial COVID-19 infection.
PBMCs from long COVID cases showed significantly higher basal oxygen consumption rate than those from healthy controls.
Oligomycin-sensitive (ATP-linked) oxygen consumption rate was significantly higher in LC PBMCs than controls.
Proton-leak oxygen consumption rate did not differ significantly between LC cases and controls, indicating no evident mitochondrial uncoupling.
No difference in aerobic glycolysis (extracellular acidification rate) was observed between LC cases and controls, in contrast to the glycolytic shift reported in acute COVID-19.
Overall net TMRM staining and calculated mitochondrial membrane potential (ψm) were not significantly different between LC cases and controls.
Mitochondrial mass, assessed by citrate synthase activity and TOM20 abundance, did not differ significantly between LC cases and controls.

LC PBMCs showed a significant reduction in mitochondrial membrane potential upon oligomycin (ATP synthase inhibitor) treatment compared to controls, indicating that Complex V is abnormally contributing to maintenance of the membrane potential (reverse/hydrolytic ATP synthase activity) rather than dissipating it as normal.
No differences in mitochondrial DNA content or damaged (deleted) mtDNA molecules were observed between LC cases and controls.
Resting heart rate (as a percentage of maximum predicted heart rate, a marker of autonomic dysfunction) correlated positively with basal oxygen consumption rate in LC cases.
Resting heart rate (% max predicted) correlated negatively with mitochondrial membrane potential in LC cases.
A statistical trend toward positive correlation between ATP-linked OCR and resting heart rate (% max predicted) was observed but did not reach significance.
EQ5D-5L quality of life scores correlated positively with ECAR in LC cases.
EQ5D-5L quality of life scores correlated negatively with oligomycin-induced changes in TMRM, supporting a link between Complex V dysfunction and reduced quality of life/fatigue.
FCCP-induced changes in TMRM were negatively correlated with time since index SARS-CoV-2 infection.
A trend toward negative correlation between oligomycin-induced TMRM changes and time since index infection was observed but did not reach significance.
In post-hoc sex-stratified analysis, female LC cases (but not males) showed significantly greater reductions in FCCP-induced and antimycin/rotenone-induced TMRM compared to female controls.
Female LC cases showed significantly higher net TMRM staining than female controls.

Sexual dimorphism was observed in the LC mitochondrial phenotype: males showed more pronounced differences in oxygen consumption rates compared to controls, while females showed more striking differences in markers of membrane polarisation.
Long COVID cases had significantly higher median BMI than controls, but BMI did not correlate significantly with any mitochondrial parameter.
LC cases exhibited severe fatigue, moderate dyspnoea on exertion, low resting heart rate relative to maximum predicted, and a high prevalence of myalgia.

The authors speculate, based on a mouse model of Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy, that (+)-Epicatechin, a selective inhibitor of ATP hydrolysis binding Complex V, which increased ATP levels and improved muscle force in that model, could be a potential treatment for the Complex V dysfunction identified in long COVID.

A cited early phase study of AXA1125, an investigational bioenergetics-targeting product, in long COVID reported improved fatigue scores but no significant difference in phosphocreatine recovery rate (an indirect marker of myocyte oxidative metabolism).

A cited study (Gunter et al.) found higher plasma tricarboxylate levels in long COVID cases, indicating altered fatty acid metabolism and dysfunctional mitochondrial-dependent lipid metabolism, consistent with the Complex V and Krebs cycle alterations described in this study.
Oxaloacetate supplementation did not significantly reduce fatigue compared to placebo as measured by the primary outcome, the Chalder Fatigue Questionnaire.

On the RAND-36 quality-of-life instrument, the OAA group reported significantly lower baseline energy scores than controls, but no significant group x time interaction was observed across the trial for the energy domain.
OAA-treated patients showed a significantly greater reduction in fatigue and total symptom burden over time on the DSQ-SF compared to controls, with earlier improvement evident by Visit 2.
A higher proportion of OAA-treated patients met the DSQ-SF responder criterion (≥10% symptom reduction) than controls, but the difference was not statistically significant.
Objectively measured upright activity time (UP Time) did not differ between OAA and control groups at any study visit.
Simple reaction time on the DANA Brain Vital improved in both groups over the trial with no statistically significant between-group differences.
OAA-treated patients showed significantly greater improvement in procedural reaction time on the DANA Brain Vital compared to controls at both Visit 2 and Visit 3.
Go/No-Go performance did not differ between groups at Visit 2 but showed significantly greater improvement in the OAA group by Visit 3.
OAA-treated patients showed a significantly greater improvement in total cognitive efficiency score than controls at both Visit 2 and Visit 3.

In OAA-treated patients, greater baseline symptom severity correlated with lower cognitive performance at Visit 1, but this correlation weakened and became non-significant by Visits 2 and 3; no significant correlation was seen in controls at any visit.
Among OAA-treated patients, DSQ-SF responder status significantly predicted greater improvement in cognitive efficiency by Visit 3, an association that was not significant in the control group.

Oxaloacetate was associated with a higher rate of treatment-emergent adverse events than placebo, including one possibly-related serious adverse event (costochondritis) that resolved by end of trial, but was overall well tolerated with mostly mild-to-moderate events.
The paper is a commentary discussing the feasibility and acceptance of transdermal auricular vagus nerve stimulation delivered via a TENS device in females with long COVID-related fatigue.
The proportion of individuals experiencing fatigue decreased from 68.2% in the acute phase of mild COVID-19 to 50.2% at 3 months post-infection.
Overall fatigue severity (MFI-20 total score) significantly decreased from the acute phase to 3 months post-COVID-19.
Physical fatigue was the most prominent dimension in the acute phase and significantly decreased by 3 months post-infection.

Although mean mental fatigue scores decreased slightly overall, mental fatigue became a proportionally dominant fatigue dimension by 3 months post-infection, alongside general fatigue and reduced activities.
Recognition memory performance significantly declined from the acute phase to 3 months post-infection, despite improvements in other cognitive domains.
PTSD symptom severity (IES-R) showed no significant improvement between the acute phase and 3 months post-infection.
Sleep disturbance (PSQI) did not significantly improve between the acute phase and 3 months post-infection.
Anxiety severity (BAI) significantly decreased from the acute phase to 3 months post-infection.
Depression severity (BDI) significantly decreased from the acute phase to 3 months post-infection.

Across cross-sectional analyses, all five fatigue dimensions were positively correlated with PTSD, anxiety, depression, and sleep disturbance, with the strongest correlation found between mental fatigue and depression.

Mental fatigue, reduced activity, and reduced motivation were negatively correlated with working memory and executive function, with the strongest correlation between reduced motivation and TMT-B performance.

Canonical correlation analysis in the acute phase identified a strong multivariate association between fatigue dimensions (general, mental, physical fatigue most heavily weighted) and neuropsychiatric symptoms, dominated by depression, anxiety, PTSD, and sleep disturbance.

At 3 months post-infection, canonical correlation analysis showed an even stronger multivariate association between fatigue (now dominated by mental fatigue) and neuropsychiatric symptoms, led by depression, anxiety, sleep disturbance, and PTSD.

Individuals with persistent fatigue (fatigue at both acute phase and 3 months) had significantly higher acute-phase scores for fatigue, PTSD, anxiety, depression, and sleep disturbance compared with those whose fatigue resolved (alleviated fatigue group).

At 3 months, individuals with persistent fatigue showed elevated scores across all fatigue dimensions plus increased psychiatric symptoms and cognitive impairments (short-term delayed recall, TMT-A) compared to those with alleviated fatigue.

Individuals who developed new-onset fatigue by 3 months had higher acute-phase reduced activity and lower immediate/long-term delayed recall than those who remained fatigue-free, and by 3 months showed markedly higher fatigue and neuropsychiatric symptoms.

In the persistent fatigue group, longitudinal increases in general, mental, and physical fatigue were mildly associated with increases in anxiety and depression, with the strongest correlation between change in mental fatigue and change in depression.

In the alleviated fatigue group, longitudinal increases in all fatigue dimensions were mildly to moderately associated with changes in anxiety, depression, and sleep disturbance, with mental fatigue showing the strongest association with depression.

Longitudinal CCA in the persistent fatigue group showed a significant multivariate association between changes in general and mental fatigue and worsening of anxiety, depression, and memory problems (recognition, short-term delayed memory) over the 4-12 week period.

In contrast to the persistent fatigue group, no canonical variable pairs reached statistical significance linking changes in fatigue dimensions to neuropsychiatric symptom changes in the alleviated fatigue, no-fatigue, or new-onset fatigue groups.
Cognitive processing speed as measured by TMT-A improved (faster completion time) from the acute phase to 3 months post-infection.
Immediate recall, short-term delayed recall, and long-term delayed recall on the AVLT-H all significantly improved from the acute phase to 3 months post-infection.

An early systematic review of 23,141 children and young people found a significantly increased risk of persisting cognitive difficulties, headache, loss of smell, sore throat and sore eyes in post-COVID cases compared to controls, with female sex and older age as risk factors.
At 3 months post-PCR testing in the CLoCk cohort, the most common persisting symptoms in test-positive CYP were fatigue, headache, shortness of breath and persisting loss of smell.
At 2 years follow-up, fatigue, headache and shortness of breath remained the most common symptoms along with sleeping difficulties, whereas loss of smell was no longer prominent.
Many persisting symptoms (other than loss of smell) were almost as common in test-negative controls as in test-positive CYP, indicating they could not be solely attributed to SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Mental health status of test-positive CYP was similar to that of test-negative CYP.
At 6 months post-testing, having a parent with ongoing problems after COVID-19 was associated with long COVID in their children.

Predictors of long COVID up to 24 months post-infection in CYP were female sex, pre-COVID-19 health problems (particularly asthma and allergy), learning difficulties at school, and family history of ongoing COVID-19 problems.
Persisting symptoms of long COVID in CYP were similar but not identical to those in adults, with cognitive problems and muscle pain being more common in adults than in CYP.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of 194 studies (735,006 patients, mean follow-up 4 months) found the prevalence among nonhospitalized adults was 34% for fatigue, 20% for breathlessness, 17% for muscle pain, 15% for sleep disorders, 12% for smell dysfunction and 8% for taste dysfunction.

Only 7% of CLoCk participants who tested PCR-positive met the research definition for long COVID persistently at all follow-up time points up to 24 months, and approximately 75% of CYP who had long COVID at 3 months no longer met the definition by 24 months.
There was evidence of a relationship between the number of SARS-CoV-2 infections and the likelihood of persisting symptoms in CYP, consistent with dose-response criteria for causality.

Findings from CYP infected with the Omicron variant were similar to those of the main CLoCk study, suggesting clinicians need not consider number of infections or variant type when developing treatment plans.

Among 576 CYP who received a COVID-19 vaccine after having previously tested PCR-positive, the proportion meeting the long COVID definition at 6 months post-test was similar to those who were not vaccinated, indicating vaccination post-infection did not mitigate long COVID risk.
CYP who received a COVID-19 vaccine followed by weekly SARS-CoV-2 testing were less likely to develop long COVID during the Omicron variant wave.
An Italian observational study showed that COVID-19 vaccination was associated with a significantly lower risk of adolescents developing long COVID at 3, 6 and 12 months post-infection.
A systematic review of 26 sources published 1986-2019 found a high prepandemic median prevalence of cough (13.6%), headache (29.9%) and fatigue (20.5%) in children aged 10-19.

Between 2012-2013 and 2021-2022, annual hospitalizations for mental health concerns in England increased by 65% (an increase that preceded the pandemic), while all-cause admissions increased by only 10%.

An updated systematic review of 60 studies (333,472 CYP) found fatigue (47%) and headache (35%) were the most commonly reported post-COVID symptoms overall, but when restricted to controlled studies the excess prevalence over controls was much lower (5% for headache, 7% for fatigue).

Only 259 CYP were admitted to paediatric intensive care in England (population ~11 million CYP) in the first year of the pandemic, suggesting persisting organ damage is unlikely to be a major cause of long COVID in CYP.
SARS-CoV-2, or parts of the virus, can persist for months in the tissues of children, and long COVID may be associated with hyperinflammation.

In some CYP with long COVID, hyperinflammation manifests as persistence of the coronavirus spike protein in the bloodstream and altered immune responses involving neutrophils, lymphocytes and cytokines.

While endothelial inflammation and microthrombi have been proposed as mechanisms in adult long COVID, there is little evidence for these in CYP, although clotting abnormalities have been described in children.
Other research found a higher likelihood of developing new mental health disorders in both COVID-19-positive and COVID-19-negative adolescents compared to younger children.
More than half of long COVID outpatients (52.2%) continued clinical follow-up beyond 180 days, defining the persistent-symptom (PS) group, while 47.8% recovered within 180 days (ER group).
Female patients made up a significantly higher proportion of the persistent-symptom group than the early-recovery group.
There was no significant difference in median age between the early-recovery and persistent-symptom groups.
Fatigue was the most common symptom overall and its prevalence was significantly higher in the persistent-symptom group than the early-recovery group.
Among female patients, insomnia prevalence was markedly higher in the persistent-symptom group than the early-recovery group.
Among female patients, memory disturbance prevalence was significantly higher in the persistent-symptom group than the early-recovery group.
Among female patients, paresthesia prevalence was significantly higher in the persistent-symptom group than the early-recovery group.
Among male patients, headache prevalence was significantly higher in the persistent-symptom group than in the early-recovery group.

The proportion of patients presenting with three or more of the 20 representative symptoms at initial visit was significantly higher in the persistent-symptom group than the early-recovery group in both men and women.
Total fatigue assessment scale scores were significantly higher (worse fatigue) in the persistent-symptom group than the early-recovery group.
Physical fatigue subscores were significantly higher in the persistent-symptom group than the early-recovery group.
Mental fatigue subscores were significantly higher in the persistent-symptom group than the early-recovery group.
Quality of life as measured by the EQ-5D-5L index was significantly lower in the persistent-symptom group than the early-recovery group.
EQ-VAS self-rated health scores were significantly lower in the persistent-symptom group than the early-recovery group.
Depression severity scores (SDS) were significantly elevated in the persistent-symptom group compared to the early-recovery group.
LDL-cholesterol levels were significantly higher in male patients with persistent long COVID than in male patients who recovered early.
LDL-cholesterol levels were slightly but significantly elevated in female patients with persistent long COVID compared to female patients who recovered early.
Serum creatinine was statistically slightly lower in female patients with persistent long COVID than in female early-recovery patients, though both remained within normal physiological range.

No significant differences were observed between early-recovery and persistent-symptom groups in hemoglobin, liver function markers, inflammatory markers, thyroid hormones, or adrenocortical hormones in either men or women.
Vaccination history, assessed across four different dose-grouping comparisons, showed no significant association with long COVID symptom duration.
The authors' prior report found that 8.4% of long COVID patients progressed to a condition meeting diagnostic criteria for myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS).

Across the 16 included studies, fatigue, headache, and cough were the most frequently reported long COVID symptoms in children and adolescents, followed by behavioral changes such as sleep disorders, mood swings, anxiety/depression, and difficulty concentrating.

Gastrointestinal symptoms including abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and constipation were also commonly reported in pediatric long COVID, along with dysgeusia, dysosmia, weight loss, dyspnea, asthenia, and fever.

Children aged 0-4 years with long COVID more frequently experienced nasal secretion and cough, whereas children 5 years and older and adolescents 11-18 years more often had emotional instability, reduced concentration, sleep disorders, anxiety/depression, fatigue, headache, dyspnea, and muscle pain.
Four of the included studies reported that the frequency of long COVID symptoms increased with increasing age among children and adolescents.

Analyses of sex differences in pediatric long COVID were inconsistent across studies: three found female predominance, one found male predominance, and one found no significant difference between sexes in clinical manifestations.
One study evaluating COVID-19 vaccination in children found it conferred temporary protection against the likelihood of developing long COVID.

Four studies found a higher frequency of comorbidities—including obesity, respiratory diseases, neurological conditions such as epilepsy, and renal disease—among children and adolescents with long COVID.
A Brazilian study cited in the discussion reported a higher incidence of long COVID among unvaccinated individuals (72%) compared with vaccinated individuals (59%).
The presence of comorbidities, biological factors, and acute-phase COVID-19 symptoms was reported to increase the risk of long COVID diagnosis by up to three times.

Obesity and SARS-CoV-2 infection were each associated with a heightened inflammatory environment; obesity is linked to release of TNF-alpha, interleukin-1, and interleukin-6 from adipose tissue, while SARS-CoV-2 infection is associated with elevated interleukin-2, interleukin-7, MCP-1, TNF-alpha, G-CSF, and CXCL10.

Children are proposed to have a relative deficiency of ACE2 receptors compared with adults, which combined with a highly responsive innate immune system and cross-reactivity from prior seasonal coronavirus exposure, may restrict inflammatory response and reduce the expressiveness of long COVID symptoms despite increased susceptibility to infection.

The functioning thymus in children up to approximately 12 years of age is proposed as a physiological mechanism contributing to a less expressive clinical picture of both acute COVID-19 and long COVID in younger children.

Persistent fatigue in long COVID is hypothesized to relate to toxicity in brain tissue from impaired lymphatic drainage/cerebrospinal fluid accumulation, alterations in muscle mitochondrial function, and decreased brain metabolism.
Chronic inflammation in long COVID is associated with functional immune changes including mast cell activation and prolonged T-cell activation.

The review discussion notes that in the general population, females have a greater risk of developing long COVID, potentially related to sex-based immunological differences and immunomodulatory effects of sex hormones, contributing to higher long COVID prevalence in adult women.
The estimated pooled prevalence of long COVID is 42%, with symptom duration reported from 6 months up to 1-2 years post-infection.
Female sex is associated with 1.5-2 times higher odds of developing long COVID, with one cited study reporting an OR of 1.8.
Older age, particularly above 65 years, increases risk of developing long COVID, with middle-aged individuals estimated at OR 1.03 per year.
Obesity/higher BMI increases the odds of long COVID, attributed to intensified inflammatory response, metabolic dysregulation, and respiratory impairment.
Having three or more comorbidities (hypertension, diabetes, chronic lung disease, depression, obesity) increases long COVID risk with an OR of 3.5.
Vaccination reduces the odds of developing long COVID (OR 0.59), with number of doses inversely correlated with risk.
Severity of the primary COVID-19 infection is positively correlated with long COVID risk (OR 2.4), attributed to exaggerated inflammatory response, viral load, and coagulation changes.
Blood group O (as well as AB and Rh-negative) is protective against long COVID; O blood type is also linked to lower risk of COVID-19 infection and adverse outcomes.

Lower socioeconomic status is a risk factor for long COVID cardiovascular complications (hazard risk 1.2), with higher risk in hospitalized versus non-hospitalized cases (1.9 vs 0.8), but no association was found for respiratory or general LC symptoms.
No association was found between socioeconomic status and respiratory or general long COVID symptoms.
Interleukin-6 is elevated in long COVID and may serve as a diagnostic biomarker.
C-reactive protein is elevated in long COVID and may serve as a diagnostic biomarker.
Tumor necrosis factor-alpha is elevated in long COVID and may serve as a diagnostic biomarker.
Long COVID cases show distinct immune profiling with increased cytotoxic immune cells compared to non-affected individuals.
Long COVID cases show higher SARS-CoV-2 and Epstein-Barr virus antibody titers than controls, suggesting viral reactivation/persistence contributes to immune dysregulation.
Systemic cortisol levels are reduced in long COVID cases compared to controls.
Machine learning integrating immunological profiling and demographic data of COVID-19 patients reliably predicted development of long COVID.
High lactate dehydrogenase, reduced T-cell levels, and elevated interleukin-6 were identified as biomarkers predicting degree of lung injury and occurrence of long COVID.
Elevated D-dimer at hospital admission was an independent predictor of lung injury within 3 months following COVID-19 infection.
Ground glass opacities and fibrotic-like changes are the most frequently reported CT radiological findings in long COVID, typically resolving within 3-6 months but persisting in more severe cases.
Vaccinated individuals had significantly lower odds of developing long COVID versus unvaccinated (OR 0.54, 95% CI 0.29-0.98).
The reported incidence of long COVID among vaccinated individuals was 3.5%.
A healthy lifestyle including balanced nutrition, regular exercise, and adequate sleep reduces long COVID risk by approximately half via enhanced immunity and reduced inflammation.
Inflammatory markers including interleukin-6, C-reactive protein, and tumor necrosis factor-alpha tend to rise in long COVID and may serve as diagnostic biomarkers.
Systemic cortisol levels were reduced in long COVID cases compared to controls, alongside altered immune profiling including increased cytotoxic immune cells and higher SARS-CoV-2 and EBV antibodies.
Elevated SARS-CoV-2 and Epstein-Barr virus antibodies were noted among long COVID cases, supporting a viral persistence/reactivation hypothesis for the syndrome.
A machine learning model integrating immunological profiling and patient demographics reliably predicted long COVID risk, potentially improving care for high-risk patients.

High LDH, reduced T-cell levels, and elevated interleukin-6 predicted degree of lung injury and long COVID occurrence, and elevated D-dimer at admission was an independent predictor of lung injury within 3 months.

CT imaging shows ground glass opacities and fibrotic-like changes in long COVID lung injury, most of which resolve within 3-6 months, though persistent changes occur more often after severe infection, mechanical ventilation, or extensive lung injury.
Vaccination reduced the odds of developing long COVID (OR 0.54, 95% CI 0.29-0.98) versus unvaccinated cases, with the vaccinated incidence of LC reported at 3.5%.
Long COVID cases showed significantly reduced quality of life with a hazard ratio of 0.94 and an odds ratio for mortality of 4.7.
Female gender was identified as a poor prognostic factor for long COVID recovery, with an odds ratio of 1.52 (95% CI 1.27-1.82) per Maglietta et al.'s meta-analysis.
Severity of primary COVID-19 infection was associated with worse long COVID prognosis (OR 1.66, 95% CI 1.03-2.68).

New-onset neurological symptoms, particularly fatigue and cognitive impairment, are among the worst prognostic indicators for long COVID, with an odds ratio of 1.67 (95% CI 1.21-2.29) and may take years or a lifetime to resolve.
Cognitive rehabilitation such as goal management training showed optimistic results in enhancing executive functions and attention deficits linked with long COVID.
Integrated psychological support, structural mental health intervention, and counselling significantly contributed to patients' recovery and better quality of life in long COVID.
Low-dose propranolol, clonidine, SSRIs, and low-dose tricyclic antidepressants are used pharmacologically for symptomatic relief of neurological long COVID symptoms.

Delta and Omicron variant spike protein mutations enhance positive charge at the likely heparan sulfate binding site.

UPF1, a component of the nonsense-mediated decay pathway, degrades BRLF1 transcripts and acts as a negative regulator of EBV reactivation.

ANO2 antibodies recognise an EBNA1 fragment via molecular mimicry, driving CNS inflammation through EBNA1-reactive T cells and triggering EBV reactivation, particularly in multiple sclerosis patients.
