Nucleocapsid-specific IgA antibody levels were significantly elevated in LC patients compared to healthy controls.
SARS-CoV-2 RNA was not detected by RT-PCR in the serum of any long COVID patients, despite elevated nucleocapsid antibodies.
SARS-CoV-2 spike and S1-specific IgM antibody levels were comparable between LC patients and healthy controls.
The spike-specific IgG/IgM ratio was significantly lower in LC patients, indicating a relatively higher proportion of IgM versus IgG, suggestive of impaired class switching.
The S1-specific IgG/IgM ratio was also significantly lower in LC patients, though less pronounced than the full spike ratio.
The spike-specific IgA/IgM ratio did not differ between LC patients and healthy controls.
SARS-CoV-2 antibody levels were not associated with fatigue or cognitive failure severity in LC patients.
LC patients had significantly higher IgG levels against the spike proteins of seasonal betacoronaviruses HKU1 and OC43 compared to healthy controls, consistent with immunological imprinting.
OC43 S2-specific IgA levels were increased in LC patients compared to healthy controls.
Antibody levels against the alphacoronaviruses NL63 and 229E were similar between LC patients and healthy controls for both IgG and IgA.
HKU1 and OC43 anti-spike antibody levels were not associated with fatigue or cognitive failure severity.
A strong positive correlation existed between IgG levels against the spike proteins of HKU1 and OC43 in both LC and HC groups, reflecting cross-reactivity between the two seasonal betacoronaviruses.
No significant correlation was found between seasonal betacoronavirus (HKU1/OC43) spike IgG and SARS-CoV-2 spike-specific IgG levels.
A weak but significant correlation was observed between seasonal betacoronavirus (HKU1/OC43) and SARS-CoV-2 spike-specific IgA levels.
Herpesvirus DNA was undetectable in serum of nearly all LC patients, with only one patient positive for HHV-6 DNA, suggesting active viremia was not present at the time of sampling.
Seroprevalence rates for EBV, CMV, HSV-1, HSV-2, and HHV-6 were comparable between healthy controls and LC patients.

IgG antibodies against the EBV reactivation-associated transcription factor Rta were elevated by 139% in LC patients compared to healthy controls, although this trend did not reach statistical significance overall for EBV antigens.
CMV p65-specific IgG antibody levels were significantly reduced in LC patients compared to healthy controls.
Lower CMV p65-specific IgG levels significantly correlated with increased fatigue severity (FAS score) in LC patients.
ANA positivity was similarly prevalent in LC patients and healthy controls, and no distinct ANA profile unique to LC patients could be identified.
Seven LC patients tested positive for three or more ANAs compared to none of the healthy controls, although overall ANA counts were not statistically different between groups.
Nearly all long COVID patients reported fatigue and a majority reported cognitive impairment, with a substantial proportion classified as severe by validated questionnaires.
Self-reported symptoms among long COVID patients most commonly included fatigue, cognitive disturbance, and muscle pain/weakness.
The proportion of patients reporting at least one persistent symptom declined progressively from diagnosis through 12 months of follow-up.
Exertional fatigue was the single most persistent symptom throughout follow-up, remaining the leading complaint at every timepoint through 12 months.
Patients initially treated in the ICU had significantly higher rates of persistent symptoms at 1, 3, 6, and 12 months than those treated in general wards or as outpatients.
At diagnosis, outpatients had significantly lower rates of fever and dyspnea but significantly higher rates of loss of smell and loss of taste compared with ward/ICU patients.

Functional status (PCFS grade 0/1) dropped sharply from 71.8% pre-COVID to 14.6% at one month, then gradually improved to 44.2% at 6 months and 50% at 12 months, without complete recovery for all patients.
Patients treated in wards or ICUs had higher rates of severe functional limitation (grade 4) at one month and moderate-to-severe limitation (grades 3-4) at three months than outpatients.
All eight SF-36 subscale scores were significantly lower than general Turkish population normative values at 1 and 3 months post-diagnosis.
SF-36 subscale scores showed significant improvement at 6 and 12 months compared with earlier timepoints.

At one month post-diagnosis, ICU-treated patients had significantly lower SF-36 scores than ward/outpatient groups in physical function, physical role difficulty, energy/vitality, social functioning, and general health perception.
At 12 months, ICU-treated patients continued to report significantly lower physical function, physical role difficulty, and social functioning scores than other groups.
Between month 1 and month 12, the ICU group showed greater improvement (delta) in physical function, emotional role difficulties, and general health perception than the outpatient and ward groups.
ICU and general ward patient groups had a higher prevalence of diabetes, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease than outpatients.
Mean age was significantly higher in patients treated in the ICU compared with those treated in the general ward or as outpatients.
Sixty-one point eight percent of patients had at least one comorbidity, most commonly hypertension, followed by cardiovascular disease and diabetes mellitus.
Of 816 patients followed after acute SARS-CoV-2 infection, 29.2% developed long COVID-19 persisting ≥3 months while 70.8% fully resolved within 3 months.
Female sex was an independent predictor of developing long COVID-19 after multivariable adjustment.
Diabetes mellitus was an independent predictor of developing long COVID-19 after multivariable adjustment.
Reinfection with SARS-CoV-2 was significantly more prevalent among patients who developed long COVID-19 compared with those who resolved.
Reinfection was independently associated with delayed symptom recovery in patients with long COVID-19.
Hospitalization during acute illness was independently associated with delayed recovery from long COVID-19.
Female sex was independently associated with delayed recovery from long COVID-19 symptoms in the Cox proportional hazards model.
Diabetes mellitus was independently associated with delayed recovery from long COVID-19 symptoms.
Full vaccination before infection was less common among patients who developed long COVID-19 compared to those who resolved, suggesting a protective association.
Vaccination status showed a non-significant protective trend for time to symptom recovery in the Cox model.
The most common symptoms in the long COVID-19 group were fatigue, post-exertional malaise, cough, cognitive dysfunction, dyspnea, chest pain/tightness, and headache.
Fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, and sleep disturbance persisted markedly longer (>32 weeks in many cases) than cough and anosmia, which typically resolved within 8-12 weeks.
Patients with long COVID-19 had significantly lower health-related quality of life across all domains of the SF-36 v2 and EQ-5D-5L at 6 and 12 months compared to the resolved group.
Return to work within 12 months was substantially lower and delayed among long COVID-19 patients compared to the resolved group.
The prevalence of long COVID-19 declined progressively across successive enrollment periods over the four-year study.
Rare neurological sequelae including cranial nerve involvement, vocal cord paralysis, and phobic/anxiety-related presentations were notably more frequent among long COVID-19 patients.

In univariate analysis, older age, female sex, comorbid diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, cardiac disease, chronic pulmonary disease, and chronic renal disease were all significantly more common among patients who developed long COVID-19.
Acute illness severity, including hospitalization and severe/critical illness, was significantly more common among patients who developed long COVID-19.

The multivariable logistic regression model predicting long COVID-19 (including age, sex, BMI, smoking, diabetes, hospitalization, reinfection, and chronic pulmonary disease) showed good calibration and strong discrimination.
A confirmed COVID-19 diagnosis was independently associated with increased odds of long COVID symptoms after adjustment for other covariates.
Among previously infected students, a BMI of 24 or higher was the strongest predictor of long COVID symptoms.
Among previously infected students, higher anxiety scores were significantly associated with increased risk of long COVID symptoms.
Being male was associated with an increased risk of developing long COVID symptoms across all students.
Older age was associated with an increased risk of developing long COVID symptoms across all students.
Not engaging in regular physical activity was associated with an increased risk of developing long COVID symptoms across all students.
Higher anxiety levels were associated with increased risk of long COVID symptoms across all students, regardless of infection status.
Almost half of students with confirmed COVID-19 more than three months prior reported long COVID physical symptoms in the past month, versus just over a third of non-diagnosed students.
Fatigue was the most commonly reported long COVID symptom among students overall.
Sleep disturbances were the second most commonly reported long COVID symptom among students overall.

Diagnosed and non-diagnosed students significantly differed in several physiological symptoms, including respiratory symptoms, fever, breathing difficulties, chest pain/tightness, muscle and joint pain, and reduced physical strength.
Diagnosed and non-diagnosed students significantly differed in reported short-term memory decline.
Mood instability differences between diagnosed and non-diagnosed students approached but did not reach statistical significance.
Over half of previously diagnosed students reported using the traditional Chinese medicine formula NRICM101 during their COVID-19 recovery.

Diagnosed and non-diagnosed students differed significantly in the frequency of exercising 1–2 times per week, unlike most other demographic and health variables which showed no significant difference.

Standardized Ginkgo biloba extracts, owing to their antioxidative, anti-inflammatory, and neuroprotective properties, may help improve cognitive impairment, fatigue, and cardiovascular symptoms in Long COVID/Post-COVID syndrome, according to early studies and case reports.
The pathophysiology of Long COVID is proposed to involve dysregulation of the autonomic nervous system, together with persistent viral particles, microvascular dysfunction, and autoimmune reactions.
Elevated IL-6 levels serve as a biomarker for predicting severe COVID-19 and are associated with increased risk of multiple organ dysfunction.
Excessively high ferritin levels (over 500 μg/L) are associated with increased risk of respiratory failure, ARDS, sepsis, death, and coagulopathy in COVID-19.
Male gender, advanced age, and pre-existing cardiovascular and respiratory conditions increase the risk of developing long COVID.
Long COVID fatigue has been linked to hypometabolism in the frontal lobe and cerebellum and to congestion of the glymphatic system affecting cerebrospinal fluid drainage.

Endothelial cell destruction by SARS-CoV-2 and cytokines such as IL-6 are proposed mechanisms driving fibrotic transformation of the lungs in long COVID, especially in older, previously hospitalized, and pulmonary-comorbid patients.
Pulmonary dysfunction in long COVID has been associated with high levels of D-dimer and blood urea nitrogen.
High density of ACE2 receptors on cardiac cells allows viral entry causing fragmentation and enucleation, making cardiac injury common in SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Increased troponin levels indicate initial myocardial inflammation that can develop into myocarditis and cardiovascular abnormalities unexplained by age or other known factors.

Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) was observed as a new pathological entity arising from cardiovascular abnormalities in long COVID, alongside mechanisms related to microthrombosis and endothelial damage.

Increased blood-brain barrier permeability during acute infection allows cytokines to enter the brain and produce neuroinflammation, contributing to cognitive impairment, headache, and brain fog, with MRI showing the frontal lobe as most affected.
Long COVID can involve acute kidney injury leading to decreased kidney function persisting even six months after infection.
High initial levels of amylase and lipase leading to acute pancreatitis have been observed, potentially due to the abundance of ACE2 receptors in the pancreas.
Patients have presented with splenic infarction and severe lymphocytopenia, explained by atrophy of lymphoid follicles, linked to ACE2 expression in the spleen.
Heavy antibiotic use during COVID-19 treatment caused gut microbiota changes and facilitated secondary Clostridioides difficile infection, in addition to direct viral action via GI ACE2 receptors.
Approximately 15-65% of COVID patients continue to have elevated transaminase and lactate dehydrogenase levels indicative of persistent liver dysfunction in long COVID.
Hypoalbuminemia, though a nonspecific marker, has been associated with negative prognosis in long COVID liver dysfunction.

Post-COVID-19 cholangiopathy involves elevated alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin, and transaminases with bile duct abnormalities on imaging, with recommendation for multidisciplinary monitoring for at least six months in hospitalized patients.

In an autopsy series of 20 deceased patients (from a larger 150-autopsy cohort at Semmelweis University), liver tissue showed steatosis, necrosis, fibrosis, inflammation, and sinusoidal ectasia with endothelial damage common to all cases; SARS-CoV-2 RNA and proteins were detected in non-parenchymal cells (endothelial and Kupffer cells) but not hepatocytes.

In an acute COVID-19 cohort, 65% of patients had elevated FIB-4 scores and 54% had increased hyaluronic acid levels, both correlating with liver function and inflammatory markers, while 5% of post-COVID patients showed signs of liver fibrosis.

A meta-analysis found MAFLD increases risk of severe COVID-19 requiring hospitalization/ICU admission but not mortality; patients with both MAFLD and obesity were six times more likely to develop severe COVID-19, and liver fibrosis predicted adverse outcomes.
Raised AST levels predicted mortality from COVID-19, although underlying liver injury mechanisms remain unclear; higher FIB-4 scores were also linked to lower IgG levels after vaccination.

In patients with pre-existing hepatitis B or C, COVID-19 can increase both the severity of liver disease and viral replication of the hepatitis virus, worsening outcomes, and immune dysregulation from COVID-19 can also trigger autoimmune hepatitis.

COVID-19 can worsen non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, particularly in individuals with obesity and/or metabolic syndrome, by exacerbating hepatic fat accumulation and potentially leading to steatohepatitis.
Patients with psychiatric comorbidities were observed to be more likely to develop long COVID.
Multivitamin supplements, including B-group vitamins and Coenzyme Q10, are recommended to prevent or counteract chronic inflammation, persistent fatigue, and cognitive dysfunction in long COVID.
In cases of mast cell activation syndrome associated with long COVID, antihistamines may be used with caution due to a possible association between dopamine fluctuations and later onset of dementia.
Exercise training significantly improved 6-minute walk test distance compared to control in Long COVID patients.
Exercise training significantly increased 30-second sit-to-stand test repetitions compared to control.
Exercise training significantly improved SF-12 mental component summary scores versus control.
Exercise training significantly increased VO2 peak (% predicted, L/kg/min, and L/min) compared to control.
Exercise training significantly reduced mMRC dyspnea scores compared to control.
Exercise training significantly reduced Fatigue Severity Scale scores compared to control.
Exercise training significantly reduced Modified Borg Dyspnea Scale scores compared to control.
Exercise training significantly reduced Visual Analogue Fatigue Scale scores compared to control.
Exercise training showed no significant benefit over control for anxiety/depression (HADS), SF-12 physical component, or spirometric measures (FVC, FEV1, FEV1/FVC, VE, VE/VO2, RER).
Respiratory muscle training significantly improved 6-minute walk test distance compared to control.
Respiratory muscle training significantly increased maximal inspiratory pressure (both % predicted and cmH2O) compared to control.
Respiratory muscle training significantly reduced mMRC dyspnea scores compared to control.

Respiratory muscle training showed no significant benefit over control on spirometry (FVC, FEV1, FEV1/FVC), fatigue (MFIS), mood (HADS), or maximal expiratory pressure (MEP), consistent with a prior meta-analysis.
Telerehabilitation-supervised interventions significantly improved 6-minute walk test distance compared to control.
Telerehabilitation significantly increased 30-second sit-to-stand repetitions compared to control.
Telerehabilitation significantly reduced Fatigue Severity Scale scores compared to control, likely by improving exercise adherence and providing more professional guidance.
Telerehabilitation showed no significant difference from control on FEV1 % predicted, FVC % predicted, and FEV1/FVC.
Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) significantly reduced the physical subscale of the Modified Fatigue Impact Scale compared to control.
tDCS did not significantly improve MFIS-cognitive, MFIS-psychosocial, or MFIS-total scores compared to control under the random-effects model.
Olfactory training showed no statistically significant improvement in UPSIT scores compared to control under the random-effects model.
Intranasal steroid sprays did not significantly improve VAS smell scores compared to control at one, two, or three weeks.
Palmitoylethanolamide plus luteolin (PEA-LUT) significantly improved TDI olfactory scores compared to control, plausibly via suppression of olfactory neuroinflammation.

The trial recruited its target of 60 participants (128 invited, 47% recruitment rate) within the planned period and randomised them to intervention (n=28) or control (n=32) groups, meeting the feasibility criterion for recruitment.
Overall study completion was 83% (n=50), with a dropout rate of 17% (10/60 participants), meeting the pre-specified feasibility criterion of <20% dropout.
More than two-thirds of participants in the intervention group (68%, n=19) completed all LC-OHP programme sessions, indicating good adherence.
Attrition in the intervention group was low, at 18% by 3 months with no further attrition (0%) by 6 months, supporting acceptability of the LC-OHP.

Among those who completed the treatment evaluation questionnaire (TEI-SF, 82% of intervention group), 87% reported positive reactions toward the LC-OHP, 87% perceived it as effective, and 70% felt it had potential for permanent improvement.
The LC-OHP could be delivered as intended in a minimum of six sessions (including a booster), fewer than the original nine-session OHP design, adapted flexibly to individual participant needs.

Withdrawal from the study was mainly attributed to long-COVID health-related issues, with additional reasons including prioritising energy for other activities, perceiving the programme as not a cure, and some tasks feeling burdensome.
Participants suggested the LC-OHP would be more beneficial if delivered earlier in the course of long COVID illness rather than after prolonged symptom duration.

In the intervention group, depression (PHQ-9) and anxiety (GAD-7) scores trended downward from baseline to 3- and 6-month follow-up, suggesting a possible favourable effect of the LC-OHP, though this is preliminary trend data only.
Fatigue (FAS) scores trended downward in the intervention group from baseline to 3- and 6-month follow-up, suggesting a possible reduction in fatigue burden, though data are preliminary.

Self-efficacy (GSE) and quality of life (EQ-5D-5L) scores trended upward in the intervention group from baseline to 3- and 6-month follow-up, suggesting possible improvement, though data are preliminary.
The control group also showed improvements in most outcomes over time except for self-efficacy (GSE), which did not improve at 6 months, complicating interpretation of intervention-specific effects.
The intervention group appeared to show more favourable outcomes than the control group in the short term (3 months), though this comparison is exploratory and not powered for efficacy.
Resting-state LF/HF ratio, a marker of sympathovagal balance, was significantly higher in adults with ADHD than in matched healthy controls.

In control subjects LF/HF increased significantly during the task compared with rest and after-task states, whereas in ADHD subjects LF/HF showed no significant change across the three behavioral states, indicating a blunted task-related autonomic response.
HF decreased significantly during the task compared with rest and after-task states in both ADHD and control subjects, with no significant difference between groups at any behavioral state.
Heart rate increased significantly during the task compared with rest and after-task states in both ADHD and control subjects, with no significant difference between groups at any state.

No significant differences were found between ADHD and control groups in the task-to-rest or after-to-rest ratios for any HRV parameter, indicating similar relative autonomic responsiveness to the task.

Within ADHD subjects, higher ADHD symptom severity (ASRS score) was positively correlated with higher resting HF, suggesting more severe ADHD symptoms are associated with greater parasympathetic activity at rest.
Within ADHD subjects, higher ADHD symptom severity (ASRS score) was negatively correlated with heart rate during the task.

The Autism-Spectrum Quotient (AQ) score, measuring comorbid autistic traits, showed no significant correlation with any HRV parameter (LF, HF, LF/HF, HR) in adults with ADHD, suggesting the high comorbidity of autism spectrum traits did not confound the autonomic findings.
Within ADHD subjects, greater total mood disturbance (depressive symptom severity) was positively correlated with resting LF.
Within ADHD subjects, greater total mood disturbance (depressive symptom severity) was negatively correlated with heart rate at rest, during the task, and after the task.
Within ADHD subjects, higher friendliness (positive mood) scores were positively correlated with heart rate during the task.

HRV and heart rate parameters at each behavioral state in the ADHD group did not differ significantly by medication status (none, atomoxetine, methylphenidate, or guanfacine), presence of comorbid depression, or ADHD presentation subtype (inattentive vs combined).

During the random number generation task, adults with ADHD showed increased nonrandomness on the count bias (CB) index, while the other two randomness indices (interval bias, RNG index) were normal, suggesting mild working-memory-related task performance alteration.

No significant difference was observed in LF between ADHD and control subjects, nor among the three behavioral states (rest, task, after), indicating LF was not significantly modulated by the paradigm in either group.

Toddlers who received gaze-contingent attention training made significantly more correct anticipatory saccades during the learning phase of a cognitive control task than toddlers in the passive-video control condition.
The proportion of correct anticipatory saccades during the learning phase was significantly higher in the attention training group compared to the control group.
During the reversal phase of the cognitive control task, the attention training group did not differ from controls on total, correct, or proportion of correct anticipatory saccades.
Attention training did not produce significant group differences in peak, mean, minimum, or looking range durations during boring or interesting sustained attention trials.
No group differences were found in saccadic reaction times across baseline, gap, overlap, facilitation, or disengagement conditions of the visual disengagement task.
Toddlers in the attention training group produced significantly more spontaneous pointing events to initiate joint attention with an examiner than the control group.
Toddlers in the attention training group responded to a greater percentage of examiner points during a book-based joint attention task than the control group.
Toddlers in the attention training group produced more imitative points in response to the examiner's points compared to controls.
The attention training group responded to a higher percentage of examiner points toward near posters than the control group.
There was no significant group difference in responding to examiner points directed at far posters.
Within the intervention group, greater composite improvement in attention performance was associated with attending more training sessions.
Higher baseline Mullen Visual Reception age-equivalent scores were associated with greater composite improvement in attention training performance.
Higher baseline ASD severity (ADOS-2 Total and Social Affect scores) was associated with lower improvement scores on the 'Stars' attention training game.
Higher ADOS-2 RRB severity scores were associated with lower improvement scores on the 'Windows' and 'Stars' attention training games.
Higher baseline Mullen Expressive Language age-equivalent was associated with lower improvement scores on the 'Butterfly' attention training game.
Greater total attention training time was associated with a larger increase in responding to joint attention on the book task.

Infants later diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder showed significantly higher resting RSA than typically developing infants from 9 to 24 months of age, with no difference detected in the first 6 months.
Infants later diagnosed with ASD showed higher mean interbeat interval (heart period) than TD infants from 9 to 24 months, paralleling the RSA elevation.
In a three-group comparison, infants with ASD showed elevated RSA compared to both neurodivergent (BAP/developmental delay) and typically developing infants, restricted to the second year of life.
Preterm infants showed lower resting RSA and mean IBI than both elevated- and low-familial-likelihood ASD groups during the first 6 months of life when measured by chronological age.
No differences in RSA or mean IBI trajectories were found among elevated-likelihood, low-likelihood, and preterm infants after 9 months of age.

When infant age was corrected for prematurity, differences in RSA and mean IBI trajectories between preterm and full-term (EL/LL) infants disappeared, indicating preterm autonomic development aligns with biological maturation rather than chronological/extrauterine experience.

Within the elevated-familial-likelihood group, infants who developed ASD (EL-ASD) showed higher RSA from 9-24 months and lower mean IBI from 1-6 months compared to their non-ASD elevated-likelihood peers (EL-TD), supporting RSA elevation as specific to ASD rather than general familial genetic risk.
Female infants showed higher resting RSA than male infants in the outcome (ASD vs TD) model, though sex did not alter the overall pattern of ASD-related RSA elevation.

Nonverbal cognitive ability and expressive language scores did not significantly influence RSA or mean IBI trajectories, and group differences in RSA/IBI remained unchanged when accounting for these covariates.

Across all infant groups (elevated-likelihood, low-likelihood, and preterm), resting RSA and mean IBI increased significantly from 1 to 24 months, with the most rapid changes in the first 6 months, reflecting normative maturation of parasympathetic/cortical control.
The ASD recurrence rate observed among elevated-likelihood siblings in this cohort was higher than recently published population recurrence rates.
Anxiety disorders co-occur in autistic individuals at estimated rates ranging from 42% to 84%.
The authors' own meta-analysis found a negative correlation between anxiety symptoms and respiratory sinus arrhythmia in autistic individuals.
Children with autism show blunted or reduced RSA withdrawal during rest and lab-interactive paradigms compared with non-autistic children.
Children with autism show reduced heart rate variability during rest and lab-interactive paradigms compared with non-autistic children.
Systematic reviews and meta-analyses report inconsistent findings regarding atypical autonomic activity in autistic samples, potentially due to failure to account for co-occurring anxiety.
In autism studies, anxiety has been associated with blunted RSA withdrawal, which contrasts with findings in the general (non-autism) anxiety literature showing greater RSA withdrawal with anxiety.
One study found that lower heart rate variability was associated with anxiety symptoms in autistic individuals.
Tiredness after physical activity was the most frequently reported symptom, reported by 97% of participants.
General tiredness was reported by 93% of participants, making it one of the most common Long COVID/PASC symptoms.
Shortness of breath was reported by 83% of participants.
Cough was reported by 77% of participants as a Long COVID/PASC symptom.
Muscle and body aches were reported by 77% of participants.
Headache was reported by 70% of participants and rated as the most severe symptom on average.
Shortness of breath after physical activity was reported by 63% of participants.
Difficulty concentrating or thinking (brain fog) was reported by 63% of participants.
Insomnia was reported by 60% of participants as a Long COVID/PASC symptom.
General tiredness had the highest average bothersomeness score among Long COVID/PASC symptoms.
Impact on activities of daily living was the most frequently reported HRQoL domain affected by Long COVID/PASC.
Physical functioning was impacted in 90% of participants who reported HRQoL effects of Long COVID/PASC.
Emotional wellbeing was impacted in 83% of participants due to Long COVID/PASC.

Exploratory comparison between participants at high versus low risk of severe COVID-19 found no notable differences in the severity, bothersomeness, or type of Long COVID/PASC signs and symptoms reported.

Clinicians most frequently identified brain fog/neurological symptoms, post-exertional malaise, and gastrointestinal symptoms as prominent in Long COVID/PASC, whereas gastrointestinal symptoms were much less frequently spontaneously reported by patients themselves.

A final 18-item Long COVID/PASC PRO instrument covering six symptom domains (respiratory, neurological, systemic, pain, cardiovascular, gastrointestinal) was retained following two rounds of concept elicitation and cognitive debriefing interviews.

Most participants demonstrated understanding of all items retained in the final Long COVID/PASC PRO instrument, with comprehension rates of 90-100% and misinterpretation instances no greater than n=2 per item.
A 7-day recall period was deemed appropriate by most participants (87%) across all items assessed in both interview rounds and was not modified.

A one-point change (improvement) was generally considered a meaningful change across most items of the Long COVID/PASC PRO instrument, though certain items required a two- or three-point change, based on very small sub-samples.

Direct SARS-CoV-2 infection of EBV-latently-infected epithelial cells (AGS-Bx1-ACE2) did not significantly increase expression of the EBV lytic transactivator BZLF1 at mRNA or protein levels over 24-72 hours post-infection.

SARS-CoV-2 infection did not increase EBV early gene BMRF1 expression, DNA replication, or production of new viral particles in the epithelial cell model, further supporting the lack of EBV reactivation.

Co-culturing SARS-CoV-2-infected Vero E6 epithelial cells with latently EBV-infected Akata-Bx1 B cells did not significantly increase EBV immediate early (BZLF1), early (BMRF1), or late (BFRF3) lytic gene expression or DNA replication, indicating that substances released from infected epithelial cells do not reactivate EBV in B cells.

Hemin treatment of latently EBV-infected Akata-Bx1 B cells significantly upregulated immediate early (BZLF1), early (BMRF1), and late (BFRF3) lytic transcripts and increased viral particle production in a dose-dependent manner, indicating heme reactivates EBV in B cells.

Hemin treatment failed to significantly increase EBV BZLF1, BMRF1, and BFRF3 expression in the EBV-latently-infected epithelial cell model (AGS-Bx1-ACE2), indicating that heme-induced EBV reactivation is specific to B cells and does not occur in epithelial cells.
According to a cited study, heme levels were increased in individuals with long COVID at 6 months compared to healthy individuals and those who recovered from COVID-19.
The authors note, citing prior literature, that heme is also elevated in patients during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection.
The authors cite literature indicating that the incidence of EBV reactivation is increased in COVID-19 patients and positively associated with COVID-19 disease severity.

SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters showed marked weight loss and 46.25% mortality within two weeks, with 13.75% of survivors failing to regain pre-infection weight by 30 dpi (classified as non-recovery/PASC), compared with IAV-infected hamsters (47.50% mortality) which all recovered weight by 30 dpi.

By 13-15 dpi neither infectious virus nor viral RNA was detectable in SARS-CoV-2 or IAV groups, indicating that persistent weight loss and lung pathology in the non-recovery group were unrelated to ongoing viral replication.
Lung fibrosis (assessed by Masson's trichrome staining) persisted until 30 dpi only in the SARS-CoV-2 non-recovery group, while it resolved by 30 dpi in both the IAV and SARS-CoV-2 recovery groups.

The SARS-CoV-2 non-recovery group showed upregulation of over 65% (26/40) of hallmark human PASC-associated genes, including S100A8, S100A9, MMP8, IL1B and TNF, across BALF, lung and spleen, a signature absent in recovery groups.

scRNA-seq showed the SARS2_PASC group had a marked increase in neutrophil proportions (61.88-78.45%) and decreased macrophages (4.16-16.02%) in BALF and lung, compared with control/recovery groups (neutrophils 3.04-23.08%, macrophages 6.12-80.05%).
Myeloid progenitor cells notably accumulated in the spleen of the SARS2_PASC group, whereas they were scarce in the recovery groups.

Multiplex immunofluorescence confirmed the SARS2_PASC group had more than a fivefold increase in MPO-positive neutrophils compared with recovery groups, along with a significant decrease in CD68-positive monocyte/macrophage cells.

Neutrophil-specific transcription factor CEBPE (along with KLF5 and GFI1) was highly upregulated in granulocyte-monocyte progenitors, neutrophil progenitors, and neutrophils of the SARS2_PASC group, driving skewed differentiation toward neutrophils.

IRF8, a transcription factor associated with monocyte/macrophage differentiation, was substantially downregulated in the SARS2_PASC group compared with recovery groups, which had higher monocyte and macrophage ratios.

The SARS-CoV-2 spike S1 antigen remained detectable in lung tissue of the SARS2_PASC group up to 30 dpi despite viral RNA clearance, whereas it was absent in the recovery group and nucleocapsid/nucleoprotein antigens cleared by 15 dpi in both SARS-CoV-2 and IAV groups.

Monocytes, M2 macrophages and alveolar macrophages in the lungs of the SARS2_PASC group persistently overexpressed extracellular matrix genes (FN1, VCAN, TIMP1, TIMP2) and the profibrotic cytokine TGFB1, linking these myeloid subsets to sustained ECM deposition and fibrotic progression.

Ingenuity pathway analysis showed neutrophils in the lung and spleen of the SARS2_PASC group had high activation of fMLP signaling, neutrophil extracellular trap signaling and IL-1 family signaling pathways, with 'neutrophil degranulation' consistently upregulated across all three tissues.

The Neu5 neutrophil subcluster, predominant in BALF, showed the highest enrichment for aging, senescence, apoptosis, lung fibrosis and TNF-alpha/NF-kB signaling gene modules but reduced leukocyte adhesion markers (SELL, ITGB2), identifying it as a functionally distinct aged neutrophil population driving chronic tissue damage in PASC.

ELISA showed elevated serum GM-CSF and G-CSF levels at 30 dpi in the SARS2_PASC group, corresponding with upregulation of their receptors CSF2RA and CSF3R across all neutrophil subclusters, supporting sustained neutrophil development and activation.

Sivelestat, a neutrophil elastase inhibitor administered from 5-11 dpi, increased recovery rate by 30% (only 8% PASC incidence) and reduced mortality by more than 50% (22% vs ~45% in controls) in SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters.
WRW4, an FPR2 antagonist, reduced PASC incidence to 10.00% compared with ~14-16% in controls, but mortality rates remained comparable to controls.
Paquinimod, an S100A8/A9 inhibitor, reduced PASC incidence to 6.00% but did not improve mortality relative to controls.

Delayed Sivelestat/inhibitor treatment initiated after 15 dpi failed to enhance recovery or prevent weight loss, indicating that irreversible pathological changes had already occurred by that time point.

qRT-PCR showed Sivelestat treatment produced the greatest reduction in lung IL1B, NFKB1 and IFNG transcript levels at 15 dpi, with suppression persisting to 30 dpi (19 days after treatment discontinuation).

Sivelestat treatment reduced lung fibrosis by more than 50% at 15 dpi and maintained marked reductions in fibrosis across all drug-treated groups by 30 dpi, compared with sustained fibrosis in untreated/DMSO controls.

Flow cytometry showed Sivelestat treatment markedly reduced neutrophil populations in both lung and spleen and decreased splenic monocyte/macrophage populations, while T and B cell frequencies remained unchanged, indicating a selective effect on innate immune cells.
Treatment with Sivelestat, Paquinimod and WRW4 all decreased the detection rate of SARS-CoV-2 S1 subunit antigen in lung tissue in addition to reducing PASC incidence.
A far greater proportion of PASC participants reported poor overall sleep quality on the PSQI than healthy controls.

NT-proBNP was elevated in the patient at presentation to the long COVID cardiac clinic, possibly as a consequence of ongoing rhythm disturbances.

The patient developed de novo atrial flutter and later atrial fibrillation alternating with junctional rhythm, beginning months after mild acute SARS-CoV-2 infection, becoming permanent AF over the following year.
Ambulatory ECG monitoring two months after acute infection revealed non-sustained ventricular tachycardia alongside atrial bradycardia and supraventricular tachycardia.
Suspected dysfunction of both the sinus and AV nodes (binodal dysfunction) was identified, precluding initiation of antiarrhythmic drug therapy.

Cardiac MRI three months after infection showed discrete myocardial edema, accentuated early arterial enhancement, and mildly reduced left ventricular ejection fraction, consistent with subacute viral myocarditis.

Repeat cardiac MRI two months after initial presentation to the long COVID clinic showed normalization of left ventricular ejection fraction and resolution of edema and late enhancement, indicating resolution of the myocarditis-like process despite ongoing arrhythmias.

At the 3-year follow-up, the patient's ECG showed first-degree AV block with markedly prolonged PQ interval and a changed P-wave morphology, indicating relocation of the atrial pacemaker site compared to her pre-COVID ECG.

The authors propose that autonomic nervous system dysfunction and decreased heart-rate variability, previously described in long COVID, may combine with structural and inflammatory factors to increase susceptibility to both brady- and tachyarrhythmias in COVID-19 convalescent patients.
The authors cite literature that SARS-CoV-2 shows tropism for cardiomyocytes and pericytes via ACE2 expression, potentially enabling direct cardiac injury.

The authors cite literature that the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein can induce fusion of human cardiomyocytes and syncytia formation, proposed as a potential pathomechanism for post-COVID arrhythmic disease.

The authors cite literature that myocardial fibrosis and gap junction disruption, including connexin remodeling, can cause delayed conduction abnormalities and arrhythmogenesis, extrapolated from viral myocarditis studies.

The authors propose atrial cardiomyopathy as a potential underlying cause of the structural and electrical remodeling producing this patient's complex arrhythmias, though it remains unclear whether prior SARS-CoV-2 infection can prompt atrial cardiomyopathy.

Oral anticoagulation with edoxaban was initiated for the newly detected atrial fibrillation/flutter and was later discontinued after 2 years once no further AF/flutter episodes were detected and CHA2DS2-VASc score was low.
Electrical cardioversion was attempted for the arrhythmia but was unsuccessful.
The authors cite recent findings suggesting that microglial activation observed in ME/CFS may be mediated in part by the interaction of advanced glycation end products with their receptor RAGE.
AGE-RAGE binding activates NF-κB, which upregulates pro-inflammatory genes involved in microglial activation and neuroimmune response, alongside increased ROS and mitochondrial dysfunction.
RAGE, expressed on endothelial cells, macrophages, and glial cells, is markedly upregulated during both acute and chronic viral infections.
In preclinical models, genetic deletion of RAGE or its pharmacological inhibition improved outcomes in sepsis and influenza by dampening cytokine storms and preserving tissue integrity.
In influenza models, RAGE deficiency enhanced viral clearance and improved survival, indicating that excessive AGE-RAGE signaling sustains harmful inflammatory responses.
EBV-encoded dUTPase activates the NF-κB pathway via TLR2/MyD88, a signaling route that overlaps with downstream RAGE signaling, potentially compounding immune dysregulation in post-viral states.
EBV infection upregulates HMGB1, a characterized RAGE ligand, thereby indirectly enhancing RAGE-mediated signaling.

Long COVID is characterized by persistent symptoms including fatigue, dyspnea, chest pain, and palpitations that can persist for months to years after acute infection.
Immune dysregulation, endothelial dysfunction, persistent viral antigens, and coagulopathy are implicated as central drivers of cardiovascular complications in Long COVID.

Direct viral infection of cardiac and vascular cells, along with autoantibody formation and cytokine-mediated injury, is proposed to contribute to myocardial inflammation, fibrosis, and arrhythmias in Long COVID.
Sex-based immunological differences and underlying comorbidities are described as further influencing individual susceptibility and disease trajectory in Long COVID cardiovascular disease.
Large-scale epidemiological studies have found significantly increased risks of pericarditis, cardiomyopathy, dysrhythmias, and heart failure among COVID-19 survivors.

Individuals who experienced severe symptoms during acute COVID-19 infection had markedly higher odds of developing long COVID compared to those with mild symptoms after adjustment for age, race, and income.
Moderate acute symptom severity was also associated with elevated (though smaller) odds of long COVID compared to mild symptoms.
Households with a member reporting pre-existing heart disease had significantly higher adjusted odds of long COVID than those without heart disease.
Asthma was significantly associated with long COVID in unadjusted models but was reported as no longer statistically significant after adjustment for covariates.
Respondents reporting poor physical health had significantly higher odds of long COVID compared to those reporting good physical health, after adjusting for age and race.
Experiencing anxiety at any time during acute COVID-19 infection was associated with markedly higher odds of developing long COVID after adjusting for age and race.
Experiencing chest pain at any time during acute infection was associated with increased odds of long COVID after adjustment for age, race, income, and health insurance coverage.
Experiencing constipation at any time during acute infection was associated with substantially increased odds of long COVID.
Experiencing heart palpitations during acute infection was associated with increased odds of long COVID after adjustment for age, race, income and healthcare access.
Experiencing shortness of breath during acute infection was associated with increased odds of long COVID after adjustment for age, race, income and healthcare access.
Sociodemographic factors including race, education, income, and healthcare access showed no statistically significant association with long COVID in crude or adjusted models.
No significant association was found between diabetes and long COVID in this study, unlike some prior literature.
Highly prevalent acute-phase symptoms (fatigue, joint/muscle pain, taste or smell changes) showed substantially reduced persistence into the long COVID period compared to their acute prevalence.
Anxiety, brain fog, and depression, though less prevalent during acute illness, showed notable persistence over time compared to other symptoms.
Roughly 12% of households had a member hospitalized for COVID-19, and about 20% reported at least one outpatient clinic visit after COVID recovery.
A large majority of long COVID patients show abnormally elevated P0.1, indicating compensatory hyperactivation of respiratory centers.

The diaphragm shows a distinctly prolonged recovery trajectory compared to peripheral skeletal muscles following COVID-19 infection.
Long COVID patients show significant impairment in neural respiratory drive with diminished cortical activation of the diaphragm, disrupting phrenic nerve stimulation and ventilatory efficiency.

Objective measurements show substantial reductions in both maximal inspiratory and expiratory pressures in long COVID patients, indicating generalized respiratory muscle weakness with diaphragmatic involvement.

RMT intervention significantly augments respiratory muscle performance, alleviates dyspnea severity, and enhances functional capacity for activities of daily living, as objectively shown by improved 6-minute walk test performance.
In acute-phase COVID-19 patients, RMT produced significant improvements in diaphragmatic thickness and thoracic expansion metrics.
The effectiveness of home-based RMT shows no significant difference compared to conventional in-person rehabilitation.
RMT consistently improves first-minute heart rate recovery (HRR1), a vagally-mediated marker of autonomic recovery, across healthy and clinical populations including long COVID.
COVID-19 infection directly damages vagal neurofunction, contributing to autonomic dysregulation that impairs bronchodilation and accelerates respiratory muscle fatigue.

Sustained high-intensity diaphragmatic contractions generate lactate accumulation that activates the diaphragmatic metaboreflex, driving tachycardia, vasoconstriction, cortical motor inhibition, and accelerated fatigue.

Among 87 long COVID patients evaluated at least one year post-infection (after excluding other causes of fatigue), 43 (49.4%) met ICD-10 SCAN criteria for neurasthenia, with associated impairment in daily functioning.
Fatigue interfering with activities of daily living, as measured by the Fatigue Severity Scale, was reported by 41.3% (36/87) of patients, though all patients reported some degree of fatigue.
Muscular aches and pains were reported by 35.6% (31/87) of the long COVID cohort.
Dizziness was reported by 5.7% (5/87) of the long COVID cohort.
Tension headaches were reported by 27.5% (24/87) of the long COVID cohort.
Weakness was reported by 31% (27/87) of the long COVID cohort.
Patients diagnosed with neurasthenia had a mean Fatigue Severity Scale score of 6.1, well above the study cut-off of 4.
Forgetfulness with inability to concentrate was reported by 8% (7/87) of the cohort.

In the 7 patients with cognitive complaints, PGI-BBD memory scale subtests were unimpaired (remote/recent memory, mental balance, delayed/immediate recall, verbal and visual retention, recognition), but all 7 showed a dysfunction rating of 2 on the attention and concentration subtest.
Sociodemographic factors (age, gender, education, occupation, marital status, and rural/urban residence) did not significantly differ between those with and without neurasthenia.
The severity of the acute COVID-19 infection (defined by hospitalization or supplemental oxygen requirement) did not correlate with the risk of developing neurasthenia.
No significant post-exertional malaise was found in this long COVID study sample, despite patients being asked whether exertion worsened their fatigue.

Unlike prior literature linking age over 50 and female gender to increased fatigue risk, this study found no such associations, attributed partly to small sample size and exclusion of patients over 60.

The 49.4% prevalence of neurasthenia in this post-COVID clinical sample is markedly higher than the previously reported 5% prevalence in a general Indian clinical sample and the 2.22% lifetime/1.19% 12-month prevalence in a US nationally representative sample, suggesting increased prevalence following COVID-19 infection.

The authors propose that neurasthenia in long COVID patients may reflect a marker of low-grade chronic inflammation from medium/long-term effects of COVID-19 infection or associated psychosocial stress, though this was not directly measured.

Recorded long COVID diagnosis prevalence in primary care records (0.33%) was far lower than self-reported long COVID prevalence from national surveys (3.3%-10.4%), indicating substantial undercoding/underdiagnosis in primary care.
Patients with a recorded long COVID diagnosis were on average older and much more likely to be female than patients without a long COVID diagnosis.
Patients recorded as Asian or Asian British ethnicity were overrepresented among long COVID patients relative to the overall population.

Asthma, anxiety, depressive disorder, hypertension and type 2 diabetes were all more prevalent before the pandemic among patients who went on to receive a long COVID diagnosis than in the overall population.
In multivariate regression, middle-aged patients had the highest adjusted odds of receiving a long COVID diagnosis compared to those aged 18-30, peaking at ages 51-60.
